words.definition: The trail of bruised and trampled grass left by a passing deer, read by hunters
words.origin: From Old French *abattre* to beat down; a hunting term.

words.definition: A hiding place for valuables or secrets; a concealed repository
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *abditorium*, from Latin *abdere* to hide.

words.definition: A person learning the alphabet; a novice at the very first steps of anything
words.origin: *abecedary* "alphabet book, primer" (going back to Middle English *abscedary*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *abecedārium* "alphabet, primer," derived from neuter of Late Latin *abecedārius* "alphabetical," from the names of the letters *a* + *b* + *c* + *d* + Latin *-ārius* -ary) + -an. First known use: 1603.

words.definition: An alphabet book or primer
words.origin: Medieval Latin, from the letters *a, b, c, d*.

words.definition: Departing from what is normal or expected
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *aberrant-, aberrans*, present participle of *aberrāre* "to wander away, stray, go wrong," from *ab-* ab- + *errāre* "to wander, drift, be in error". First known use: circa 1536.
examples: I don't intend to suggest that his psychology was in some way **aberrant** or neurotic … — Michael Chabon

words.definition: A state of temporary suspension
words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French *abeyaunce* "absence of a claimant or owner, lapse in succession," from *abaer, abair* "to open wide" (from *a-*, prefix in transitive verbs—from Latin *ad-* ad- — + *baer, baier* "to have the mouth wide open, gape, pant," from Vulgar Latin **batāre*, perhaps of imitative origin) + *-ance* -ance. First known use: circa 1530.
examples: … new contracts on all but one existing mine … are **in abeyance** pending the outcome of a government inquiry to be carried out into Australia's role in the nuclear fuel cycle. — Vimala Sarma
A plan that is currently being held **in abeyance**

words.definition: The fear of running out of things to read
words.origin: From Greek *a-* without + *biblion* book + *-phobia* fear; a modern coinage.

words.definition: A strong urge to avoid or withdraw from something
words.origin: From Latin *abiens*, present participle of *abire* to go away.

words.definition: The origin of life from non-living matter
words.origin: A-:2 + bio- + genesis. First known use: 1870.
examples: According to the conventional hypothesis, the earliest living cells emerged as a result of chemical evolution on our planet billions of years ago in a process called **abiogenesis**. — David Warmflash et al.

words.definition: To solemnly renounce a belief or claim
words.origin: Middle English *abjuren*, borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French *abjurer*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *abjūrāre*, "to repudiate, renounce (a right or claim), swear to stay away from," going back to Latin, "to deny knowledge of falsely under oath, repudiate," from *ab-* ab- + *jūrāre* "to swear". First known use: 15th century.
examples: He **abjured** his allegiance to his former country.

words.definition: Extravagance, especially in matters of food and drink
words.origin: From Latin *abligurire* to squander on luxuries, from *ligurire* to lick.

words.definition: The act of washing oneself, especially as a religious rite; one's washing up
words.origin: Middle English *ablucioun* "cleansing of oil (in alchemy)," borrowed from Late Latin *ablūtiōn-, ablūtiō* "washing, cleansing" (Medieval Latin, "cleansing of oil"), from Latin *abluere* "to wash off, cleanse," from *ab-* ab- + *-luere*, form in combination of *lavere* "to wash" + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns. First known use: 1533.

words.definition: Land lost gradually to the action of water
words.origin: From Latin *abluere* to wash away.

words.definition: The denial or giving up of one's own interests
words.origin: Middle English *abnegacioun*, borrowed from Late Latin *abnegātiōn-, abnegātiō*, from Latin *abnegāre* "to refute, decline, deny" + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Monks practice **abnegation** of the material aspects of human life.
… Rennie Stennett, the Giants' $600,000-a-year bust of a second baseman, had, in a rush of **abnegation**, given away his money and was living on the beach, subsisting on abalone.

words.definition: To scrape or wear away by friction
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abrādere* "to remove by rubbing, scrape off," from *ab-* ab- + *rādere* "to scrape". First known use: 1675.

words.definition: To repeal or do away with a law or agreement
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abrogātus*, past participle of *abrogāre*, "to repeal (a law), repudiate, cancel," from *ab-* ab- + *rogāre* "to ask, ask an assembly for approval of". First known use: circa 1520.
examples: The company's directors are accused of **abrogating** their responsibilities.

Continued progress in measurement and characterization of antibodies and strategies to **abrogate** antibody production both prior to and following heart transplant have been encouraging. — Peter M Eckman

words.definition: The natural shedding of a leaf, fruit or flower
words.origin: Middle English *abscisioun*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *abscīsiōn-, abscīsiō* "cutting off, felling, amputation," going back to Latin, "aposiopesis," from *abscīdere* "to cut off or away, remove" + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns; spelling *abscission* (in Late and Medieval Latin as *abscissiōn-, abscissiō*) by construing the noun as a derivative of Latin *abscindere* "to tear off or away". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To leave hurriedly and secretly, typically to escape arrest or take what isn't yours
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abscondere* "to conceal, hide," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *condere* "to put, store up, put away, conceal". First known use: 1652.

words.definition: To make off abruptly, often to dodge a debt or duty; a jocular 19th-century Americanism
words.origin: A mock-Latin American coinage of the 1830s, perhaps from *ab-* + *squat* + *perambulate*.

words.definition: To hold oneself back from indulging
words.origin: Middle English *absteinen, abstenen*, borrowed from Anglo-French *asteign-, absteign-*, stem of *astenir, abstenir*, borrowed (with conjugation change, conformed to *tenir*) from Latin *abstinēre* "to keep from, hold back, refrain, withhold oneself from," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *tenēre* "to hold, occupy, possess". First known use: 14th century.
examples: Ten members voted for the proposal, six members voted against it, and two **abstained**.

words.definition: Sparing in eating and drinking
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abstēmius* "refraining from wine, careful with one's means," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *-tēmius*, from a base *tēm-* "intoxicating" (also in *tēmētum* "intoxicating beverage," *tēmulentus* "drunken"); if going back to an Indo-European root **temH-*, akin to Sanskrit *tāmyati* "(he/she) is stunned, loses consciousness, is exhausted," *tamayati* "(he/she) chokes (someone)," Armenian *tʿmrim* "(he/she) is stunned" (perhaps going back to **tēmiro-*). First known use: 1609.

words.definition: Having a cleansing or purging action; a cleansing agent or detergent
words.origin: From Latin *abstergere* to wipe away.

words.definition: Difficult to understand; obscure
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abstrūsus* "concealed, recondite," from past participle of *abstrūdere* "to conceal," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *trūdere* "to push, thrust". First known use: circa 1549.

words.definition: A pathological loss of willpower; an inability to act or make decisions
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin, probably borrowed from Greek *aboulía* "thoughtlessness, irresolution, indecision," derivative of *áboulos* "inconsiderate, ill-advised," from *a-* a-:2 + *-boulos*, adjective derivative of *boulḗ* "will". First known use: 1847.

words.definition: Of the deep ocean zone, far below where light reaches
words.origin: From Greek *abyssos* bottomless + *pelagos* sea.

words.definition: The impossibility of truly knowing anything
words.origin: From Greek *akatalēpsia*, from *a-* not + *katalambanein* to grasp.

words.definition: Feigned refusal of something one in fact desires, in hopes of being pressed to accept
words.origin: From Greek *akkismos* affectation, coyness.

words.definition: An upward slope, as of a hill, seen from below; the opposite of a declivity
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *acclīvitāt-, acclīvitās*, from *acclīvis, acclīvus* "sloping upwards" (from *ad-* ad- + *clīvus* "slope, incline") + *-itāt-, -itās* -ity. First known use: 1614.

words.definition: An award or expression of high praise
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *acolade, accolade* "embrace," from *acoler* "to embrace" (going back to Old French, from *a-*, prefix forming transitive verbs—going back to Latin *ad-* ad-— + *col* "neck," going back to Latin *collum*) + *-ade* -ade. First known use: 1591.
examples: Received the highest **accolade** of his profession
A movie that has drawn **accolades** from both fans and critics

words.definition: An additional item of dress or equipment; the trappings that identify a role
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *accoutrement, accoustrement*, from *accoutrer* "to accoutre" + *-ment* -ment. First known use: circa 1550.
examples: Shops offering the physical **accoutrements** of polite manners—lace, gloves, linen underclothing, snuff, and gentleman's powdered wigs … — Arthur Herman
… some of the other **accouterments** of power that define our diplomacy. — Elizabeth Drew

words.definition: Gradual growth by the addition of layers
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *accrētiōn-, accrētiō* "increase," from *accrē-* (stem of *accrēscere* "to increase, be added") + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Listless indifference to duty and to life itself; to medieval monks, a sin of the soul
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *acēdia* "apathy, torpor, sloth," borrowed from Late Greek *akēdía* "negligence, apathy," going back to Greek *akḗdeia* "carelessness, indifference," noun derivative of *akēdḗs* "uncared for, without care or worry, careless, heedless," from *a-* a-:2 + *-kēdēs,* adjective derivative of * kêdos* "care, anxiety, grief". First known use: 1607.
examples: A wily demon, **acedia** is difficult to pin down. … The term itself defies translation: despondency, sloth, lassitude, ennui, melancholy—each displays an aspect, none the full image. — Jeff Reimer

But I can at least console myself that Richard [Edwards] never succumbed to **acedia**. On the contrary, he filled every unforgiving minute and lived a rich and happy life, overflowing with love and meaning. — Toby Young

words.definition: Characterized by apathy, boredom or sloth
words.origin: From *acedia*, from Greek *akēdia* indifference, from *a-* + *kēdos* care.

words.definition: A field or place of bloodshed; from the potter's field bought with Judas's silver
words.origin: Greek *Akeldama*, from Aramaic *ḥăqēl dĕmā*, literally, field of blood. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Sharp and biting in tone
words.origin: Acerb + -ic. First known use: 1865.

words.definition: One whose hair has never been cut
words.origin: From Greek *akersekomēs* with unshorn hair, from *a-* + *keirein* to cut + *komē* hair.

words.definition: Growing in heaps or tight clusters, as some fungi and lichens do
words.origin: From Latin *acervatus*, past participle of *acervare* to heap up.

words.definition: A ringing or roaring heard in the head
words.origin: From Greek *akouein* to hear.

words.definition: To accept something reluctantly but without protest
words.origin: Borrowed from French *acquiescer,* going back to Middle French, borrowed from Latin *acquiēscere* "to rest, find peace, be satisfied (with)," from *ad-* ad- + *quiēscere* "to repose, be quiet". First known use: 1613.
examples: **Acquiesced** to their request with a simple nod
The public is not only **acquiescing** in but is actually supporting the move … — Jeffrey Sachs

words.definition: Bitterness or ill feeling
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *acrimonie,* borrowed from Latin *ācrimōnia,* from *ācr-, ācer* "sharp, biting, keen" + *-mōnia,* suffix of abstract nouns (going back to the Indo-European noun-forming suffix **-mĕ̄n-/*-mŏ̄n-* + the abstract noun formative **-i-*). First known use: 1542.

words.definition: The ability to make good judgments and quick, shrewd decisions in a given field
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *acūmen* "sharp point, stinger, acuteness of mind," from *acū-,* stem of *acuere* "to sharpen" + *-men,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: circa 1579.
examples: His business **acumen** led to his appointment as the chair of the economic-development team … — David Frum

words.definition: Unbreakable; impossible to move or persuade; having the lustre of a diamond
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *adamantinus,* borrowed from Greek *adamántinos,* derivative of *adamant-, adámas* adamant. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: To muddle or confuse the mind; of an egg, to become rotten and fail to hatch
words.origin: Middle English *adel-* (in *adel eye* "putrid egg"), attributive use of Old English *adela* "filth, filthy or foul-smelling place," going back to Germanic **adela-, *adelōn-* (whence Middle Dutch *ael* "liquid manure," Middle Low German *ādel, ādele,* Middle High German —east Upper German— *adel,* regional Swedish *adel, al* "animal urine"), of obscure origin. First known use: 1682.

words.definition: To warn or reprimand firmly
words.origin: Middle English *amonysshen, admonisshen, amonescen,* alteration (with assimilation to the verbal suffix *-issh, -esce,* borrowed from Anglo-French *-iss-,* going back to the Latin inceptive suffix *-ēsc-, -īsc-*) of *amonesten,* borrowed from Anglo-French *amonester,* going back to Vulgar Latin **admonestāre,* probably derivative of **admonestus,* past participle of Latin *admonēre* "to give a reminder to, give advice to, caution" (modelled on *comestus,* past participle of *comedere* "to eat up, consume") from *ad-* ad- + *monēre* "to bring to the notice of, give warning". First known use: 14th century.
examples: She **admonished** them to follow proper procedures.

words.definition: Fine writing on a trivial or base subject
words.origin: From Greek *adoxos* inglorious + *-graphia* writing.

words.definition: Clever and skilful, especially with the hands or mind
words.origin: Borrowed from French, going back to Old French, "handsome, elegant, skilled (in combat)," from *a-,* prefix, perhaps with intensive value (going back to Latin *ad-* ad-) + *droit* "straight, direct, true, regular," going back to Latin *directus* "straight, direct". First known use: 1652.

words.definition: Added or derived from outside; supplemental rather than inherent
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *adscītīcius, ascītīcius,* from Latin *adscītus, ascītus,* past participle of *adscīscere, ascīscere* "to take to oneself, admit, adopt" (from *ad-* ad- + *scīscere* "to get to know, ascertain, vote for, approve," inchoative derivative of *scīre* "to know") + *-īcius* -itious. First known use: 1620.

words.definition: Excessive admiration or praise
words.origin: Middle English *adulacioun* "insincere praise, flattery," borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *adūlātiōn-, adūlātiō,* from *adūlārī* "to fawn upon (of dogs), praise insincerely" (of uncertain origin) + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Celebrities often feed off the **adulation** of fans, but that acclaim can be fleeting and illusory. — Ruben Castenada
During the campaign, he basked in the **adulation** of his fans and emphasized the promises that drew the biggest applause and the most retweets … — Peter Coy

words.definition: To outline faintly or foreshadow
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *adumbrātus,* past participle of *adumbrāre* "to shade, represent by means of light and shade, sketch, outline," from *ad-* ad- + *-umbrāre,* verbal derivative of *umbra* "shadow". First known use: 1537.
examples: The social unrest that **adumbrated** the French Revolution
Bubbling optimism, not at all **adumbrated** by difficulties

words.definition: Scorched or sunburnt; gloomy in temperament
words.origin: Middle English "treated with intense heat (of medical ingredients), altered by body heat (of humours)," borrowed from Medieval Latin *adustus,* going back to Latin, "burnt, scorched," from past participle of *adūrere*" to scorch, burn up, cauterize," from *ad-* ad- + *ūrere* (past participle *ustus*) "to expose to fire, burn, scorch," going back to Indo-European **h1eu̯s-* "burn (transitive), singe," whence Greek *heúō, heúein* "to scorch" (with presumed metathesis of *h*), Sanskrit *óṣati* "(s/he) burns," *uṣṭáḥ* "burnt up". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Happening by chance or from outside rather than by design; incidental
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *adventīcius* "coming from outside, external, foreign," from *adventus*, past participle of *advenīre* "to arrive, approach" + *-īcius* -itious. First known use: 1603.
examples: A Federal house without **adventitious** later additions

words.definition: Evening approaches; it grows toward dusk
words.origin: Latin, it is growing toward evening, from *vesper* evening.

words.definition: The innermost sanctuary of an ancient temple, open only to priests; a sanctum
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *adytum,* borrowed from Greek *ádyton,* neuter of *ádytos* "not to be entered," from *a-* a-:2 + *-dytos,* verbal adjective of *dýein* "to enter, make one's way into, sink," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Protection or sponsorship
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, borrowed from Greek *aigís* "goatskin, mantle of Zeus," derivative of *aig-, aíx* "goat"; akin to Armenian *aic* "goat" (perhaps going back to Indo-European **h2eiǵ-ih2-*), and perhaps to Avestan *izaēna* "of leather". First known use: 15th century.
examples: Passed new laws under the **aegis** of national security

words.definition: A consuming, lasting passion
words.origin: From Greek *aei* ever + *pathos* feeling.

words.definition: Produced, carried or shaped by the wind, as dunes or the sighing of a wind harp
words.origin: *Aeolus,* god of the winds (borrowed from Latin, borrowed from Greek *Aíolos*) + -ian. First known use: 1595.

words.definition: A harp played by the wind
words.origin: From *Aeolus*, Greek god of the winds.

words.definition: A pompous bore who claims inspiration
words.origin: From *Aeolus*, god of the winds; coined by Jonathan Swift.

words.definition: One with a refined appreciation of art and beauty
words.origin: Probably derivative of aesthetic or aesthetics, on the model of athletics : athlete and similar pairs. First known use: 1866.

words.definition: Of or belonging to summer
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French or Latin; Anglo-French, from Latin *aestivalis*, from *aestivus* of summer, from *aestas* summer. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Friendly and easy to talk to
words.origin: Middle English *affabyl,* borrowed from Anglo-French *affable,* borrowed from Latin *affābilis,* from *affārī* "to speak to, address" (from *ad-* ad- + *fārī* "to speak") + *-bilis* "capable of (being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A sudden creative impulse or inspiration, as if breathed in by a god
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *afflātus,* literally, "emission of breath, exhalation," from *afflāre* "to breathe on or toward, inspire" (from *ad-* ad- + *flāre* "to blow, breathe") + *-tus,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 1649.

words.definition: Selfless, unconditional love
words.origin: A-:1 + gape. First known use: 1667.

words.definition: The doctrine that, in the end, all things tend toward good
words.origin: From Greek *agathos* good.

words.definition: Made up of both good and evil
words.origin: From Greek *agathos* good + *kakos* bad; coined by Robert Southey.

words.definition: Looking worse after a haircut
words.origin: Japanese, from *ageru* to raise + *otoru* to be inferior.

words.definition: A person who never laughs; one immune to humour of any kind, however good the joke
words.origin: From Greek *agelastos* not laughing, from *a-* + *gelan* to laugh.

words.definition: Not growing old or looking younger than one's age
words.origin: From Greek *agērasia*, from *a-* not + *gēras* old age.

words.definition: The bringing up to date of an institution or doctrine; modernization
words.origin: Borrowed from Italian, from *aggiornare* "to bring up to date" (from *a-,* verbal prefix — going back to Latin *ad-* ad- — + *giorno* "day," going back to Late Latin *diurnum,* from neuter of Latin *diurnus* "daily") + *-mento* -ment. First known use: 1962.
examples: Dedicated to the **aggiornamento** of the church

words.definition: To collect or form into a mass or cluster; a jumbled mass of things
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *agglomerātus,* past participle of *agglomerāre* "to heap up, mass together, join forces," from *ad-* ad- + *glomerāre* "to form into a ball, collect into a mass," verbal derivative of *glomer-, glomus* "ball-shaped mass". First known use: 1632.

words.definition: To make greater in power, rank or reputation
words.origin: Borrowed (with assimilation of the ending to -ize) from French *agrandiss-,* stem of *agrandir,* going back to Old French, from *a-,* verb-forming prefix (going back to Latin *ad-* ad-) + *-grandir,* verbal derivative of *grand* "large, great," going back to Latin *grandis* "fully grown, large, great". First known use: 1634.

words.definition: , adjective 1. Awry
words.origin: Scots *agley, aglee* "obliquely, askance, awry," from *a-* a-:1 + *gley, glee* "to squint, look askance," going back to Old Scots *gley* (in the participle *gleyit* "squinting") & Middle English (north, northwest Midlands) *glien, gleen, gleien* "to be squint-eyed, glance, glisten," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1785.
examples: The best-laid schemes o' Mice an' Men Gang aft **agley** … — Robert Burns

words.definition: The study of ignorance or the investigation of the unknowable
words.origin: From Greek *agnoia* ignorance + *-logy*; coined by James Ferrier in 1854.

words.definition: A name or nickname added to one's own in recognition of some deed or trait
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *agnōmen,* alteration of **adnōmen* (by analogy with *nōscere* "to get to know" : *agnōscere* "to acknowledge, recognize"), from *ad-* ad- + *nōmen* name. First known use: 1654.

words.definition: Very eager or curious to hear or see something; in a state of excitement
words.origin: Probably borrowed from Middle French *en gogues* "in good humour, mirthful," from *en* "in" + *gogues,* plural of *gogue* "good humour, joking, pleasantry, mockery," going back to a Gallo-Romance expressive base **gog-*. First known use: 1664.
examples: “… That was the year the **Twilight** movie was going to come out, and the kids were **agog** with all things vampire. …” — Shelley Dorrill
“… There goes Mrs. Tony now, **all agog** to spread such a delectable bit of gossip.” — Lucy Maud Montgomery

words.definition: , plural agones (AG-uh-neez) A conflict, contest or struggle
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *agṓn* "gathering, assembly, contest". First known use: 1600.
examples: Normally the hostility between two opposed characters is such that the **agon** clearly continues for as long as they are on stage together. — Michael A. Lloyd

words.definition: Causing great physical or mental pain
words.origin: From present participle of agonize. First known use: 1570.

words.definition: Sick with fright
words.origin: An old English dialect word of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Loss of the ability to write
words.origin: A-:2 + Greek *-graphia* -graphy, probably after German *Agraphie* or French *agraphie*. First known use: 1565.

words.definition: The study of grasses
words.origin: From Greek *agrōstis* grass + *-logy*.

words.definition: Divination by watching the movements of cats
words.origin: From Greek *ailouros* cat + *manteia* divination.

words.definition: One who loves cats
words.origin: Greek *aiélouros, aílouros* "the wild or domestic cat" + -o- + -phile. First known use: 1914.

words.definition: The worship of filth or obscenity
words.origin: From Greek *aischros* shameful + *latreia* worship.

words.definition: A vision or dream, especially an Irish poetic vision
words.origin: Irish, vision, dream.

words.definition: With hands on the hips and elbows turned outward; of limbs, flung out at angles
words.origin: Middle English *in kenebowe,* of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Acting against one's better judgment; weakness of will
words.origin: Greek, lack of self-control, from *a-* + *kratos* power.

words.definition: Brisk and eager; acting with cheerful readiness and speed, without being asked twice
words.origin: Latin *alacritas*, from *alacr-, alacer* lively, eager. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Cheerful readiness or eagerness
words.origin: Latin *alacritas*, from *alacr-, alacer* lively, eager. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Half-dead; utterly dejected
words.origin: From French *à la mort* to the death.

words.definition: An avenger
words.origin: Greek, avenging spirit.

words.definition: Having wings; winged
words.origin: Latin *alatus*, from *ala*. First known use: 1661.

words.definition: A person characterized by arrogance, braggadocio, lack of self awareness
words.origin: Greek, boaster, impostor.

words.definition: Depending on chance or luck
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *āleātōrius* "of gamblers or games of chance," derivative of *āleātor* "gambler," from *ālea* "game of chance, gamble" (of obscure origin) + *-ā-,* verb formative + *-tor,* agent suffix. First known use: 1693.

words.definition: An old distilling vessel; anything that refines or transforms what passes through it
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French & Medieval Latin; Middle French *alambic* & Medieval Latin *alembicum*, from Arabic *al-anbīq*, from *al* the + *anbīq* still, from Late Greek *ambik-, ambix* alembic, from Greek, cap of a still. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … philosophy … filtered through the **alembic** of Plato's mind. — B. T. Shropshire

words.definition: The study of the nature of truth
words.origin: From Greek *alētheia* truth + *-logy*.

words.definition: Acting as an antidote to poison; a remedy against venom or infection
words.origin: From Greek *alexipharmakos*, from *alexein* to ward off + *pharmakon* poison.

words.definition: Difficulty recognizing and describing one's own emotions
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *a-* without + *lexis* word + *thymos* spirit, feeling; coined by psychiatrist Peter Sifneos in 1973.

words.definition: Cold or chilly; marked by extreme coldness of the body, as in some fevers
words.origin: Latin *algidus*, from *algēre* to feel cold. First known use: circa 1623.
examples: The rescuers searching the **algid** waters of the Bering Sea

words.definition: An exaggerated show of emotion over something small
words.origin: Spanish, from Arabic *al-haraka* the movement.

words.definition: Nutritious; nourishing
words.origin: From Latin *alibilis*, from *alere* to nourish.

words.definition: To make suffering less severe
words.origin: Late Latin *alleviatus*, past participle of *alleviare*, from Latin *ad-* + *levis* light. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Smelling or tasting of garlic or onions; belonging to the onion family
words.origin: Latin *allium* garlic. First known use: 1757.

words.definition: Having the power to attract; appealing
words.origin: From Latin *alliciens*, present participle of *allicere* to entice.

words.definition: The striking of a moving ship against a fixed object
words.origin: From Latin *allidere* to strike against.

words.definition: The repetition of initial sounds in nearby words
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *allīterātiōn-, allīterātiō,* from Latin *ad-* ad- + *lītera* "letter" + *-ātiōn-, -ātiō* -ation. First known use: circa 1624.

words.definition: The name of another real person, assumed by an author as a pen name
words.origin: From Greek *allos* other + *onyma* name.

words.definition: An abnormal desire to eat things not usually eaten, such as chalk or clay. Also known as pica
words.origin: From Greek *allotrios* strange + *-phagia* eating.

words.definition: The rosy light on mountain peaks at sunrise or sunset
words.origin: Partial translation of German *Alpenglühen*, from *Alpen* Alps + *Glühen* glow. First known use: 1862.

words.definition: Otherness: the state or quality of being other or different
words.origin: Middle English *alterite* "change, state of being changed, difference," borrowed from Late Latin *alteritāt-, alteritās* (as translation of Greek *heterótēs*), from Latin *alter* "second, other" + *-itāt-, -itās* -ity. First known use: 1560.
examples: … we are likely always to discover unexplored places—an **alterity**—within ourselves. — Virginia Anderson
[Jeannette] Lander reflects on food as a marker of difference and cultural **alterity**, but also as a means of coming together: "Cooking connects all of my worlds." — Heike Henderson

words.definition: Pompous or pretentious
words.origin: From Latin *altus* high + *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: Thundering from on high
words.origin: From Latin *altitonans*, from *altus* high + *tonare* to thunder.

words.definition: Lofty in thought or aspiration
words.origin: From Latin *altitudo* height.

words.definition: Born in an undeveloped and helpless condition and requiring parental care and feeding for some time
words.origin: New Latin *Altrices,* proposed division of birds having altricial young (plural of Latin *altrīc-, altrīx* "foster mother, wet nurse," from *alere* "to nurse, nourish" + *-trīx,* feminine agent suffix) + -ial. First known use: 1869.

words.definition: With all one's strength
examples: The soul strives **amain** to live and work … — R. W. Emerson
They whom I favour thrive in wealth **amain** … — John Milton

words.definition: To combine into one whole
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *amalgamātus,* past participle of *amalgamāre* "to combine (a metal) with mercury," verbal derivative of *amalgama* amalgam. First known use: 1599.
examples: They **amalgamated** the hospital with the university.

words.definition: A literary assistant who takes dictation or copies manuscripts; a scribe
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *āmanuensis,* from (*servus*) *ā manū* "slave with secretarial duties," literally, "(slave) from the hand" + *-ensis,* suffix of appurtenance. First known use: 1619.
examples: Composed her autobiography with the help of an **amanuensis**

words.definition: An imaginary flower that never fades
words.origin: Latin *amarantus*, a flower, from Greek *amaranton*, from neuter of *amarantos* unfading, from *a-* + *marainein* to waste away. First known use: 1616.

words.definition: Undying or unfading, like the legendary amaranth flower; deep purplish-red
words.origin: From *amaranth* + *-ine*. *Amaranth*: Latin *amarantus*, a flower, from Greek *amaranton*, from neuter of *amarantos* unfading, from *a-* + *marainein* to waste away. First known use: 1667.

words.definition: A pretend or insignificant lover
words.origin: From Latin *amatorculus* a little lover, diminutive of *amator*.

words.definition: Relating to love or sexual desire
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *amātōrius,* adjective derivative of *amātōr-, amātor* "lover". First known use: 1571.

words.definition: Partial or total loss of sight without visible change to the eye
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *amaurōsis,* borrowed from Greek *amaúrōsis* "dimming of sight, loss of sight without a visible cause," from *amaurō-,* variant stem of *amaroún* "to make dim or faint, weaken, impair" (verbal derivative of *amaurós* "dim, faint, having little or no sight," of uncertain origin) + *-sis* -sis. First known use: circa 1657.

words.definition: The scope, extent or bounds of something; the range of one's authority
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *ambitus* "circuit, circumference, strip of ground around the outside of a building," from *ambīre* "to visit in rotation, surround, encircle" + *-tus,* suffix of action nouns. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings
words.origin: Borrowed from German, from *ambi-* ambi- + *-valent,* in *äquivalent* equivalent. First known use: 1912.
examples: … people whose relationship to their job is **ambivalent**, conflicted. — Terrence Rafferty
Americans are deeply **ambivalent** about the country's foreign role. Isolationist yearnings coexist uneasily with superpower policies. — David P. Calleo

words.definition: One having the characteristics of both an extrovert and an introvert
words.origin: Ambi- + *-vert* (in extrovert, introvert). First known use: 1923.

words.definition: Exceptionally delicious or fragrant
words.origin: Latin, from Greek, literally, immortality, from *ambrotos* immortal, from *a-* + *-mbrotos* (akin to *brotos* mortal). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A recess in a church wall for sacred vessels; any storeroom or cupboard
words.origin: Middle English *almerie, almary* "pantry, wardrobe, cabinet," borrowed from Anglo-French *almarie, almaire* (continental Old French *armaire, armairie*). First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The lowest throw at dice, double ones; bad luck or the worst of fortune
words.origin: Middle English *ambes as*, from Anglo-French, from *ambes* both + *as* aces. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: To make something bad better
words.origin: Alteration (after French *améliorer*) of meliorate. First known use: 1653.

words.definition: Open and responsive to suggestion
words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French, from *amener* "to bring, bring to a court (as witnesses, pledges), summon, take, lead" (also continental Old French) (from *a-* —going back to Latin *ad-* ad-— + *mener* "to lead, bring") + *able* -able. First known use: circa 1599.
examples: She said her peers wanted her to bend the rules, but she wasn't **amenable**. — Erin Osmon
His boss was **amenable** to the idea of his working from home.

words.definition: Without a clear shape or form
words.origin: Greek *amorphos*, from *a-* + *morphē* form. First known use: circa 1727.

words.definition: A phrase that can be read two ways because of loose grammar, not word choice
words.origin: Middle English *amphibologie* "double meaning, ambiguity," borrowed from Late Latin *amphibologia,* alteration (by assimilation to the final element *-logia* -logy) of Latin *amphibolia,* borrowed from Greek *amphibolía* "state of being attached on two sides, double meaning, ambiguity," from *amphíbolos* "attached on both sides, doubtful, ambiguous" + *-ia* -y. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A piece of nonsense verse or burlesque writing that seems to mean something
words.origin: From French *amphigouri*, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A small item of food served as an appetizer
words.origin: French, literally amuse the mouth.

words.definition: The inability to recognize, reproduce or appreciate music
words.origin: From Greek *amousia* lack of harmony, from *a-* + *mousa* muse.

words.definition: A military advance into the interior; an arduous upward or inland journey
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *anábasis* "way up, ascent, journey up," from *anaba-,* variant stem of *anabaínein* "to go or come up, ascend" (from *ana-* ana- + *baínein* "to step, go, come") + *-sis* -sis; (sense 2) from the retreat of Greek mercenaries in Asia Minor described in the *Anabasis* of Xenophon. First known use: circa 1706.

words.definition: A herb said to restore lost love
words.origin: From Greek *anakampserōs*, from *anakamptein* to bend back + *erōs* love.

words.definition: Something out of its proper time
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *anachronismus,* borrowed from Middle Greek *anachronismós,* from Late Greek *anachronízein* “to be late, (middle voice) be an anachronism” (from Greek *ana-* ana- + *chrónos* “time” + *-izein* -ize) + Greek *-ismos* -ism. First known use: 1617.
examples: I think the concept of the draft is an **anachronism** from the time before laptops and word processing software. — Sarah Manguso

words.definition: An abrupt change in the middle of a sentence making one part inconsistent with the other
words.origin: Late Latin, from Late Greek *anakolouthon* inconsistency in logic, from Greek, neuter of *anakolouthos* inconsistent, from *an-* + *akolouthos* following, from *ha-, a-* together + *keleuthos* path. First known use: 1583.

words.definition: Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *anadiplōsis*, literally, repetition, from *anadiploun* to double, from *ana-* + *diploun* to double. First known use: circa 1526.

words.definition: The moment in a drama when a character recognizes the truth of their situation
words.origin: Greek *anagnōrisis*, from *anagnōrizein* to recognize, from *ana-* + *gnōrizein* to make known; akin to Greek *gnōrimos* well-known, *gignōskein* to come to know. First known use: 1783.

words.definition: Recollection, especially of a supposed previous existence; a patient's history
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *anamnēsis*, from *anamimnēskesthai* to remember, from *ana-* + *mimnēskesthai* to remember. First known use: circa 1593.

words.definition: Repeating a word at the start of successive phrases
words.origin: Late Latin, from Late Greek, from Greek, act of carrying back, reference, from *anapherein* to carry back, refer, from *ana-* + *pherein* to carry. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: Lincoln's "we cannot dedicate—we cannot consecrate—we cannot hallow—this ground" is an example of **anaphora**

words.definition: The inversion of the usual order of words
words.origin: Medieval Latin, from Greek *anastrophē*, literally, turning back, from *anastrephein* to turn back, from *ana-* + *strephein* to turn. First known use: circa 1550.

words.definition: Something or someone intensely disliked
words.origin: Late Latin *anathemat-, anathema*, from Greek, thing devoted to evil, curse, from *anatithenai* to set up, dedicate, from *ana-* + *tithenai* to place, set. First known use: 1582.
examples: Slashing tech work forces would have **been anathema** in Silicon Valley just a few years ago. — Mike Isaac
… this notion **was anathema to** most of his countrymen. — Stephen Jay Gould

words.definition: To denounce, condemn or curse
A religious recluse who lives walled up in a cell for prayer; a hermit
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *anchorita*, alteration of Late Latin *anachoreta*, from Late Greek *anachōrētēs*, from Greek *anachōrein* to withdraw, from *ana-* + *chōrein* to make room, from *chōros* place. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Providing support; secondary
words.origin: From *ancilla* + *-ry*. *Ancilla*: Latin, female servant. First known use: 1663.
examples: The main factory and its **ancillary** plants
… backers [of a proposed park] see all kinds of **ancillary** benefits, from health to traffic. — Lisa W. Foderaro

words.definition: Anecdotal information gleaned from casual observation
words.origin: A blend of *anecdote* and *data*.

words.definition: Growing in windy conditions
words.origin: From Greek *anemos* wind.

words.definition: A windflower
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *anemōnē*. First known use: 1548.

words.definition: Lack of energy
words.origin: International Scientific Vocabulary a-:2 + *-ergy* (as in *allergy*). First known use: 1890.

words.definition: A winding channel; intricate twisting
Full of twists, turns and winding passages; sinuous and circuitous
words.origin: Middle English *amfractuous,* borrowed from Late Latin *anfrāctuōsus,* from *anfrāctu-,* stem of *anfrāctus* "bend, circular motion, winding course" (from *an-,* assimilated form of *amb-* "around" + *-frāctus,* action noun derivative of *frangere* "to break") + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The inability to feel pleasure
words.origin: New Latin, from a-:2 + Greek *hēdonē* pleasure. First known use: 1887.

words.definition: Like a feeble old woman; doddering, weak-minded or senile, as anile superstitions
words.origin: Latin *anilis*, from *anus* old woman. First known use: circa 1624.

words.definition: Criticism or censure; a remark that comments critically on someone
words.origin: Latin *animadversion-, animadversio*, from *animadvertere*. First known use: 1583.

words.definition: A microscopic animal, of the kind first glimpsed under early microscopes
words.origin: New Latin *animalculum*, diminutive of Latin *animal*. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: Hostility or ill will
words.origin: Latin, spirit, mind, courage, anger. First known use: 1795.
examples: … the sixties mentality, with its strong **animus** against what it defines as "elitism" … — Daniel J. Singal

words.definition: Not likely to offend or provoke, and thus bland; a painkilling medicine
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *anōdynus* "allaying pain," borrowed from Greek *anṓdynos* "free from pain, causing no pain, harmless, allaying pain," from *an-* an- + *-ōdynos,* adjective derivative (with compositional lengthening) of *odýnē* "pain," of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … his speech contained a single **anodyne** reference to the man who preceded him. — John F. Burns

words.definition: Deviating from what is standard
words.origin: Late Latin *anōmalus* "irregular (of grammatical paradigms), unequal in size (of planets)" (borrowed from Greek *anṓmalos* "not uniform, unequal, inconsistent, irregular [in grammar]," from *an-* an- + *homalόs* "even, uniform, equal, like") + -ous. First known use: 1606.
examples: Researchers could not explain the **anomalous** test results.
An **anomalous** figure in the world of politics

words.definition: Difficulty recalling the names of things
words.origin: From Greek *a-* without + *onoma* name.

words.definition: Repeating a word in two different senses
words.origin: From Greek *antanaklasis* reflection, from *anaklan* to bend back.

words.definition: Occurring or existing before a war, especially the American Civil War
words.origin: Latin *ante bellum* before the war. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: Ridiculously old-fashioned
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *antedīluviānus,* from Latin *ante-* ante- + *dīluvium* "flood, inundation" + *-ānus* -an. First known use: 1646.
examples: That **antediluvian** relic known as a slide rule

words.definition: Before dawn
words.origin: From Latin *antelucanus*, from *ante* before + *lux* light.

words.definition: Preventing nightmares
words.origin: From Greek *anti* against + *ephialtēs* nightmare.

words.definition: Of the rays that converge opposite the setting sun
words.origin: From *anti-* + Latin *crepusculum* twilight.

words.definition: Out of line; lopsided; out of whack
words.origin: American dialect, perhaps from *anti-* + *godling*; recorded from the 1800s.

words.definition: A cloth laid over a chair back to protect it from Macassar hair oil; a Victorian staple
words.origin: *anti- + Macassar* (*oil*) (a hairdressing). First known use: 1844.

words.definition: Repeating words in reverse order, as "eat to live, not live to eat"
words.origin: From Greek *antimetabolē* turning about.

words.definition: A contradiction between two beliefs or conclusions that each seem reasonable
words.origin: Earlier, "opposition of one law or rule to another," borrowed from Latin *antinomia* "contradiction between laws," borrowed from Greek *antimonía* "conflict between the requirements of different laws," from *anti-* anti- + *nómos* "custom, convention, law" (noun derivative of *némein* "to pasture [animals], rule, direct, distribute, apportion") + *-ia* -y; as a philosophical term after German *Antinomie,* used by Immanuel kant in *Critique of Pure Reason* (*Kritik der reinen Vernunft*). First known use: 1585.
examples: … **antinomies** of beauty and evil, freedom and slavery … — Stephen Holden

words.definition: A deep-seated dislike
words.origin: Latin *antipathia*, from Greek *antipatheia*, from *antipathēs* of opposite feelings, from *anti-* + *pathos* experience. First known use: 1592.
examples: … perhaps his greatest **antipathies** were cabs, old women, doors that would not shut … — Charles Dickens

words.definition: A short chant sung before or after a psalm, often by alternating choirs
words.origin: Middle English *antiphone*, from Middle French, from Late Latin *antiphona*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Using a word to mean its opposite, usually ironically, as "giant" for a tiny dog
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek, from *anti-* + *phrasis* diction. First known use: 1533.

words.definition: Old-fashioned or outdated; too old to be useful
words.origin: From *antiquate* to make old, from Late Latin *antiquare*, from Latin *antiquus* ancient.

words.definition: People living on the same meridian on opposite sides of the equator
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *antiscii*, from Greek *anti* opposite + *skia* shadow.

words.definition: The direct opposite
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek, literally, opposition, from *antitithenai* to oppose, from *anti-* + *tithenai* to set. First known use: 1529.
examples: Her temperament is the very **antithesis** of mine.

words.definition: A cave, cavern, cavity
words.origin: French, from Latin *antrum*. First known use: 1585.

words.definition: At any time
words.origin: From *any* + *when*, on the model of *anywhere*.

words.definition: Provision made for younger royal children; a perquisite that comes with a station
words.origin: French *apanage*, from Old French, from *apaner* to provide for a younger offspring, from Medieval Latin *appanare*, from Latin *ad-* + *panis* bread. First known use: 1602.

words.definition: A desire to be away from people; a love of solitude
words.origin: From Greek *apanthrōpia*, from *apo* away + *anthrōpos* human.

words.definition: Lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *apathie,* borrowed from Latin *apathīa,* borrowed from Greek *apatheîa,* noun derivative of *apathḗs* "not suffering, without passion or feeling, impassive," from *a-* a-:2 + *-pathēs,* adjective derivative of *páthos* "experience, misfortune, emotion". First known use: 1594.
examples: The professor described sociopaths as people prone to **apathy** who behave badly out of a desperation to feel something. — Manvir Singh

words.definition: The point in the orbit of a planet or comet at which it is farthest from the sun
words.origin: New Latin, from *apo-* + Greek *hēlios* sun. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: The gradual loss of an unstressed vowel at the start of a word, as squire from esquire
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek, release, from *aphienai* to let go, from *apo-* + *hienai* to send. First known use: 1880.

words.definition: A short, pithy statement of a truth
words.origin: Middle French *aphorisme*, from Late Latin *aphorismus*, from Greek *aphorismos* definition, aphorism, from *aphorizein* to define, from *apo-* + *horizein* to bound. First known use: 1528.
examples: The high-minded **aphorism**, "Let us value the quality of life, not the quantity"
These are dazzling chapters, packed with perfectly chosen anecdotes and pithy with **aphorism**. — John Keegan

words.definition: A writer or speaker of aphorisms
words.origin: Middle French *aphorisme*, from Late Latin *aphorismus*, from Greek *aphorismos* definition, aphorism, from *aphorizein* to define, from *apo-* + *horizein* to bound. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: A person who keeps bees, especially on a commercial scale; a beekeeper
words.origin: Apiary + -ist. First known use: 1785.

words.definition: A place where bees are kept
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *apiārium,* from *apis* "bee" (of obscure origin) + *-ārium* -ary. First known use: 1654.

words.definition: Self-confidence and assurance, especially in a demanding situation; poise
words.origin: French, literally, perpendicularity, from Middle French, from *a plomb*, literally, according to the plummet. First known use: 1818.
examples: She played several roles with equal **aplomb**.

words.definition: The loss of a sound or sounds at the end of a word, as in sing from singan
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *apocopē,* borrowed from Greek *apocopḗ,* literally, "a cutting off," noun derivative from the base of *apokóptein* "to cut off, chop off," from *apo-* apo- + *kóptein* "to strike, knock, hew, fell with a weapon," perhaps going back to dialectal Indo-European **kop-* "strike, fell," whence also Lithuanian *kapiù, kàpti* "to hew, fell," *kapóti* "to hew, chop," Russian *kopát'* "to dig". First known use: circa 1550.

words.definition: Of doubtful authenticity, though widely repeated
words.origin: Apocrypha + -al. First known use: 1553.

words.definition: Clearly established or beyond dispute; demonstrably and necessarily true
words.origin: Latin *apodicticus*, from Greek *apodeiktikos*, from *apodeiknynai* to demonstrate, from *apo-* + *deiknynai* to show. First known use: circa 1645.

words.definition: The highest point; the climax
words.origin: French *apogée*, from New Latin *apogaeum*, from Greek *apogaion*, from neuter of *apogeios, apogaios* far from the earth, from *apo-* + *gē, gaia* earth. First known use: 1640.
examples: Aegean civilization reached its **apogee** in Crete.

words.definition: Freedom from bodily pain, prized by the Epicureans as a highest good
words.origin: Greek *aponia*, from *a-* without + *ponos* pain, toil.

words.definition: Raising a subject by saying one won't mention it
words.origin: Late Latin, repudiation, from Greek, denial, negation, from *apophanai* to deny, from *apo-* + *phanai* to say. First known use: 1656.
examples: … he indulges himself in **apophasis** about his ex-wives (“No, I am most definitely not making any charges or accusations. It's merely that …”). — John Brooks

words.definition: The perception of connections or
words.origin: Borrowed from German *Apophänie,* perhaps from Greek *apophaínein* "to reveal, represent" (from *apo-* apo- + *phaínein* "to make visible, cause to appear") + German *-ie* -ia. First known use: 1999.
examples: What psychologists call **apophenia**—the human tendency to see connections and patterns that are not really there—gives rise to conspiracy theories. — George Johnson

words.definition: An expression of doubt; a puzzling impasse in reasoning
words.origin: French *aporie*, ultimately from Greek *aporia* difficulty, perplexity, from *aporos* impassable, from *a-* + *poros* passage. First known use: circa 1550.

words.definition: An abrupt breaking off in the middle of a sentence, as if one is unable or unwilling to proceed
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *aposiōpēsis*, from *aposiōpan* to be fully silent, from *apo-* + *siōpan* to be silent, from *siōpē* silence. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: The abandonment of a belief or cause
words.origin: Middle English *apostasie,* borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed from Late Latin *apostasia,* borrowed from Greek *apostasía* "defection, revolt, (Septuagint) rebellion against God" (Late Greek, "defection, apostasy"), variant (with *-ia* -ia) of *apóstasis,* from *aposta-,* variant stem of *aphístamai, aphístasthai* "to stand away from, keep aloof from, revolt," middle voice of *aphístēmi, aphistánai* "to put away, remove, cause to revolt" (from *aph-,* assimilated variant of *apo-* apo- + *histánai* "to cause to stand, place") + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To address an absent person, idea or thing as if present, as in poetry
words.origin: Apostrophe + -ize. First known use: 1676.

words.definition: One who prepared and sold medicines
words.origin: Middle English *apothecarie, apotecarie, pothecarie,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French *apothecaire, ipotecaire,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *apotēcārius, apothēcārius,* going back to Late Latin, "shopkeeper," from Latin *apothēca* "storeroom, storehouse, repository" (borrowed from Greek *apothḗkē,* from *apothē-,* variant stem of *apotithénai* "to put away, stow away" —from *apo-* apo- + *tithénai* "to put, place"— + *-kē,* noun suffix) + *-ārius* -ary. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A concise saying or maxim expressing a general truth; an aphorism
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *apothegma, apophthegma,* borrowed from Greek *apophthegmat-, apóphthegma*, from *apophtheg-,* stem of *apophthéngomai, apophthéngesthai* "to speak one's opinion plainly, utter a pithy saying" (from *apo-* apo- + *phthéngomai, phthéngesthai* "to utter a sound, speak clearly," of obscure origin) + *-mat-, -ma,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 1548.

words.definition: The highest point of something; elevation to divine status
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *apotheōsis* "transformation into a god, deification," borrowed from Greek *apothéōsis,* from *apotheō-,* variant stem of *apotheóō, apotheoûn* "to transform into a god, deify" (from *apo-* apo- + *theoûn* "to make a god of," verbal derivative of *theós* "god") + -sis -sis. First known use: circa 1580.
examples: … Nelson Rockefeller, the other top contender and the **apotheosis** of liberal Republicanism. — Sam Tanenhaus

words.definition: To pacify by giving in to demands
words.origin: Middle English *appesen*, from Anglo-French *apeser, apaiser*, from *a-* (from Latin *ad-*) + *pais* peace. First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Appeased** the dictator by accepting his demands
Placaters, who try hard to **appease** others so as to keep the peace, fear getting hurt in some way. — Mike Cote

words.definition: A strong natural craving or desire; an instinctive inclination
To place next to or side by side: to juxtapose
words.origin: Middle French *aposer*, from Old French, from *a-* + *poser* to put. First known use: 1593.

words.definition: Apt in the circumstances
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *appositus* "situated near, ready at hand, suitable, apt," from past participle of *appōnere* "to place near, put or fit on, contribute as an additional element," from *ap-* ap-:1 + *pōnere* "to place, set, put in position". First known use: 1621.

words.definition: Approval or praise
words.origin: From *approbate* + *-ion*. *Approbate*: Middle English, from Latin *approbatus*, past participle of *approbare*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A plan that has won the **approbation** of the mayor

words.definition: An accessory, equipment, gear, etc. associated with an activity or style of living
words.origin: Middle English *appurtenaunce* "subsidiary or incidental right or privilege, accessory, appendage," borrowed from Anglo-French *apartenance, apurtenance,* from *apartenant, appurtenant* appurtenant + *-ance* -ance. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **appurtenance** of welcome is fashion and ceremony. — William Shakespeare

words.definition: To bask in the sun
words.origin: From Latin *apricari* to bask in the sun, from *apricus* sunny.

words.definition: The warmth of the sun on a winter's day
words.origin: From Latin *aprīcitās* "sunniness," from *aprīcus* "sunny". First known use: 1623.

words.definition: The inability to concentrate
words.origin: From Greek *aprosexia* inattention, from *a-* + *prosechein* to attend.

words.definition: A water-drinker
words.origin: From Latin *aqua* water + *bibere* to drink.

words.definition: Based on whim rather than reason
words.origin: Middle English, "depending on individual discretion," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *arbitraire, arbitrarie* "relating to arbitration," borrowed from Latin *arbitrārius* "relating to or depending on the discretion of an arbiter," from *arbitr-, arbiter* arbiter + *-ārius* -ary. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Until we understand it, advice on which foods to eat … will always seem **arbitrary** … — Nicholas Florko
You can tell a well-written show when you realize not a single note, word or marking is **arbitrary**. — Charlie Henderson

words.definition: Living in or relating to trees; resembling a tree in form or character
words.origin: Latin *arboreus* of a tree, from *arbor*. First known use: circa 1667.

words.definition: A garden of trees
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, plantation of trees, from *arbor*. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: The killing of a tree
words.origin: From Latin *arbor* tree + *-cide* killing.

words.definition: Idyllically pastoral and simple
Understood by few; mysterious
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *arcānus* "secret, private, intimate," from *arca* "chest, coffer, box" + *-ānus* -an. First known use: 1547.

words.definition: A perfect, original example of something
words.origin: Latin *archetypum*, from Greek *archetypon*, from neuter of *archetypos* archetypal, from *archein* + *typos* type. First known use: 1545.
examples: … the House of Commons, the **archetype** of all the representative assemblies which now meet … — T. B. Macaulay
He is the **archetype** of a successful businessman.

words.definition: Someone who is very fond of teddy bears or collects them
words.origin: From Greek *arktos* bear + *-phile* lover.

words.definition: Passionate and enthusiastic
words.origin: Middle English *ardaunt, ardent* "burning, fiery, passionate," borrowed from Middle French *ardent, ardant,* going back to Old French, borrowed from Latin *ardent-, ardens* "burning, fiercely hot, shining, eager, passionate," from present participle of *ardēre* "to burn, emit light or flame, be fiercely hot, be violently excited, be eager," derivative of *āridus, ārdus* "dry, waterless". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Requiring great effort
words.origin: Latin *arduus* high, steep, difficult; akin to Old Irish *ard* high. First known use: 1549.
examples: … a life of **arduous** toil. — A. C. Cole

words.definition: Of the colour silver or white
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *argentum* "silver, money," going back to Indo-European **h2 r̥ǵ-n̥t-o-* (whence also Old Irish *argat* "silver," Middle Welsh *aryant* "silver, money," Breton *arcʼhant,* Sanskrit *rajatáḥ* "shining white, silvery" [for **ṛjatáḥ*], Avestan* ərəzata* "silver," Armenian *arcatʻ*), derivative of **h2erǵ-, *h2r̥ǵ-* "bright, white" whence, with varying suffixation, Greek *árgyros* "silver," Tocharian B *ārkwi* "white," Sanskrit *árjunaḥ* "shining, white," Hittite *ḫarki-* "white, bright". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Silvery
words.origin: From *argent* + *-ine*. *Argent*: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *argentum* "silver, money," going back to Indo-European **h2 r̥ǵ-n̥t-o-* (whence also Old Irish *argat* "silver," Middle Welsh *aryant* "silver, money," Breton *arcʼhant,* Sanskrit *rajatáḥ* "shining white, silvery" [for **ṛjatáḥ*], Avestan* ərəzata* "silver," Armenian *arcatʻ*), derivative of **h2erǵ-, *h2r̥ǵ-* "bright, white" whence, with varying suffixation, Greek *árgyros* "silver," Tocharian B *ārkwi* "white," Sanskrit *árjunaḥ* "shining, white," Hittite *ḫarki-* "white, bright". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Copious but meaningless talk; wordy, contentious dispute over nothing
words.origin: Reduplication of Scots & English *argle*, alteration of *argue*. First known use: 1834.

words.definition: The jargon or slang of a particular group, often kept secret from outsiders
words.origin: From French *argot*. First known use: 1825.
examples: He has been bombarded by thousands of scathing messages—known as being "flamed" in the **argot** of cyberspace. — Peter H. Lewis

words.definition: Having little or no rain; dry, barren and lifeless
words.origin: Borrowed from French & Latin; French *aride,* going back to Middle French, borrowed from Latin *āridus, ārdus* "dry, waterless, withered, austere (of style)," derivative, with the adjective suffix *-idus,* of *ārēre* "to be dry, parched, withered," going back to Indo-European **h2eh1s-eh1-,* stative derivative of a verbal base **h2eh1s-* "make dry with heat," whence also Tocharian A *asatär* "(it) dries up," Tocharian B *osotär*; also from the same base a root noun **h2eh1s-,* whence Hittite *ḫāšš-* "ashes, dust," from which as thematic derivatives Sanskrit *ā́saḥ* "ashes, dust," and (as a collective or noun of appurtenance?) **h2eh1s-eh2-,* whence Latin *āra* "altar," Oscan *aasaí* (locative), Hittite *ḫāššā-* "hearth," Old High German *essa, esse* "forge" (from **asjō-*), Old Swedish *æsia, æssia* "smith's fire," Old Icelandic *esja* "soapstone (used in hearths)" (both from **asjōn-*). First known use: 1652.

words.definition: The art of dining
words.origin: From Greek *ariston* breakfast or lunch + *-logy*.

words.definition: An obsessive preoccupation with numbers, calculations and counting
words.origin: From Greek *arithmos* number + *mania*.

words.definition: Entitled to bear a heraldic coat of arms, as a family of the gentry
words.origin: Latin *armiger* "bearing arms, armed" + -ous. First known use: circa 1727.

words.definition: Strong in war, battle, contest
words.origin: From Latin *armipotens*, from *arma* arms + *potens* powerful.

words.definition: Love, compassion, empathy, warmth of feeling
words.origin: Māori, love, compassion.

words.definition: An ambitious newcomer, often one thought to be unscrupulous; a social climber
words.origin: Borrowed from French, from *arriver* "to reach a destination, achieve success" (going back to Old French *ariver* "to reach a destination by ship") + *-iste* -ist. First known use: 1895.

words.definition: A hidden motive or mental reservation
words.origin: French, literally rear thought.

words.definition: Clever trickery or skill
words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French & Middle French, "trade, craft, craftsmanship, contrivance," borrowed from Latin *artificium* "artistry, craftsmanship, craft, craftiness, cunning," from *artific-, artifex* "practitioner of an art, specialist, craftsman, creator" (from *art-, ars* "acquired skill, craftsmanship" + *-fic-, -fex,* agentive derivative of *facere* "to make, bring about, do") + *-ium,* denominal or deverbal suffix of function or state. First known use: 1540.
examples: … believing that characters had to be created from within rather than with **artifice**. — Garson Kanin
… revising the state's constitution through a series of legal stratagems and **artifices** … — W. Haywood Burns

words.definition: Without guile; sincere; simple
words.origin: Art + -less. First known use: 1586.

words.definition: Practising severe self-discipline and abstention
words.origin: Greek *askētikos*, literally, laborious, from *askētēs* one that exercises, hermit, from *askein* to work, exercise. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: To attribute to a particular cause or source
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *ascribere*, from *ad-* + *scribere* to write. First known use: 15th century.
examples: These poems are usually **ascribed** to Homer.
They **ascribe** most of their success to good timing and good luck.

words.definition: With suspicion or disapproval
words.origin: Probably a sense development (influenced by *asqwynt* "obliquely, askew," and phonetically similar words) of earlier and Middle English *askaunce, a-skans, a-skaunces* "in such a way that, as if, as if to say, artificially, deceptively," from *as-* as + Old French *quanses, canses* "as if, appearing as though," from *quanse-, canse-* (going back to Latin *quam sī* "as if") + *-s,* adverbial suffix. First known use: circa 1530.
examples: Many critics have **looked askance** at the proposal.

words.definition: A brush or perforated globe used to sprinkle holy water in a ceremony
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *aspergere*. First known use: 1649.

words.definition: Harshness of tone or manner; roughness of surface; severity of weather
words.origin: Middle English *asprete*, from Anglo-French *aspreté*, from *aspre* rough, from Latin *asper*, from Old Latin **absperos*, from *ab-* ab- + *-speros*; akin to Sanskrit *apasphura* repelling, Latin *spernere* to spurn. First known use: 13th century.
examples: He asked with some **asperity** just what they were implying.
… whether hearing herself described as a 'lovely woman' softened the **asperity** of her grief … — Charles Dickens

words.definition: A damaging accusation: slander
examples: The **aspersion** of the congregation before Mass

words.definition: An immortal flower said to grow in the Elysian fields
words.origin: Latin *asphodelus*, from Greek *asphodelos*. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: To test the purity or quality of a metal; to attempt or try something difficult
examples: **Assayed** the gold to determine its purity
**Assay** the results of the new changes

words.definition: Showing great care and perseverance
words.origin: Latin *assiduus*, from *assidēre* to sit beside. First known use: circa 1552.
examples: She tended her garden with **assiduous** attention.

words.definition: The echoing of vowel sounds in nearby words, as in "a hot pot of rot"
words.origin: French, from Latin *assonare* to answer with the same sound, from *ad-* + *sonare* to sound, from *sonus* sound. First known use: 1727.

words.definition: To ease or soothe a feeling
words.origin: Middle English *aswagen,* borrowed from Anglo-French *asuager* (continental Old French *assuagier*), going back to Vulgar Latin **assūaviāre,* from Latin *ad-* -ad- + Vulgar Latin **-sūaviāre,* derivative of Latin *sūavis* "agreeable to the senses, sweet, pleasant". First known use: 14th century.
examples: No explanation or rationale could **assuage** our shock, pain and grief. — Ian T. Douglas

words.definition: An exclamation introducing a speech, as in "Behold!"
words.origin: Greek, a marking with a star, from *astēr* star.

words.definition: Severe and incisive in criticism; tending to shrink skin and stop bleeding
words.origin: Probably from Middle French, from Latin *astringent-, astringens*, present participle of *astringere* to bind fast, from *ad-* + *stringere* to bind tight. First known use: circa 1541.

words.definition: Shrewd and quick to see what matters
words.origin: Latin *astutus*, from *astus* craft. First known use: 1565.
examples: … a very **astute** move to increase … chances of re-election … — Bryce Edwards

words.definition: Leaving out conjunctions, as "I came, I saw, I conquered"
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek, from neuter of *asyndetos* unconnected, from *a-* + *syndetos* bound together, from *syndein* to bind together, from *syn-* + *dein* to bind. First known use: 1555.

words.definition: A state of serene calm, free from worry
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Greek; Middle French *ataraxie,* borrowed from Greek *ataraxía,* from *atáraktos* "calm, unexcited" (from *a-* a-:2 + *taraktós,* verbal adjective of *tarássein,* (Attic) *taráttein* "to stir up, disturb, agitate mentally or emotionally") + *-ia* -y; *tarássein* going back to Indo-European **dhr̥h2gh-i̯é-,* zero grade ablaut derivative of **dhreh2gh-* "be stirred up, become turbulent," whence also Old Church Slavic raz*dražǫ,* raz*dražiti* "to provoke, make angry," Lithuanian *dérgiu, dérgti* "to make dirty, besmirch, defame". First known use: 1881.
examples: The highest goal of an Epicurean disciple was **ataraxia**—tranquility of mind. — Erich Segal

words.definition: Reverting to something ancestral or primitive
words.origin: French *atavisme*, from Latin *atavus* ancestor, from *at-* (probably akin to *atta* daddy) + *avus* grandfather. First known use: 1833.

words.definition: The fear of not being good enough
words.origin: From Greek *atelēs* imperfect + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Procrastination; putting things off
words.origin: French, from *atermoyer* to put off.

words.definition: The fear of being forgotten or ignored
words.origin: A modern coinage, perhaps from Greek *athazagoria* forgetfulness + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Melancholy or ill-tempered; once thought caused by an excess of black bile
words.origin: Latin *atra bilis* black bile. First known use: 1651.

words.definition: A bore who buttonholes people with tedious, sad stories
words.origin: Italian, from *attaccare* to attach + *bottoni* buttons.

words.definition: A fragrant essential oil, especially one distilled from rose petals
words.origin: Persian *ʽaṭir* perfumed, from Arabic, from *ʽiṭr* perfume. First known use: 1790.

words.definition: To weaken or reduce in force
examples: … shows great skill in the use of language to moderate or **attenuate** the impact of awkward facts. — Bernard Lewis

words.definition: Regretting one's wrongdoing only because of the fear of punishment
words.origin: From Latin *attritus*, past participle of *atterere* to rub away.

words.definition: The fear of failure
words.origin: From Greek *atychēs* unlucky + *-phobia*.

words.definition: A song or poem greeting the dawn, or lovers parting at dawn
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from Old Occitan *aubada*, from *alba, auba* dawn, from Vulgar Latin **alba*, from Latin, feminine of *albus* white. First known use: circa 1678.

words.definition: Showing bold, daring disregard for risk
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *audacieux,* from *audace* "daring, recklessness" (borrowed from Latin *audācia,* from *audāc-, audāx* "daring, bold, excessively daring, reckless" + *-ia* -ia) + *-ieux* -ious; *audāx* from *audēre* "to intend, dare, venture" (verbal derivative of *avidus* "ardent, eager, greedy") + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance (probably going back to Indo-European **-eh2,* noun ending + **-k-,* suffixal formative). First known use: 1550.

words.definition: To portend a good or bad outcome
words.origin: Middle English *augurre, augure,* borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *augure,* borrowed from Latin *augur,* perhaps going back to **aug-u-s* "the increased, one who receives the signs of increase," noun derivative of an s-stem adjective **aug-u-s* "increased, grown," derivative of a u-stem adjective **aug-u-* with the same sense, derivative from the base of *augeō, augēre* "to increase, make greater, heighten". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A sign or omen of what will happen; the art of reading omens, as from birds
words.origin: Middle English *augurie,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *augorrye, augurrie,* borrowed from Latin *augurium* "divination by an augur, art of divination, omen, portent," from *augur* augur + *-ium,* suffix of function or state. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Ancient **augury** involved the interpretation of the flight patterns of birds.
"… the best **augury** of a man's success in his profession is that he thinks it the finest in the world." — George Eliot

words.definition: Golden or gold-coloured; elaborately ornamented, especially in literary style
words.origin: Middle English *aureat*, from Medieval Latin *aureatus* decorated with gold, from Latin *aureus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to golden hair
words.origin: From Latin *auricomus*, from *aurum* gold + *coma* hair.

words.definition: The dawn; a glowing display of light in polar skies
words.origin: From Latin *aurora*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The act of listening to sounds from the heart, lungs or other organs
words.origin: Latin *auscultation-, auscultatio* act of listening, from *auscultare* to listen; akin to Latin *auris* ear. First known use: 1820.

words.definition: Promising success; favourable
words.origin: Latin *auspicium* auspice + -ous. First known use: 1593.
examples: … a festival that takes place during the hottest months of spring, just before the monsoon rains, and that is considered an **auspicious** time for weddings. — Cynthia Gorney

In days of old, seers entered a trance state and then informed anxious seekers what kind of mood the gods were in, and whether this was an **auspicious** time to begin a journey, get married, or start a war. — Harvey Cox

words.definition: Severely plain and simple
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *austerus*, from Greek *austēros* harsh, severe; akin to Greek *hauos* dry. First known use: 14th century.
examples: An **austere**… figure too remote for love from his children. — Eileen Lockwood
**… austere** critics who decry sentimentality … — Fisun Güner

words.definition: Native to a place rather than introduced; formed where it is found, as a rock
words.origin: Autochthon + -ous. First known use: 1803.

words.definition: A self-taught person, especially one who has learned widely without schooling
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin & Greek; New Latin *autodidactus* "self-taught," borrowed from Greek *autodídaktos,* from *auto-* auto- + *didaktós* "taught, learned". First known use: 1784.

words.definition: Self-worship
words.origin: From Greek *autos* self + *latreia* worship.

words.definition: Having a purpose, motivation, or
words.origin: Greek *autotelḗs* "having an end in itself, having one's own authority, final, unconditional" (from *auto-* auto- + *-telēs,* adjective derivative of *télos* "fulfillment, completion, end") + -ic. First known use: 1864.

words.definition: An overstatement or hyperbole, especially when arranged in a sequence of increasing intensity
words.origin: Greek, increase, growth.

words.definition: Extreme greed for wealth
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *avaritia*, from *avarus* avaricious, from *avēre* to crave. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … an era of nearly unbridled **avarice** on Wall Street … — Matthew Campbell and Kit Chellel

words.definition: Keenly enthusiastic
words.origin: French or Latin; French *avide*, from Latin *avidus*, from *avēre* to desire, crave; akin to Welsh *ewyllys* desire, Old Irish *con-oí* he protects. First known use: 1769.

words.definition: A forcible tearing away; the sudden shift of land by flood or a river's change
Kind and friendly, like an uncle
words.origin: Latin *avunculus* maternal uncle. First known use: 1831.
examples: Jovial and **avuncular**, the President's chief of staff seems oblivious to the pressures that accompany what is arguably the second most powerful job in the land. — Craig Unger
Two weeks of poker had led to his writing to his uncle a distressed, but confident, request for more funds; and the **avuncular** foot had come down with a joyous bang. — P. G. Wodehouse

words.definition: Away from the appropriate, planned or expected course; askew or crooked
The emptiness felt after visitors leave
words.origin: Baining, a language of Papua New Guinea.

words.definition: A self-evident truth
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *axiome,* borrowed from Latin *axiōma* "fundamental proposition," borrowed from Greek *axíōma* "honour, honoured status, prestige, that which is reasonable (though not demonstrated to be true), self-evident principle," from *axiō-,* variant stem of *axióō, axioûn* "to consider worthy, value, consider appropriate, claim, think" (verbal derivative of *áxios* "valued [at a sum of money], worth, equal, of an equivalent status, worthy, suitable," of uncertain origin) + *-ma,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 15th century.
examples: One of the **axioms** of the theory of evolution
Cites the **axiom** "no one gives what he does not have"

words.definition: Bright blue, like a cloudless sky
words.origin: Middle English *asur*, from Anglo-French *azeure*, probably from Old Spanish, modification of Arabic *lāzaward*, from Persian *lāzhuward*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A face that begs to be slapped
words.origin: German, from *Backpfeife* slap + *Gesicht* face.

words.definition: Witty, playful conversation
words.origin: Borrowed from French, going back to Middle French, "foolishness, stupidity," from *badiner* "to banter, jest, play the fool" (verbal derivative of *badin* "silly, foolish," as noun, "fool, simpleton," borrowed from Occitan, from *badar* "to have the mouth wide open, gape"—going back to Vulgar Latin **batāre*, perhaps of imitative origin + *-in*, adjective suffix) + *-age* -age. First known use: circa 1658.

words.definition: Something of little value or importance; a trifle; a short, light piece of music
words.origin: French, from Italian *bagattella*. First known use: 1633.

words.definition: One's sphere of operations, knowledge or authority; a bailiff's district
words.origin: Middle English *baillifwik*, from *baillif* + *wik* dwelling place, village, from Old English *wīc*, from Latin *vicus* village. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … concerns at the spy agency that the Pentagon is intruding into its traditional **bailiwick**. — Scott Shane and Mark Mazzetti

words.definition: A kiss on the hand
words.origin: French, from *baiser* to kiss + *main* hand.

words.definition: A small sum given as a tip, alms or bribe, especially in parts of the East
words.origin: Persian *bakhshīsh*, from *bakhshīdan* to give; akin to Greek *phagein* to eat, Sanskrit *bhajati* he allots. First known use: 1686.

words.definition: Senseless talk or writing; nonsense; once a jumbled mix of liquors
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1674.

words.definition: Threatening harm; menacing
words.origin: Middle English *balefull* "(of humans or animals) bent upon mischief or destruction, malevolent, (of things) pernicious," also "wretched, miserable," going back to Old English *bealluful* "full of evil, sinful," from *bealu* bale + *-ful* -ful. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Clamor or uproar
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1868.

words.definition: A bathing place; a public bath or a spa resort with medicinal springs
words.origin: From Latin *balnearius*, from *balneum* bath.

words.definition: To dance clumsily but with relish
words.origin: Perhaps of Scandinavian origin; compare Danish *baltre* to romp.

words.definition: To deceive
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1703.
examples: I got **bamboozled** by the salesperson to buy a more expensive model.
A quarterback **bamboozled** by an unexpected defence

words.definition: Lacking originality; dull
