words.origin: Borrowed from French, "pertaining to a feudal lord's right to extract usage fees for mills, ovens, etc., within his jurisdiction, available for general use, ordinary, commonplace, trite," going back to Old French *bannel* "subject to a feudal lord's jurisdiction, of seigneurial authority," borrowed from Medieval Latin *bannālis, banālis* "ordered by a ban, invested with public authority," from *bannus, bannum* "order given by a public authority, authority, jurisdiction" (borrowed from Old Low Franconian **banna-* "call to arms by a lord") + Latin *-ālis* -al. First known use: 1825.
examples: The writing was **banal**, but the story was good.
We've all gotten mired in **banal** small talk at some point. — Sue Shellenbarger

words.definition: Merely practical or mechanical; mundane work done only for money
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *banausikós* "of an artisan, pedestrian, in bad taste" from *bánausos* "artisan, craftsman," as an adjective "of an artisan, vulgar" (of uncertain origin) + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 1845.
examples: … contempt for the **banausic** occupations. — T. S. Eliot
… such mundane and **banausic** considerations as comfort and durability … — G. B. Boyer

words.definition: To destroy, damage, defeat, injure
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1939.

words.definition: Loss of the ability to sense weight
words.origin: From Greek *baros* weight + *a-* + *gnōsis* knowledge.

words.definition: A blessing or spiritual power passed from a holy person
words.origin: Arabic *baraka* blessing.

words.definition: Having a small or sparse beard
words.origin: From Latin *barbatulus*, diminutive of *barbatus* bearded.

words.definition: The outer fortification of a castle or town, especially a gate tower
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *barbecane*, from Medieval Latin *barbacana*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Excessive admiration of William Shakespeare
words.origin: *Bard* (*of Avon*), epithet of Shakespeare + *-o-* + *-later*. First known use: 1903.

words.definition: Offering only the illusion of plenty, as the imaginary feast in the Arabian Nights
words.origin: *Barmecide*, a wealthy Persian, who, in a tale of *The Arabian Nights' Entertainments*, invited a beggar to a feast of imaginary food. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: One giving only the illusion of abundance or some benefits
words.origin: *Barmecide*, a wealthy Persian, who, in a tale of *The Arabian Nights' Entertainments*, invited a beggar to a feast of imaginary food. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: The vexatious stirring up of lawsuits; fraud or gross negligence by a ship's master
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *barratrie*, from Anglo-French **baraterie*, literally, deception, from Old French *barater* to be active, do business, cause strife, deceive, perhaps from Vulgar Latin **prattare*, from Greek *prattein, prassein* to do. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One's destined soulmate
words.origin: Yiddish, destined.

words.definition: The least prestigious variety of a language
words.origin: From *basi-* base + *-lect*, as in *dialect*.

words.definition: A punishment or torture of beating on the soles of the feet with a stick
words.origin: Spanish *bastonada*, from *bastón* stick, from Late Latin *bastum*. First known use: 1572.

words.definition: An abrupt, ludicrous drop from the lofty to the trivial
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *báthos* "depth," neuter s-stem derivative of *bathýs* "deep". First known use: 1727.

words.definition: A broadax used as a weapon of war
An old, worn-out shoe
words.origin: Scots, an old worn shoe; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A minor parish or church official who keeps order; a ceremonial university officer
words.origin: Middle English *bedel* messenger, from Old English *bydel*; akin to Old High German *butil* bailiff, Old English *bēodan* to command. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: Blissfully happy, as if blessed; showing serene, saintly joy
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *beātificus* "making happy," from *beātus* "happy, fortunate" (from past participle of *beāre* "to make happy, gladden, bless," perhaps, if going back to **dwe-jo-*, akin to *bonus* "good," going back to **dwe-nos*) + *-ficus* -fic. First known use: 1635.

words.definition: To dress up or decorate gaudily, in a vulgar or tasteless way
words.origin: Be- + dizen. First known use: 1661.

words.definition: An unfaithful spouse
words.origin: From *bed* + *swerver*; coined by Shakespeare in *The Winter's Tale*.

words.definition: To charm, often in a deceptive way
words.origin: Middle English *bigilen, beguilen*, from *bi-, be-* be- + *gile* guile or *gilen* "to deceive, cheat," borrowed from Old French *guiler*, derivative of *guile*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: **Beguiled** her classmates into doing the work for her

words.definition: An old woman, especially a malicious or ugly one; a hag; once, a grandmother
words.origin: Middle English *beldam* grandmother, from Anglo-French *bel* beautiful + Middle English *dam*. First known use: 1520.

words.definition: To give a false impression of
words.origin: Middle English *belien*, going back to Old English *belēogan*, from *be-* be- + *lēogan* "to lie". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: His manner and appearance **belie** his age.

words.definition: A golden age of peace and refinement
words.origin: French, beautiful era.

words.definition: A writer of literature valued for elegance of style, as essays or criticism
words.origin: *belles lettres*. First known use: 1801.

words.definition: Eager to fight
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *bellicosus*, from *bellicus* of war, from *bellum* war. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The leading sheep of a flock, with a bell; an indicator of trends to come
words.origin: Middle English *bellewether, belleweder* "castrated ram with a bell around his neck followed by the other sheep in a flock, leader," from *belle* bell + *wether, weder* wether. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A summer house, gallery or tower built to command a fine view
words.origin: Italian, literally, beautiful view. First known use: 1549.

words.definition: Well-meaning and kindly
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *benevolent-, benevolens*, from *bene* + *volent-, volens*, present participle of *velle* to wish. First known use: 15th century.
examples: In stark contrast to … gold-hoarding dragons of medieval Europe, Chinese dragons were perceived as **benevolent** creatures. — Catherine Duncan
In post-Civil War America, **benevolent** societies also found a foothold aiding people freed from slavery. — Ashawnta Jackson

words.definition: In a state of ignorance
examples: **Benighted** travellers … have seen his midnight candle glimmering. — W. B. Yeats
Spreading their message among these poor **benighted** people

words.definition: Kind and gracious
words.origin: *benign* + *-ant* (as in *malignant*). First known use: 1631.

words.definition: A blessing; a spoken prayer of benediction, as a benison upon the house
words.origin: Middle English *beneson*, from Anglo-French *beneiçon*, from Late Latin *benediction-, benedictio*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Relating to the lowest level of a sea or lake and the life on its floor
words.origin: *benthos*. First known use: 1902.

words.definition: To scold or criticize someone angrily and at length, as a sergeant berates recruits
examples: Being **berated** by her parents when she came home late

words.definition: Deprived of something; lonely and abandoned
examples: Both players are instantly **bereft** of their poise … — A. E. Wier
… the book is … completely **bereft** of an index.

words.definition: A grandfather's father: great-grandfather
words.origin: From Old French *besaiel* great-grandfather.

words.definition: To spatter with filth
words.origin: From *be-* + obsolete *scumber* to void dung.

words.definition: To damage the reputation of someone in the opinion of others; to soil
examples: High ideals were **besmirched** by cruelty and greed … — R. A. Newhall
Although the accusations against Normand were unsupported, her name was **besmirched**. — John Lahr

words.definition: To scatter things over a surface; to lie scattered across something
To be a sign or warning of something to come, as dark clouds betoken rain; to signify
The state of lying in the interval separating two conditions, qualities, extremes
words.origin: From *between* + *-ity*.

words.definition: A hard mass found in the stomach of some animals, once prized as a poison antidote
words.origin: Middle French, from Medieval Latin, from Arabic dialect *bezuwār*, from Arabic *bāzahr*, from Persian *pād-zahr*, from *pād* protecting (against) + *zahr* poison. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: To eat or drink noisily. verb intr
words.origin: Imitative, perhaps from Latin *bibere* to drink.

words.definition: A small, decorative object valued for its beauty or rarity; a curio
words.origin: From French *bibelot*. First known use: 1873.

words.definition: People who read too much
words.origin: Coined by H. L. Mencken, from Greek *biblion* book + Latin *bibulus* drinking freely.

words.definition: One who destroys or mutilates books
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *klastēs* breaker.

words.definition: One who steals books
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *kleptēs* thief.

words.definition: One with extreme devotion to books
Excessive reverence for books or for the literal words of a sacred book
An obsessive passion for collecting books
words.origin: Borrowed from French *bibliomanie,* from *biblio-* biblio- + *-manie* -mania. First known use: 1734.

words.definition: A voracious reader; one who devours books as others devour meals
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *-phagos* eating.

words.definition: One who loves to read books; a bookworm
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *-phagos* eating.

words.definition: A lover or collector of books
words.origin: French, from *bibli-* + *-phile*. First known use: 1820.

words.definition: A bookseller, especially of rare works
words.origin: Latin *bibliopola* bookseller, from Greek *bibliopōlēs*, from *bibli-* + *pōlein* to sell. First known use: circa 1541.

words.definition: The pleasure of smelling a good book
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *osmē* smell.

words.definition: One who hoards books and keeps them locked away, as if burying them from others
words.origin: From Greek *biblion* book + *taphos* tomb.

words.definition: A librarian
words.origin: From *bibliotheca* + *-ry*. *Bibliotheca*: Latin, from Greek *bibliothēkē*, from *bibli-* + *thēkē* case; akin to Greek *tithenai* to put, place.

words.definition: The use of reading to support healing
Excessively fond of drinking alcohol; absorbent, as blotting paper
words.origin: Latin *bibulus*, from *bibere* to drink. First known use: 1675.

words.definition: A novel about a young person's growth into adulthood
words.origin: German, from *Bildung* education + *Roman* novel. First known use: 1906.

words.definition: Bad-tempered; also, sickly in colour
words.origin: Middle French *bilieux*, from Latin *biliosus*, from *bilis*. First known use: 1541.
examples: With clapboards painted red and **bilious** yellow — Sinclair Lewis

words.definition: To cheat or defraud, especially by evading payment; to elude or thwart
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of balk. First known use: 1641.
examples: **Bilking** investors out of their life savings
The Tampa couple sent out phony sonograms and **bilked** money from couples wanting children, authorities say. — Brady Dennis

words.definition: A love letter, especially a playful or sentimental one, from the French sweet note
words.origin: French *billet doux*, literally, sweet letter. First known use: 1673.

words.definition: Relating to two seas
words.origin: From Latin *bi-* two + *mare* sea.

words.definition: Relating to the leap year or the extra day in a leap year
words.origin: From Latin *bisextilis*, from *bisextus* the leap day.

words.definition: A temporary encampment, in the open air, typically without tents or cover
words.origin: French, from Low German *biwacht*, from *bi* by + *wacht* guard. First known use: 1811.

words.definition: A scoundrel
words.origin: Black + guard. First known use: 1535.

words.definition: Flattering, smooth or ingratiating speech, meant to soothe or win someone over
words.origin: From Latin *blandus* flattering + *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: Flattery meant to persuade
words.origin: Blandish + -ment, probably after Anglo-French *blandisement, blaundissement* and continental Old & Middle French *blandissement*. First known use: circa 1553.
examples: … refuses to yield to their **blandishments** … — Irving Babbitt

words.definition: A person who talks at great length without making much sense; nonsense
words.origin: Scots, alteration of *blather skate*, from *blather, blether* blather + *skate* a contemptible person. First known use: circa 1650.

words.definition: A babbler
words.origin: From Latin *blatero* babbler, from *blaterare* to babble.

words.definition: A coat of arms
words.origin: Middle English *blason*, from Anglo-French. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An idle, talkative person
words.origin: Scots, an idle, talkative man; used by Robert Burns.

words.definition: To flinch or shy away suddenly out of fear or pain; to turn pale
words.origin: Middle English *blenchen* "to move suddenly or sharply, flinch, change direction, evade, mislead" (also "to shine, gleam"), going back to Old English *blencan* "to deceive, cheat" (attested once), probably going back to Germanic **blankjan-* (whence also Old Icelandic *blekkja* "to impose upon"), causative derivative from **blanka-* "bright". First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Cheerfully carefree, sometimes too much so
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *blīthe*; akin to Old High German *blīdi* joyous. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: A **blithe** disregard for the rights of others

words.definition: To talk at length in a pompous and boastful way, especially in politics
words.origin: Perhaps irregular from blow. First known use: 1845.

words.definition: The deep blue twilight just before sunrise or after sunset
words.origin: From French *l'heure bleue*.

words.definition: Excellent, admirable or attractive; audaciously bold or remarkable
words.origin: Probably blend of *bold* and *audacious*. First known use: 1845.

words.definition: A thick, blunt needle for drawing tape through a hem; a small dagger
words.origin: Middle English *bodekin*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A person engaged in scientific or technical research, often with eccentricity
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1942.

words.definition: The soft, pleasing blur of an out-of-focus background in a photograph
words.origin: Borrowed from Japanese *boke* "blur, haziness". First known use: 1997.

words.definition: Gazing vacantly into the distance, thinking of nothing
words.origin: Japanese, from *boke* absent-mindedness.

words.definition: To support or strengthen
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English; akin to Old English *belg* bag. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A place of escape, hiding or seclusion
Pompous, inflated language
words.origin: Earlier, "cotton or other material used as padding or stuffing," extension (with parasitic *t*) of *bombace, bombage,* going back to Middle English *bombace,* borrowed from Anglo-French *bombés, bombace,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *bambac-, bambax, bombax* (also *banbax, bonbax*) "cotton plant, cotton fibre or wadding," borrowed from Middle Greek *bámbax, pámbax,* going back to a Greek stem *pambak-* (as in *pambakís* "item of clothing, probably of cotton"), probably borrowed from Middle Persian *pambak* "cotton" (or from an unknown source from which both words were borrowed). First known use: 1577.

words.definition: A twilled dress fabric of silk and worsted, once worn in mourning
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *bombasine, bombazine* "cotton fabric, fabric with a cotton weft and another material as warp" (Old French *drap bombasin* "cotton cloth"), borrowed from Upper Italian (Lombardy) *bombasina,* corresponding to Tuscan *bambagino,* derivative (with *-ino, -ina* -ine) of *bambagia, bambagio* "cotton" (borrowed from Middle Greek *bambákion,* derivative of *bámbax, pámbax* "cotton"), probably conflated with Latin *bombȳcinus* "of silk" (Medieval Latin, "of cotton," as neuter noun, "cotton"), pseudo-Greek derivative (with *-inos* -ine) of *bombyc-, bombyx* "silkworm, silk," borrowed from Greek **bómbyx,* presumed on the basis of *bombýkion* "cocoon of a kind of moth, probably *Pachypasa otus,*" of uncertain origin. First known use: 1572.

words.definition: To buzz or hum, as a bee or insect does on a summer day; to drone on
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *bombinātus,* past participle of *bombināre,* word of uncertain meaning formed from the base of Latin *bombīre* or *bombilāre* "to buzz, hum" (in New Latin taken to be synonymous with these words), derivatives of *bombus* "buzzing, humming," borrowed from Greek *bómbos*. First known use: 1748.

words.definition: A person who enjoys good food, drink and company
words.origin: French, literally, good liver. First known use: 1674.
examples: … eating and drinking and generally plunging himself into the life of a **bon vivant** … — Raymond Sokolov

words.definition: A piece of banal religious art, devotional object, ornament
words.origin: French, from *bon Dieu* good God.

words.definition: Cheerful friendliness
words.origin: French *bonhomie*, from *bonhomme* good-natured man, from *bon* good + *homme* man. First known use: 1777.
examples: … exuded an aura of cheerful **bonhomie**. — Alistair MacLean

words.definition: Ignorant or uncultured people regarded as a class
words.origin: Blend of boob and *bourgeoisie*. First known use: 1921.

words.definition: An illegal payment, as in graft
words.origin: Borrowed from Dutch *boedel* "personal estate, goods and chattels, large quantity (now usually *boel* in this sense)," going back to Middle Dutch *bōdel* "wealth, inheritance, bride's possessions," going back to Germanic **boþla-* "residence, property" (whence also Old English *boðl, botl, bold* "dwelling, house, hall," Old Frisian *bōdel, bōdil, bōl* "movable property, inheritance," Old Saxon *bodal* "dwelling, estate," Old Icelandic *ból* "farm, abode"), from **bō-/*bū-* "live, dwell" + **-þla-,* suffix of instruments (going back to Indo-European **-tlo-*). First known use: 1625.

words.definition: An imaginary or elusive goal whose pursuit may lead to ruin
words.origin: Perhaps from *boojum*, an imaginary creature in *The Hunting of the Snark* by Lewis Carroll; from its grotesque appearance. First known use: 1951.

words.definition: Devoted to reading; studious
words.origin: From *book* + *-ish*. *Book*: Middle English, from Old English *bōc*; akin to Old High German *buoh* book, Goth *boka* letter. First known use: 1542.

words.definition: Work or activity that wastes time and money, especially at public expense
words.origin: Coined by Robert H. Link †1957 American scoutmaster. First known use: 1928.
examples: The project is a complete **boondoggle**—over budget, behind schedule, and unnecessary.

words.definition: Rough and bad-mannered
words.origin: From *boor* + *-ish*. *Boor*: Dutch *boer*; akin to Old English *būan* to dwell. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: Having a stern, angry or sad expression
words.origin: From *boot* + *faced*, with a face as expressionless as leather.

words.definition: A sudden violent gust of wind, typically accompanied by rain, snow or sleet. Also known as a squall
words.origin: From Spanish *borrasca* storm.

words.definition: A rumbling or gurgling noise made by moving gas in the intestines
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *borborygmos*, from *borboryzein* to rumble. First known use: circa 1724.

words.definition: Northern; relating to the north, north wind, northern regions
words.origin: Middle English *boriall*, from Late Latin *borealis*, from Latin *boreas* north wind, north, from Greek, from *Boreas*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A mass of trees or shrubs; a thicket or thick foliage, as in a painted landscape
words.origin: Middle English *boskage,* borrowed from Anglo-French *boscage* "wood, woodland," from *bois, bos* "grove, forest, wood (the material)" (Old French also *bosc*) + *-age* -age. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A thicket or grove
words.origin: Borrowed from French, "grove, thicket," going back to Middle French, probably borrowed from Old Occitan, from *bosc* "forest, wood" (going back to Germanic **boska-, *buska-* "shrub, thicket") + *-et* -et. First known use: circa 1737.

words.definition: Covered with trees or bushes; wooded and shady, as a bosky dell
words.origin: *bosk, boske* "shrub, thicket" (going back to Middle English *bosk, boske, buske,* by-forms of *bussh, bosch*) + -y. First known use: circa 1616.

words.definition: A wealthy, fashionable man-about-town who frequents the boulevards
words.origin: French, from *boulevard*. First known use: 1870.

words.definition: A complete overturning or reversal, as of fortune or opinion; an upheaval or turmoil
words.origin: From French *bouleversement*. First known use: 1782.

words.definition: Obligatory; binding
words.origin: From Middle English *bounden*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An ill-bred, vulgar man
To remove material considered improper from a text
words.origin: Thomas *Bowdler* †1825 English editor. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: To quarrel noisily about trivial matters; a paltry squabble over nothing much
words.origin: Perhaps from Middle Dutch *brabbelen*, of imitative origin. First known use: 1568.

words.definition: To move by swinging from hand to hand along branches, as gibbons do
Boastful or arrogant behaviour; a braggart or empty boasting
words.origin: Brag or brag + Italian *-occhio,* noun suffix (going back to Vulgar Latin **-uculus,* diminutive suffix); after *Braggadocchio,* personification of boasting in *The Faerie Queene* (book 2, canto 3) by Edmund spenser. First known use: 1594.
examples: … doubts about his creative activities beset him from time to time and, paradoxically, led to frequent outbursts of **braggadocio**. — Bernard Denvir
… the air of swaggering **braggadocio** that all important men are expected to show in fighting … — C. W. M. Hart

words.definition: A noisy brawl or quarrel, as in a tavern; a drunken spree or bender
words.origin: Probably from the name *Brannigan*. First known use: 1892.

words.definition: Miscellaneous small ornaments and trinkets
words.origin: French *bric-à-brac*. First known use: 1830.

words.definition: Construction or creation from a diverse range of whatever things are at hand
words.origin: French, from *bricoler* to putter about. First known use: 1960.

words.definition: Gray or tawny with streaks or spots of a darker colour
words.origin: *brindle*, adjective. First known use: 1696.

words.definition: Vigour or vivacity of style or performance; spirited liveliness
words.origin: From Italian *brio*. First known use: 1731.

words.definition: Gigantic; enormous, as the giants of Brobdingnag in Gulliver's Travels
words.origin: *Brobdingnag*, imaginary land of giants in *Gulliver's Travels*, by Jonathan Swift. First known use: 1728.

words.definition: A low rumble like distant thunder, heard far off
words.origin: From Greek *brontē* thunder.

words.definition: A noisy, overexcited reaction or fuss
words.origin: From French *brouhaha*. First known use: 1890.

words.definition: To spread a report or rumour widely, as in it was bruited about town; a rumour
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, noise. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Fog or mist
words.origin: French, mist, winter, from Old Occitan *bruma*, from Latin, winter solstice, winter; akin to Latin *brevis* short. First known use: 1694.

words.definition: Cheap, showy or counterfeit; from the old dialect name for Birmingham
words.origin: Alteration of *Birmingham*, England, the source in the 17th century of counterfeit groats. First known use: 1679.
examples: … a bilious combination of **brummagem** melodrama and synthetic seascapes. — John McCarten

words.definition: Dark brown
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *brunneus* brown.

words.definition: Abrupt or offhand in speech or manner
words.origin: Borrowed from French, borrowed from Italian *brusco* "(of a person's manner) rough, rude, abrupt," also "(of wine, food) sharp, pungent," going back to a pre-Latin expressive base **brūsk-,* denoting prickliness, roughness. First known use: circa 1639.

words.definition: Habitual grinding or clenching of the teeth, often in sleep
words.origin: Irregular from Greek *brychein* to gnash the teeth + English *-ism*. First known use: 1932.

words.definition: Relating to the pleasant aspects of country life
words.origin: Latin *bucolicus*, from Greek *boukolikos*, from *boukolos* cowherd, from *bous* head of cattle + *-kolos* (akin to Latin *colere* to cultivate). First known use: circa 1609.

words.definition: Something lovely seen only in a fleeting moment
words.origin: A coinage listed on the Other-Wordly blog; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A cause of obsessive fear, irritation or loathing; an imaginary terror
A defensive wall; a person or thing acting as a defence or safeguard
words.origin: Middle English *bulwerke*, from Middle Dutch *bolwerc*, from *bolle* tree trunk + *werc* work. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Democratic principles that stand as a **bulwark** against tyranny

words.definition: An umbrella; a whimsical American coinage blending umbrella and parachute
words.origin: *bumber-* (alteration of *umbr-* in *umbrella*) + *-shoot* (alteration of *-chute* in *parachute*). First known use: 1876.
examples: A **bumbershoot** is exactly the same as an umbrella, but it's a much better word. The **bumber** bit is a variant of brolly, and the **shoot** is there because it looks a little bit like a parachute. — Mark Forsyth
… the sort of writer who won't say umbrella when he can say **bumbershoot**. — Malcolm Jones

words.definition: Fussy, petty officialdom
words.origin: From *Bumble*, the pompous beadle in Dickens's *Oliver Twist*.

words.definition: Useless or tedious printed information; paperwork; originally, toilet paper
words.origin: From *bumf* toilet paper, short for *bumfodder*, from bum + *fodder*. First known use: circa 1889.

words.definition: To confuse or fluster completely
words.origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps a fanciful alteration of *bamboozle*; an American and British dialect word.

words.definition: Irritatingly self-assertive
words.origin: Bump + *-tious* (as in *fractious*). First known use: 1801.

words.definition: An impostor
words.origin: From Wemba-wemba (Aboriginal Australian) *banib*.

words.definition: Making a gentle bubbling sound
words.origin: From Middle English *burble*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To grow or increase rapidly
words.origin: Middle English *burjonen*, from Anglo-French *burjuner*, from *burjun* bud, from Vulgar Latin **burrion-, burrio*, from Late Latin *burra* fluff, shaggy cloth. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … when the flame trees and jacaranda are **burgeoning** … — Alan Carmichael
The market has **burgeoned** in recent years.

words.definition: A citizen of a town or city, typically a member of the solid middle class
To polish by rubbing; to enhance or perfect an image or reputation
words.origin: Middle English *burnischen*, from Anglo-French *burniss-*, stem of *burnir*, alteration of Old French *brunir*, literally, to make brown, from *brun*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A thick-soled boot worn by ancient tragic actors; tragic drama itself
words.origin: Probably modification of Middle French *brozequin*. First known use: 1503.

words.definition: Excessively complicated and intricate
A secret group of plotters
words.origin: French *cabale* cabala, intrigue, cabal, from Medieval Latin *cabbala* cabala, from Late Hebrew *qabbālāh*, literally, received (lore). First known use: 1614.

words.definition: Giving inspiration
words.origin: From Latin *caballinus*, from *caballus* horse.

words.definition: A gem polished into a smooth dome rather than cut with facets
words.origin: Middle French, diminutive of Middle French dialect (Picard) *caboche* head. First known use: 1825.

words.definition: To laugh loudly and immoderately, often in a harsh or convulsive way
words.origin: Latin *cachinnatus*, past participle of *cachinnare*, of imitative origin. First known use: 1824.
examples: … **cachinnated** till his sides must have ached. — John Burroughs

words.definition: An evil spirit or demon, the opposite of a guardian spirit; a malevolent person
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *cacodaemōn* "calamitous," borrowed from Greek *kakodaímōn* "possessed by a malevolent spirit, ill-fated, (as noun) malevolent spirit," from *kako-* caco- + *daímōn* "personal spirit, bringing luck or ill, that accompanies an individual". First known use: 1538.

words.definition: An irresistible urge to do something unwise, as the itch to write or meddle
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *cacoēthes* "malignant tumor at an early stage, disease of character," borrowed from Greek *kakóēthes* "malignancy, wickedness," noun derivative from neuter of *kakoḗthēs* "ill-disposed, malicious, (of things) abominable, (of tumors, fevers, etc.) malignant," from *kako-* caco- + *-ēthēs,* adjective derivative of *êthos* "custom, disposition, character". First known use: circa 1587.

words.definition: Bad handwriting or incorrect spelling; poor writing of any kind
words.origin: Caco- + -graphy (in orthography), perhaps after French *cacographie*. First known use: 1574.

words.definition: Harsh-sounding
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *cacophōnus* (borrowed from Greek *kakóphōnos* "disagreeable-sounding," from *kako-* caco- + *-phōnos* "having a sound [of the kind specified]," adjective derivative of *phōnḗ* "sound made by something living, voice, speech") + -ous. First known use: 1782.
examples: Like an old battlefield, once **cacophonous** / with the clash of steel, the roar of cannon, / the screams of wounded and dying men … — Brian Moore

words.definition: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds
words.origin: Borrowed from French & New Latin; French *cacophonie,* going back to Middle French, borrowed from New Latin *cacophōnia,* borrowed from Greek *kakophōnía,* from *kakóphōnos* "disagreeable-sounding, cacophonous" + *-ia* -ia. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: Very pale, thin or bony, like a corpse; gaunt and deathly in appearance
words.origin: From *cadaver* + *-ous*. *Cadaver*: Latin, from *cadere* to fall. First known use: 1627.
examples: Grossly underweight, he appeared **cadaverous**, like a living skeleton

words.definition: The rise and fall of a voice or rhythm
words.origin: Middle English, “rhythm of prose or verse, rhetorical periods,” borrowed from Medieval Latin *cadentia* “rhythm in verse,” noun derivative (formally feminine singular from neuter plural) of Latin *cadent-, cadens,* present participle of *cadere* “to fall, sound rhythmically, end, terminate (of words or clauses)”. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Falling off early, as some leaves or petals do; transient and perishable
words.origin: Latin *cadūcus* “on the verge of collapsing, ready to fall (of fruit), transitory” (from *cadere* “to fall” + *-ūcus* “performing the action [of the verb specified]”) + -ous. First known use: 1775.

words.definition: Bluish or grayish green
words.origin: From Latin *caesius* bluish grey.

words.definition: Running one's fingers tenderly through a loved one's hair
words.origin: Brazilian Portuguese, from Kimbundu *kifunate* to twist.

words.definition: A circle of protection drawn around oneself
words.origin: Scottish Gaelic, a sanctuary or encircling.

words.definition: A contemptible or cowardly person; a base wretch, a word common in old romances
words.origin: Middle English *caitif*, from Anglo-French *caitif, chaitif* wretched, despicable, from Latin *captivus* captive. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To persuade by flattery or coaxing
words.origin: Borrowed from French *cajoler* "to give much attention to, make a fuss over, flatter, persuade with flattery," going back to Middle French *cajoller* "to flatter out of self-interest," perhaps the same verb as Middle French *cageoller* "to vocalize, sing (of a jay or other bird)," expressive formation of uncertain origin. First known use: 1630.

words.definition: A prison
words.origin: Spanish *calabozo* dungeon. First known use: 1792.

words.definition: Causing a sensation of warmth when applied; a warming remedy
words.origin: From Latin *calefaciens*, from *calere* to be warm + *facere* to make.

words.definition: A fever with delirium once suffered by sailors in the tropics; burning zeal
words.origin: Spanish *calentura*, from *calentar* to heat, from Latin *calent-, calens*, present participle of *calēre* to be warm. First known use: 1582.

words.definition: Having shapely, well-proportioned buttocks, as in a famous Greek statue
words.origin: Greek *kallipygos*, from *kalli-* + *pygē* buttocks. First known use: 1831.

words.definition: A noisy, boisterous parade with tin horns and pans; a mock serenade
words.origin: Back-formation from *callithumpian*, adjective, alteration of English dialect *gallithumpian* disturber of order at elections in 18th century. First known use: 1843.

words.definition: Showing a cruel disregard for others
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *callosus*, from *callum, callus* callous skin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Young and inexperienced
words.origin: Middle English *calu* bald, from Old English; akin to Old High German *kalo* bald, Old Church Slavic *golŭ* bare. First known use: 1580.

words.definition: A false statement made to damage someone's reputation
words.origin: Middle English *calumnye*, from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *calomnie*, from Latin *calumnia*, from *calvi* to deceive; perhaps akin to Old English *hōlian* to slander, Greek *kēlein* to beguile. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Denounced his opponent for his defamatory insinuations and **calumny**
He was the target of **calumny** for his unpopular beliefs.

words.definition: A small group of secret, scheming advisers to a ruler; a cabal
words.origin: Spanish, literally, small room. First known use: 1820.

words.definition: The common people, regarded with contempt; the rabble or mob
words.origin: French, from Italian *canaglia*, from *cane* dog, from Latin *canis*. First known use: 1588.

words.definition: A false or baseless rumour
words.origin: French, literally, duck; in sense 1, from Middle French *vendre des canards à moitié* to cheat, literally, to half-sell ducks. First known use: 1843.
examples: The report about a conspiracy proved to be a **canard**.
The widespread **canard** that every lawyer is dishonest

words.definition: Frank and truthful
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *candide* "brilliant, favourably disposed," borrowed from Latin *candidus* "bright, white, light-coloured, clear (of liquids), favourable, kind," adjective derivative corresponding to *candēre* "to shine, be white, gleam," going back to Indo-European **(s)kn̥d-C-,* zero-grade stative derivative of **(s)kend-* "shine/make shine," whence Latin *-cendere* in *accendere, incendere* "to set on fire, kindle"; in nominal derivatives Middle Welsh *cann* "white, shining," Middle Breton *cann* "full moon," Sanskrit *candráḥ, ścandráḥ* "bright, the moon". First known use: 1597.
examples: She was very **candid** about her past.
… a **candid** critic of the Police Department's accountability practices. — Steve Miletich

words.definition: Frankness and honesty
words.origin: Borrowed from French & Latin; French *candeur,* borrowed from Latin *candōr-, candor* "brightness, radiance, whiteness, disposition to think well (of)," noun derivative in *-ōr-* corresponding to *candēre* "to shine, be white," *candidus* "bright, white". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a rare moment of **candour** from a master of obfuscation … — Anthony Faiola

words.definition: Relating to the dog days
words.origin: Middle English *caniculer* of the star Sirius, from Late Latin *canicularis*, from Latin *Canicula* Sirius, diminutive of *canis*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: One who destroys good things
words.origin: From *canker* + *blossom*; used by Shakespeare.

words.definition: To kiss and cuddle amorously
words.origin: Perhaps from English dialect *canoodle*, noun, donkey, fool, foolish lover. First known use: 1859.
examples: … used to sit in the sun porch in the evening, among the geraniums and the begonias, whispering, holding hands, **canoodling**. — Edna O'Brien

words.definition: A person who loves dogs
words.origin: From Latin *canis* dog + Greek *-philos* loving.

words.definition: Melodious or resonant, as birdsong or a fine voice; pleasantly musical in sound
words.origin: Latin *canorus*, from *canor* melody, from *canere* to sing. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: Bad-tempered and argumentative
words.origin: Perhaps irregular from obsolete *contack* contention. First known use: circa 1736.
examples: … I have developed into a **cantankerous** old man who shouts at the television … — Bryan Forbes

words.definition: A hymn or chant forming part of a church service, taken from the Bible
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *canticulum*, diminutive of *canticum* song, from *cantus*, past participle of *canere*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: A long beam or projection fixed at only one end, supporting a balcony or bridge
words.origin: Perhaps from cant + *-i-* + *lever*. First known use: 1667.

words.definition: A magic spell
words.origin: Probably alteration of *caltrop*. First known use: 1719.

words.definition: Cheerful and lively
words.origin: Cant. First known use: 1719.

words.definition: Having a lot of space inside; roomy; wide-ranging in mind or scope
words.origin: Latin *capac-, capax* capacious, capable, from Latin *capere* to take. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: An ornamental covering spread over a horse's saddle; rich clothing or trappings
words.origin: Middle French *caparaçon*, from Old Spanish *caparazón*. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: To surrender; to give in
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *capitulātus,* past participle of *capitulāre* "to summarize point by point, stipulate in an agreement, censure in a conventual assembly," derivative of *capitulum* "heading or division of a document, chapter". First known use: 1596.
examples: The enemy was forced to **capitulate** unconditionally.
The company **capitulated** to the labour union to avoid a strike.

words.definition: Given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *capricieux,* borrowed from Italian *capriccioso,* from *capriccio* caprice + *-oso* -ous. First known use: 1588.
examples: … the belief … that we were mere pieces in the games of **capricious** gods. — Diane Weber Bederman
The **capricious** nature of the stock market

words.definition: An attempt to win favour or applause by flattery or artful appeal
words.origin: From Latin *captatio*, from *captare* to strive to seize.

words.definition: Inclined to find fault over trifles
words.origin: Middle English *capcious*, from Middle French or Latin; Middle French *captieux*, from Latin *captiosus*, from *captio* deception, verbal quibble, from *capere* to take. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A hard protective shell
words.origin: French, from Spanish *carapacho*. First known use: 1836.
examples: The **carapace** of reserve he built around himself … — M. M. Mintz

words.definition: To worry or trouble someone, as in carking cares; a burden of care or anxiety
words.origin: From Anglo-French *carkier* to load, burden.

words.definition: To drink plenty of alcohol and enjoy oneself with others noisily
words.origin: Middle French *carrousse*, from *carous*, adverb, all out (in *boire carous* to empty the cup), from German *gar aus*. First known use: 1559.

words.definition: A quibbling question; a pun or riddle
words.origin: A whimsical 17th-century coinage of unknown origin.

words.definition: A carved scroll-shaped ornament; an oval frame enclosing a pharaoh's name
words.origin: Middle French *cartouche*, from Italian *cartoccio*, from *carta*. First known use: circa 1611.

words.definition: Deep reddish-brown
words.origin: From Latin *castanea* chestnut.

words.definition: To reprimand severely
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *castīgātus,* past participle of *castīgāre* "to discipline for a fault or lapse, reprove, censure," perhaps from **casti-,* stem of **castis* "reprimand" (going back to Indo-European **ḱHs-ti-,* whence also Sanskrit *śiṣṭi-* "instruction") + **-ig-,* going back to Indo-European *-h2ǵ-,* zero-grade of **h2eǵ-* "drive, impel, lead". First known use: 1606.
examples: The judge **castigated** the lawyers for their lack of preparation.

words.definition: One who employs deceptive or excessively subtle reasoning, especially on moral issues
words.origin: Probably from Spanish *casuista*, from Latin *casus* fall, chance. First known use: 1609.

words.definition: Clever but unsound reasoning, especially about moral questions; sophistry
words.origin: From *casuist* + *-ry*. *Casuist*: Probably from Spanish *casuista*, from Latin *casus* fall, chance. First known use: 1712.

words.definition: The misuse of a word, or its strained use in a mixed or far-fetched metaphor
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *katachrēsis* misuse, from *katachrēsthai* to use up, misuse, from *kata-* + *chrēsthai* to use. First known use: 1550.

words.definition: A decorated wooden platform on which a coffin rests at a lying in state
words.origin: Italian *catafalco*, from Vulgar Latin **catafalicum* scaffold, from *cata-* + Latin *fala* siege tower. First known use: circa 1660.

words.definition: Kissing with the tongue
words.origin: From Greek *kataglōttisma*, from *glōtta* tongue.

words.definition: A wild cat, especially a cougar or lynx; a fierce, untamed person
words.origin: Short for *cat-a-mountain*. First known use: 1664.

words.definition: Excessive build-up of mucus in the nose or throat, as with a heavy cold
words.origin: Middle English *catarre*, from Middle French or Late Latin; Middle French *catarrhe*, from Late Latin *catarrhus*, from Greek *katarrhous*, from *katarrhein* to flow down, from *kata-* + *rhein* to flow. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Designed to sell quickly with little regard for quality; cheap and showy
The curve formed by a chain or cable hanging freely from two points
words.origin: New Latin *catenaria*, from Latin, feminine of *catenarius* of a chain, from *catena*. First known use: 1788.

words.definition: To make a shrill howling or wailing noise, like a cat in heat
words.origin: Middle English *caterwawen*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Release of strong emotion, bringing relief
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *katharsis*, from *kathairein* to cleanse, purge, from *katharos*. First known use: circa 1775.

words.definition: The concentration of mental or emotional energy on a person, idea or object
words.origin: New Latin (intended as translation of German *Besetzung*), from Greek *kathexis* holding, from *katechein* to hold fast, occupy, from *kata-* + *echein* to have, hold. First known use: 1922.

words.definition: A watery drink, especially weak tea or milk
words.origin: From *cat* + *lap*, a drink fit only for a cat.

words.definition: Askew; not lined up properly
words.origin: American dialect, perhaps from *cater* diagonally + a fanciful ending.

words.definition: Sarcastic in a scathing way
words.origin: Latin *causticus*, from Greek *kaustikos*, from *kaiein* to burn. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The chemical was so **caustic** that it ate through the pipe.

words.definition: To raise petty objections
words.origin: Latin *cavillari* to jest, cavil, from *cavilla* raillery; akin to Latin *calvi* to deceive. First known use: 1542.
examples: The author **caviled** about the design of the book's cover.
He **caviled** the conditions of the agreement.

words.definition: Trying to revive a dead love affair
words.origin: Italian, literally reheated cabbage.

words.definition: A social gathering, typically involving folk music, dancing and storytelling
words.origin: Irish *céilí* & Scottish Gaelic *cèilidh* visit, social evening, party with music and dancing, from Old Irish *céilide* visit, from *céile* servant, companion, neighbour; akin to Welsh *cilydd* companion, Old Breton *kiled*. First known use: 1875.

words.definition: Swiftness of movement
words.origin: Middle English *celerite*, borrowed from Anglo-French *celeritee*, borrowed from Latin *celeritāt-, celeritās* from *celer* "swift, speedy" + *-itāt-, -itās* -ity. First known use: 15th century.
examples: **Celerity** of movement is vital in war.

words.definition: A small group of writers, artists or thinkers; the room of the Last Supper
words.origin: Late Latin *cenaculum* the room where Christ and his disciples had the Last Supper, from Latin, top story, probably from *cena* dinner. First known use: 1855.

words.definition: A monument to someone buried elsewhere, especially to those fallen in war
words.origin: French *cénotaphe*, from Latin *cenotaphium*, from Greek *kenotaphion*, from *kenos* empty + *taphos* tomb. First known use: 1578.

words.definition: Formal, severe disapproval
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *censure*, borrowed from Latin *cēnsūa* "office of censor, assessment, moral oversight," from *cēnsēre* "to give as an opinion, perform the duties of a censor" + *-ūra* -ure. First known use: 1539.
examples: Unorthodox practices awaiting the **censure** of the city council
The country faces international **censure** for its alleged involvement in the assassination.

words.definition: Waxy
words.origin: From Latin *cera* wax.

words.definition: Intellectual rather than emotional
words.origin: French *cérébral*, from Latin *cerebrum* brain; akin to Old High German *hirni* brain, Greek *kara* head, *keras* horn, Sanskrit *śiras* head. First known use: 1801.

words.definition: The working of the brain; thinking
words.origin: Back-formation from *cerebration*, from *cerebrum*. First known use: 1915.

words.definition: Waxed cloth for wrapping a corpse; a burial garment or shroud
Drooping, nodding or bending forward
words.origin: From Latin *cernuus* facing earthward, stooping.

words.definition: Certainly
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French, going back to Vulgar Latin **certās*, feminine plural accusative (with adverbial value) of Latin *certus* "fixed, settled, indisputable". First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Deep blue like a clear summer sky; azure, a favourite of painters and poets
words.origin: Latin *caeruleus* dark blue. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: An oily, hypocritical person
words.origin: From Mr Chadband, a hypocritical preacher in Dickens's *Bleak House*.

words.definition: Annoyance at having failed or been humiliated
words.origin: French, from *chagrin* sad. First known use: 1661.

words.definition: A rooster, especially in fables and medieval tales; a crowing cock
words.origin: Middle English *Chantecleer*, rooster in verse narratives, from Old French *Chantecler*, rooster in the *Roman de Renart*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … now that that antisocial **chanticleer** has bitten the dust, the henhouse is as gentle and peaceful as a nunnery …
… to brag as lustily as **chanticleer** in the morning, standing on his roost, if only to wake my neighbours up. — Henry David Thoreau

words.definition: Dejected or dispirited, as if with a drooping jaw; crestfallen
An insult veiled as a joke
words.origin: From Greek *charientismos* gracefulness, from *charis* grace.

words.definition: A noisy mock serenade of pans and kettles for newlyweds; a cacophony
words.origin: French, perhaps from Late Latin *caribaria* headache, from Greek *karēbaria*, from *kara, karē* head + *barys* heavy. First known use: circa 1681.

words.definition: Cautiously wary
words.origin: Middle English *charri* "sorrowful, dear, cherished," going back to Old English *cearig* "troubled, troublesome, taking care," going back to Germanic **karaga-* (whence Old Saxon & Old High German *karag* "sorrowful"), from **karō* "sorrow, worry" + **-aga-,* by-form of **-iga-* -y. First known use: 15th century.
examples: A government **chary** of getting involved in foreign entanglements

words.definition: Having a changeable lustre or colour, like a cat's eye in the dark
words.origin: French, from present participle of *chatoyer* to shine like a cat's eyes. First known use: 1816.

words.definition: A summer gathering of lectures, concerts and plays for education and amusement
words.origin: *Chautauqua* Lake. First known use: 1884.

words.definition: The act of saving by using extremely frugal measures
Having the plump, rosy innocence of a cherub; angelic and childlike
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *cheroub*, from Hebrew *kĕrūbh*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An expedition, raid or campaign
words.origin: From Old French *chevauchée* a raid on horseback, from *cheval* horse.

words.definition: The treatment of light and shade in art; a striking contrast of light and dark
words.origin: Italian, from *chiaro* clear, light + *oscuro* obscure, dark. First known use: 1686.
examples: The artist uses **chiaroscuro** to create the perception of depth in a two-dimensional work.
A spotlight revealing a **chiaroscuro** of ridges and craters on a mountainside

words.definition: A reversal of grammatical structure in parallel phrases
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *chiasmos*, from *chiazein* to mark with a chi. First known use: 1871.

words.definition: Trickery or deception, especially in legal matters; a sharp double bend on a racetrack
words.origin: Borrowed from French *chicaner* "to dispute by means of quibbles, raise issues with minor points of law in order to complicate a judicial suit," going back to Middle French, "to sue, prosecute," perhaps a blend of the Gallo-Romance expressive base *čik-* expressing diminutiveness (as in Old Occitan *chic* "small," French *chiquet* "small piece") and *ricaner* "to snicker, laugh affectedly or contemptuously," going back to Middle French, "to bray," probably alteration (by association with *rire* "to laugh") of Old French (Norman) *recaner, rechaner* "to bray," from *re-* re- + *-caner,* derivative of *cane* "tooth," going back to Old Low Franconian **kinni-* "cheek," going back to Germanic **kinnu-*. First known use: circa 1671.

words.definition: Trickery used to deceive
words.origin: Borrowed from French *chicanerie* "quibbling on minor points of law brought up to complicate a judicial case," going back to Middle French *chiquanerie,* from *chicaner* "to dispute by means of quibbles," earlier "to sue, prosecute" + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 1589.
examples: He wasn't above using **chicanery** to win votes.

words.definition: A tall chest of drawers
words.origin: French *chiffonnier*, from *chiffon*. First known use: 1765.

words.definition: A group of a thousand things; a period of a thousand years; a millennium
words.origin: Late Latin *chiliad-, chilias*, from Greek, from *chilioi* thousand. First known use: 1598.

words.definition: An illusion or fanciful hope that can never be realized
words.origin: Latin *chimaera*, from Greek *chimaira* she-goat, chimera; akin to Old Norse *gymbr* yearling ewe, Greek *cheimōn* winter. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a fancy, a **chimera** in my brain, troubles me in my prayer. — John Donne

words.definition: Wildly fanciful; imaginary
words.origin: *chimera*. First known use: 1638.
examples: She's a **chimerical** optimist infused with utopian visions.

words.definition: To form something from parts that are very different
words.origin: From *chimera*, the monster of Greek myth.

words.definition: To cheer. verb intr.: To make a shrill noise
words.origin: Middle English *charken, chirken* to creak, chirp, from Old English *cearcian* to creak; akin to Old English *cracian* to crack. First known use: 1843.
examples: … play with her and **chirk** her up a little. — Harriet Beecher Stowe

words.definition: Handwriting, especially when regarded as an art or a field of study
Anger or irritability, once attributed to an excess of yellow bile
words.origin: Middle English *colre, colera, coler* "bile (either of the two humours), gastric upset thought to be caused by excess bile," borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French *colre, colere,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *colera, cholera* "cholera, acute gastroenteritis, bile (by association of the word with Greek *cholḗ* "gall, bile")," going back to Latin *cholera* "acute gastroenteritis," borrowed from Greek *choléra,* of uncertain origin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Bad-tempered or irritable
words.origin: Middle English *colerik* "of the humour bile, having excess bile," borrowed from Anglo-French *colerique,* borrowed from Late Latin *colericus, cholericus* "bilious," borrowed from Greek *cholerikós* "of cholera," from *choléra* cholera + *-ikos*. First known use: 1556.

words.definition: A literary style that describes objects rather than interpreting them
words.origin: French, from *chose* thing.

words.definition: A selection of passages from an author or language, used to aid learning
words.origin: New Latin *chrestomathia*, from Greek *chrēstomatheia*, from *chrēstos* useful + *manthanein* to learn. First known use: 1832.

words.definition: The hard case in which a caterpillar transforms; any stage of development
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *chrȳsallid-, chrȳsallis,* borrowed from Greek *chrȳsallid-, chrȳsallís,* from *chrȳsós* "gold" (referring to the metallic gold-like sheen of some butterfly pupae) + *-allid-, -allis,* noun suffix of some plant and animal names. First known use: 1601.
examples: … a budding writer could not emerge from his **chrysalis** too soon. — William DuBois

words.definition: Rule by the wealthy
words.origin: From Greek *chrysos* gold + *-kratia* rule.

words.definition: Relating to or inhabiting the underworld, as gods and spirits of the earth
words.origin: Greek *chthon-, chthōn* earth. First known use: 1882.

words.definition: Rude in a mean-spirited way
words.origin: Middle English *cherlyssh* "of churls, rustic, uncouth," going back to Old English *ceorlisc, cyrlisc,* from *ceorl* "male person, countryman, member of the lowest class of free men" + *-isc* -ish. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: He didn't like the **churlish** tone in his voice. — Margaret Truman
Outrage is among your more **churlish** emotions — Robert Goldsborough

words.definition: , also chutzpa Shameless boldness; brazen nerve; gall
words.origin: Yiddish *khutspe*, from Late Hebrew *ḥuṣpāh*. First known use: 1867.
examples: It took a lot of **chutzpah** to stand up to him the way she did.

words.definition: The scar left by a healed wound; a mark left on a stem where a leaf has fallen
words.origin: From Latin *cicatrix* scar.

words.definition: To heal by forming a scar
A guide who gives information about antiquities and places of interest
words.origin: Italian, from *Cicerone* Cicero. First known use: 1726.

words.definition: To tame; to reclaim from wildness
words.origin: From Latin *cicurare* to tame, from *cicur* tame.

words.definition: Roundabout and indirect
words.origin: Perhaps from Medieval Latin *circuitosus*, from Latin *circuitus*. First known use: 1664.
examples: His **circuitous** form of logic was mind-boggling.

words.definition: To walk all the way around something, especially a sacred place, as a rite
words.origin: Late Latin *circumambulatus*, past participle of *circumambulare*, from Latin *circum-* + *ambulare* to walk. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: Using many words where few would do
words.origin: Middle English *circumlocucyon*, from Latin *circumlocution-, circumlocutio*, from *circum-* + *locutio* speech, from *loqui* to speak. First known use: circa 1518.

words.definition: Wary and unwilling to take risks; carefully considering all circumstances
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French or Latin; Middle French *circonspect*, from Latin *circumspectus*, from past participle of *circumspicere* to look around, be cautious, from *circum-* + *specere* to look. First known use: 15th century.
examples: They are **circumspect** in all their business dealings.

words.definition: To surround with a rampart or trench, as a besieging army does; enclosed by a ridge
words.origin: Latin *circumvallatus*, past participle of *circumvallare* to surround with siege works, from *circum-* + *vallum* rampart. First known use: circa 1798.

words.definition: A wispy, feathery cloud high in the sky
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, curl. First known use: 1708.

words.definition: Able to perceive things beyond the senses
words.origin: French, from *clair* clear (from Latin *clarus*) + *voyant*, present participle of *voir* to see, from Latin *vidēre*. First known use: 1844.

words.definition: Loud
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *clāmant-, clāmans,* present participle of *clāmāre* "to shout, utter a loud cry". First known use: 1639.

words.definition: Loud and noisy; insistently demanding
words.origin: Middle English *clamourus, clamorous,* from *clamour* clamour + *-ous, -us* -ous. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A loud and confused noise, especially of protest
words.origin: Middle English *clamour,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *clamur, clamour,* borrowed from Latin *clāmor,* from *clāmāre* "to shout, utter a loud cry" + *-or* -or. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Kept secret or done secretively
words.origin: Middle French or Latin; Middle French *clandestin*, from Latin *clandestinus*, from *clam* secretly; akin to Latin *celare* to hide. First known use: circa 1528.

words.definition: A group of people hired to applaud or heckle a performer; a band of flatterers
words.origin: French, from *claquer* to clap, of imitative origin. First known use: 1848.

words.definition: Loud and clear, like a medieval trumpet; a stirring call to action
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French & Medieval Latin; Middle French *clairon*, from Medieval Latin *clarion-, clario*, from Latin *clarus*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An ancient water clock that measured time by the flow of water
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *klepsydra*, from *kleptein* to steal + *hydōr* water. First known use: 1580.

words.definition: Learned or literary people regarded as a class; the intelligentsia
words.origin: German *Klerisei* clergy, from Medieval Latin *clericia*, from Late Latin *clericus* cleric. First known use: circa 1818.

words.definition: A critical period or turning point in life; the onset of menopause
words.origin: Latin *climactericus*, from Greek *klimaktērikos*, from *klimaktēr* critical point, literally, rung of a ladder, from *klimak-, klimax* ladder. First known use: 1582.

words.definition: An excessive desire to stay in bed
words.origin: From Greek *klinē* bed + *mania*.

words.definition: Glittering with gold or silver; tinselly finery or imitation gold leaf
words.origin: Middle French, from present participle of *clinquer* to glitter, literally, to clink, of imitative origin. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: A sewer or cesspool; a place of moral filth; a single body cavity in birds
words.origin: Latin; akin to Greek *klyzein* to wash. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: A clumsy, awkward or boorish person, especially a country one; a large, heavy shoe
Sickeningly sweet or sentimental
words.origin: From *cloy* + *-ing*. *Cloy*: Middle English, to hinder, lame, alteration of *acloyen* to harm, maim, modification of Anglo-French *encloer* to nail, prick a horse with a nail in shoeing, from Medieval Latin *inclavare*, from Latin *in* + *clavus* nail. First known use: 1594.
examples: Her coyness grows **cloying** after a while … — Elysa Gardner

words.definition: A miser
words.origin: From *clutch* + *fist*.

words.definition: To come together to form one whole
words.origin: Latin *coalescere*, from *co-* + *alescere* to grow. First known use: circa 1541.
examples: … separate townships have **coalesced** into a single, sprawling colony … — Donald Gould

words.definition: Rough in texture; crude or vulgar in manner
words.origin: Middle English *cors*, perhaps from *course*, noun. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Of what **coarse** metal ye are molded … — Shakespeare

words.definition: An imaginary land of great luxury, idleness and plenty, where roast geese fly about
words.origin: Middle English *cokaygne*, from Middle French (*pais de*) *cocaigne* land of plenty. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A self-important little man, strutting like a bantam rooster; boastful talk
words.origin: Probably modification of obsolete Dutch dialect *kockeloeren* to crow, of imitative origin. First known use: circa 1798.

words.definition: Ridiculous, implausible or absurd, as a cockamamie scheme; muddled and nonsensical
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of *decalcomania*. First known use: 1962.
examples: Of all the **cockamamy** excuses I ever heard — Leo Rosten

words.definition: Dawn; the time when the cock first crows, at the very start of the day
A small loft just below the roof
words.origin: Probably from cock. First known use: circa 1580.

words.definition: A vain, silly fop
An elderly man, especially one who is eccentric or crotchety
words.origin: Probably alteration of *cadger*. First known use: circa 1738.

words.definition: Nonsense; foolish talk or ideas, said with blunt British dismissiveness
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1959.
examples: The notion that Scott was waylaid by bad luck is "a lot of **codswallop**," said Roland Huntford, a British historian. — Kenneth Chang
"Some say he died. **Codswallop**, in my opinion …" — J. K. Rowling

words.definition: Having the same age, date of origin or period; a contemporary
words.origin: Late Latin *coaevus* "of the same age" (from Latin *co-* co- + *-aevus,* adjective derivative of *aevus, aevum* "time as the medium in which events occur, age, lifetime") + -al. First known use: 1645.

words.definition: Clear, logical and convincing
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *cōgent-, cōgens,* present participle of *cōgere* "to drive together, gather, compress, force, compel," from *co-,* variant before a vowel and *h* of *com-* com- + *agere* "to drive (cattle), be in motion, do". First known use: 1659.

words.definition: To think deeply about something; to meditate or ponder at length
words.origin: Latin *cogitatus*, past participle of *cogitare* to think, think about, from *co-* + *agitare* to drive, agitate. First known use: 1582.
examples: **Cogitating** the possible consequences of my decision

words.definition: Deep, careful thought
words.origin: From *cogitate* + *-ion*. *Cogitate*: Latin *cogitatus*, past participle of *cogitare* to think, think about, from *co-* + *agitare* to drive, agitate. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Having knowledge or awareness
words.origin: Cogniz(ance) + -ant. First known use: 1820.
examples: … they should have been a little more **cognizant** of what the airport's needs would be. — Tom Gougeon, quoted in *The Denver Post*

words.definition: People with expert knowledge in a field
words.origin: Borrowed from Italian (now spelled *conoscente*), from *cognoscente, conoscente* adjective, "knowing," from present participle of *cognoscere, conoscere* "to know, have knowledge of," going back to Latin *cognōscere* "to get to know, acquire knowledge of". First known use: 1776.

words.definition: A close-fitting cap covering the top, back and sides of the head; a hairstyle
words.origin: Middle English *coife*, borrowed from Anglo-French, going back to early Medieval Latin *cofea, cuphia*, of uncertain origin. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … wore her hair teased into a dramatic **coif**. — Lawrence Wright

words.definition: To confer in secret; to conspire
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: A formal conversation or dialogue
words.origin: Middle English *colloquie* "discourse," borrowed from Latin *colloquium* "talk, conversation, conference, discussion," from *colloquor, colloquī* "to talk, converse, discuss" (from *col-* col- + *loquī* "to talk, speak") + *-ium,* suffix of deverbal compounds. First known use: 15th century.
examples: A **colloquy** between the trial judge and defendant

words.definition: Stomach pain or queasiness, especially from nervousness or fear
words.origin: Perhaps by folk etymology from New Latin *cholera morbus*, literally, the disease cholera. First known use: circa 1823.

words.definition: A publisher's emblem; a note at the end of a book giving details of its making
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *kolophōn* summit, finishing touch; perhaps akin to Latin *culmen* top. First known use: 1733.

words.definition: A peddler of books, especially one who distributes religious tracts
words.origin: French, alteration of Middle French *comporteur*, from *comporter* to bear, peddle. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: Pleasant to look at; attractive
words.origin: Middle English *comly*, alteration of Old English *cȳmlic* glorious, from *cȳme* lively, fine; akin to Old High German *kūmig* weak. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Going in with him, they observed that all was neat and **comely** … — Willa Cather

words.definition: An item of food, usually in the plural, as in a shop's comestibles; edible
words.origin: Medieval Latin *comestibilis*, from Latin *comestus*, past participle of *comedere* to eat, from *com-* + *edere* to eat. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Courtesy and considerate behaviour toward others
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *cōmitāt-, cōmitās* "friendliness, courtesy, graciousness," from *cōmis* "kind, obliging, gracious" (probably going back to Old Latin *cosmis,* of uncertain origin) + *-itāt- -itās* -ity. First known use: 1543.

words.definition: Improvised Italian comedy with stock characters
words.origin: Italian, literally, comedy of art. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: In proportion to; corresponding in size or degree
words.origin: Late Latin *commensuratus*, from Latin *com-* + Late Latin *mensuratus*, past participle of *mensurare* to measure, from Latin *mensura* measure. First known use: 1641.
examples: Was given a job **commensurate** with her abilities
Lived a life **commensurate** with the early years of the republic

words.definition: Threatening punishment or vengeance, as a comminatory sermon; denunciatory
words.origin: Middle English *comminacion* "threat of punishment or vengeance," borrowed from Anglo-French *comminacioun,* borrowed from Latin *comminātiōn-, comminātiō* "act of threatening or menacing," from *comminor, comminārī* "to make a threat of, threaten" (from *com-* com- + *minor, minārī* "to threaten") + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To be moved to tears by something touching
words.origin: Italian, from Latin *commovere* to move deeply.

words.definition: Containing or presenting the essential facts in a full yet concise way
words.origin: Middle English *compendious, compendiose,* borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *compendieux,* borrowed from Latin *compendiōsus* "advantageous, short (of a route), both comprehensive and succinct," from *compendium* "profit, short cut, abridgement, summary" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Smugly satisfied, unaware of danger
words.origin: Latin *complacent-, complacens*, present participle of *complacēre* to please greatly, from *com-* + *placēre* to please. First known use: 1767.
examples: The American people, so **complacent** up to then, suddenly buzzed with wild rumours. — Evan Thomas
… it is perhaps the most **complacent**, satisfied, petit bourgeois nation in Europe, if not on earth. — Robert D. Kaplan

words.definition: Willing to please others or accept their behaviour without protest; obliging
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from present participle of *complaire* to gratify, acquiesce, from Latin *complacēre*. First known use: 1638.

words.definition: Able to coexist with something else without contradiction; compatible
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *compossibilis*, from *com-* together + *possibilis* possible.

words.definition: A feeling of guilt that prevents wrongdoing
words.origin: Middle English *compunccioun*, from Anglo-French *compunction*, from Late Latin *compunction-, compunctio*, from Latin *compungere* to prick hard, sting, from *com-* + *pungere* to prick. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … showed no **compunction** in planning devilish engines of … destruction. — Havelock Ellis
… he had no **compunction** about brushing aside legal technicalities. — Robert Penn Warren

words.definition: To link together in a chain or series, as events or computer strings; connected like links
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *concatenatus*, past participle of *concatenare* to link together, from Latin *com-* + *catena* chain. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Meant to placate or win over
examples: But while the conference call might have been seen as a **conciliatory** gesture, an olive branch to his critics after weeks of bitter back-and-forth, the meeting seemed anything but. — Colin Deppen

words.definition: Skilful and harmonious arrangement of parts, especially in literary style
words.origin: Latin *concinnitas*, from *concinnus* skillfully put together. First known use: 1531.

words.definition: Naturally accompanying or associated
words.origin: Latin *concomitant-, concomitans*, present participle of *concomitari* to accompany, from *com-* + *comitari* to accompany, from *comit-, comes* companion. First known use: 1607.

words.definition: Strong desire, especially sexual desire; ardent longing for worldly things
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *concupiscentia*, from Latin *concupiscent-, concupiscens*, present participle of *concupiscere* to desire ardently, from *com-* + *cupere* to desire. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Fitting and deserved, especially of punishment; well merited
words.origin: Middle English *condigne*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *condignus*, from *com-* + *dignus* worthy. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To converse informally; to fabricate memories unknowingly to fill gaps
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *confābulātus,* past participle of *confābulārī* "to talk together, converse," from *con-* con- + *fābulārī* "to talk, converse, invent a story, make up a fable," derivative of *fābula* "talk, gossip, tale, legend"; (sense 3) translation of German *konfabulieren*. First known use: circa 1604.
examples: A major characteristic of brain-damaged patients is the tendency to **confabulate**—to hide and dissemble about their damage. — Peter R. Breggin

words.definition: A large, destructive fire
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *conflagrātiōn-, conflagrātiō,* from *conflagrāre* "to be destroyed by fire, be burnt down" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 1600.
examples: The **conflagration** between the two countries lasted for ten years.

words.definition: To combine two things into one, often wrongly
words.origin: Latin *conflatus*, past participle of *conflare* to blow together, fuse, from *com-* + *flare* to blow. First known use: 1557.
examples: Even more often, outsiders **conflate** the couple, and credit them with each other's characteristics. — Alison Lurie
This unsettling book—**conflating** journalism, personal reportage, sociology and philosophical inquiry … — Rosemary Mahoney

words.definition: A flowing together, as of rivers or ideas
words.origin: From *confluent*. *Confluent*: Middle English, from Latin *confluent-, confluens*, present participle of *confluere* to flow together, from *com-* + *fluere* to flow. First known use: 15th century.
examples: At the **confluence** of Native American, Hispanic, and Anglo cultures, Santa Fe is the symbolic heart of the Southwest. — Jeffrey Steingarten
A hip urban **confluence** of tasting rooms, galleries, and surfboard designers, it's a place where wine, art and beach culture coalesce.

words.definition: A flowing together of streams, rivers or crowds into one; a confluence
words.origin: Medieval Latin *confluxus*, from Latin *confluere*. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: Pleasant because suited to one's tastes
words.origin: *com-* + *genius*. First known use: circa 1625.

words.definition: A disorderly collection or heap of things, ideas or people; an aggregation
words.origin: Latin, from *congerere*. First known use: circa 1619.

words.definition: A fit of rage, hysteria or alarm, as in having a conniption; a tantrum
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1833.
examples: He had a **conniption** when his favourite TV program was preempted by a political speech.

words.definition: To secretly allow or conspire in wrongdoing
words.origin: French or Latin; French *conniver*, from Latin *conivēre, connivēre* to close the eyes, connive, from *com-* + *-nivēre* (akin to *nictare* to wink); akin to Old English & Old High German *hnīgan* to bow. First known use: 1601.
examples: The government **connived** in the rebels' military buildup.
The captain **connived** at the smuggling of goods aboard his ship.

words.definition: Relationship by blood or by descent from a common ancestor; close kinship
Growing old together
words.origin: From Latin *consenescere* to grow old together.

words.definition: The linking or agreement of different disciplines when forming a theory or coming to a conclusion
words.origin: *com-* + re*silience*. First known use: 1840.

words.definition: Anxiety or dismay, often at something unexpected
words.origin: French or Latin; French, from Latin *consternation-, consternatio*, from *consternare* to throw into confusion, from *com-* + *-sternare*, probably from *sternere* to spread, strike down. First known use: 1604.
examples: … the two … stared at each other in **consternation**, and neither knew what to do. — Pearl Buck

words.definition: To treat or regard with contempt; to scorn or disdain as beneath one's notice
words.origin: Middle English *contempnen* "to slight, spurn," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *contempner* "to despise, disdain," borrowed from Latin *contemnere* "to look down on, show no respect for, despise," from *con-* con- + *temnere* "to scorn, despise," of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to counterpoint, in which independent melodies are combined
words.origin: Italian *contrappunto* counterpoint, from Medieval Latin *contrapunctus*. First known use: 1816.

words.definition: A minor dispute, disagreement or embarrassing mishap; an unlucky hitch
words.origin: French, from *contre-* counter- + *temps* time, from Latin *tempus*. First known use: 1769.

words.definition: Feeling remorse for wrongdoing
words.origin: Middle English *contrit,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Medieval Latin *contrītus,* past participle of Latin *conterere* "to pound to pieces, crush, wear out or down, exhaust mentally or physically" (Medieval Latin also, "to crush in spirit with a sense of one's sin, render contrite"), from *con-* con- + *terere* "to rub, grind, crush, wear down". First known use: 14th century.
examples: I have a sense now of his feeling somewhat **contrite**, or perhaps only abashed. — Renata Adler
Ford executives had hoped their efficient, well-publicized recall efforts and **contrite** approach to customers would enable them to put the tire crisis behind them. — Cathy Booth Thomas

words.definition: Stubbornly or wilfully disobedient to authority, especially a court
words.origin: From *contumacy* + *-ous*. *Contumacy*: Middle English *contumacie*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *contumacia*, from *contumac-, contumax* rebellious. First known use: 1583.
examples: Was warned that any **contumacious** conduct would not be tolerated

words.definition: Stubborn rebelliousness or insubordination
words.origin: Middle English *contumacie*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *contumacia*, from *contumac-, contumax* rebellious. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Insolent or insulting treatment
words.origin: Middle English *contumelie*, from Middle French, from Latin *contumelia*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To thrash or bruise
words.origin: From Latin *contundere* to bruise.

words.definition: A confusing, difficult problem
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1645.
examples: He is faced with the **conundrum** of trying to find a job without having experience.
… resorts seeking to maintain their postcard-perfect beaches face the same **conundrum**: What should be done with plastic waste once it is collected? — Aryn Baker

words.definition: Living together in harmony
words.origin: Spanish, living together.

words.definition: Friendly, lively and enjoyable
words.origin: Late Latin *convivialis*, from Latin *convivium* banquet, from *com-* + *vivere* to live. First known use: circa 1668.

words.definition: Abundant in supply
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *copiosus*, from *copia* abundance, from *co-* + *ops* wealth. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … Shakespeare, whose soul was so **copious** … — Gilbert Highet

words.definition: A small wood cut back regularly for growth
words.origin: Middle English *copies* cutover area overgrown with brush, from Middle French *copeis*, from Old French, from Vulgar Latin **colpaticium*, from **colpare* to cut, from Late Latin *colpus* blow. First known use: 1534.

words.definition: The involuntary use of obscene words
words.origin: From New Latin *coprolalia*. First known use: 1886.

words.definition: A small group of trees
words.origin: By alteration. First known use: 1578.

words.definition: Of orangish-red or reddish-orange colour
words.origin: French, the corn poppy; imitative of a cock's crow.

words.definition: A woman who flirts lightheartedly
words.origin: French, feminine of *coquet*. First known use: circa 1611.
examples: … the book brought to mind a true Southern **coquette**, flashy and sweet and alluring all at the same time. — Tina Jordan
