… the rufous-crested **coquette**, a tiny hummingbird (with a red mohawk "hair-do") that was just as … flirty as its name. — Thelma Dalmas

words.definition: Heart-shaped
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *cordiformis,* from Latin *cord-, cor* "heart" + *-iformis* -iform. First known use: 1828.

words.definition: A chain of mountains or mountain ranges
words.origin: Borrowed from Spanish, from *cuerda* "string, rope, line of mountain peaks" (going back to Latin *chorda, corda* "tripe, string of a musical instrument") + *-ill-,* diminutive suffix (going back to Latin *-illus*) + *-era,* suffix of place (going back to Latin *-āria,* feminine of *-ārius* -ary). First known use: 1704.

words.definition: A shoemaker, especially one working in fine new leather rather than repairing shoes
words.origin: Middle English *cordewaner,* borrowed from Anglo-French, from *cordewan* cordwain + *-er* -er. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Rustic; folksy; countrified
A natural consequence or result
words.origin: Middle English *correlary, corolarie,* borrowed from Late Latin *corōllārium,* going back to Latin, "garland (given as a reward), unsolicited payment, gratuity," from *corōlla* "small wreath of flowers" + *-ārium* -ary. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … love was a stormy passion and jealousy its normal **corollary**. — Ida Treat
A **corollary** to the problem of the number of vessels to be built was that of the types of vessels to be constructed. — Daniel Marx

words.definition: To confirm or give support to
words.origin: Latin *corroboratus*, past participle of *corroborare*, from *com-* + *robor-, robur* strength. First known use: 1529.
examples: The documents … **corroborate** this sequence of events. — Jennifer Bjorhus

words.definition: A meeting
words.origin: Dharuk (Australian Aboriginal language of the Port Jackson area) *garaabara*. First known use: 1811.

words.definition: To flash or sparkle, as light on water; to show brilliance or dazzling wit
words.origin: Latin *coruscatus*, past participle of *coruscare* to flash. First known use: 1705.

words.definition: To care for and protect in an overindulgent way, as a pet lamb; to pamper
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1579.

words.definition: A small, exclusive group of people
words.origin: Borrowed from French, "group of persons joined by a common interest," earlier, "group of peasants owing labour service or rent to a lord," going back to Middle French (Picard) "tenure of a free peasant," from *cotier* "peasant on a smallholding, cottar" + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 1738.

words.definition: Having the same boundaries or extent in space, time or meaning
words.origin: Alteration of *conterminous*. First known use: 1799.
examples: A voting district **coterminous** with the city
… an experience of life **coterminous** with the years of his father. — Elizabeth Hardwick

words.definition: A person's face or expression
words.origin: Middle English *contenance*, from Anglo-French *cuntenance, contenance*, from Medieval Latin *continentia*, from Latin, restraint, from *continent-, continens*, present participle of *continēre* to hold together. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … a **countenance** which expressed both good humour and intelligence … — Sir Walter Scott
… startled, and also somewhat out of **countenance**. — Arnold Bennett

words.definition: Love at first sight; a sudden, overwhelming event
words.origin: French, literally a stroke of lightning.

words.definition: Cultured; refined; sophisticated
words.origin: Back-formation from *uncouth*. First known use: 1896.
examples: Although they disagreed with the speaker, they were **couth** enough to listen to him respectfully.

words.definition: Friendly and cosy
words.origin: From *couth* + *-y*. *Couth*: Back-formation from *uncouth*.

words.definition: To yearn to possess something belonging to another
words.origin: Middle English *coveiten*, from Anglo-French *coveiter*, from Vulgar Latin **cupidietare*, from Latin *cupiditat-, cupiditas* desire, from *cupidus* desirous, from *cupere* to desire. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A vain, conceited man; a dandy; once, the cap worn by a professional jester
words.origin: Middle English *cokkes comb*, literally, cock's comb. First known use: circa 1529.

words.definition: Foolish vanity
words.origin: From *coxcomb* + *-ry*. *Coxcomb*: Middle English *cokkes comb*, literally, cock's comb. First known use: 1770.

words.definition: To trick or deceive, especially by small, charming deceits; to obtain by cheating
words.origin: Perhaps from obsolete Italian *cozzonare*, from Italian *cozzone* horse trader, from Latin *cocion-, cocio* trader. First known use: 1573.
examples: **Cozened** his supper out of the old couple

words.definition: Bad-tempered; grumpy
words.origin: Scots form of *crabbed*.

words.definition: Good times involving pleasant company, enjoyable conversation
words.origin: Borrowed from Irish, borrowed (via Hiberno-English) from Scots and northern English crack in sense "lively conversation, gossip, news". First known use: 1972.
examples: Life is very quiet and you have to make your own **craic**. =fun — Sandra Cribben
… a (sort of) grown-up mystery-comedy-drama series that's proper **craic**. — Shannon Connellan

words.definition: Sickness from excess eating or drinking
words.origin: From Latin *crapula* intoxication, from Greek *kraipalē* hangover.

words.definition: Suffering the effects of drinking or eating to excess; given to intemperance
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *crāpulōsus,* from Latin *crāpula* "intoxication" (borrowed from Greek *kraipálē* "drinking bout, intoxication," of uncertain origin) + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: circa 1540.

words.definition: Contemptibly cowardly
words.origin: Middle English *cravant*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … **craven** mercenaries who would not fight … — Thomas Fleming

words.definition: Too ready to believe things
words.origin: Latin *credulus*, from *credere* to believe, entrust. First known use: 1553.
examples: Few people are **credulous** enough to believe such nonsense.

words.definition: A fear of precipices or cliffs
words.origin: From Greek *krēmnos* cliff + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Having battlements, with regular gaps along the top of a wall
words.origin: From past participle of *crenellate* "to furnish with crenellations," borrowed (with -ate replacing *-é*) from French *crenelé* "having crenellations," going back to Old French *quernelé,* from *crenel, quernel* "crenellation" (from *cren, cran* "notch"—going back to Gallo-Romance **crēn-* or **crĭn-,* of uncertain origin— + *-el,* diminutive suffix) + *-é* -ee. First known use: circa 1823.

words.definition: To make a crackling or rattling sound, as of stiff joints or burning wood
words.origin: Latin *crepitatus*, past participle of *crepitare* to crackle, frequentative of *crepare* to rattle, crack. First known use: circa 1828.

words.definition: Relating to twilight
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *crepusculāris,* from Latin *crepusculum* "twilight" + *-āris* -ar. First known use: 1668.

words.definition: Sunbeams streaming through gaps in clouds
words.origin: From Latin *crepusculum* twilight.

words.definition: Twilight
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Latin *crepusculum,* from presumed earlier **krepos-* "twilight" (of obscure origin) + *-culum,* probably after *dīlūculum* "dawn, daybreak" (from *dīlūcēre* "to be clear" + *-ulum,* diminutive suffix). First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Sad and disappointed after a setback
examples: After losing the playoff game, the team was **crestfallen**.

words.definition: Firm, dry and brittle; fresh and bracing; briskly clear
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English, from Latin *crispus*; akin to Welsh *crych* curly. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: To cuddle up together, as against the cold
words.origin: Of English dialect origin, perhaps related to *cruddle* to curdle or *cuddle*.

words.definition: Irritable, cranky and peevish, often with age, as a crotchety old neighbour
words.origin: From *crotchet* + *-y*. *Crotchet*: Middle English *crochet*, from Anglo-French *crochet, croket*. First known use: 1825.

words.definition: A blow on the head with a club
words.origin: Scots, a blow on the head; of imitative origin.

words.definition: An ancient stringed instrument that's typically associated with Welsh music. Also called a crowd
words.origin: Borrowed from Welsh. First known use: 1793.

words.definition: A burial chamber in a catacomb; a small bedroom in a Roman house
words.origin: Latin, bedroom, from *cubare* to lie down.

words.definition: A short, thick stick used as a weapon; to beat with such a stick
words.origin: Middle English *kuggel*, from Old English *cycgel*; perhaps akin to Middle High German *kugele* ball. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: … grasped more firmly a stout oaken **cudgel** … — Jane G. Austin

words.definition: A piece of armour of breastplate and backplate fastened together
words.origin: Middle English *curas*, from Middle French *cuirasse*, probably from Old Occitan *coirassa*, from Late Latin *coreacea*, feminine of *coreaceus* leathern, from Latin *corium* skin, leather; akin to Old English *heortha* deerskin, Latin *cortex* bark, Greek *keirein* to cut. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Deserving blame
words.origin: Middle English *coupable*, from Anglo-French *cupable, culpable*, from Latin *culpabilis*, from *culpare* to blame, from *culpa* guilt. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The defendant is **culpable** for her actions.

words.definition: A useless person who just takes up space
words.origin: From *cumber* to burden + *ground*.

words.definition: A useless person
words.origin: From *cumber* to burden + *world*.

words.definition: Delay or procrastination, especially as a deliberate and cautious strategy
words.origin: Latin *cunctation-, cunctatio*, from *cunctari* to hesitate; akin to Sanskrit *śaṅkate* he wavers, Old English *hangian* to hang. First known use: 1585.

words.definition: Greed for money or possessions
words.origin: Middle English *cupidite*, from Anglo-French *cupidité*, from Latin *cupiditat-, cupiditas*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A small rounded dome forming or adorning a roof or ceiling, often with a lantern
words.origin: Italian, from Latin *cupula*, diminutive of *cupa* tub. First known use: 1549.

words.definition: A rare, unusual or intriguing object, often an ornamental one
words.origin: Short for *curiosity*. First known use: 1849.

words.definition: A bad-tempered, often older person
words.origin: Of uncertain origin. First known use: 1568.
examples: The film follows Otto, an older man who has become a **curmudgeon** upon the loss of his wife from cancer. — Adrianna Freedman
This is a story about a **curmudgeon** who is so disgruntled with life but starts to make connections with his new neighbours. — Abby Corson

words.definition: Hasty and not thorough
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *cursōrius* "of running, swift" (Late Latin in nominal derivatives, as *cursōria* "shoe for running"), adjectival derivative of Latin *cursor* "runner". First known use: 1601.
examples: Only a **cursory** inspection of the building's electrical wiring was done.

words.definition: A woodwind instrument, an early form of bassoon, also known as a dulcian
words.origin: Middle French *courtault*, from *court* short, from Latin *curtus*. First known use: 1576.

words.definition: A thief, especially one who steals from people's pockets
A steep bowl-shaped mountain basin, carved by glaciers. Also known as a cirque
words.origin: Welsh, valley. First known use: 1853.

words.definition: A loving cuddle; a cosy, safe place
words.origin: Welsh, a cuddle or a cubbyhole.

words.definition: Made of massive irregular stones fitted without mortar; gigantic
A delusion in which one believes oneself to be a dog
words.origin: From Greek *kyōn* dog + *anthrōpos* human.

words.definition: Relating to the chase or hunting
words.origin: From Greek *kynēgetikos*, from *kyōn* dog + *hēgeisthai* to lead.

words.definition: A person or thing that is the centre of attention or admiration; a guide
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *Cynosure* "Ursa Minor," borrowed from Latin *Cynosūra,* borrowed from Greek *Kynósoura,* from *kynós,* genitive of *kýōn* "dog" + *ourá* "tail". First known use: 1565.
examples: … they have turned an eyesore into a **cynosure**. — Catherine Reynolds
… his rapidly increasing wealth has made him a **cynosure** in political circles. — Larissa MacFarquhar

words.definition: Having a metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones
words.origin: Middle English *dactyl, dactile* "fruit of the date palm, a dactyl in verse," borrowed from Latin *dactylus* "dactyl in verse, kind of date," borrowed from Greek *dáktylos* "digit (finger or toe), finger's width as a measurement, dactyl in verse, date," of uncertain origin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A fingerprint, especially one taken in ink for the purpose of identification
words.origin: From Greek *daktylos* finger + *-gram*.

words.definition: Intricately and skilfully made; ingenious, like the work of Daedalus
words.origin: Latin *daedalus*, from Greek *daidalos*. First known use: 1590.
examples: … visions of cloud and light and **daedal** earth are the airman's daily scene. — Laurence Binyon

words.definition: A casual romantic or sexual relationship
words.origin: From *dally* + *-ance*. *Dally*: Middle English *dalyen*, from Anglo-French *dalier*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A rich, reversible fabric with a pattern woven into it; a soft greyish pink
words.origin: Middle English *damaske*, from Medieval Latin *damascus*, from *Damascus*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Involving imminent danger
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *Damoklēs*. First known use: 1578.

words.definition: Temper or anger, as in getting one's dander up; tiny flakes of animal skin
words.origin: Alteration of *dandruff*. First known use: 1786.

words.definition: An inconsequential person
words.origin: Originally a small 16th-century coin; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: To mark with spots or rounded patches of colour or light, as sun through leaves
words.origin: Middle English *dappel-gray*, adjective, grey marked with spots of another colour. First known use: circa 1586.

words.definition: Fearless and determined
words.origin: Daunt + -less. First known use: 1588.

words.definition: So loud as to make hearing impossible
words.origin: From present participle of *deafen*, from *deaf* + *-en*.
examples: Their silence on the issue was **deafening**.

words.definition: A scarcity or lack
words.origin: Middle English *derthe*, from Old English **dierth*, from *dēore* dear. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: In a clockwise direction
words.origin: Scottish Gaelic *deiseil*, from Middle Irish *dessel*, from Old Irish *dess* right, south + *sel* turn; akin to Latin *dexter* right hand. First known use: 1771.

words.definition: A sudden, humiliating failure
words.origin: French *débâcle*, from *débâcler* to clear, from Middle French *desbacler*, from *des-* de- + *bacler* to block, perhaps from Vulgar Latin **bacculare*, from Latin *baculum* staff. First known use: 1802.

words.definition: To corrupt morally or lead away from virtue; a bout of excessive indulgence
words.origin: Borrowed from French *débaucher* "to divert or distract (a person) from work, obligations, etc., tempt into excess or immorality," going back to Middle French, "to cause (a servant, worker) to leave his master's service," going back to Old French *desbauchier* "to scatter, disperse (people, a crowd)," presumably from an earlier sense "to rough-hew a beam from a larger log" (hence, "to split, separate") from *des-* dis- + *-bauchier,* verbal derivative of *bauch* (Walloon, Picard) "beam," borrowed from Old Low Franconian **balk-,* going back to Germanic **balkōn* "beam". First known use: 1595.
examples: … a heavy drinker who later became wholly **debauched**. — Alistair Horne

words.definition: Severely weakened, as by illness or hardship
words.origin: Latin *debilitatus*, past participle of *debilitare* to weaken, from *debilis* weak. First known use: 1533.
examples: An economy **debilitated** by years of civil war

words.definition: Confident, stylish and charming
words.origin: Middle English *debonere, debonaire* "mild, meek, kind, courteous," borrowed from Anglo-French *deboneire, debonaire* "mild, meek, noble, highborn," from *de* "of" + *bon* "good" + Old French *aire, ere* "family, stock, sort, kind". First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: To emerge from a narrow place, such as a valley or ravine, into open country
words.origin: French *déboucher*, from *dé-* de- + *bouche* mouth, from Old French *boche*, from Latin *bucca* cheek. First known use: 1745.

words.definition: To expose as false
The process of transferring a design from a specially prepared paper onto another surface
words.origin: Borrowed from French *décalcomanie,* from *décalquer* "to trace, transfer by tracing" (from *dé-* de- + *calquer* "to trace, copy") + *-o-* -o- + *-manie* -mania, after *potichomanie* "the art of imitating painted porcelain ware," earlier presumably "craze for vases imitating Chinese porcelain," compound with *potiche* "rounded or polygonal vase with a separate cover, originally one made in China". First known use: 1864.

words.definition: To behead; to separate a continuous printout into individual sheets
words.origin: Latin *decollatus*, past participle of *decollare*, from *de-* + *collum* neck. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Polite and in good taste
words.origin: Latin decōrus "good-looking, handsome, worthy of approval, suitable" (derivative of *decōr-, decor* "pleasing appearance, beauty, grace, seemliness, propriety," derivative from the stem of *decet, decēre* "to add grace to, adorn, be fitting or proper") + -ous. First known use: 1653.
examples: Ever **decorous**, she periodically excuses herself to another room rather than allow a guest to witness her blowing her nose. — Will Hermes

words.definition: Behaviour in keeping with good taste
words.origin: From neuter of Latin *decōrus* "good-looking, worthy of approval, suitable". First known use: 1568.
examples: According to strict neoclassic **decorum** only the aristocracy had the right to appear in tragedy … — Irving Babbitt
… strict in her notions of **decorum** … — Jane Austen

words.definition: To publicly denounce or disparage; to speak of as worthless or dangerous
words.origin: Borrowed from French *décrier* "to discredit, depreciate," going back to Middle French *descrier* (15th century), from *des-* de- + *crier* "to cry". First known use: 1614.
examples: The king may at any time **decry** … any coin of the kingdom … — William Blackstone

words.definition: To cross or intersect in the form of an X; arranged in crossing pairs
words.origin: Latin *decussatus*, past participle of *decussare* to arrange crosswise, from *decussis* the number ten, numeral X, intersection, from *dec*em + *ass-, as* unit. First known use: 1658.

words.definition: To embezzle or misappropriate money held in trust, as a dishonest treasurer does
words.origin: Medieval Latin *defalcatus*, past participle of *defalcare*, from Latin *de-* + *falc-, falx* sickle. First known use: 1541.

words.definition: Capable of being revised, defeated or annulled
words.origin: Alteration (conformed to -ible) of earlier *defesable,* borrowed from Anglo-French, from *de-* de- + *fesable* "doable, feasible," after *defaire, desfaire* "to undo, put an end to, destroy, nullify". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To throw out of a window
words.origin: *de-* + Latin *fenestra* window. First known use: 1619.

words.definition: Polite submission and respect
words.origin: Borrowed from French *déférence,* going back to Middle French *deference* "act of submitting," from *deferer* "to submit to another, defer" + *-ence* -ence. First known use: 1660.

words.definition: Quick and skilful
words.origin: Perhaps continuing Middle English *daffte, daft, defte* "well-mannered, gentle, dull, foolish". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A person skilled in the art of dinner-table conversation; a learned dinner guest
words.origin: From Greek *deipnosophistēs*, from *deipnon* meal + *sophistēs* wise man; after a work by Athenaeus.

words.definition: A look
words.origin: British Army slang, from Hindi *dekho* look!

words.definition: Causing harm or damage
words.origin: Greek *dēlētērios*, from *dēleisthai* to hurt. First known use: 1587.

words.definition: To take a small amount of something: to taste or sip
words.origin: From Latin *delibare* to take a little of.

words.definition: To melt away or become liquid by absorbing moisture; to dissolve or dwindle
words.origin: Latin *deliquescere*, from *de-* + *liquescere*, inchoative of *liquēre* to be fluid. First known use: 1756.

words.definition: A fainting fit or loss of consciousness; a melting away of strength or substance
words.origin: Latin, a failing, a swoon.

words.definition: Obscure or ambiguous
A leader who exploits popular prejudice
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *dēmagōgós,* from *dêmos* "people" + *-agōgos* "leading, impelling". First known use: 1629.
examples: The most fervent devotees of a cult or **demagogue** are those who mistake courtship for love and the power of a leader for their own. — Greg Jackson

words.definition: Land attached to a manor and kept for the owner's use; a domain or realm
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *demesne, demeine*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A group on the fringes of respectable society, once of kept women
words.origin: French *demi-monde*, from *demi-* + *monde* world, from Latin *mundus*. First known use: 1855.
examples: Opening as an underworld drama, set among the **demimonde** of Viennese sex workers and gangsters, it soon shifted gear—and location, moving to the countryside and becoming something far richer and more unexpected …
Yet, when he wanders from the leafy, comfortable districts into the criminal and sexual **demimondes** of Bombay, he is transfixed …

words.definition: To give up an office or a position; to dismiss. verb intr.: To resign
words.origin: Middle English *dimitten*, from Anglo-French *demettre*. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: A being who shapes the material world; a powerful creative force
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *dēmiurgus,* borrowed from Greek *dēmiourgós,* literally, "master of a craft, artisan" (Homeric *dēmioergós* "one skilled in an art or craft that benefits the community"), contraction of **dēmioworgos,* from *dḗmios* "of the people, public" (adjective derivative of *dêmos* "people") + **-worgos,* ablaut derivative of Indo-European **u̯erǵ-* "make, bring about" (whence, as a nominal derivative, Greek *érgon* "work"). First known use: 1840.

words.definition: Of or for ordinary people; denoting the everyday form of a language
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *dēmotikós* "of the people, common, ordinary, of the cursive Egyptian script," from *dēmótēs* "one of the people, commoner" (from *dêmos* "people" + *-tēs,* suffix of persons) + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 1822.

words.definition: Soothing, especially to irritated or inflamed mucous membranes
words.origin: Latin *demulcent-, demulcens*, present participle of *demulcēre* to soothe, from *de-* + *mulcēre* to soothe. First known use: 1732.

words.definition: To raise doubts or show reluctance
words.origin: Middle English *demuren, demeren* to linger, from Anglo-French *demurer, demoerer*, from Latin *demorari*, from *de-* + *morari* to linger, from *mora* delay. First known use: 13th century.
examples: It would seem hazardous to **demur** to a proposition which is so widely accepted. — Samuel Alexander

words.definition: Reserved, modest and shy
words.origin: From Middle English *demure*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … cultural stereotypes of women being feminine and **demure**. — Jacqueline Fitzgerald
… looked prim and proper in a **demure** dress … — Yaron Steinbuch

words.definition: To criticize unfairly; to belittle
words.origin: Latin *denigratus*, past participle of *denigrare*, from *de-* + *nigrare* to blacken, from *nigr-, niger* black. First known use: 1526.

words.definition: An inhabitant or occupant of a place; a regular frequenter of somewhere
words.origin: Middle English *denizeine*, from Anglo-French *denisein, denzein* inhabitant, inner part, inner, from *denz* within, from Late Latin *deintus*, from Latin *de-* + *intus* within. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … daylilies, purple loosestrife, and other roadside **denizens** now firmly rooted in Maine … — Rebecca Sawyer-Fay

words.definition: The final resolution of a plot
words.origin: French *dénouement*, literally, untying, from Middle French *desnouement*, from *desnouer* to untie, from Old French *desnoer*, from *des-* de- + *noer* to tie, from Latin *nodare*, from *nodus* knot. First known use: 1705.
examples: In the novel's **denouement**, the two hostages escape to freedom.
It is an intentionally unsettling **denouement**, which is in keeping with the tone and purpose of the entire miniseries. — David Wiegand

words.definition: The habit of speaking through clenched teeth, as in suppressed anger
words.origin: From Latin *dens* tooth + *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: Deserving strong condemnation; shockingly bad
words.origin: From French *déplorable*, from *déplorer* to lament, from Latin *deplorare* to weep bitterly.

words.definition: To express disapproval of
words.origin: Latin *deprecatus*, past participle of *deprecari* to avert by prayer, from *de-* + *precari* to pray. First known use: 1628.
examples: … speaks five languages … but **deprecates** this facility …

words.definition: An act of attacking, plundering or ravaging; a destructive raid
words.origin: Late Latin *depraedatus*, past participle of *depraedari*, from Latin *de-* + *praedari* to plunder. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: To uproot; to remove from one's native culture or natural environment
words.origin: Middle French *desraciner*, from *des-* de- + *racine* root, from Late Latin *radicina*, from Latin *radic-, radix*. First known use: 1609.

words.definition: The shameful failure to fulfil one's obligations; the state of being abandoned
To mock with contempt
words.origin: Latin *deridēre*, from *de-* + *ridēre* to laugh. First known use: circa 1526.
examples: … how they mock and **deride** him as he slinks away. — Charles Dickens
These artists were a plucky band of underdogs and the conventional art community found all kinds of ways to **deride** them. — Diane Urbani de la Paz

words.definition: Imitative of others' work; unoriginal
The very latest fashion or newest thing; literally, the last cry
words.origin: French, literally, last cry. First known use: 1896.

words.definition: Action displaying heroic courage, often with a touch of mockery
words.origin: Middle English *dorring don* daring to do, from *dorring* (gerund of *dorren* to dare) + *don* to do. First known use: 1579.

words.definition: A very poor person
words.origin: Spanish, shirtless.

words.definition: To catch sight of something distant or barely visible; to discover by looking
words.origin: In sense 1 Middle English *descrien, descriven, descreven* "to catch sight of, discover, discern," apparently developed from *descriven* (rarely *descrien*) "to describe, recount, characterize," borrowed from Anglo-French *descrire, descriver, descrier* "to describe, give an account of," going back to Latin *dēscrībere* "to represent by drawing, describe"; in sense 2 Middle English *descrien* "to announce, make known, reveal, betray," perhaps borrowed from Middle French *descrier* "to cry, make known," from *des-* de- + *crier* "to cry". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Improvising a clever way out of trouble
words.origin: Portuguese, from *desenrascar* to disentangle.

words.definition: The state of being only partly or carelessly dressed; casual or loose attire
words.origin: French *déshabillé*, from past participle of *déshabiller* to undress, from *dés-* dis- + *habiller* to dress. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: To remove the moisture from
words.origin: Latin *desiccatus*, past participle of *desiccare* to dry up, from *de-* + *siccare* to dry, from *siccus* dry. First known use: 1575.
examples: … a charming little romance … not **desiccated** and compressed within the pages of a book … — Elinor Wylie
Lake Valencia has been … steadily **desiccating** for more than 200 years. — J. Platt Bradbury et al.

words.definition: In low spirits from loss of hope
words.origin: Latin *despondent-, despondens*, present participle of *despondēre*. First known use: circa 1699.

words.definition: Extremely poor; lacking necessities
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *destitutus*, past participle of *destituere* to abandon, deprive, from *de-* + *statuere* to set up. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A state of disuse, as of a custom, law or word no longer observed
words.origin: Middle English *dissuetude*, from Latin *desuetudo*, from *desuescere* to become unaccustomed, from *de-* + *suescere* to become accustomed; akin to Latin *sodalis* comrade. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Lacking a plan or purpose; half-hearted
words.origin: Latin *desultorius*, literally, of a circus rider who leaps from horse to horse, from *desilire* to leap down, from *de-* + *salire* to leap. First known use: 1581.
examples: … a dragged-out ordeal of … **desultory** shopping. — Herman Wouk

words.definition: Reckless mischief or charming wildness; dealings with the devil; sorcery
words.origin: Borrowed from French, going back to Old French, from *diable* "devil, the Devil" (borrowed from Late Latin *diabolus*) + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 1726.

words.definition: Relating to changes occurring over time
words.origin: Borrowed from French *diachronique,* from *diachronie* diachrony + *-ique* -ic. First known use: 1917.

words.definition: The entire compass of musical tones; a swelling burst of harmony
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin, from Greek *(hē) dia pasōn (chordōn symphōnia)*, literally, the concord through all the notes, from *dia* through + *pasōn*, genitive feminine plural of *pas* all. First known use: 1519.
examples: … registers the full **diapason** of her responses … — Mindy Aloff

words.definition: Light, delicate and translucent
words.origin: Extension with -ous of Medieval Latin *diafanus, diaphanus,* borrowed from Greek *diaphanḗs* "transparent, manifest, conspicuous," adjective derivative from the stem of *diaphaínein* "to let be seen through," *diaphaínesthai* "to show through, be seen through," from *dia-* dia- + *phaínein* (active voice) "to bring to light, cause to appear," and *phaínesthai* (middle voice) "to become visible, come to light, appear". First known use: 1614.
examples: Had only a **diaphanous** hope of success

words.definition: Sweating, especially heavy perspiration brought on by illness or medicine
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *diaphorēsis*, from *diaphorein* to dissipate by perspiration, from *dia-* + *phorein*, frequentative of *pherein* to carry. First known use: circa 1681.

words.definition: A forceful, bitter verbal attack
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin, "disputation," going back to Latin, "school (of rhetoric or philosophy)," borrowed from Greek *diatribḗ* "wearing down, attrition, spending of time, discussion, discourse, school," derivative of *diatrī́bein* "to crush, wear out, spend time, occupy oneself," from *dia-* dia- + *trī́bein* "to rub, grind, wear down," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: A division into two contrasting parts
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *dichotomia,* borrowed from Greek *dichotomía* "division into two parts (of the moon, in logic), bisection," from *dichótomos* "cut in half, dichotomous" + *-ia* -ia. First known use: 1588.
examples: It's the **dichotomy** of what is shown to Wall Street and to the tax man. — Erik Sherman

words.definition: Of or relating to Charles Dickens or his works
words.origin: From *dickens* + *-ian*. *Dickens*: Euphemism. First known use: 1842.
examples: … a **Dickensian** density of imaginative detail. — Thomas M. Disch
In spite of the **Dickensian** reputation that outlives them orphanages … represented a significant social reform for their time … — Mary-Lou Weisman

words.definition: Intended to teach, often moralizing
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *didacticus,* borrowed from Greek *didaktikós* "apt at teaching," from *didaktós* "taught, learned" (verbal adjective of *didáskein*, aorist *edídaxa* "to teach, instruct," factitive derivative of *daênai* "to learn") + *-ikos* -ic; *daênai* going back to Indo-European **dens-, *dn̥s-* "become knowledgeable or skillful," whence also Avestan *dīdaiŋ́hē* "(I) learn, experience" and, in nominal derivatives, Sanskrit *dáṃsaḥ* "marvelous power," *dasráḥ* "accomplishing wonderful deeds," and perhaps Greek *dḗnea* "plans, intentions". First known use: 1658.
examples: The first part of the book is more **didactic**, with lengthy descriptions of how the operating system actually works. — Richard C. Leinecker
The best of her poems are brilliant and compelling; others are uneven and feel talky or **didactic**. — Elizabeth Lund

words.definition: A mischievous prank or caper; an antic, as in cutting didoes
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1807.

words.definition: Happening inside a story
examples: One of the primary qualities of those texts we understand as fiction is that they generate a **diegetic** order that has an astonishing independence from its text. — Robert Scholes

words.definition: Modest or shy from a lack of confidence
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Latin *diffīdent-, diffīdens* "distrustful, lacking in confidence," from present participle of *diffīdere* "to lack confidence (in), have no trust (in)," from *dif-,* assimilated form of *dis-* dis- + *fīdere* "to trust, have confidence (in)," going back to Indo-European **bhei̯dh-* "trust, entrust". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To dress, adorn or equip, as a knight for battle; to prepare or make ready
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *dihtan* to arrange, compose, from Latin *dictare* to dictate, compose. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Slow to act; causing delay
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *dilatorie*, Late Latin *dilatorius*, from Latin *differre* (past participle *dilatus*) to postpone, differ. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A dabbler in the arts without real commitment
words.origin: Borrowed from Italian, agentive derivative of *dilettare* "to please, delight," borrowed from Latin *dēlectāre*. First known use: 1748.
examples: Mr. Carroll often criticizes the superficial lives of the **dilettantes** … who mingle in New York. — Mark Stevens
Whitman ran an amateurish campaign … and was painted as an aristocratic **dilettante**. — Eleanor Clift

words.definition: Showing care and effort
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *diligent-, diligens*, from present participle of *diligere* to esteem, love, from *di-* (from *dis-* apart) + *legere* to select. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Many hours of **diligent** research were required.
Even those who are **diligent** about using sunscreen every day will still likely experience some unprotected exposure to the sun, such as getting in and out of the car. — Nick Blackmer

words.definition: To waste time through indecision
words.origin: Reduplication of *dally*. First known use: 1740.

words.definition: Extremely or unusually small
words.origin: Middle English *diminutif*, from Medieval Latin *diminutivum*, alteration of Late Latin *deminutivum*, from neuter of *deminutivus*, adjective, from *deminutus*, past participle of *deminuere* "to lessen". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A deep, wooded valley
words.origin: Middle English, deep hollow. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: One who is wasteful and reckless with money or resources
words.origin: From *ding* to strike + *thrift*.

words.definition: A person with a recurring, uncontrollable craving for alcohol
words.origin: Borrowed from German *Dipsomanie,* from Greek *dípsa* "thirst" (of uncertain origin) + German *-o-* -o- + *-manie* -mania. First known use: circa 1844.

words.definition: To thrill or vibrate, as from a blow or strong feeling
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of *thirl*. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: To free someone from a mistaken idea or belief; to set right
words.origin: French *désabuser*, from *dés-* dis- + *abuser* to abuse. First known use: 1669.
examples: Was quickly **disabused** of the idea that anything had changed

words.definition: Barefoot
words.origin: From Latin *discalceatus* unshod, from *calceus* shoe.

words.definition: Barefoot or wearing only sandals, as certain religious orders are
words.origin: Partial translation of Latin *discalceatus*, from *dis-* + *calceatus*, past participle of *calceare* to put on shoes, from *calceus* shoe, from *calc-, calx* heel. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Having good judgment
words.origin: From present participle of discern. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: To tear off or to rip into pieces
words.origin: From Latin *discerpere* to tear in pieces.

words.definition: To disconcert or confuse someone completely; to throw into disarray
words.origin: Probably alteration of *discompose*. First known use: 1879.
examples: … inventing cool new ways to **discombobulate** the old order. — Kurt Andersen
Executives of other NHL clubs are hopping mad at St. Louis president Jack Quinn and general manager Ron Caron for once again **discombobulating** the NHL's salary structure. — Austin Murphy

words.definition: To make uneasy or embarrassed
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *descumfit*, past participle of *descumfire*, from *des-* dis- + *cumfire* to prepare. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … was **discomfited** in a great battle … — Edward Gibbon

words.definition: Unhappy beyond comfort
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *disconsolatus*, from Latin *dis-* + *consolatus*, past participle of *consolari* to console. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a clutch of **disconsolate** houses. — D. H. Lawrence
The team returned **disconsolate** from three losses

words.definition: Wandering from subject to subject
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *discursīvus* "showing reasoned thought, logical," from *discursus,* past participle of *discurrere* "to range over, discuss" (going back to Latin, "to run off in different directions, [of a mind or speaker] branch out, range") + Latin *-īvus* -ive. First known use: 1595.

words.definition: The feeling that something is unworthy of respect
words.origin: Middle English *desdeyne*, from Anglo-French *desdaign*, from *desdeigner*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Had a look of utter **disdain** on his face

words.definition: The state of being carelessly or partly dressed
words.origin: French *déshabillé*, from past participle of *déshabiller* to undress, from *dés-* dis- + *habiller* to dress. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: To scatter or disperse
words.origin: From Latin *disjicere* to scatter.

words.definition: To speak of as of little worth
words.origin: Middle English *disparagen* "to degrade by marriage below one's class, defile (a woman)," borrowed from Anglo-French *desparager* (continental Old French *desparagier*), from *des-* dis- + *parage* "equality of rank, lineage, high birth," from *per* "equal, match, member of the hereditary nobility" + *-age* -age. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … but let every man … not think himself **disparaged**, if another of his neighbours have better than he. — Richard Allestree

words.definition: Essentially different in kind
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *disparātus* "separate, distinct," from past participle of *disparāre* "to divide, separate off, make different," from *dis-* dis- + *parāre* "to supply, provide, make ready" (influenced in sense by association with *dispar-, dispār* "unequal, different"). First known use: 1566.
examples: Its **disparate** parts don't quite jell, and the ending feels rushed. — Don Aucoin

words.definition: To enjoy oneself unrestrainedly; to frolic or play; a diversion
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *desporter*, to carry away, comfort, entertain, from *des-* dis- + *porter* to carry, from Latin *portare*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A long or elaborate essay or discussion on a particular subject
words.origin: Latin *disquisition-, disquisitio*, from *disquirere* to investigate, from *dis-* + *quaerere* to seek. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: To conceal one's true motives or feelings
words.origin: Middle English *dissymbulen, dissymblen,* probably reshaping of *dissimulen* in same sense (after *resemblen* "to resemble," *semblance* semblance, and like forms), borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *dissimuler, dissumuler* "to hide under a false appearance," borrowed from Latin *dissimulāre*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: He had **dissembled** about the risks involved.

words.definition: To disperse or squander
words.origin: Latin *dissipatus*, past participle of *dissipare, dissupare*, from *dis-* + *supare* to throw. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … one's sympathy is eventually **dissipated**. — Andrew Feinberg
**Dissipated** the family fortune in reckless business ventures

words.definition: Lax in morals; given to vice
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *dissolutus*, from past participle of *dissolvere* to loosen, dissolve. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **dissolute** and degrading aspects of human nature — Wallace Fowlie

words.definition: A lack of harmony
words.origin: From *dissonant*. *Dissonant*: Middle English *dissonaunte*, from Latin *dissonant-, dissonans*, present participle of *dissonare* to be discordant, from *dis-* + *sonare* to sound. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **dissonance** between the truth and what people want to believe
The mingling of bitter comedy and stark tragedy produces sharp **dissonances** … — F. B. Millett

words.definition: A wildly enthusiastic speech or piece of writing; a choral hymn to Dionysus
words.origin: Greek *dithyrambos*. First known use: circa 1647.

words.definition: Of or during the daytime
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *diurnalis*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To stray or digress from a course or subject; to wander off the point
words.origin: Late Latin *divagatus*, past participle of *divagari*, from Latin *dis-* + *vagari* to wander. First known use: 1816.

words.definition: A wandering from the subject; a digression
words.origin: Late Latin *divagatus*, past participle of *divagari*, from Latin *dis-* + *vagari* to wander. First known use: 1816.

words.definition: To branch off or diverge
words.origin: Latin *divaricatus*, past participle of *divaricare*, from *dis-* + *varicare* to straddle. First known use: 1673.

words.definition: Desiring strife
words.origin: From Latin *diversus* different + *volens* wishing.

words.definition: The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by signs
words.origin: Middle English *divinacioun*, from Latin *divination-, divinatio*, from *divinare*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To reveal something secret
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *divulgare*, from *dis-* + *vulgare* to make known, from *vulgus* mob. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Refused to **divulge** the name of her informant

words.definition: Shaky or slow, typically because of old age; infirm and feeble
words.origin: Middle English *dadiren*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Badly written, comic verse
words.origin: Middle English *dogerel*, probably diminutive of *dogge* dog. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Asserting opinions as undeniably true
words.origin: From *dogma* + *-tic*. *Dogma*: Latin *dogmat-, dogma*, from Greek, from *dokein* to seem. First known use: 1681.

words.definition: A person given boring, menial tasks to do for others; a drudge or general helper
words.origin: British naval slang *dogsbody* pudding made of peas, junior officer. First known use: 1922.

words.definition: A short watch, especially one of the two two-hour watch duties on a ship: 4-6 pm or 6-8 pm
The sweetness of doing nothing
words.origin: Italian, literally, sweet doing nothing. First known use: 1814.

words.definition: A prehistoric tomb of large upright stones capped by a flat slab
words.origin: French, probably modification of Cornish *tolmen*, from *tol* hole + *men* stone. First known use: 1831.
examples: "Dusted with magic," is how one archaeologist described the famously atmospheric hills to me, in a region long known for its intriguing stone circles, **dolmens**, and other megalithic monuments. — Caroline Alexander

There's a lot more to discover such as the prehistoric **dolmen** structures and menhirs at Filitosa and the Scandola Nature Reserve, one of the richest marine diversity hotspots in Europe … — Susan Gough Henly

words.definition: Something that banishes or mitigates grief or pain, as a friend's company
words.origin: From Latin *dolor* pain + *fugare* to drive away.

words.definition: Feeling or expressing great sorrow
words.origin: From *dolor* + *-ous*. *Dolor*: Middle English *dolour*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *dolor* pain, grief, from *dolēre* to feel pain, grieve. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A state of great sorrow or distress; grief, a word now mainly found in poetry
words.origin: Middle English *dolour*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *dolor* pain, grief, from *dolēre* to feel pain, grieve. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A place of wickedness
words.origin: From French *Dom Daniel*, an undersea hall of sorcerers in the *Arabian Nights* sequels.

words.definition: A scene of uproar or disorder; a heated public brawl or argument
words.origin: *Donnybrook* Fair, annual Irish event known for its brawls. First known use: 1852.

words.definition: An apparition or double of a living person; an uncanny lookalike
words.origin: German, double-goer.

words.definition: A pedantic, tiresome scholar
words.origin: From Nicolas d'Orbellis, a 15th-century French scholastic.

words.definition: A pedantic, nagging critic
words.origin: From French *doryphore* Colorado beetle, from Greek *doryphoros* spear-bearer.

words.definition: An old person, especially one who has become weak, foolish or senile
Brave, persistent and resolute, as a doughty campaigner; stout-hearted
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *dohtig*; akin to Old High German *toug* is useful, Greek *teuchein* to make. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Severe or gloomy in manner
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *durus* hard. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … an insistent hunger for learning and a **dour** … determination to achieve it. — Walter Moberly

words.definition: A widow with a title or property from her late husband; a dignified elderly woman
words.origin: Middle French *douagiere*, from *douage* dower, from *douer* to endow. First known use: 1530.

words.definition: The most respected or prominent person in a particular field; the senior member
words.origin: French, from Old French *deien*, from Late Latin *decanus* dean. First known use: 1670.

words.definition: Hell; a place of torment
words.origin: Persian *dūzakh* hell.

words.definition: Excessively harsh and severe
words.origin: Latin *Dracon-, Draco*, from Greek *Drakōn* Draco (Athenian lawgiver). First known use: 1752.

words.definition: To make dirty or wet by trailing through mud; to straggle behind
words.origin: Frequentative of *drag*. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: Dirty or untidy
words.origin: From *draggle* to drag through mud + *tail*.

words.definition: An interpreter or guide in countries where Arabic, Turkish or Persian is spoken
words.origin: Middle English *drugeman*, from Anglo-French, from Old Italian *dragomanno*, from Middle Greek *dragomanos*, from Arabic *tarjumān*, from Aramaic *tūrgĕmānā*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To endure or suffer
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *drēogan*; akin to Goth *driugan* to perform military service. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Dreary and bleak, as weather
words.origin: Middle English, of Scandinavian origin; akin to Old Norse *drjūgr* lasting. First known use: 1786.

words.definition: Quaint or dry humour; a comical act or story; a whimsical jest
A compulsive desire to travel
words.origin: From Greek *dromos* running + *mania*.

words.definition: Rotten inside though sound outside, as timber
words.origin: Perhaps from obsolete *drucksy* rotten; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A nymph inhabiting a forest or a tree, especially an oak, in Greek mythology
words.origin: Latin *dryad-, dryas*, from Greek, from *drys* tree. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a sunrise stroll with a **dryad** in a dew-drenched forest … — Edith Wharton

words.definition: A feeling of offence or deep resentment, usually in high dudgeon
words.origin: Middle English *dogeon*, from Anglo-French *digeon, dogeon*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A heightened, soulful intensity in art
words.origin: Spanish dialect, charm, from Spanish, ghost, goblin, probably from *duen de casa*, from *dueño de casa* owner of a house. First known use: 1956.

words.definition: Sweet and soothing to the ear
words.origin: Middle English *doucet*, from Anglo-French, from *duz, douz* sweet, from Latin *dulcis*; perhaps akin to Greek *glykys* sweet. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To sweeten; to soften or make more agreeable, as a temper or harsh words
words.origin: Late Latin *dulcificare*, from Latin *dulcis*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: A stringed instrument played by striking or plucking strings over a soundbox
words.origin: Middle English *dowcemere*, from Middle French *doulcemer*, from Old Italian *dolcimelo*, from *dolce* sweet, from Latin *dulcis*. First known use: 1509.
examples: Introduced by the gentle twanging of hammers on the strings of the **dulcimer**, Veris Dulcis In Tempore turned out to be a lovely duet in praise of the sweetness of love. — William Littler
Fretted and usually three-stringed, the **dulcimer** is both a solo and an accompanying instrument. — Lee Wilcox

words.definition: Like a dunce; stupid or foolish, as in Pope's satire the Dunciad
words.origin: From *dunce*, after the scholar John Duns Scotus.

words.definition: Deceitfulness; double-dealing
words.origin: Middle English *duplicite*, from Middle French, from Late Latin *duplicitat-, duplicitas*, from Latin *duplex*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the simplicity and openness of their lives brought out for him the **duplicity** that lay at the bottom of ours. — Mary Austin

words.definition: Contemplating dust and the impermanence of things
words.origin: Old English, from *dūst* dust + *scēawung* contemplation.

words.definition: A sleeping potion; deadly nightshade
words.origin: From Old English *dwala* error, delusion.

words.definition: A daydream; a stupor
words.origin: Scots, from Old English *dwolma* confusion.

words.definition: Difficulty getting out of bed in the morning
words.origin: From Greek *dys-* bad + *ania* trouble; a modern coinage.

words.definition: Suffering from indigestion; irritable or gloomy in temperament
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, borrowed from Greek *dyspepsía,* from *dys-* dys- + *pépsis* "cooking, ripening, digestion" (from *pep-,* base of *péttein, péssein, péptein* "to cook, ripen, digest" + *-sis* -sis) + *-ia* -ia. First known use: circa 1706.

words.definition: A harsh, derogatory or offensive word used in place of a neutral one
words.origin: Dys- + *-phemism* (in euphemism). First known use: 1884.

words.definition: A profound state of unease or dissatisfaction
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin, borrowed from Greek *dysphoría* "malaise, discomfort, vexation," from *dýsphoros* "hard to bear, grievous" (from *dys-* dys- + *-phoros,* nominal ablaut derivative from the base of *phérein* "to carry, bear") + *-ia* -ia. First known use: circa 1842.
examples: Paradoxically, chronic cocaine use eventually leads to **dysphoria**—a depressed, low-energy state characterized by flattened emotions, a lack of interest in sex, and physical immobility. — James Lieber

words.definition: The disorientation of being away from home
words.origin: French, from *dépayser* to remove from one's country.

words.definition: An unplanned wander through a city, led by its moods
words.origin: French, drift.

words.definition: One who testifies or can testify to something heard
A catchy song or tune that keeps involuntarily repeating in one's mind
To flow back; to decline gradually
words.origin: Middle English *ebbe*, from Old English *ebba*; akin to Middle Dutch *ebbe* ebb, Old English *of* from. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Dark brown or black, like ebony; dark and lustrous, as ebon hair or night
Drunkenness; intoxication, the opposite of sobriety
words.origin: From Latin *ebrietas*, from *ebrius* drunk.

words.definition: Bubbling enthusiasm and high spirits
words.origin: From *ebullient*. *Ebullient*: Latin *ebullient-, ebulliens*, present participle of *ebullire* to bubble out, from *e-* + *bullire* to bubble, boil. First known use: 1749.

words.definition: Cheerful and full of energy
words.origin: Latin *ebullient-, ebulliens*, present participle of *ebullire* to bubble out, from *e-* + *bullire* to bubble, boil. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Like ivory
words.origin: From Latin *eburneus*, from *ebur* ivory.

words.definition: Unconventional and slightly strange
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *ecentricus, excentricus* "not concentric with another circle, (of a planetary orbit in Ptolemaic astronomy) not having the earth exactly at its centre," from Late Latin *eccentros, eccentrus* "not having the earth at its centre" (borrowed from Greek *ékkentros,* from *ek-* ec- + *-kentros,* adjective derivative of *kéntron* "sting, goad, point, stationary point of a pair of compasses, midpoint of a circle or sphere") + Latin *-icus* -ic. First known use: 1642.
examples: … book publishing's **eccentric** distribution system … — John Mutter

words.definition: A striptease performer; a word coined by H. L. Mencken from the Greek for moulting
words.origin: Ecdysi(s) + -ast. First known use: 1940.

words.definition: The formation of words by imitating sounds; also a word created in this manner
words.origin: From *echo* + *-ism*.

words.definition: Brilliant display or effect; conspicuous success; acclaim, as done with great eclat
words.origin: French, splinter, burst, éclat, from Old French *esclat* splinter. First known use: 1672.

words.definition: Drawing on a wide range of sources
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *eklektikós* "picking out, selecting what appears to be best," from *eklektós* "picked out, select" (verbal adjective of *eklégein* "to pick out, select," from *ek-* ec- + *légein* "to collect, gather, count, say") + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 1683.

words.definition: A vivid literary description of a work of art, real or imagined
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *ecphrasis,* borrowed from Greek *ékphrasis* "description," from *ekphrad-,* stem of *ekphrázein* "to tell over, recount, describe" (from *ek-* ec- + *phrázein* "to point out, show, tell, explain," of uncertain origin) + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 1715.

words.definition: Devouring; voracious; consuming everything in its path, as edacious time
words.origin: Latin *edac-, edax*, from *edere* to eat. First known use: circa 1798.

words.definition: To instruct or improve morally or intellectually
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *edifier*, from Late Latin & Latin; Late Latin *aedificare* to instruct or improve spiritually, from Latin, to erect a house, from *aedes* temple, house; akin to Old English *ād* funeral pyre, Latin *aestas* summer. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To erase; to make oneself inconspicuous
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *esfacer, effacer*, from *e-* + *face* face. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Bubbly; vivacious and enthusiastic
examples: She was a marvel with the press: fresh, direct, **effervescent**. — Bruce Anderson

words.definition: Weak and ineffectual; overrefined
words.origin: Latin *effetus*, from *ex-* + *fetus* fruitful. First known use: 1660.
examples: … the **effete** monarchies … of feudal Europe … — G. M. Trevelyan
… macrophages that recycle used iron from **effete** red cells. — Nancy C. Andrews

words.definition: Producing the intended result
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *efficace* "effective" or its source Latin *efficāc-, efficāx* "capable of fulfilling a function, effective" (from *efficere* "to make, bring about, produce, carry out" + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: The ability to produce a desired result
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *efficācia,* from *efficāc-, efficāx* "capable of fulfilling a function, efficacious" + *-ia* -y. First known use: 1527.
examples: The **efficacy** of this treatment has not yet been proved.

words.definition: A light, stroking massage
words.origin: French, from *effleurer* to touch lightly.

words.definition: To burst into flower; to reach an optimal stage of development; to blossom
words.origin: Latin *efflorescere*, from *ex-* + *florescere* to begin to blossom. First known use: 1775.
examples: Bricks may **effloresce** owing to the deposition of soluble salts

words.definition: The act of flowering; a peak of development
examples: … periods of … intellectual and artistic **efflorescence**. — Julian Huxley

words.definition: An unpleasant or harmful vapour or smell
words.origin: Latin *effluvium* act of flowing out, from *effluere*. First known use: 1651.

words.definition: Shameless boldness
words.origin: French *effronterie*, ultimately from Medieval Latin *effront-, effrons* shameless, from Latin *ex-* + *front-, frons* forehead. First known use: 1641.

words.definition: Shining brightly; radiant
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *effulgentia* "radiance," noun derivative of Latin *effulgent-, effulgens,* present participle of *effulgēre* "to shine or blaze forth, flash," from *ef-,* variant before *f* of *ex-* ex-:1 + *fulgēre* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten". First known use: 1667.

words.definition: Gushing with feeling
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *effūsīvus* "generating profusely, lavish," from Latin *effūsus* (past participle of *effundere* "to pour out, discharge, expend") + *-īvus* -ive. First known use: circa 1687.

words.definition: Soon afterward; again; an archaic word beloved of Spenser and Coleridge
words.origin: Middle English *eftsones*, alteration of Old English *eftsōna*, from Old English *eft* after + *sōna* soon; akin to Old English *æfter* after. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Outstandingly bad; shocking
words.origin: Latin *egregius*, from *e-* + *greg-, grex* herd. First known use: circa 1550.
examples: Is there one lie that seems to be the most repeated or, in your view, is the most **egregious**? — Meredith Blake
**Egregious** padding of the evidence — Christopher Hitchens

words.definition: The action of going out of or leaving a place; a way out; an exit
words.origin: Latin *egressus*, from *egredi* to go out, from *e-* + *gradi* to go. First known use: 1530.

words.definition: Able to recall images in vivid and precise detail, as if still seeing them
words.origin: Greek *eidētikos* of a form, from *eidos* form. First known use: 1888.

words.definition: An idealized person or thing; a spectre or phantom; an insubstantial image
words.origin: Greek *eidōlon*. First known use: 1763.

words.definition: The dark grey seen in total darkness
words.origin: German, intrinsic grey.

words.definition: A description of or commentary on a work of visual art
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *ecphrasis,* borrowed from Greek *ékphrasis* "description," from *ekphrad-,* stem of *ekphrázein* "to tell over, recount, describe" (from *ek-* ec- + *phrázein* "to point out, show, tell, explain," of uncertain origin) + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 1715.

words.definition: Ecstatically happy
words.origin: Latin *elatus* (past participle of *efferre* to carry out, elevate), from *e-* + *latus*, past participle of *ferre* to carry. First known use: 1638.

words.definition: Weird and sinister or ghostly
words.origin: Perhaps from Middle English **elfriche* fairyland, from Middle English *elf* + *riche* kingdom, from Old English *rīce*. First known use: 1508.
examples: And the woman, whose voice had risen to a kind of **eldritch** singsong, turned with a skip, and was gone. — Robert Louis Stevenson
… the film works its whimsically **eldritch** spell through inspired casting, brilliant editing, and subtly astonishing special effects … — Ty Burr

words.definition: Relating to or dependent on charity; charitable, as an eleemosynary foundation
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *eleēmosynārius,* from *eleēmosyna* "charitable gift, act of charity" (borrowed from Greek *eleēmosýnē* "pity, act of kindness, alms," from *eleḗmōn* "compassionate" —adjective derivative of *eleeîn* "to take pity on," derivative of *éleos* "pity, compassion," of uncertain origin— + *-synē,* abstract noun suffix) + Latin *-ārius* -ary. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: A mournful poem, often for the dead
words.origin: Latin *elegia* poem in elegiac couplets, from Greek *elegeia, elegeion*, from *elegos* song of mourning. First known use: 1501.

words.definition: An intense desire for freedom
words.origin: From Greek *eleutheros* free + *mania*.

words.definition: A tangled lock of hair, as if knotted by elves in the night while one slept
To omit a sound or syllable when speaking; to merge or suppress
words.origin: Latin *elidere* to strike out, from *e-* + *laedere* to injure by striking. First known use: 1540.

words.definition: To remove to a distance; to conceal or carry off, especially property
words.origin: Middle English *eloynen*, from Anglo-French *esloigner, eloigner*, from *es-* ex- (from Latin *ex-*) + *luin, loing* (adverb) far, from Latin *longe*, from *longus* long. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Fluent and persuasive in speech
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *ēloquent-, ēloquens* "capable of speech, expressing oneself fluently," from present participle of *ēloquī* "to utter, put into words," from *ē-* e-:1 + *loquī* "to talk, speak," probably going back to dialectal Indo-European **tlokw-* "talk," whence also Old Irish *ad-tluichethar* "(s/he) gives thanks" (originally with *buide* "thanks" as object, as in *atluchedar buidi do Día* "he thanks God"), *do-tluichethar* "(s/he) desires, beseeches, asks," Old Church Slavic *tlŭk* "interpreter" (from **tl̥kw-o-*). First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: At another time
words.origin: From *else* + *when*.

words.definition: In a different direction
words.origin: From *else* + *whither*.

words.definition: To make clear; explain
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *ēlūcidātus,* past participle of *ēlūcidāre* "to enlighten, explain," from Latin *ē-,* variant of *ex-* ex-:1 + *-lūcidāre,* derivative of *lūcidus* "bright, shining, clear to the understanding". First known use: circa 1568.

words.definition: Difficult to find, catch or grasp
words.origin: Latin *ēlūsus,* past participle of *ēlūdere* "to trick, avoid, elude" + -ive. First known use: 1725.

words.definition: Blissful or heavenly, like Elysium, the ancient paradise of the blessed
examples: The stillness, the repose, the peace, / They win the quiet soul away, / To visit that **Elysian** world, / Where breaketh an eternal day.
Reading … transports the subconscious to **elysian** and empyrean bliss. — Bobson Gbinije

words.definition: To decorate; to add fictitious detail
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *embeliss-*, stem of *embelir*, from *en-* + *bel* beautiful. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To make larger
words.origin: Em- + big + -en. First known use: 1996.
examples: This incredible chart was the final product. (Click to **embiggen**.) — Erik Malinowski

words.definition: Plumpness or fleshiness, especially a woman's full bosom; stoutness
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from *en bon point* in good condition. First known use: 1670.

words.definition: A liquid rubbed on the body to relieve muscular pain; a liniment
words.origin: Middle English *embrocacioun*, from Middle French *embrocacion*, from Medieval Latin *embrocation-, embrocatio*, from Late Latin *embrocare* to rub with lotion, from Greek *embroche* lotion, from *en-* + *brechein* to wet. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Famous and respected
words.origin: Middle English, "standing out, exceed other things in quality or degree," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, "high, lofty" (also continental Old French), borrowed from Latin *ēminent-, ēminens* "standing out above a surface, projecting, outstanding in merit or importance," from present participle of *ēminēre* "to stick out, protrude, project, be preeminent, excel," from *ē-,* variant of *ex-* ex-:1 + *-minēre,* taken to mean "stand out, rise above" (unattested without a prefix). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Soothing; attempting to calm
words.origin: Latin *emollient-, emolliens*, present participle of *emollire* to soften, from *e-* + *mollis* soft. First known use: 1612.
examples: … soothe us in our agonies with **emollient** words … — H. L. Mencken

words.definition: A salary, fee or profit from employment or office, usually in the plural
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *emolumentum* advantage, from *emolere* to produce by grinding, from *e-* + *molere* to grind. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To enclose in complete armour
words.origin: From *em-* + *panoply* full armour.

words.definition: Mania for holding public office
words.origin: From Spanish *empleomanía*, from *empleo* employment + *manía*.

words.definition: A display of warmth, eagerness or cordiality, as in greeting a guest
words.origin: French, from (*s'*)*empresser* to hurry, from *en-* + *presser* to press. First known use: 1709.

words.definition: Belonging to or deriving from the sky or highest heaven; celestial and sublime
words.origin: Late Latin *empyrius, empyreus*, from Late Greek *empyrios*, from Greek *em-* en-:2 + *pyr* fire. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The highest heaven; the sky
To match or surpass by imitation
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *aemulātus,* past participle of *aemulārī* "to vie with, rival, imitate," derivative of *aemulus* "rivaling, emulous". First known use: 1582.

words.definition: Eager to equal or outdo others
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *aemulus* "striving to equal or surpass, rivaling, envious," (as noun) "rival, competitor," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1535.

words.definition: In the open air, especially of painting
words.origin: French, in the open air.

words.definition: A deliberate grammatical mistake for effect
words.origin: From Greek *enallagē* interchange.

words.definition: The tendency of things, beliefs, etc., to change into their opposites
words.origin: From Greek *enantios* opposite + *dromos* running; used by Carl Jung.

words.definition: Pregnant; an enclosure or wall of fortification around a place
words.origin: French, perhaps from Vulgar Latin **incenta*, alteration of Latin *incient-, inciens* being with young, modification of Greek *enkyos* pregnant, from *en-* + *kyein* to be pregnant. First known use: 1602.

words.definition: The brain, the part of the central nervous system enclosed in the skull
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *enkephalos*. First known use: 1741.

words.definition: A handbook or manual containing essential information or a body of teaching
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *encheiridion*, from *en* in + *cheir* hand. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A person who delivers high praise in speech or writing; a eulogist or flatterer
words.origin: Greek *enkōmiastēs*, from *enkōmiazein* to praise, from *enkōmion*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: A speech or text in high praise
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *enkōmion*, from *en* in + *kōmos* revel, celebration. First known use: 1567.

words.definition: To make dark, less clear or gloomy
words.origin: From *en-* + *darken*.

words.definition: From end to end; lengthwise
words.origin: Middle English *endelong*, alteration of *andlong*, from Old English *andlang* along, from *andlang*, preposition. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: The custom of marrying only within one's own group, clan or caste
A person possessed by a devil; a fanatical enthusiast or zealot
words.origin: From Greek *energoumenos* one worked on by a spirit.

words.definition: To drain of energy or vitality
words.origin: Latin *enervatus*, past participle of *enervare*, from *e-* + *nervus* sinew. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: Drained of energy or vitality; exhausted
words.origin: Latin *enervatus*, past participle of *enervare*, from *e-* + *nervus* sinew. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: A volley of gunfire directed along a line from end to end; rooms in a row
words.origin: French, from *enfiler* to thread, enfilade, from Old French, to thread, from *en-* + *fil* thread. First known use: circa 1730.

words.definition: To cause or give rise to
words.origin: Middle English *engendren*, from Anglo-French *engendrer*, from Latin *ingenerare*, from *in-* + *generare* to generate. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A mysterious person or thing
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *aenigmat-, aenigma* "obscure expression, riddle," borrowed from Greek *ainigmat-, aínigma* "statement phrased in oblique or allusive language, riddle, puzzle," derivative with the resultative suffix *-mat-, -ma* from the base of *ainíssomai, ainíssesthai* "to hint at a truth, speak in obscure language, hint at, allude to," derivative of *aînos* "tale, allegory, riddle," of obscure origin. First known use: 1539.
examples: Before the Apollo program, the origin of the moon was an **enigma**. — Eva Botkin-Kowacki
How frustrated profile writers sum him up: "He remains an **enigma**."

words.definition: The running of a sentence from one line of verse into the next without a pause
words.origin: French *enjambement*, from Middle French, encroachment, from *enjamber* to straddle, encroach on, from *en-* + *jambe* leg. First known use: circa 1839.

words.definition: Deep hostility
words.origin: Middle English *enmite*, from Anglo-French *enemité, enemisté*, from *enemi* enemy. First known use: 14th century.
examples: There's a long history of **enmity** between them.
… as personal **enmities** go, they don't get much more vicious than this. — Richard Innes

words.definition: Listless weariness from lack of interest
words.origin: French, from Old French *enui* annoyance, from *enuier* to vex, from Late Latin *inodiare* to make loathsome. First known use: 1732.
examples: Suffered from a general sense of **ennui**
… chronicling the existential **ennui** of modern life … — Eli Glasner

words.definition: Bored; weary of everything
words.origin: French, bored.

words.definition: To fill with intense delight
To enchant or fascinate someone, as if by sorcery; to bewitch
words.origin: Middle French *ensorceler*, alteration of Old French *ensorcerer*, from *en-* + *-sorcerer*, from *sorcier, sorcer* sorcerer. First known use: circa 1541.

words.definition: A short closing stanza of a poem, often addressed to a patron
words.origin: Middle English *envoye*, from Middle French *envoi*, literally, message, from Old French *envei*, from *enveier* to send on one's way, from Vulgar Latin **inviare*, from Latin *in-* + *via* way. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Relating to or caused by the wind
words.origin: Latin *Aeolus*, Aeolus. First known use: 1622.

words.definition: Lasting for eons; everlasting
words.origin: From *eon* + *-ian*. *Eon*: Borrowed from Late Latin *aeōn* "age (in the world's history), evil spirit (in Gnosticism)," borrowed from Greek *aiṓn* "lifetime, long period of time, age".

words.definition: Correcting oneself mid-sentence for emphasis
words.origin: From Greek *epanorthōsis* correction.

words.definition: The worship of words
words.origin: From Greek *epos* word + *latreia* worship.

words.definition: An ornamental centrepiece for a dining table, with several branches or bowls
words.origin: Probably from French *épargne* saving. First known use: 1754.

words.definition: A young man of 18 to 20 in ancient Greece, in training for citizenship; a youth
words.origin: Latin *ephebus*. First known use: 1880.

words.definition: Things that last only a short time
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *ephēmera*, neuter plural of *ephēmeros*. First known use: 1650.

words.definition: Lasting a very short time
words.origin: Greek *ephēmeros* lasting a day, daily, from *epi-* + *hēmera* day. First known use: 1576.
examples: Their fame turned out to be **ephemeral**.
… the **ephemeral** nature of journalism … — Evelyn Toynton

words.definition: Something short-lived; an insect, such as a mayfly, that lives for only a day
words.origin: From Greek *ephēmeron*, from *epi* upon + *hēmera* day.

words.definition: Taking joy in the misfortune of others
words.origin: From Greek *epichairekakia*, from *epi* upon + *chara* joy + *kakon* evil.

words.definition: Having characteristics of both sexes or of neither; effete or effeminate
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *epicoenus*, from Greek *epikoinos*, from *epi-* + *koinos* common. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A quotation followed by a commentary upon it
words.origin: From Greek *epikrisis* determination.

words.definition: A person devoted to refined food and drink
words.origin: *Epicurus*. First known use: 1551.

words.definition: A less distinguished follower or imitator of an artist or philosopher
words.origin: German, from Latin *epigonus* successor, from Greek *epigonos*, from *epigignesthai* to be born after, from *epi-* + *gignesthai* to be born. First known use: 1865.

words.definition: A short, witty saying
words.origin: Middle English *epigrame,* borrowed from Latin *epigrammat-, epigramma* "inscription, epitaph, epigram," borrowed from Greek *epigrammat-, epígramma* "inscription on a tomb, monument or work of art" (Late Greek, "short poem, epigram"), from *epigráphein* "to mark the surface of, graze, scratch a mark on, inscribe" (from *epi-* epi- + *gráphein* "to cut into, scratch, inscribe, write") + *-mat-, -ma,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A sudden, striking realization
words.origin: Middle English *Epiphanie,* borrowed from Anglo-French *Epiphane, Epiphanie,* borrowed from Late Latin *epiphanīa, epiphania* "appearance, manifestation, Christ's first manifestation (to the Gentiles in Western tradition)," borrowed from Late Greek *epipháneia* "appearance, manifestation (of God in the Old Testament, of Christ's first coming or of the Second Coming)," going back to Greek, "appearance, coming into view, manifestation (of a deity to a worshipper), Christ's coming (in the New Testament), visible surface, outward show, fame," noun derivative of *epiphanḗs* "coming into view, appearing, manifest, evident," adjective derivative from the stem of *epiphaínein* "to show, display," mediopassive *epiphaínesthai* "to come into view, be manifested, appear on the surface," from *epi-* epi- + *phaínein* "to bring to light, cause to appear," *phaínesthai* "to become visible, appear". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … the experience is an **epiphany** whereby the true essence of cooking is revealed. — John Mariani

words.definition: Relating to knowledge or to the degree of its validation, as epistemic doubt
words.origin: Greek *epistḗmē* "skill, expertise, knowledge, scientific knowledge (as opposed to practical skill)" + -ic; *epistḗmē,* from *epístamai, epístasthai* "to have the skill, know how (with infinitive), have knowledge of, understand" (from *epi-* epi- + Greek *hístēmi, histánai* "to cause to stand, place," middle voice *hístamai, hístasthai* "to take up a position, come and stand") + *-mē,* abstract noun suffix. First known use: 1922.

words.definition: Written in the form of letters
examples: … an endless sequence of … **epistolary** love affairs.

words.definition: The art or practice of letter writing, as once taught in rhetoric
words.origin: From Greek *epistolē* letter + *-graphia* writing.

words.definition: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a name
words.origin: Latin *epitheton*, from Greek, from neuter of *epithetos* added, from *epitithenai* to put on, add, from *epi-* + *tithenai* to put. First known use: 1579.

words.definition: A perfect example
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *epitomē*, from *epitemnein* to cut short, from *epi-* + *temnein* to cut. First known use: 1520.
examples: … J. D. Salinger managed to forge, in Holden Caulfield, the **epitome** of American adolescent disgruntlement for decades of young readers … — Laura Miller
Utilizing his summary but expanding upon it, I present my own **epitome** of the book … — David B. Ruderman

words.definition: Repeating a word in quick succession for emphasis
words.origin: From Greek *epizeuxis* fastening together.

words.definition: Skill or proficiency in a situation or a task
words.origin: A back-formation from *ineptitude*.

words.definition: Calmness and composure, especially under strain
words.origin: Latin *aequanimitas*, from *aequo animo* with even mind. First known use: 1663.

words.definition: Calm and even-tempered
words.origin: From Latin *aequanimis*, from *aequus* even + *animus* mind.

words.definition: Balance of forces or interests; a counterbalance or equilibrium
Equal in power, force, effect
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *aequipollent-, aequipollens*, from *aequi-* equi- + *pollent-, pollens*, present participle of *pollēre* to be able. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Ambiguous; open to more than one interpretation
words.origin: Late Latin *aequivocus*, from *aequi-* equi- + *voc-, vox* voice. First known use: 1599.
