words.definition: To speak ambiguously to avoid commitment
, conjunction Before (earlier in time)
words.origin: Middle English *er*, from Old English *ǣr*, from *ǣr*, adverb, early, soon; akin to Old High German *ēr* earlier, Greek *ēri* early. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: 'The wind is north from the snows,' said Aragorn. 'And **ere** morning it will be in the East,' said Legolas. — J. R. R. Tolkien

words.definition: A hermit or recluse, especially a Christian one living alone in the desert
words.origin: From Middle English *eremite*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: The fear of being alone
words.origin: From Greek *erēmos* lonely + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Opposed to machines and technology, like a Luddite
words.origin: From Samuel Butler's satire *Erewhon*, an anagram of *nowhere*.

words.definition: An extreme or irrational fear of work, often used jokingly
words.origin: From Greek *ergon* work + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Of or characterized by debate or argument for its own sake, rather than for truth
words.origin: Greek *eristikos* fond of wrangling, from *erizein* to wrangle, from *eris* strife. First known use: 1637.
examples: We have frequently devolved … into **eristic** argument: conversations devoid of reason, logic, and evidence replaced by name-calling … — Irvin Peckham

words.definition: A deeply felt experience
words.origin: German, experience, from *erleben* to live through.

words.definition: Irregularly notched or jagged
words.origin: Latin *erosus*, past participle of *erodere*. First known use: 1793.

words.definition: Aveling, especially in search of adventure
words.origin: Middle English *erraunt* "wandering, itinerant, notorious, reprobate," borrowed from Anglo-French *errant,* present participle of *errer* "to journey, travel, behave, act, fare" (continental Old French also *edrer, esrer*) going back to early Medieval Latin *iterāre,* re-formation (after the base noun *iter*) of Late Latin *itinerārī* "to travel"; in sense 1 influenced by Middle French & French *errant,* present participle of *errer* "to go off course, be deceived or mistaken," going back to Latin *errāre*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Formerly: in the past
words.origin: Middle English *erest* earliest, formerly, from Old English *ǣrest*, superlative of *ǣr* early. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: Former
words.origin: Erst + *while* "at one time, formerly," going back to Middle English, going back to Old English *hwīle,* accusative of *hwīl* while. First known use: 1569.
examples: … cultures, **erstwhile** unknown to each other … — Robert Plank

words.definition: A belch
Having or showing great learning
words.origin: Middle English *erudit*, from Latin *eruditus*, from past participle of *erudire* to instruct, from *e-* + *rudis* rude, ignorant. First known use: 15th century.
examples: There was the **erudite**-but-humble professor next door and upstairs. — Maria Shine Stewart
In the telling of a life lived through books, and in her own sometimes floridly **erudite** sentences, the deep magic of writing is revealed. — Nina Renata Aron

words.definition: Great learning and knowledge
Bursting forth; breaking through a surface, as some fungi do
words.origin: From Latin *erumpere* to break out.

words.definition: Theology concerned with death, judgment and the final destiny of humankind
words.origin: Greek *eschatos* last, farthest. First known use: 1838.

words.definition: To deliberately avoid
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *eschiver* (3rd present *eschiu*) of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *sciuhen* to frighten off. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Some investigative efforts avoid risk by **eschewing** anonymous sources …

words.definition: A small writing desk with drawers and compartments for papers and letters
words.origin: Obsolete French, writing desk, scriptorium, from Medieval Latin *scriptorium*. First known use: 1664.

words.definition: Fit to be used as food; edible, especially of plants and roots
words.origin: Latin *esculentus*, from *esca* food, from *edere* to eat. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: Having the capability of moulding diverse ideas or things into unity
words.origin: Greek *es hen* into one + English *plastic*. First known use: 1817.
examples: The **esemplastic** power of the poetic imagination … — W. H. Gardner

words.definition: Understood only by a small group
words.origin: Late Latin *esotericus*, from Greek *esōterikos*, from *esōterō*, comparative of *eisō, esō* within, from *eis* into; akin to Greek *en* in. First known use: circa 1660.
examples: … a body of **esoteric** legal doctrine … — Benjamin N. Cardozo
The titles of some concert tours can be a bit **esoteric**. — Matt Wake

words.definition: A fruit tree or shrub trained to grow flat against a wall or trellis
words.origin: French, ultimately from Italian *spalla* shoulder, from Late Latin *spatula* shoulder blade. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: Belonging to or appearing in summer, as estival flowers or heat
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French or Latin; Anglo-French, from Latin *aestivalis*, from *aestivus* of summer, from *aestas* summer. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To spend a hot or dry season in a dormant state, as some animals do
examples: Snails combat desiccation by **estivating**, that is, burrowing into the mud and sealing up the shell with mucus until conditions improve. — Mark Woolhouse
… I asked him to Skype in from the Connecticut coastline, where he is **estivating** while on a prestigious writing fellowship … — Glen Weldon

words.definition: Relating to or found in an estuary, where a river meets the sea
Hungry or greedy; eager to devour, whether food, wealth or knowledge
words.origin: Latin *esurient-, esuriens*, present participle of *esurire* to be hungry; akin to Latin *edere* to eat. First known use: circa 1672.

words.definition: One who believes the soul is immortal
words.origin: From *eternity* + *-arian*.

words.definition: Extremely delicate and light; heavenly
examples: … the rise of a peaking full moon, which bathed the wild shore in an **ethereal** glow. — Simon Peter Groebner
… a wood thrush sang its **ethereal** song. — Taylor Piephoff

words.definition: The science of animal behaviour, especially in natural conditions
words.origin: Greek *ethos* + English *-logy*. First known use: 1843.

words.definition: Pale and drawn out from lack of light; feeble, weakened or lacking vigour
words.origin: French *étioler*. First known use: 1784.

words.definition: A sudden happy turn that rescues a story from looming disaster
words.origin: Coined by J. R. R. Tolkien from Greek *eu-* good + *katastrophē* overturning.

words.definition: A state of happiness and flourishing, especially from a virtuous life
words.origin: From Greek *eudaimonia*, from *eu-* good + *daimōn* spirit.

words.definition: A state of flourishing and true well-being
words.origin: Greek, from *eu-* good + *daimōn* spirit.

words.definition: The idea that gods are based on historical heroes whose stories became exaggerated in retelling
words.origin: *Euhemerus*, 4th century b.c. Greek mythographer. First known use: 1788.

words.definition: Fortunate through being good or innocent; lucky in a deserved way
words.origin: From Greek *eumoiros* fortunate, from *eu-* good + *moira* fate.

words.definition: Peace of mind after a pleasant dream
words.origin: From Greek *eu-* good + *oneiros* dream + *phrēn* mind.

words.definition: Beautiful thinking; goodwill toward others
words.origin: Greek, goodwill, from *eu-* good + *nous* mind.

words.definition: A mild word used in place of a harsh one
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *euphēmismus,* borrowed from Greek *euphēmismós* "substitution of an auspicious word for an inauspicious one," from *euphēmízesthai* "to use words of good omen" (from *eúphēmos* "uttering sounds of good omen, fair-sounding, auspicious" + *-izesthai,* middle voice of *-izein* -ize) + *-ismos* -ism; *eúphēmos* from *eu-* eu- + *-phēmos,* nominal derivative, with a suffixal *-m-,* from the base of *phēmí, phánai* "to say, speak". First known use: 1656.
examples: "Privy" and "closet" are examples of **euphemism** by metonymy … — Daniel Balado-Lopez

words.definition: Pleasing to the ear
words.origin: Late Latin *euphōnia* euphony + -ous. First known use: 1774.

words.definition: Pleasing sound, especially in words
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *euphōnia,* borrowed from Greek *euphōnía* "good voice quality (of a public speaker), good tone (of horns)," from *eúphōnos* "pleasant-sounding, musical" (from *eu-* eu- + *-phōnos* "having a sound [of the kind specified]," adjective derivative of *phōnḗ* "sound made by something living, voice, speech") + *-ia* -ia. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: Intensely happy and excited
words.origin: From *euphoria*, New Latin, from Greek *euphoros* healthy, from *eu-* well + *pherein* to bear.
examples: He knew he was going to win big, big, big, and he was **euphoric** about it. — Russell Baker

words.definition: An artificial, highly elaborate way of writing or speaking, after Lyly's Euphues
words.origin: *Euphues*, character in prose romances by John Lyly. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: Affectedly elaborate in style
words.origin: *Euphues*, character in prose romances by John Lyly. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: A positive, beneficial form of stress
words.origin: Eu- + stress. First known use: 1968.
examples: … during positive stress ("**eustress**"), such as a promotion or vacation, feel-good chemicals called endorphins are released. — Tracy Boyd

words.definition: A calm, steady and contented state of mind
words.origin: Greek, cheerfulness, from *eu-* good + *thymos* spirit.

words.definition: Pleasantness of the sound of a word
words.origin: From Greek *eutonos* well strung.

words.definition: Liveliness and ease of conversation
words.origin: From Greek *eutrapelia* wit, from *eu-* well + *trepein* to turn.

words.definition: To fade away like vapour
words.origin: Latin *evanescere*. First known use: 1822.

words.definition: The quality of quickly fading from sight
words.origin: From *evanescent*. *Evanescent*: Latin *evanescent-, evanescens*, present participle of *evanescere*. First known use: 1751.

words.definition: Quickly fading from sight or memory
words.origin: Latin *evanescent-, evanescens*, present participle of *evanescere*. First known use: 1717.

words.definition: The evening time
To make worse
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *exacerbātus,* past participle of *exacerbāre* "to irritate, exasperate, make worse," from *ex-* ex-:1 + *acerbāre* "to make bitter, make worse," verbal derivative of *acerbus* "acid, bitter, bitterly hostile, distressing". First known use: 1660.
examples: A skin condition **exacerbated** by too much sun
The new law only **exacerbates** the unemployment problem.

words.definition: Lifeless; spiritless
words.origin: Latin *exanimatus*, past participle of *exanimare* to deprive of life or spirit, from *ex-* + *anima* breath, soul. First known use: circa 1534.

words.definition: The removing of flesh, especially from a corpse before burial
words.origin: From Latin *ex-* out of + *caro* flesh.

words.definition: Ever upward
words.origin: Trade name, from Latin, higher, comparative of *excelsus* high, from past participle of *excellere*. First known use: 1868.

words.definition: To criticize severely, as a reviewer may excoriate a book; to strip or abrade the skin
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *excoriatus*, past participle of *excoriare*, from Latin *ex-* + *corium* skin, hide. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: On guard
words.origin: From Latin *excubans*, present participle of *excubare* to keep watch.

words.definition: To clear from blame
words.origin: Medieval Latin *exculpatus*, past participle of *exculpare*, from Latin *ex-* + *culpa* blame. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: Extremely bad or unpleasant
words.origin: From *execrate* + *-able*. *Execrate*: Latin *exsecratus*, past participle of *exsecrari* to put under a curse, from *ex* + *sacr-, sacer* sacred. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Critical explanation of a text
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *exēgēsis,* borrowed from Greek *exḗgēsis* "detailed account, description, exposition," from *exēgē-,* variant stem of *exēgéomai, exēgeîsthai* "to lead forth, direct, prescribe, order, dictate, expound, explain, relate" (from *ex-* ex-:3 + *hēgeîsthai* "to lead, act as guide, rule, consider, believe") + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 1627.
examples: As an **exegesis**, though, it's nicely done, and Kennedy traces Sontag's main themes deftly along tortuous paths through both essays and fiction. — Larissa MacFarquhar

words.definition: Serving as a model
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *exemplāris,* with ending conformed to -ary. First known use: circa 1507.
examples: … they serve **exemplary** pastries … — G. V. Higgins
This story is **exemplary** of her style.

words.definition: An example or model
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, example. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Pressing; demanding
words.origin: Latin *exigent-, exigens*, present participle of *exigere* to demand. First known use: 1624.

words.definition: Very small in size or amount; scanty or meagre, as an exiguous income
words.origin: Latin *exiguus*, from *exigere*. First known use: 1630.
examples: Wrest an **exiguous** existence from the land

words.definition: Obsolete
words.origin: From Latin *exoletus*, past participle of *exolescere* to grow out of use.

words.definition: To clear of blame
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *exoneratus*, past participle of *exonerare* to unburden, from *ex-* + *oner-, onus* load. First known use: 1524.

words.definition: Unreasonably high, as a price; far beyond what is fair
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *exorbitant-, exorbitans*, present participle of *exorbitare* to deviate, from Latin *ex-* + *orbita* track of a wheel, rut, from *orbis* disk, hoop. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The beginning or introduction of a speech or treatise, meant to win the audience
words.origin: Latin, from *exordiri* to begin, from *ex-* + *ordiri* to begin. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: To speak or write at length or in detail, as on a favourite subject
words.origin: Latin *exspatiatus*, past participle of *exspatiari* to wander, digress, from *ex-* + *spatium* space, course. First known use: circa 1552.
examples: … **expatiating** upon the value of the fabric … — Thomas Hardy

words.definition: Convenient though perhaps improper
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French or Latin; Anglo-French, from Latin *expedient-, expendiens*, present participle of *expedire* to extricate, prepare, be useful, from *ex-* + *ped-, pes* foot. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Awakening or arousing
words.origin: From Latin *expergefacere* to awaken.

words.definition: To atone for guilt or sin
words.origin: Latin *expiatus*, past participle of *expiare* to atone for, from *ex-* + *piare* to atone for, appease, from *pius* faithful, pious. First known use: circa 1500.
examples: … permission to **expiate** their offences by their assiduous labours … — Francis Bacon

words.definition: To erase or remove completely
words.origin: Latin *expungere* to mark for deletion by dots, from *ex-* + *pungere* to prick. First known use: 1602.

words.definition: To drain of blood, as in surgery or slaughter; to become bloodless
words.origin: Latin *exsanguinatus* drained of blood, from *ex-* + *sanguin-, sanguis* blood. First known use: 1833.

words.definition: Spoken or done without preparation
words.origin: Late Latin *extemporāneus* "done on the spur of the moment" (from Latin *ex tempore* "on the spur of the moment, extempore" + *-āneus,* suffix forming adjectives from temporal adverbs) + -ous. First known use: 1673.
examples: A great deal of criminal and delinquent behaviour is … **extemporaneous**. — W. C. Reckless

words.definition: To destroy completely; root out
words.origin: Latin *exstirpatus*, past participle of *exstirpare*, from *ex-* + *stirp-, stirps* trunk, root. First known use: 1538.

words.definition: To praise enthusiastically
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *extollere*, from *ex-* + *tollere* to lift up. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Irrelevant; unrelated
words.origin: Latin *extrāneus* "not belonging to one's family or household, coming from abroad, foreign, external" + -ous. First known use: 1638.

words.definition: To shed or cast off
words.origin: From Latin *exuviae* cast skins.

words.definition: A small island in a river, especially in the Thames; also spelled ait
words.origin: From Old English *īgeth*, diminutive of *īeg* island.

words.definition: A person who composes fables; a liar, especially one who invents elaborate stories
words.origin: Probably borrowed from Middle French *fabuliste,* from Latin *fābula* "talk, account, fable" + French *-iste* -ist. First known use: 1593.

words.definition: Treating serious matters with flippant humour
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *facetieux, facecieux,* from *facetie* "joke, jesting remark" (borrowed from Latin *facētia, facētiae* "cleverness, wit," in plural sense, "amusing things, jests") + *-eux* (going back to Latin *-ōsus* -ous). First known use: 1594.
examples: … a … possibly **facetious** suggestion that Texas should secede if Washington doesn't ease off … — Todd J. Gillman

words.definition: Easily done; overly simple, glib or superficial
words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *facilis* "easy, accommodating, nimble," from *fac-,* stem of *facere* "to make, bring about, perform, do" + *-ilis* -ile. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … I am not concerned … with offering any **facile** solution for so complex a problem … — T. S. Eliot

words.definition: Atrociously wicked or villainous; capable of heinous crimes
words.origin: From Latin *facinorosus*, from *facinus* crime.

words.definition: An employee who does all kinds of work
words.origin: From the Latin phrase *fac tōtum* "do all!", from *fac* (singular imperative of *facere* "to make, do" + *tōtum* "the whole, entirety," from neuter of *tōtus* "all, the whole of"). First known use: 1562.

words.definition: A bright spot on the sun's surface, often appearing near sunspots
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, diminutive of *fac-, fax* torch. First known use: 1706.

words.definition: To waste time without accomplishing much
words.origin: English dialect, imitative of a puff of wind.

words.definition: With pleasure; gladly; willing or obliged under the circumstances
words.origin: Middle English *fagen, fayn*, from Old English *fægen*; akin to Old English *gefēon* to rejoice, Old High German *gifehan*, Old Norse *feginn* happy. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A backless couch for reclining
words.origin: From *fainting* + *couch*, a Victorian piece of furniture.

words.definition: A thing already done and beyond reversal
words.origin: French, accomplished fact. First known use: 1845.
examples: He charged that the members were presented with a **fait accompli** instead of being called to a meeting to discuss the policy change. — Daniel Thomases

words.definition: A cheat or impostor
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French, "maker, creator, agent, idler, waster," going back to Latin *factor* "maker, perpetrator". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Based on a mistaken belief
words.origin: From *fallacy* + *-ous*. *Fallacy*: Latin *fallacia*, from *fallac-, fallax* deceitful, from *fallere* to deceive. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Capable of making mistakes
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *fallibilis*, from Latin *fallere*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The annihilation of the self in divine love
words.origin: Arabic *fanāʼ* passing away, annihilation.

words.definition: A useless or fanciful ornament; nonsense or tomfoolery, said with scorn
words.origin: Perhaps an alteration of *fandango*.

words.definition: Arrogant or boastful talk; swaggering bluster; a flourish of trumpets
words.origin: French *fanfaronnade*, from Spanish *fanfarronada*, from *fanfarrón* braggart. First known use: 1652.

words.definition: A tangle; a muddle
words.origin: Scots, from *fank* a coil.

words.definition: To paint the face with cosmetics; to gloss over or disguise faults
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *farder*, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *faro* coloured. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A bundle or pack; a burden, especially of sorrow, as in Hamlet
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, ultimately from Arabic *farda* part, bundle. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Wild; fierce
words.origin: French, wild, shy, from Old French, alteration of *forasche*, from Late Latin *forasticus* living outside, from Latin *foras* outdoors; akin to Latin *fores* door. First known use: 1765.

words.definition: A confused mixture of things, as a farrago of lies; a hodgepodge or jumble
words.origin: Latin *farragin-, farrago* mixed fodder, mixture, from *far* spelt. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: A hooped petticoat or circular pad once worn to widen a skirt
words.origin: Modification of Middle French *verdugale*, from Old Spanish *verdugado*, from *verdugo* young shoot of a tree, from *verde* green, from Latin *viridis*. First known use: 1552.

words.definition: A separately published instalment of a book; a small bundle of fibres
words.origin: Latin *fasciculus*, diminutive of *fascis*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; fussy
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *fastidiosus*, from *fastidium* disgust, probably from *fastus* arrogance (probably akin to Latin *fastigium* top) + *taedium* irksomeness. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … regulators are guaranteed to take a **fastidious** approach in evaluating safety … — Alex Carchidi
… he took **fastidious** care of his cars. — Marga Lincoln

words.definition: A mirage seen over water
words.origin: Italian, literally, Morgan le Fay (sorceress of Arthurian legend). First known use: 1785.
examples: … had been taken in by a mirage known as a **Fata Morgana**, in which atmospheric conditions stretch, invert, and otherwise distort distant objects, making them appear taller. — Stanley A. Freed
The non-existent mountainous region in the Arctic called Crockerland … is an example of a **Fata Morgana**.

words.definition: Prophetic; relating to prophecy or the foretelling of fate, as an oracle's words
words.origin: Latin *fatidicus*, from *fatum* fate + *dicere* to say. First known use: 1607.

words.definition: Complacent foolishness or stupidity; a fatuous remark or act
words.origin: Middle French *fatuité* foolishness, from Latin *fatuitat-, fatuitas*, from *fatuus*. First known use: circa 1548.

words.definition: Silly and pointless
words.origin: Latin *fatuus* foolish. First known use: 1633.
examples: A **fatuous** socialite with a near-pathological love of parties and shopping — Janet Maslin

words.definition: Relating to the west wind
words.origin: Latin *favonianus*, from *Favonius*, the west wind. First known use: circa 1681.

words.definition: A feudal tenant's sworn loyalty to a lord; faithfulness and allegiance
words.origin: Middle English *feute, fealtye,* borrowed from Anglo-French *feelté, fealté,* going back to Latin *fidēlitāt-, fidēlitās* "faithfulness, loyalty". First known use: 14th century.
examples: The vassal vowed **fealty** to the king.
… the **fealty** of country music fans to their favourite stars … — Nicholas Dawidoff

words.definition: Having or showing the symptoms of a fever; feverishly excited or agitated
words.origin: Medieval Latin *febrilis*, from Latin *febris* fever. First known use: 1651.
examples: A **febrile** reaction caused by an allergy

words.definition: Fertile; intellectually productive
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *fecundus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Lacking initiative or strength of character
words.origin: From Scots, earlier *fectles* "valueless, futile," from *fek, fect* (later *feck*) "value, efficacy" (aphetic form of *effect* effect) + *-les* -less. First known use: circa 1585.
examples: She can't rely on her **feckless** son.
… a **feckless** maneuver that could only serve to strengthen the enemy … — Simon Schama

words.definition: The festive mood at the end of a working day
words.origin: German, from *Feier* celebration + *Abend* evening.

words.definition: Well chosen; apt
words.origin: From *felicity* + *-ous*. *Felicity*: Middle English *felicite*, from Anglo-French *felicité*, from Latin *felicitat-, felicitas*, from *felic-, felix* fruitful, happy. First known use: 1789.
examples: Handled the delicate matter in a most **felicitous** manner
The ride through the countryside is a **felicitous** journey for city people.

words.definition: A high, barren hill or moor
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English; akin to Old High German *fel* skin, Latin *pellis*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Low, marshy land
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *fenn*; akin to Old High German *fenna* fen, Sanskrit *paṅka* mud. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: The arrangement of windows in a building; an opening made in a membrane
words.origin: From *fenestrate* + *-ion*. *Fenestrate*: Latin *fenestratus*, from *fenestra*. First known use: 1846.

words.definition: Relating to ordinary weekdays, not feast days
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *feria*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An ache for distant places
words.origin: German, from *fern* far + *Weh* ache.

words.definition: A metal cap or ring that strengthens the end of a handle, stick or tube
words.origin: Alteration of Middle English *virole*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *viriola*, diminutive of *viria* bracelet, of Celtic origin; akin to Old Irish *fiar* oblique. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Intensely passionate
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, from Latin *fervent-, fervens*, present participle of *fervēre* to boil, froth. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … they've built one of the most **fervent** fan bases in electronic music … — Niyaz Pirani

words.definition: Intensely enthusiastic, sometimes excessively
words.origin: Latin *fervidus*, from *fervēre*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Intense and passionate feeling
words.origin: Middle English *fervour*, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *fervur*, from Latin *fervor*, from *fervēre*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … booing and cheering with almost equal **fervour** … — Alan Rich

words.definition: Scurrilous or obscene, like the bawdy verses sung at Roman weddings
words.origin: Latin *fescennini* (*versus*), ribald songs sung at rustic weddings, probably from *Fescinninus* of Fescennium, from *Fescennium*, town in Etruria. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: A chain of flowers or ribbons hung in a curve; to adorn lavishly
words.origin: From French *feston*, from Italian *festone* festive ornament.

words.definition: Of a pale yellow or straw-like colour
words.origin: From Latin *festuca* stalk, straw.

words.definition: Smelling extremely unpleasant
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *foetidus*, from *foetēre* to stink. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To restrain or restrict
words.origin: Middle English *feter*, from Old English; akin to Old English *fōt* foot. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Condition or state of health and spirits, as in fine fettle; to put in order
words.origin: Fettle. First known use: 1740.
examples: I proved to her I was **in fine fettle** by consuming a herculean portion of eggs scrambled with onions and smoked salmon. — Lawrence Sanders

He stopped practicing or even warming up before tournament rounds in order to spare strain on the risky hip. His golf game was nonetheless **in fine fettle**—provided he could keep swinging. — Alfred Wright

words.definition: The colour of a faded, dead leaf
words.origin: French *feuille morte* dead leaf.

words.definition: A section of a newspaper given to fiction, criticism or light literature
words.origin: French, from *feuillet* sheet of paper, from Old French *foillet*, diminutive of *foille* leaf. First known use: 1845.

words.definition: Otherworldly and whimsical
words.origin: Middle English *feye*, from Old English *fǣge*; akin to Old High German *feigi* doomed and perhaps to Old English *fāh* hostile, outlawed. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: … another and lesser man … gave a **fey** lonely warning. — Hodding Carter
Not being **fey**, he never suspected what it would lead to.

words.definition: An authoritative decree
words.origin: Latin, let it be done, 3rd singular present subjunctive of *fieri* to become, be done. First known use: circa 1631.
examples: According to the Bible, the world was created by **fiat**.

words.definition: Trivial matters; nonsense; to fuss or trifle over things of no importance
words.origin: Reduplication of *fiddle* (fiddlesticks). First known use: 1577.

words.definition: The bow with which the fiddle is played
Involving trust, especially one person acting for another in money matters
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *fīdūciārius* "holding in trust, of a trustee, (of property) held on trust," from *fīdūcia* "transference of a property on trust, trust, reliance, confidence" (from **fīdūcus* "trusting" —from *fīdere* "to trust [in], have confidence [in]" + *-ūcus,* deverbal adjective suffix— + *-ia* -ia) + *-ārius* -ary. First known use: circa 1641.

words.definition: A break for coffee, cake and conversation
words.origin: Swedish, from a back-slang reversal of *kaffi* coffee.

words.definition: A slender thread or fibre
words.origin: Middle French, from Medieval Latin *filamentum*, from Late Latin *filare* to spin. First known use: 1594.

words.definition: To pilfer or steal something, especially something of small value
words.origin: From Middle English *filch*. First known use: 1561.

words.definition: The fact of being descended or derived from someone or something
Excessively reverent toward one's ancestors, forebears or tradition
words.origin: *fil*ial + *-o-* + *pietistic*. First known use: 1893.

words.definition: Hanging by a thread
words.origin: From Latin *filum* thread + *pendulus* hanging.

words.definition: To obtain something by devious or dishonest means; to wangle
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of *fainaigue* to renege. First known use: circa 1924.
examples: He **finagled** his way into the concert.
I have long craved a convention where someone had to wheel and deal, … maneuver and **finagle**, to win the crown. — Mark Plotkin

words.definition: A post with one or more signs pointing toward one or more places
A decorative ornament at the top of a spire, gable, post or lamp
words.origin: Middle English, from *final, finial* final. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Shunning endings; avoiding the end of things
words.origin: From Latin *finis* end + *fugere* to flee.

words.definition: One who stirs others to passion for a cause
A small cask used for liquids, butter or fish; a quarter-barrel
words.origin: Middle English, ultimately from Middle Dutch *veerdel* fourth, from *veer* four; akin to Old English *fēower*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The vault of the sky
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin & Latin; Late Latin *firmamentum*, from Latin, support, from *firmare*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: She's a rising star in the city's artistic **firmament**.

words.definition: To astonish greatly
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1772.
examples: We were **flabbergasted** by the news that he had won the lottery.

words.definition: To flog or whip, especially as religious discipline or punishment
words.origin: Latin *flagellatus*, past participle of *flagellare*, from *flagellum*, diminutive of *flagrum* whip; perhaps akin to Old Norse *blaka* to wave. First known use: circa 1623.
examples: He **flagellated** himself for years over the failure.

words.definition: Criminal or villainous; extremely and shamefully wicked, as flagitious crimes
words.origin: Middle English *flagicious*, from Latin *flagitiosus*, from *flagitium* shameful thing. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Conspicuously offensive
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *flagrant-, flagrans* "flaming, fiery, (of a person) burning with desire, passionate," present participle of *flagrāre* "to be ablaze, burn, shine, burn (with passion, zeal)," probably derivative of an adjective **flagro-* "burning," going back to Indo-European **bhl̥g-ro-,* adjective derivative from the verbal base *bhleg-* "shine, be bright"; (sense 1) after in flagrante delicto and parallel Latin phrases. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: An idle man-about-town who strolls the streets observing society
words.origin: French *flâneur*. First known use: 1854.

words.definition: Nonsense
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1878.

words.definition: To laugh impudently or jeeringly at someone; a mocking look or word
words.origin: Middle English *fleryen*, of Scandinavian origin; akin to Norwegian *flire* to giggle. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A flighty, frivolous and overly talkative person
words.origin: Middle English *flepergebet*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Nonsense
words.origin: Perhaps of Scandinavian origin; akin to Old Norse *flim* mockery. First known use: circa 1538.

words.definition: Small fragments or splinters, as when something is smashed to flinders
words.origin: Middle English *flendris*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Not showing proper seriousness
words.origin: Probably from flip. First known use: 1675.

words.definition: Judging something to be worthless
words.origin: A jocular Eton coinage from Latin *flocci, nauci, nihili, pili*, all meaning of little value.

words.definition: Having or resembling tufts of wool; fluffy or loosely clumped
words.origin: Latin *flocc*us + English *-ulent*. First known use: 1800.

words.definition: Elaborately ornate; also, flushed red
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *flōridus* "abounding in flowers, brightly coloured, in the bloom of youth, highly coloured (of rhetoric)," adjective derivative, with the suffix *-idus,* corresponding to *flōrēre* "to bloom". First known use: 1651.

words.definition: Producing many flowers; bearing blooms in abundance, as a prized rose
words.origin: Latin *flōrifer* "producing flowers, flowery" (from *flōri-* flori- + *-fer* "bearing") + -ous. First known use: 1678.

words.definition: , plural florilegia A compilation of excerpts; anthology
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *flōrilegium,* from Latin *flōrilegus* "culling flowers" (from *flōri-* flori- + *-legus,* adjective derivative of *legere* "to gather, pick") + *-ium,* suffix of deverbal compounds (formed after Latin *spīcilegium* "gathering of stray ears of grain"); loan-translation of Greek *anthología* anthology. First known use: 1647.

words.definition: To grow or develop well; to thrive
words.origin: Middle English *florisshen* "to put forth flowers, bloom, grow luxuriantly, prosper, brandish (a weapon)," borrowed from Anglo-French *floriss-,* stem of *florir, flurir* "to bloom, grow abundantly, thrive," going back to Vulgar Latin **flōrīre,* restructuring of Latin *flōrēscere* "to begin to flower, increase in vigor," inchoative derivative of *flōrēre* "to bloom, prosper, be at the peak of one's powers," stative verbal derivative of *flōr-, flōs* flower. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The company **flourished** with record profits under the new owner.

words.definition: To perplex or bewilder someone greatly; to baffle completely
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1836.
examples: He was **flummoxed** by the legal jargon.
A hapless innocent who had been **flummoxed** by wily city slickers — Andy Logan

words.definition: A small dot made by the excrement of an insect, such as a fly
A contest of poetic insults, as in medieval Scots poetry; a heated exchange
words.origin: Scots, literally, contention, gerund of *flyte* to contend, argue, from Middle English *fliten*, from Old English *flītan*; akin to Old High German *flīzan* to argue. First known use: 1508.

words.definition: Aimless strolling and idle observation
words.origin: French, from *flâner* to stroll.

words.definition: A pale, white rainbow seen in fog
A person, typically an old one, with old-fashioned or conservative attitudes
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1792.
examples: … all of the young, smug newcomers … considered him an old **fogy**. — Theodore Dreiser

words.definition: A minor weakness or eccentricity
words.origin: Obsolete French (now *faible*), from obsolete *foible* weak, from Old French *feble* feeble. First known use: circa 1648.
examples: … talent is always balanced by **foible**. — Janna Malamud Smith

words.definition: To thrust with a weapon; lunge
words.origin: Middle English, from *foin* fork for spearing fish, from Anglo-French *fuin*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A general assembly of the people of a town, city, county
words.origin: Alteration of Old English *folcmōt, folcgemōt*, from *folc* people + *mōt, gemōt* meeting. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: To stir up trouble or rebellion
words.origin: Middle English, to apply a warm substance to, from Late Latin *fomentare*, from Latin *fomentum* compress, from *fovēre* to heat, soothe; akin to Lithuanian *degti* to burn, Sanskrit *dahati* it burns. First known use: circa 1613.

words.definition: Excessive fuss or showy ornamentation over something trivial
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1848.

words.definition: To engage in fruitless activity; to mess about or waste time
words.origin: Probably alteration of *footer* to waste time. First known use: 1891.

words.definition: A fool; a silly, insignificant person
words.origin: From *fop* a foolish person + *doodle* a simpleton. First known use: 17th century.

words.definition: Excessively concerned with one's clothes and appearance, like a fop
words.origin: From *fop* + *-ish*. *Fop*: Middle English; akin to Middle English *fobben* to deceive, Middle High German *voppen*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Patient self-control and restraint
words.origin: From *forbear* + *-ance*. *Forbear*: Middle English *forberen*, from Old English *forberan* to endure, do without, from *for-* + *beran* to bear. First known use: 1570.
examples: The policy provides a means of **forbearance** for borrowers meeting certain criteria.
… a sudden formality in his manner, which showed that his **forbearance** was at last failing him. — Wilkie Collins

words.definition: The euphoria of falling in love
words.origin: Norwegian and Danish, in love.

words.definition: To prevent or forbid, as in heaven forfend; to avert or keep away
The capacity to forget easily
words.origin: A jocular blend of *forget* and *memory*.

words.definition: Pitifully sad and lonely
words.origin: Middle English *forloren*, from Old English, past participle of *forlēosan* to lose, from *for-* + *lēosan* to lose. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Worn out from too much work
words.origin: Middle English *forswonke*, from Old English *forswuncen*, past participle of *forswincan* "to toil hard," from *for-* (intensive) + *swincan* "to toil".

words.definition: A small fort or outwork of a fortification, as on a Scottish estate
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *fortalitia*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to paranormal phenomena
words.origin: From Charles Fort, an American writer on unexplained phenomena.

words.definition: Courage in pain or adversity
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *fortitudin-, fortitudo*, from *fortis*. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: Happening by chance, often luckily
words.origin: Latin *fortuitus*; akin to Latin *fort-, fors* chance. First known use: 1653.
examples: … from a cost standpoint, the company's timing is **fortuitous**.
… belted down the stairs, and there was a **fortuitous** train. — Doris Lessing

words.definition: To rummage or search about; to search for gold in abandoned workings
words.origin: English dialect *fossick* to ferret out. First known use: 1852.

words.definition: Dazzling or stunning; striking suddenly and with great force, like lightning
words.origin: French, striking like lightning, from *foudre* lightning.

words.definition: A pretender, bluffer or fraudster
words.origin: From poker, a player bluffing with four cards of a suit instead of five.

words.definition: The eerie glow of fungi on rotting wood
words.origin: From *fox* + *fire*; perhaps from Old French *faux* false.

words.definition: A noisy disturbance or quarrel, often involving several people; a brawl
words.origin: French, din, row, from Italian *fracasso*, from *fracassare* to shatter. First known use: 1716.

words.definition: Irritable and quarrelsome; unruly
words.origin: Fract(ion) (in sense "rupture, discord, breach of the peace") + -ious (after captious, factious). First known use: 1714.

words.definition: Fragile; capable of being easily broken, as frangible china or bullets
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Middle French & Medieval Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Medieval Latin *frangibilis,* from Latin *frangere* "to break, shatter" + *-ibilis* -ible. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Embarrassment felt on behalf of someone else
words.origin: German, from *fremd* other + *schämen* to be ashamed.

words.definition: Fast, energetic and wildly uncontrolled
words.origin: Middle English *frenetik, frentik, frantike* "temporarily deranged, delirious," borrowed from Anglo-French *frenetic, frenetique,* borrowed from Latin *phrenēticus* "suffering from madness," borrowed from Greek *phrenētikós,* late variant of *phrenītikós,* from *phrenîtis* "inflammation of the brain, delirium, insanity" (from *phren-, phrḗn* "midriff, seat of the passions, mind, wit" —of uncertain origin— + *-ītis* -itis) + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: circa 1529.
examples: A **frenetic** attempt to beat a deadline
… succumb to exhaustion merely trying to keep up with the president's **frenetic** schedule.

words.definition: To eat greedily and often
words.origin: Yiddish, from German *fressen* to devour.

words.definition: Easily crumbled
words.origin: Middle French or Latin; Middle French, from Latin *friabilis*, from *friare* to crumble. First known use: 1563.

words.definition: A frivolous or foolish person; to waste time in trifles and idle pursuits
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1633.

words.definition: Open-air living; joy in nature
words.origin: Norwegian, free-air life; popularized by Henrik Ibsen.

words.definition: Showy or unnecessary ornament in architecture, dress or language
words.origin: Middle French *friperie*, alteration of Old French *freperie*, from *frepe* old garment. First known use: 1568.

words.definition: A sudden strong feeling of excitement, fear or thrill; a shiver
words.origin: French, shiver, from Old French *friçon*, from Late Latin *friction-, frictio*, from Latin, literally, friction (taken in Late Latin as derivative of *frigēre* to be cold). First known use: 1777.
examples: … produce a genuine **frisson** of disquiet. — Patricia Craig

words.definition: Lively and playful, as a frolicsome puppy or lamb; full of fun and mischief
Difficult to deal with; contrary
words.origin: Middle English, turned away, froward, from *fro* from + *-ward* -ward. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Stuffy and close in a warm, stale way, as of an unaired room
words.origin: Alteration of *frowsy*. First known use: 1865.

words.definition: To be or to make untidy, tangled or ruffled
words.origin: Back-formation from *frowzy*.

words.definition: Scruffy, dingy and neglected
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1681.
examples: … a **frowsy** smell of stale beer and stale smoke. — W. Somerset Maugham
… a couple of **frowsy** stuffed chairs … — R. M. Williams

words.definition: Sparing with money or food
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Late Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Late Latin *frūgālis* "not given to excess, temperate, sober, simple" (early Medieval Latin also "thrifty, sparing"), back-formation from Latin *frūgālior, frūgālissimus* and *frūgāliter,* comparative and superlative degrees and adverbial derivative (with the suffix *-āl-* -al) of *frūgī* "(of people, especially slaves) having merit or worth, deserving, sober, thrifty," "(of things) moderate, sober," predicative dative of *frūg-, frūx* (usually in plural) "edible produce of plants, fruit, crops, grain," root noun from the base of *fruor, fruī* "to enjoy the produce or proceeds of, derive advantage from". First known use: 1542.

words.definition: Feeding on fruit, as many bats, birds and monkeys do
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *frūgivorus* "crop-devouring," from Latin *frūg-, frūx* "edible produce of plants, fruit, crops" + *-i-* -i- + *-vorus* -vorous. First known use: 1713.

words.definition: A dish of hulled wheat boiled in milk and spiced; an old harvest pudding
words.origin: Middle English *frumenty, furmenty,* borrowed from Anglo-French *formenté, fromenté, frumenté* (continental Middle French *fromentee*), from *furment, frument* "wheat" (going back to Vulgar Latin **frumentum,* alteration of Latin *frūmentum* "the fruit of cereal plants, grain") + *-é,* reduced from *-ee,* suffix of association or containment, going back to Late Latin *-āta* (going back to Latin, feminine of *-ātus* -ate); *frūmentum* going back to *frūg-,* base of *frūx* (usually in plural) "edible produce of plants, fruit, crops, grain" and *fruor, fruī* "to enjoy the produce or proceeds of, derive advantage from" + *-mentum* -ment. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Very angry
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll, a blend of *fuming* and *furious*.

words.definition: Fat and squat; chubby, as a fubsy little dog or teapot
words.origin: Obsolete English *fubs* chubby person. First known use: 1780.

words.definition: To confuse or befuddle, especially with drink
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1588.
examples: … corridors, archways, recesses … combined to **fuddle** any sense of direction … — Elizabeth Bowen

words.definition: A person who is very old-fashioned and pompous or fussy, resistant to change
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1868.

words.definition: A warm, stuffy or smoky atmosphere in a closed room, as of a crowded pub
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of fog. First known use: 1888.

words.definition: Fleeting; tending to disappear
words.origin: Latin *fugac-, fugax*, from *fugere*. First known use: 1635.

words.definition: Shining brightly; dazzling, as fulgent jewels or a fulgent sunrise
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Latin *fulgent-, fulgens,* present participle of *fulgēre* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Flashing like lightning
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *fulgurant-, fulgurans,* present participle of *fulgurāre* "to flash (of lightning), shine, gleam," derivative of *fulgur* "flash of lightning, lightning". First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Sooty or smoky; dusky or dark in colour, as fuliginous clouds
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *fūlīginōsus* "covered with soot," from Latin *fūlīgin-, fūlīgō* "soot" + *-ōsus* -ous; *fūlīgō,* from *fūlī-* (going back to Indo-European **dhuh2-li-* "smoke, dust," whence also Sanskrit *dhūli-* "dust," Lithuanian *dū́lis* "mist, dust from tree rot used to drive out bees") + *-gin-, -gō,* suffix denoting something coating or enveloping, usually undesirable, as *rōbīgō* "rust," *mellīgō* "bee glue". First known use: 1597.

words.definition: To protest strongly and loudly
words.origin: Middle English *fulminaten* "to direct (condemnation at an offender)," borrowed from Late Latin *fulminātus,* past participle of *fulmināre* "to strike down, confound (an opponent)" (Medieval Latin, "to thunder [threats, denunciations]"), going back to Latin, "to strike (of lightning), strike like lightning," derivative of *fulmin-, fulmen* "lightning," from *fulg-* (base of *fulgēre* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten") + *-min-, -men,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Excessively complimentary or flattering
words.origin: Middle English *fulsom, foulsome* "abundant, well-fed, plump, arousing disgust," from *ful, foul* full + *-som, -some* -some. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … describes in **fulsome** detail … — G. N. Shuster
**Fulsome** bird life. The feeder overcrowded — Maxine Kumin

words.definition: Tawny; brownish-yellow or orange
words.origin: Latin *fulvus*; perhaps akin to Latin *flavus* yellow. First known use: 1664.

words.definition: An opening in or near a volcano through which hot sulphurous gases emerge
words.origin: Italian *fumarola*, from Italian dialect (Neapolitan), from Late Latin *fumariolum* vent, from Latin *fumarium* smoke chamber for aging wine, from *fumus*. First known use: 1811.

words.definition: Tightrope walking
words.origin: Latin *funambulus* ropewalker, from *funis* rope + *ambulare* to walk. First known use: 1801.

words.definition: A tightrope walker, especially a performer who balances high above a crowd
words.origin: Latin *funambulus* ropewalker, from *funis* rope + *ambulare* to walk. First known use: 1801.

words.definition: A flounce on a skirt or petticoat; showy ornaments or trimmings
words.origin: By folk etymology from French dialect *farbella*. First known use: 1702.

words.definition: Sly and secretive
words.origin: French or Latin; French *furtif*, from Latin *furtivus*, from *furtum* theft, from *fur* thief, from or akin to Greek *phōr* thief; akin to Greek *pherein* to carry. First known use: 1612.

words.definition: One who worries or complains about unimportant things: a fussy person
Pompous or pretentious language
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *fustian, fustayn*, from Medieval Latin *fustaneum*, probably from *fustis* tree trunk, from Latin, stick, cudgel. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: A low, shabby scoundrel
words.origin: Coined by Shakespeare, perhaps from *fusty*.

words.definition: Smelling stale, damp or stuffy; old-fashioned in attitude or style
words.origin: Probably alteration of Middle English *foisted, foist* musty, from *foist* wine cask, from Anglo-French *fust, fuist* wood, tree trunk, cask, from Medieval Latin *fustis*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Pointless; incapable of success
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Latin *fūtilis, futtilis* "brittle, fragile (of containers), serving no purpose, pointless," perhaps (if original sense was "leaky") from *fū-* (going back to Indo-European **ǵheu̯-* "pour, shed") + *-tilis* "obtained by, characterized by (the action of the verb)". First known use: circa 1555.
examples: A **futile** attempt to control the flooding

words.definition: Things that evoke a particular season
words.origin: Japanese, from *fū* wind + *butsu* thing + *shi* poem.

words.definition: A tax, especially the hated salt tax of prerevolutionary France
words.origin: Middle English *gabell*, borrowed from Middle French *gabelle*, going back to Old French, "tax on certain commodities," borrowed from Italian *gabella*, borrowed from Arabic *qabāla* "tribute," derivative of *qabila* "receive". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A wandering beggar, especially a licensed one in old Scotland
words.origin: Scots, a licensed beggar; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A person who habitually travels from place to place in search of pleasure
words.origin: From the verb phrase *gad about*, from gad. First known use: 1757.

words.definition: Headlong and reckless, like the swine of Gadara
words.origin: From the demon-possessed *Gadarene* swine in Matthew 8:28 that rushed into the sea. First known use: 1895.

words.definition: An archaic exclamation of surprise or annoyance, a mild oath of old
words.origin: Perhaps from *God's hooks*, the nails of the Crucifixion. First known use: circa 1652.

words.definition: A long thick glove: gauntlet
words.origin: From Old French *gaigne-pain* bread-winner, a hired soldier's sword.

words.definition: To deny or contradict
words.origin: Middle English *yein seyen, gein-seyen* "to speak in opposition to, deny," from *yein-, gein-* "away, back, against, in opposition to" (going back to Old English *gēan-* "in opposition to," or marking returning or reciprocal action, going back to Germanic **gagna-*) + *seyen* "to say". First known use: 14th century.
examples: Did not dare to **gainsay** the king

words.definition: The delusion that one has become a cat
words.origin: From Greek *galē* weasel, cat + *anthrōpos* human.

words.definition: Confused, meaningless talk; gibberish, often pompously delivered
words.origin: French, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Loose, wide breeches worn in the 16th and 17th centuries; leggings
words.origin: Earlier also *garragascoynes*, perhaps reshaping (after gascon) of Middle French *garguesques, greguesques* (also *chausses à la gregesque* "leggings in the *gregesque* style"), borrowed from Spanish *gregüescos*, plural of *gregüesco*, probably for **greguesco*, from *griego* "Greek" (going back to Latin *Graecus*) + *-esco* -esque. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: A confused jumble or medley of things; once a hash of leftover meats
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *galimafree* "stew made with various meats," earlier *calimafree* "kind of sauce," perhaps blend of *galer* "to squander in pleasures, have a good time" and Middle French dialect (Picard) *mafrer* "to gorge oneself," borrowed from Middle Dutch *moffelen, maffelen* "to work the jaws," of imitative origin. First known use: circa 1556.

words.definition: Indifferent or uncaring
words.origin: From Gallio, the Roman official in Acts who cared nothing for the dispute before him.

words.definition: A small glazed earthenware pot used by apothecaries for ointments
words.origin: Middle English *galy pot*, perhaps from *galey, galy* galley + *pott* pot. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To go around from one place to another in pursuit of pleasure
words.origin: Perhaps extended form of gallant. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: A mercenary or retainer of an Irish chief, armed with a battleaxe
words.origin: Borrowed from Irish *gallóglach* "soldier from a Scottish clan in the service of an Irish chief," from *gall* "Gaul, Scandinavian invader, foreigner" (going back to Middle Irish, borrowed from Latin *Gallus* "a gaul") + *óglach* "young man, warrior, soldier," going back to Middle Irish *óclach, óglaech*, originally derivative (probably after *echlach* "messenger, attendant," *midlach* "man incapable of bearing arms, coward") of *óc* "young," going back to Old Irish *óac*, going back to Celtic **yowanko-* (whence also Welsh *ieuanc* "young," Breton *yaouank*), going back to Indo-European **h2i̯̯u-h2n-ḱo-*. First known use: circa 1515.

words.definition: A clumsy, oafish or uncouth person, often said with some affection
words.origin: Of obscure origin. First known use: circa 1818.

words.definition: A coterie; an unpleasant situation one is caught in
words.origin: French, galley; from Molière's line about a galley.

words.definition: Enduring the unbearable with patience and dignity
words.origin: Japanese, endurance, of Buddhist origin.

words.definition: An opening move made to gain an advantage
words.origin: Borrowed from Spanish *gambito*, borrowed from Italian *gambetto*, literally, "act of tripping someone," from *gamba* "leg" (going back to Late Latin) + *-etto*, diminutive suffix. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: To run or jump about playfully, as lambs in spring; a playful frolic
words.origin: In part verbal derivative of gambol, in part borrowing (assimilated to the noun) from Middle French *gambader*, verbal derivative of *gambade*. First known use: 1508.

words.definition: A girl with mischievous, boyish charm, as in Audrey Hepburn's roles; a street urchin
words.origin: Borrowed from French, feminine derivative of *gamin* gamin. First known use: 1848.

words.definition: Playfully impudent or mischievous
words.origin: From French *gamin* street urchin.

words.definition: Nonsense or humbug intended to deceive; ham cured like bacon
words.origin: Assimilated form of earlier *gambon*, borrowed from Anglo-French *gamboun, jaumbeun* (continental Old French *jambon*), from *gambe, jambe* "hock of a horse, leg" + *-on*, diminutive or particularizing suffix, going back to Latin *-ō, -ōn-*, suffix of persons with a prominent feature. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A vagrant or drifter
words.origin: Middle English (north) & early Scots *gangrel, gangerall*, probably from *gang* gang + *-rel*, noun suffix with diminutive or pejorative force (borrowed from Old French *-erel*, expansion of *-el*, diminutive suffix, going back to Latin *-ellus*). First known use: 15th century.
examples: Wholly a **gangrel**, he neither worked nor wanted … — D. C. Thomson

words.definition: Something that makes one stare
words.origin: From *gape* + *seed*, something sown to make people stare.

words.definition: A warning cry once given in Edinburgh before throwing slops from a window
words.origin: Perhaps from French *garde à l'eau!* look out for the water! First known use: 1622.

words.definition: Excessively talkative
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *garrulus,* from *garrīre* "to chatter, talk rapidly" (probably of imitative origin) + *-ulus,* deverbal suffix denoting inclination or repetitive action (going back to Indo-European *-l-,* participial suffix). First known use: circa 1611.

words.definition: Extravagant boasting, as the Gascons were said to indulge in; to boast extravagantly
words.origin: French *gasconnade*, from *gasconner* to boast, from *gascon* Gascon, boaster. First known use: 1709.

words.definition: A gourmet; a connoisseur of good food and its preparation and history
words.origin: French, back-formation from *gastronomie*. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: Socially awkward
words.origin: French, literally, left. First known use: 1751.
examples: It would be **gauche** to mention the subject

words.definition: Awkward, embarrassing or unsophisticated ways; a tactless act
words.origin: From French *gaucherie*. First known use: 1810.

words.definition: A small open pavilion with a view
words.origin: Perhaps from gaze + Latin *-ebo* (as in *videbo* I shall see). First known use: 1752.

words.definition: A geographical dictionary or directory of place names and their features
To raise the price after accepting an offer from a buyer
words.origin: British slang, perhaps from Yiddish *gezumph* to overcharge.

words.definition: A deep feeling of safety, warmth and belonging
words.origin: German, from *geborgen* sheltered, safe.

words.definition: To play a hoax or practical joke
words.origin: Scots, a trick or hoax; of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Icy cold; extremely chilly
words.origin: Latin *gelidus*, from *gelu* frost, cold. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Cosy and pleasantly comfortable
words.origin: German, from *Gemüt* disposition, heart.

words.definition: Warmth, friendliness and cosy good cheer
words.origin: German, from *gemütlich* cosy.

words.definition: The substitution of a word that is believed to be more polite or refined
words.origin: Genteel + -ism. First known use: 1926.

words.definition: To lower one's body briefly by bending one knee, as in worship; to defer
words.origin: Late Latin *genuflectere*, from Latin *genu* knee + *flectere* to bend. First known use: 1630.

words.definition: The fear of growing old
words.origin: From Greek *gēraskein* to grow old + *-phobia*.

words.definition: A ruler or manager
words.origin: Latin *gerent-, gerens*, present participle of *gerere* to bear, carry on. First known use: 1576.

words.definition: Relevant to the subject
words.origin: Middle English *germain*, literally, having the same parents, from Anglo-French. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Omit details that are not **germane** to the discussion

words.definition: A whole that is more than the sum of its parts
words.origin: German, literally, shape, form. First known use: 1922.
examples: When he gets rolling, you're not responding to single jokes—it's the whole **gestalt** of the movie that's funny. — Pauline Kael
When new employees are recruited fresh out of college and can look forward to working for the same company for 40 years, it changes the **gestalt** of management. — Brenton R. Schlender

words.definition: A showy but worthless trinket
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1529.

words.definition: Cosy, convivial and companionable
words.origin: Dutch, from *gezel* companion.

words.definition: Of the moon, more than half but less than full
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *gibbosus* humpbacked, from Latin *gibbus* hump. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An insulting or mocking remark
words.origin: Perhaps from Middle French *giber* to shake, handle roughly. First known use: 1567.
examples: Boxers **gibing** each other before a fight

words.definition: A dancing reflection of light on a wall
words.origin: Italian dialect (Lombard); of uncertain origin.

words.definition: The urge to squeeze something unbearably cute
words.origin: Tagalog.

words.definition: A clove-scented pink or stock
words.origin: By folk etymology from Middle English *gilofre* clove, from Anglo-French, alteration of Old French *girofle*, from Latin *caryophyllum*, from Greek *karyophyllon*, from *karyon* nut + *phyllon* leaf. First known use: 1551.

words.definition: A pivoted support that keeps an instrument, such as a compass, level
words.origin: Alteration of obsolete *gemel* double ring, from Middle English, from Anglo-French *gemel, jomel*, from Latin *gemellus*, diminutive of *geminus*. First known use: circa 1780.

words.definition: Showy but flimsy and worthless, as gimcrack furniture; a cheap, showy ornament
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1676.

words.definition: , plural glabellae (-BEL-ee) The area between the eyebrows, just above the nose
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, feminine of *glabellus* hairless, diminutive of *glaber*. First known use: circa 1823.

words.definition: Free from hair or down; smooth, as a leaf, a stem or skin
words.origin: Latin *glabr-, glaber* smooth, bald. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: Foolish and thoughtless
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *glaikit*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Of a dull greyish-green or blue; covered with a powdery bloom like a plum
words.origin: Latin *glaucus*, from Greek *glaukos* gleaming, grey. First known use: 1671.

words.definition: A piece of land serving as part of a clergyman's benefice; soil or land
words.origin: Latin *gleba* clod, land. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A glowing coal
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *glēd*; akin to Old English *glōwan* to glow. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A jest or trick
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: Fluent but insincere and shallow
words.origin: Probably modification of Low German *glibberig* slippery. First known use: 1584.
examples: Their **glib** assurances that "everything will be fine"

words.definition: A slide down a steep slope of snow or ice; a gliding step in ballet
words.origin: French, noun, slide, glissade, from *glisser* to slide, from Old French *glicier*, alteration of *glier*, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *glītan* to glide. First known use: 1837.

words.definition: Twilight
words.origin: Scots *gloam* to become twilight, back-formation from *gloaming*. First known use: circa 1821.

words.definition: Twilight; dusk
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *gloming*, from Old English *glōming*, from *glōm* twilight; akin to Old English *glōwan* to glow. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A ring of rainbow light around a shadow on cloud
words.origin: Middle English *glorie*, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, from Latin *gloria*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **glory** of the city is its Gothic cathedral.

words.definition: The phenomenon of speaking in an unknown language; speaking in tongues
words.origin: Probably borrowed from German *Glossolalie, Glossolalia,* from *glosso-* glosso- + Greek *laliá* "talk, speech" (from *laléō, laleîn* "to talk, chat"—of onomatopoeic origin— + *-ia* -ia), after Greek *laleîn glṓssais* and variants in the New Testament (as Acts 2:4), conventionally translated "to speak in tongues". First known use: 1879.

words.definition: To explain away or gloss over, as faults; to flatter or fawn upon someone
words.origin: Middle English *glosen* to gloss, flatter, from *glose* gloss. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Weather that is lovely to look at from indoors
words.origin: Icelandic, from *gluggi* window + *veður* weather.

words.definition: Expressed in short, pithy maxims or aphorisms; enigmatic and hard to interpret
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *gnōmikós* "dealing in maxims, didactic," from *gnṓmē* "maxim" + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 1784.

words.definition: The projecting piece on a sundial that casts the shadow marking the hour
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *gnōmōn* "pointer of a sundial," borrowed from Greek *gnṓmōn* "examiner, interpreter, carpenter's square, pointer of a sundial," from *gnō-,* base of *gignṓskein* "to perceive, know" + *-mon-, -mōn,* agent suffix. First known use: 1546.

words.definition: Wordy, jargon-laden language that is hard to understand
words.origin: Irregular from *gobble*, noun. First known use: 1944.

words.definition: A gullible or credulous person
words.origin: French, fly-swallower, from *gober* to gulp + *mouche* fly.

words.definition: A busybody who meddles in others' affairs
words.origin: Irish English, from French *gobemouche* gullible person.

words.definition: Utterly surprised; flabbergasted
words.origin: Gob + smack + -ed. First known use: 1956.
examples: Thus, when the cell-phone video surfaced, fashion insiders were so **gobsmacked** that to this day they'll tell you where they were when they first heard about it. — Ingrid Sischy

words.definition: Waking early to hear the first birdsong
words.origin: Swedish, from *gå* go + *ut* out + *otta* dawn.

words.definition: To shirk work
A banner or pennant hung from a crossbar, often with streamers
words.origin: Borrowed from Italian *gonfalone,* dissimilated from *gonfanone,* borrowed from Old French *gunfanun, gonfanon* "battle standard, banner," going back to Old Low Franconian **gundfanōn,* going back to Germanic **gunþfanōn* (whence also Old English *gūþfana* "battle standard, banner," Old Saxon *gūthfano,* Old High German *gundfano,* Old Icelandic *gunnfani*), from **gunþī, gunþjō* "battle, combat" + **fanōn* "piece of cloth". First known use: 1595.

words.definition: One who idly watches boats on a canal
words.origin: English canal slang, perhaps from Lincolnshire dialect *gawn* and *gooze* to gape.

words.definition: Having a large belly: fat
words.origin: From *gore* dirt + *belly*; used by Shakespeare.

words.definition: To paralyze, petrify or hypnotize
Lacking sense or initiative; foolish, in a gaping, vacant sort of way
words.origin: Alteration of English dialect *gaumless*, from *gaum* attention, understanding (from Middle English *gome*, from Old Norse *gaum, gaumr*) + *-less*. First known use: 1883.

words.definition: Very light, thin and delicate
words.origin: Middle English *gossomer*, from *gos* goose + *somer* summer. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … the **gossamer** of youth's dreams … — Andrea Parke

words.definition: A person who enjoys eating and often eats too much; a glutton
words.origin: Middle English *gourmaunt*, from Middle French *gourmant*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A foolish person
words.origin: From Old Norse *gaukr* cuckoo.

words.definition: Two hands cupped together
words.origin: Scots, from Old Norse *gaupn* the hollowed hands.

words.definition: Slender or thin, especially in a charming or attractive way; gracefully slight
words.origin: Latin *gracilis*. First known use: 1623.

words.definition: Magic; occult learning
words.origin: From Middle English *gramarye* grammar, learning, magic.

words.definition: An archaic expression of thanks or surprise, from the French grand merci
words.origin: Middle English *grand mercy*, from Anglo-French *grand merci* great thanks. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A Spanish or Portuguese nobleman of the highest rank; a person of eminence
words.origin: Spanish *grande*, from *grande*, adjective, large, great, from Latin *grandis*. First known use: 1593.

words.definition: Grandeur, greatness, magnificence
words.origin: Italian, greatness, from *grande* great.

words.definition: Pompous or extravagant in language
words.origin: Probably from Middle French, from Latin *grandiloquus* using lofty language, from *grandis* + *loqui* to speak. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: Impressive or magnificent in appearance or style, especially pretentiously so
words.origin: French, from Italian *grandioso*, from *grande* great, from Latin *grandis*. First known use: 1818.
examples: They did not believe his **grandiose** claims.

words.definition: Uncalled for; done without good reason
words.origin: Latin *gratuitus*, from *gratus* grateful. First known use: 1617.
examples: We mistake the **gratuitous** blessings of Heaven for the fruits of our own industry. — Roger L'Estrange

words.definition: Soft hail or snow pellets formed when supercooled droplets freeze on snowflakes
words.origin: From German *graupel*. First known use: 1889.

words.definition: The essence or most serious part of a complaint or accusation
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *gravāmen* "burden, discomfort, annoyance," from Latin *gravāre* "to make heavy, oppress, weigh heavily upon" (derivative of *gravis* "heavy, oppressive, serious") + *-men,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 1602.

words.definition: Dignity and seriousness of manner
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *gravitās* "heaviness, weight, dignity, seriousness". First known use: 1869.
examples: Had the **gravitas** of a deep thinker

words.definition: The characters, such as @#%$*!, used to convey profanity in a comic
words.origin: Coined by the American cartoonist Mort Walker (1923-2018). First known use: 1968.
examples: … it's impossible to quote Ryan directly without liberal use of the **grawlix** … — Steve Rushin

words.definition: To weep
words.origin: Middle English *greten*, from Old English *grētan*; akin to Old English *grǣtan* to weep. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Fond of company; sociable
words.origin: Latin *gregarius* of a flock or herd, from *greg-, grex* flock, herd. First known use: 1668.

words.definition: A colour between grey and beige
words.origin: Borrowed from French *grège* "raw, unfinished (of silk)," going back to Middle French, borrowed from Italian *greggio* (Upper Italian *grezzo*) "in its natural state, unfinished," perhaps going back to Vulgar Latin **gregius* "plain, ordinary" (formed as a counterpart to Latin *ēgregius* "outstanding, first-rate"), derivative of Latin *greg-, grex* "flock, herd, troop"; later construed in English as a blend of grey and beige. First known use: 1835.

words.definition: A cat, especially an old female one, as kept by a witch; a spiteful old woman
words.origin: *gray* + *malkin*. First known use: 1630.

words.definition: One who is always grinning
words.origin: From *grin* + a fanciful ending.

words.definition: A method of painting in shades of grey to imitate sculpture or relief
words.origin: French, from *gris* grey, from Middle French. First known use: 1848.

words.definition: To watch others eat in hope of being offered some
words.origin: Of uncertain, perhaps Scottish, origin.

words.definition: A coarse, buffoonish person
words.origin: From German *Grobian*, from *grob* coarse.

words.definition: Strangely distorted or ugly; absurdly incongruous
words.origin: French, from Italian *grottesca*, a style of painting found in excavated Roman ruins, from *grotta* grotto.

words.definition: Relating to needy hack writers or their mediocre work, after a London street
words.origin: From Grub Street in London, once home to hack writers.

words.definition: To shudder with fear or horror
words.origin: Scots and Middle English, of Scandinavian origin.

words.definition: Surly, gloomy or stern
words.origin: Perhaps a blend of *grim* and *glum*.

words.definition: A habitual grumbler or complainer
words.origin: From *grumble* + *-tonian*, modelled on sect names like *Muggletonian*; first used of 17th-century critics of the English court.

words.definition: Contented; happy
words.origin: Back-formation from disgruntled. First known use: 1904.
examples: Once, he was **gruntled**—a wife and a kid, a good job—but because he devoted too much time to the latter, the formers packed up and left. — Steven Rea
I returned to my interrupted slumber in a mood far from **gruntled**. — Lawrence Sanders

words.definition: A network of personal relationships and favours
words.origin: Mandarin *guānxi* relationship, connection.

words.definition: A small freshwater fish used as bait; a credulous or easily cheated person
words.origin: Middle English *gojoun*, from Middle French *goujon*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A reward or recompense, especially one given for service or valour
words.origin: Middle English *gerdoun, guerdoun,* borrowed from Anglo-French *gueredun, guerdun* (also continental Old French), going back to Old Low Franconian **wiđarlōn* (attested as *withirlon,* translating Late Latin *retribūtiō* in the Wachtendonck Psalms), from **wiđar-* "against, back" (going back to Germanic **wiþra-,* whence also Old English *wiþer-* "against, in return") + **lōn* "reward, recompense," replaced in Gallo-Romance by Latin *dōnum* "gift, offering, benefit"; **lōn* going back to Germanic **launa-* (whence Old English *lēan* "recompense, reward," Old Frisian *lān,* Old Saxon & Old High German *lōn,* Old Icelandic & Gothic *laun*), derivative with the suffix **-no-* from the Indo-European verbal base **leh2u-* "seize, capture". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Sly or cunning intelligence
words.origin: Middle English *gile*, from Anglo-French, probably of Germanic origin; akin to Old English *wigle* divination. First known use: 13th century.
examples: A war that called for **guile** rather than firepower

words.definition: Greediness; gluttony; an excessive appetite for food
words.origin: Middle English *gulosite*, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *gulositas*, from Latin *gulosus* gluttonous, from *gula* gullet. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Shrewd or spirited initiative and resourcefulness; common sense
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1719.

words.definition: The action or faculty of tasting; the sense of taste itself
words.origin: Latin *gustation-, gustatio*, from *gustare*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Relating to the sense of taste
Government by women or a woman; rule exercised by women
words.origin: From Greek *gynē* woman + *-archia* rule.

words.definition: A spiral or vortex
words.origin: Latin *gyrus*, from Greek *gyros*. First known use: 1566.

words.definition: A fetter or shackle. verb tr.: To restrain
words.origin: From Middle English *gyve*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Moonlight shimmering on water
words.origin: Turkish, from *gümüş* silver + *servi* cypress.

words.definition: A cold sea fog on the east coast of Britain
words.origin: Of Dutch or Scandinavian origin; compare Dutch *harig* misty.

words.definition: Clothing or attire; equipment or apparatus for a particular role
words.origin: Middle English *abiliments, habilementes*, from Middle French *abillement, habillemens*, from Old French *abiller* to prepare, equip, from *bille* trimmed wood, log. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the **habiliments** of civilization … — W. P. Webb

words.definition: Clothing suited to an office or occasion
words.origin: Middle English *abiliments, habilementes*, from Middle French *abillement, habillemens*, from Old French *abiller* to prepare, equip, from *bille* trimmed wood, log. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the **habiliments** of civilization … — W. P. Webb

words.definition: The physical characteristics of a person, especially as relating to disease
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin. First known use: 1886.

words.definition: Delusions of a cheerful nature
words.origin: From Greek *habros* graceful, delicate + *mania*.

words.definition: One's few humble, treasured possessions
words.origin: German, from *Habe* possessions + *Seligkeit* bliss.

words.definition: The quality that makes a thing uniquely itself
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *haecceitas*, from *haec* this; coined by Duns Scotus.

words.definition: The writing of the lives of saints; a biography that idealizes its subject
To torment or harass, as if ridden by a hag in a nightmare; to obsess
A spreading halo of light around a bright object
words.origin: *halo* + *-ation*. First known use: 1859.

words.definition: Idyllically happy and peaceful, as in times past
examples: **Classics Illustrated** have become pricey nostalgia items for those who grew up in the supposedly **halcyon** years after World War II. — Donna Richardson

words.definition: A holy place or sanctuary; a sacred relic once used in swearing oaths
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *hāligdōm*, from *hālig* holy + *-dōm* -dom. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A fatal flaw leading to the downfall of a tragic hero or heroine
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *hamartía* "error in conduct, fault, wrongdoing," noun derivative from the base of *hamartánein,* aorist *hḗmarton* "to miss the mark, fail, err," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1900.

words.definition: The custom of viewing cherry blossoms
words.origin: Japanese, from *hana* flower + *mi* viewing.

words.definition: A contract or agreement, especially about a betrothal or marriage
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *handfæst*. First known use: circa 1616.

words.definition: To feel a strong, restless desire
