words.origin: Probably from Dutch dialect *hankeren*. First known use: 1627.

words.definition: A word or form recorded only once in a language or in an author's works
words.origin: Greek, something said only once. First known use: 1692.

words.definition: Unfortunate
words.origin: Middle English *happelesse,* from *happe* "luck, fortune, hap" + *-lesse* -less. First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Hapless** beings caught in the grip of forces we can do little about — W. H. Whyte

words.definition: Relating to the sense of touch, especially in perceiving objects
words.origin: Back-formation from haptics. First known use: 1860.

words.definition: A lengthy, aggressive speech
words.origin: Middle French *arenge*, from Old Italian *aringa*, from *aringare* to speak in public, from *aringo* public assembly, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *hring* ring. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … listening to his capacious **harangue** and its immaculate delivery … — Sir Winston Churchill
… emotional and frequently violent **harangues** … — K. E. Read

words.definition: A sign of what is to come
words.origin: Middle English *herbergere, herberjour, herbeger, harbenyowre* "member of a noble or royal retinue who assigns lodgings to guests or rides ahead to prepare an encampment, host, innkeeper," borrowed from Anglo-French *herberger, herberjur* (continental Old French *herbergeor*), from *herberger* "to lodge, shelter, encamp" (continental Old French *herbergier,* borrowed from Old Low Franconian **haribergōn,* going back to Germanic **haribergōjan-* "to set up quarters for an army") + *-er, -eor* -er. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Robins, crocuses, and other **harbingers** of spring
… I suspect the mural is a **harbinger** of things to come, that new printing techniques will usher in a revival of architectural ornament. — Karrie Jacobs

words.definition: To listen attentively
words.origin: Middle English *herkien*; akin to Old High German *hōrechen* to listen, Old English *hīeran* to hear. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … only natural for them to **hark** to him … — G. G. Black

words.definition: A strict, bossy or belligerent old woman, especially a scolding one
words.origin: Perhaps modification of French *haridelle* old horse, gaunt woman. First known use: 1678.

words.definition: Acutely distressing
words.origin: From present participle of harrow. First known use: 1799.
examples: Mr. Wu's work in a coal mine was particularly **harrowing**. — Charles Horner

words.definition: A Roman religious official who interpreted omens from the entrails of victims
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *haruspex, harispex,* from a stem *haru-, hari-,* presumed to mean "intestines" (probably going back to Indo-European **ǵhr̥H-u-,* u-stem derivative of **ǵhr̥H-* "gut, cord made from animal intestines") + *-spex,* noun derivative of a verbal base *-spec-* "see, observe". First known use: 1584.

words.definition: Arrogantly superior
words.origin: Obsolete *haught*, from Middle English *haute*, from Anglo-French *halt, haut*, literally, high, from Latin *altus*. First known use: 1530.
examples: … Mr. Yorke talked about equality, but at heart he was … **haughty** as Beelzebub to whomsoever the world deemed (for he deemed no man) his superior. — Charlotte Brontë

words.definition: Haughtiness of manner
words.origin: French, from *haut* high. First known use: circa 1628.
examples: … he distances himself with customary **hauteur** from the world … — Martin Amis

words.definition: To talk nonsense
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1866.

words.definition: A thick rope or cable for mooring or towing a ship, often of steel
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *haucer*, from Anglo-French *halcer, haucer* to raise, hoist, from Vulgar Latin **altiare*, from Latin *altus* high. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: The wild pansy; peace of mind
Open, uncultivated land with heather
words.origin: Middle English *heth*, from Old English *hǣth*; akin to Old High German *heida* heather, Old Welsh *coit* forest. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Weekly; meeting or appearing every seven days, as a hebdomadal council
words.origin: From *hebdomad* + *-al*. *Hebdomad*: Latin *hebdomad-, hebdomas*, from Greek, from *hebdomos* seventh, from *hepta* seven. First known use: 1711.

words.definition: Relating to or happening at puberty
words.origin: From Greek *hēbētikos*, from *hēbē* youth.

words.definition: Mental dullness or lethargy; a sluggish, blunted state of mind
words.origin: Late Latin *hebetudo*, from *hebēre* to be dull; akin to Latin *hebes* dull. First known use: circa 1621.

words.definition: To talk to in a bullying way
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *Hektōr*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A sneaking, shifty person
words.origin: From *hedge* + *creeper*, one who skulks along hedgerows.

words.definition: Careless; showing no caution
examples: … **heedless** follies of unbridled youth … — John DeBruyn

words.definition: Dominance of one group over others
words.origin: Greek *hēgemonia*, from *hēgemōn* leader, from *hēgeisthai* to lead. First known use: 1567.
examples: The rise of Health Management Organizations (HMOs) and managed care in general has weakened physician **hegemony** over medicine. — Amy Agigian

words.definition: A journey made to escape danger; Muhammad's flight from Mecca in 622
words.origin: The *Hegira*, flight of Muhammad from Mecca in a.d. 622, from Medieval Latin, from Arabic *hijra*, literally, departure. First known use: 1753.

words.definition: A deep sense of home and belonging
words.origin: German, home, homeland.

words.definition: Relating to the rising or setting of a star at about the same time as the sun
words.origin: Late Latin *heliacus*, from Greek *hēliakos*, from *hēlios*. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: A love of sunlight
words.origin: From Greek *hēlios* sun + *-philia* love.

words.definition: Fond of or adapted to sunlight
words.origin: From Greek *hēlios* sun + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: A plant that turns its flowers toward the sun; a light purple colour
words.origin: Latin *heliotropium*, from Greek *hēliotropion*, from *hēlio-* heli-:1 + *tropos* turn; from its flowers' turning toward the sun. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: A rowdy, mischievous or troublesome person, especially a child
words.origin: Probably alteration (influenced by *hell*) of *hallion* scamp. First known use: 1787.

words.definition: Expressing a single idea by two words joined by and, as nice and warm
words.origin: Late Latin *hendiadys, hendiadyoin*, modification of Greek *hen dia dyoin*, literally, one through two. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: Belief in or worship of one god without denying the possibility of others
words.origin: German *Henotheismus*, from Greek *hen-, heis* one + *theos* god. First known use: 1860.

words.definition: Requiring great strength or effort, as a herculean task
words.origin: From *Hercules*, the Greek hero famed for his twelve great labours.

words.definition: A belief contrary to orthodox doctrine
words.origin: Middle English *heresie,* borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed (with assimilation to the suffix *-ie* -y) from Late Latin *haeresis, heresis* "school (of philosophy or theology), sect, belief contrary to church dogma," borrowed from Greek *haíresis* "act of taking, choice, course of action or thought, system of principles, sect, faction," from *haireîn* "to take, grasp, (middle voice) obtain, choose, prefer" (of obscure origin) + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 13th century.
examples: To disagree with the party leadership was **heresy**.

words.definition: Concerning interpretation, especially of scripture or literary texts
Having many different colours
words.origin: From German *heterochromatin*. First known use: 1932.

words.definition: Abnormal or irregular; deviating from the ordinary rule, as a word with odd inflections
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *heterocliton,* noun derivative from neuter of *heteroclitos* "irregularly inflected". First known use: 1580.

words.definition: Not conforming to accepted standards or beliefs
words.origin: Late Latin *heterodoxus*, from Greek *heterodoxos*, from *heter-* + *doxa* opinion. First known use: circa 1650.

words.definition: The use of a word different from the one intended
words.origin: From Greek *heteros* other + *-phēmia* speech.

words.definition: A pause or gap in a sequence
words.origin: Latin, from *hiare* to yawn. First known use: 1563.
examples: The … weedy **hiatus** between the town and the railroad. — Willa Cather
… the **hiatus** between the theory and the practice of the party … — J. G. Colton

words.definition: A shelter where an animal hibernates
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, winter residence, from *hibernare*. First known use: 1770.

words.definition: Relating to winter; wintry, as hibernal frosts or the hibernal sleep of bears
A member of the lower nobility in Spain, like Don Quixote; a gentleman by birth
words.origin: Spanish, from Old Spanish *fijo dalgo*, literally, son of something. First known use: 1594.

words.definition: Unwilling to change because of convention
A person, especially a priest, who interprets sacred mysteries
words.origin: Late Latin *hierophanta*, from Greek *hierophantēs*, from *hieros* + *phainein* to show. First known use: 1677.

words.definition: In confusion or disorder; jumbled together without any sense or system
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1598.

words.definition: A swindler, gangster or a corrupt politician
words.origin: The *Highbinders*, gang of ruffians in New York City about 1806. First known use: 1876.

words.definition: Named or called
words.origin: Middle English, past participle (earlier past) of *hoten* to command, call, be called, from Old English *hātan*; akin to Old High German *heizzan* to command, call. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The remote areas beyond a coast or city
words.origin: German, from *hinter* hinder + *Land*. First known use: 1879.

words.definition: Poetic or literary inspiration
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *Hippokrēnē*. First known use: 1613.

words.definition: A mythical creature with the body of a horse and the wings and head of an eagle
words.origin: French *hippogriffe*, from Italian *ippogrifo*, from *ippo-* (from Greek *hippos* horse) + *grifo* griffin, from Latin *gryphus*. First known use: 1612.

words.definition: A deep longing for a home one can't return to, or that never was
words.origin: Welsh, longing, homesickness.

words.definition: Hairy
words.origin: Latin *hirsutus*; akin to Latin *horrēre* to bristle. First known use: 1621.

words.definition: Overly theatrical or dramatic
words.origin: Late Latin *histrionicus*, from Latin *histrion-, histrio* actor. First known use: 1648.

words.definition: To or toward this place
words.origin: Middle English *hider, hither*, from Old English *hider*; akin to Goth *hidre* hither, Latin *citra* on this side. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A greyish-white crystalline deposit of frozen vapour on grass and branches
Gray or white, as from age
words.origin: From *hoar* + *-y*. *Hoar*: Middle English *hor*, from Old English *hār*; akin to Old High German *hēr* hoary. First known use: 1530.
examples: You can't fight city hall, says the **hoary** adage. — Jack Kroll
Of all the **hoary** old monsters, dragons are the most persistent, appearing everywhere from mall crystal shops to Disney movies. — Donald G. McNeil, Jr.

words.definition: A clumsy or awkward youth, no longer a boy but not yet a man
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1540.

words.definition: A favourite topic that someone keeps returning to; a child's toy horse
words.origin: *hobby* small light horse, from Middle English *hoby, hobyn*, perhaps from *Hobbin*, nickname for *Robert* or *Robin*. First known use: circa 1553.

words.definition: To mix socially, especially with the powerful
words.origin: From the obsolete phrase *drink hobnob* to drink alternately to one another. First known use: 1813.

words.definition: A confused mixture of unrelated things; a jumble, as of styles or ideas
words.origin: Alteration of *hotchpotch*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The common people; the masses, often used with disdain by those who think themselves above them
words.origin: Greek, the many. First known use: 1837.

words.definition: Nonsense; trite, sentimental or melodramatic material in a play or film
words.origin: Probably blend of *hocus-pocus* and *bunkum*. First known use: 1906.

words.definition: A sunken lane worn deep by centuries of feet
words.origin: From Old English *hola weg* sunken road.

words.definition: A whole idea expressed in a single word
words.origin: From Greek *holos* whole + *phrasis* phrase.

words.definition: All at once; all in a lump, as when swallowing something whole
words.origin: Probably reduplication of *bolus*. First known use: 1857.
examples: … she … put it back, **holus-bolus**, in her pocket. — Wilkie Collins

words.definition: A soft sandstone used to scour the wooden decks of ships, on bended knee as if in prayer
A repetition of the same or similar endings in a sequence of words
words.origin: From Greek *homoioteleuton*, from *homoios* like + *teleutē* ending.

words.definition: A moralizing lecture
words.origin: Middle English *omelie*, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *homilia*, from Late Greek, from Greek, conversation, discourse, from *homilein* to consort with, address, from *homilos* crowd, assembly; akin to Greek *homos* same. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A word that looks the same as another on the lips, as "my" and "pie"
words.origin: From Greek *homos* same + *phainein* to show.

words.definition: A very small human or humanlike creature; a tiny person once thought to be in sperm
words.origin: Latin, diminutive of *homin-, homo* human being. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: One's true feelings, kept private
words.origin: Japanese, true sound.

words.definition: An informal gathering with folk music
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1929.

words.definition: To jump into puddles
words.origin: Icelandic, from *hoppa* to hop + *í* into + *polla* puddles.

words.definition: To get the better of someone by cheating or deception; to bamboozle
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1829.
examples: … trying to avoid getting **hornswoggled** by advertising claims … — Jennifer Rude Klett
By the end of the call, Santillo had allegedly **hornswoggled** Olson into parting with her life savings … — Gary Craig

words.definition: A timepiece, such as a clock, watch or sundial; an instrument for telling the hours
words.origin: Middle English *orloge*, from Anglo-French *oriloge*, from Latin *horologium*, from Greek *hōrologion*, from *hōra* hour + *legein* to gather. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The erection of hairs on the skin from cold, fear or excitement; goosebumps
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *horripilātiōn-, horripilātiō* "bristling of hair," from *horripilāre* "to shudder" (Latin, "to become bristly or hairy," from *horrēre* "to be stiffly erect, bristle, shudder, shiver" + *-i-* -i- + *-pilāre,* verbal derivative of *pilus* "hair," of obscure origin) + Latin *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: circa 1656.
examples: Suddenly he was swept by **horripilation**. The goosebumps swept up from his ankles all the way to the nape of his neck, where the hairs stirred and tried to lift. — Stephen King

words.definition: Strongly urging
words.origin: Late Latin *hortativus*, from Latin *hortatus*, past participle of *hortari* to urge. First known use: 1623.

words.definition: Tending or aiming to exhort; strongly encouraging, as a hortatory speech
A rash, hotheaded person
words.origin: From the nickname of Sir Henry Percy, a rash 14th-century warrior.

words.definition: To cripple, disable or to make ineffective
words.origin: From Old English *hōh* heel.

words.definition: A favourite haunt, especially a pub
words.origin: Dutch *hof* enclosure; akin to Old English *hof* enclosure, and perhaps to *hufil* hill. First known use: 1711.

words.definition: A boisterous, carefree girl who ignores the rules of decorum; a tomboy
words.origin: Perhaps from obsolete Dutch *heiden* country lout, from Middle Dutch, heathen; akin to Old English *hǣthen* heathen. First known use: 1676.

words.definition: Harmony, balance and beauty in all things
words.origin: Navajo *hózhǫ́* beauty, harmony.

words.definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *hýbris* "arrogance, abuse, violence, outrage," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1884.
examples: Shocked by the sheer **hubris** of their comments/actions
Their story … depicts a team that became the victim of its own **hubris**.

words.definition: Swaggering; showily boastful
words.origin: A 16th-century reduplication of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Confusion or disorder; secrecy or concealment, as in hugger-mugger dealings
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: A commotion; a fuss
words.origin: Perhaps from *hallo* + Scots *balloo*, interjection used to hush children. First known use: 1762.
examples: Why do roosters crow? If they're like insects and frogs, that **hullabaloo** is an ad for a mate …
Somebody heard the splash and they raised an awful **hullabaloo**. He's gone! Lower the boats! … — Joseph Conrad

words.definition: Someone or something outstanding, remarkable or unusual
words.origin: Probably alteration of *hummer*. First known use: 1896.
examples: That was one **humdinger** of a storm.

words.definition: An imaginary illness; low spirits or a fit of the sulks
words.origin: Perhaps from *hum* + *dudgeon* resentment.

words.definition: A hillock or knoll; a hump or ridge in an ice field; a wooded rise in a marsh
words.origin: Alteration of hammock. First known use: 1555.

words.definition: A stringed instrument played by turning a crank
words.origin: Probably imitative. First known use: 1745.

words.definition: Busy, boisterous activity, as of city life; commotion and tumult
words.origin: Probably alteration & reduplication of *hurling*, gerund of *hurl*. First known use: 1539.

words.definition: Like glass: transparent or translucent
words.origin: Late Latin *hyalinus*, from Greek *hyalinos*, from *hyalos*. First known use: circa 1661.

words.definition: A cosy mood of comfort and contentment
words.origin: Borrowed from Danish, "comfort, coziness," borrowed from Norwegian *hygge* (Bokmål), *hyggje* (Nynorsk), probably noun derivative of *hygge* (Bokmål), *hyggje* (Nynorsk) "to make comfortable," also regionally "to notice, understand, take care of, be fond of," going back to an Old Norwegian equivalent of Old Icelandic *hyggja* "to think, believe," going back to Germanic **hugjan-* (whence also Old English *hycgan* "to think, meditate, consider," Old Frisian *hugia* "to be recalled," Old Saxon *huggian* "to think [of], be mindful of, consider, plan," Old High German *huggen* "to think, have in mind, be mindful of," Gothic *hugjan* "to be of a [specified] state of mind"), noun derivative of **hugi-* "mind" (whence Old English *hyge* "mind, thought, intention," Old Frisian *hei* "mind," Old Saxon *hugi* "thought, mind, intention," Old High German *hugu* "mind, understanding," Old Norse *hugr* "mind, heart, wish," Gothic *hugs* "mind"), of uncertain origin. First known use: 1960.
examples: During the long, dark winters when Danes retreat inside their homes, **hygge** is what brings them a great sense of comfort and joy. — Mary Holland
And after the recent trend of cozy, comforting **hygge**, there's another Scandinavian state of mind to embrace. — Leanne Italie

words.definition: Relating to a wedding or marriage
words.origin: Latin *hymenaeus* wedding song, wedding, from Greek *hymenaios*, from *Hymēn*. First known use: 1602.

words.definition: A transferred epithet, as in a sleepless night, where the night didn't sleep
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *hypallagē*, literally, interchange, from *hypallassein* to interchange, from *hypo-* + *allassein* to change, from *allos* other. First known use: 1586.

words.definition: A heightened sensitivity to sounds
words.origin: From Greek *hyper* over + *akousis* hearing.

words.definition: Deliberate exaggeration
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *hyperbolē* excess, hyperbole, hyperbola, from *hyperballein* to exceed, from *hyper-* + *ballein* to throw. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Often, referring to an athlete as an icon is an act of obvious **hyperbole**. — Chad Finn
… the show is famous for constantly using **hyperboles** like “the most shocking season” or “jaw-dropping” … — Shivani Gonzalez

words.definition: Relating to the extreme north of the earth; of the far north; frigid
words.origin: Latin *Hyperborei* (plural), from Greek *Hyperboreoi*, from *hyper- + Boreas*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to the drowsy state immediately before falling asleep
words.origin: Borrowed from French *hypnagogique,* from Greek *hýpnos* “sleep” + *-agōgos* “leading, drawing forth” + French *-ique* -ic. First known use: 1886.

words.definition: A pet name or term of endearment, as Bill for William; the use of such names
words.origin: Late Latin *hypocorisma*, from Greek *hypokorisma*, from *hypokorizesthai* to call by pet names, from *hypo-* + *korizesthai* to caress, from *koros* boy, *korē* girl. First known use: 1850.

words.definition: Relating to a pet name or diminutive form of a name
words.origin: Late Latin *hypocorisma*, from Greek *hypokorisma*, from *hypokorizesthai* to call by pet names, from *hypo-* + *korizesthai* to caress, from *koros* boy, *korē* girl. First known use: 1850.

words.definition: An underground chamber or vault, especially an ancient burial chamber
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *hypogēum, hypogaeum* "underground chamber," borrowed from Greek *hypógeion, hypógaion,* noun derivative from neuter of *hypógeios, hypógaios* "underground, subterranean". First known use: circa 1706.

words.definition: A diminished sense of taste
words.origin: From Greek *hypo* under + *geusis* taste.

words.definition: Putting the last thing first
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek, literally, (the) later earlier, (the) latter first. First known use: 1555.

words.definition: A gentle, communal melancholy
words.origin: Turkish, from Arabic *ḥuzn* sadness.

words.definition: Caused by medical examination or treatment, as an illness or injury
words.origin: Greek *iātro-,* combining form of *iātrós* "physician, healer" + -genic. First known use: 1920.

words.definition: The ethereal fluid said to flow like blood in the veins of the Greek gods
words.origin: Greek *ichōr*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *īconoclastēs* "person who destroys religious images," borrowed from Middle Greek *eikonoklástēs,* from Greek *eikono-* icono- + *-klastēs,* derivative, with the agent suffix *-tēs,* from the base of *kláō, klân* "to break off, break in pieces". First known use: 1641.

words.definition: To form an idea or conception of something; to imagine or envisage
A vivid, evocative word that depicts sensory experiences
words.origin: From Greek *idea* form + *phōnē* sound.

words.definition: Self worship
words.origin: From Greek *idios* one's own + *latreia* worship.

words.definition: The speech habits, vocabulary and quirks of language peculiar to one person
words.origin: *idio-* + *-lect* (as in *dialect*). First known use: 1948.

words.definition: A peculiar habit or way of behaving
words.origin: Greek *idiosynkrasia*, from *idio-* + *synkerannynai* to blend, from *syn-* + *kerannynai* to mingle, mix. First known use: 1604.
examples: When you know someone a long time, you become accustomed to their **idiosyncrasies**, which is a fancy word for their unique habits. — Lemony Snicket (Daniel Handler)
GE executives examine each country's **idiosyncrasies** microscopically, then tailor a mix of products … and retail approaches to wring the best performance from each. — Linda Grant

words.definition: Peculiar to one person; distinctively individual
words.origin: Greek *idiosynkrasia*, from *idio-* + *synkerannynai* to blend, from *syn-* + *kerannynai* to mingle, mix. First known use: 1604.

words.definition: An extremely happy, peaceful or picturesque scene
words.origin: Latin *idyllium*, from Greek *eidyllion*, from diminutive of *eidos* form; akin to Greek *idein* to see. First known use: 1586.

words.definition: Peaceful and picturesque
words.origin: From *idyll* + *-ic*. *Idyll*: Latin *idyllium*, from Greek *eidyllion*, from diminutive of *eidos* form; akin to Greek *idein* to see. First known use: 1856.

words.definition: Formed from solidified lava or magma, as granite is; relating to fire
words.origin: Latin *igneus*, from *ignis* fire; akin to Sanskrit *agni* fire. First known use: 1664.

words.definition: A will-o'-the-wisp flickering over marshes; a delusive hope or goal
words.origin: Medieval Latin, literally, foolish fire. First known use: 1563.

words.definition: Public shame or disgrace
words.origin: Middle French or Latin; Middle French *ignominie*, from Latin *ignominia*, from *ig-* (as in *ignorare* to be ignorant of, ignore) + *nomin-, nomen* name, repute. First known use: circa 1527.
examples: Suffered the **ignominy** of another losing season

words.definition: A reason for being; what makes life worth living
words.origin: Japanese, from *iki* life + *kai* worth.

words.definition: Repeatedly going outside to see if someone is coming
words.origin: Inuktitut.

words.definition: Each; every
words.origin: Middle English, from *ilk* + *a* (indefinite article). First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Introducing or stating an inference, as the word therefore does
Alluring; enticing
words.origin: From Latin *illecebrosus*, from *illecebra* allurement.

words.definition: People claiming special enlightenment or knowledge; a secretive elite
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *illūminātī,* plural of *illūminātus,* going back to Latin, past participle of *illūmināre* "to give light to, light up, brighten". First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Deceptive; not real
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Late Latin; Middle French *illusoire,* borrowed from Late Latin *illūsōrius* "mocking, derisive, deceptive," from Latin *illūdere* "to make fun of, fool, dupe" + *-tōrius,* deverbal adjective suffix originally forming derivatives from agent nouns ending in *-tōr-, -tor*. First known use: circa 1631.

words.definition: One who forgives a first and second wrong, but never a third
words.origin: Tshiluba, a Bantu language of the Congo.

words.definition: The final, adult stage of an insect; an idealized mental image of a parent
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *imāgō,* going back to Latin *imāgin-, imāgō* "representation, semblance, image". First known use: 1787.

words.definition: Overlapping like roof tiles or fish scales, as the leaves of some buds
words.origin: Late Latin *imbricatus*, past participle of *imbricare* to cover with pantiles, from Latin *imbric-, imbrex* pantile, from *imbr-, imber* rain; akin to Greek *ombros* rain. First known use: circa 1610.

words.definition: A complicated, embarrassing situation
words.origin: Italian, from *imbrogliare* to entangle, from Middle French *embrouiller*. First known use: 1750.
examples: America's president and scientific establishment became furiously embroiled with a few writers of popular nature books for children. The **imbroglio** ended in the rout of the nature writers … — Matt Cartmill

words.definition: To stain or drench, especially with blood, as a sword or one's hands
words.origin: Middle English *enbrewen, embrowen*, from Anglo-French *embrower* to soil, probably alteration of Old French *abevrer, abreuver* to water, soak, ultimately from Latin *bibere* to drink. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: Perfectly clean and tidy; free from flaw or error
words.origin: Middle English *immaculat*, from Latin *immaculatus*, from *in-* + *maculatus* stained. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Existing or operating within; inherent; of God, present throughout creation
words.origin: Late Latin *immanent-, immanens*, present participle of *immanēre* to remain in place, from Latin *in-* + *manēre* to remain. First known use: 1535.
examples: … beauty is not something imposed but something **immanent**. — Anthony Burgess

words.definition: To impoverish or to make miserable
words.origin: In-:2 + *miser*able + *-ation*. First known use: 1942.

words.definition: To kill or offer as a sacrifice, especially by burning; to destroy utterly
words.origin: Latin *immolatus*, past participle of *immolare* to sprinkle with meal before sacrificing, sacrifice, from *in-* + *mola* sacrificial barley cake, literally, millstone; akin to Latin *molere* to grind. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Unchanging over time
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *immutabilis*, from *in-* + *mutabilis* mutable. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A situation in which no progress is possible
words.origin: French, from *in-* + *passer* to pass. First known use: 1851.
examples: An impossible **impasse** in which accepting a pardon meant admitting guilt

words.definition: The quality of showing no emotion
Paint laid on a canvas so thickly that brush or knife marks stand out
words.origin: Italian, from *impastare*. First known use: 1784.

words.definition: Fearless; undaunted in the face of danger or threat
words.origin: From Latin *impavidus* fearless.

words.definition: Flawless
words.origin: Latin *impeccabilis*, from *in-* + *peccare* to sin. First known use: 1531.

words.definition: Having little or no money
words.origin: In-:1 + obsolete English *pecunious* rich, from Middle English, from Latin *pecuniosus*, from *pecunia* money. First known use: 1596.

words.definition: Equipment, especially bulky baggage, that slows one's progress
words.origin: Latin, plural of *impedimentum* impediment, from *impedire*. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: Arrogant and domineering
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *imperiōsus* "exercising authority, domineering," from *imperium* "authority over family members and slaves exercised by the head of a household, supreme administrative authority, dominion" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 1529.
examples: … a kind of arrogant potentate too **imperious** to acknowledge weaknesses common to ordinary men. — Robert Dalleck
… the **imperious** problems of the new age. — John F. Kennedy

words.definition: The quality of remaining calm under any strain
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *imperturbabilis*, from Latin *in-* + *perturbare* to perturb. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Unable to be affected; impenetrable
words.origin: Latin *impervius*, from *in-* + *pervius* pervious. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Acting quickly without thought
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *impetuosus*, from Latin *impetus*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A driving force
words.origin: Latin, assault, impetus, from *impetere* to attack, from *in-* + *petere* to go to, seek. First known use: 1641.
examples: The push serves as the **impetus**, the child and the swing reach the highest point on their own, and then gravity returns the child and swing to the starting place. — Natalie Willman Duffy
People were short on **impetus** to spend big as well, relatively speaking. — George Nelson

words.definition: To pawn, pledge or mortgage, as goods or property against a debt
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *impignorare*, from *pignus* pledge.

words.definition: Unable to be appeased
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *implacabilis*, from *in-* + *placabilis* placable. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To ask persistently and annoyingly
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Medieval Latin; Middle French *importuner* "to tire, annoy by inappropriate persistence," borrowed from Medieval Latin *importūnāre* "to harass, pester," verbal derivative of Latin *importūnus* "unfavorable, inconvenient, adverse, troublesome, relentless". First known use: 1530.
examples: … he was **importuned** relentlessly by the hostess to bestow … a name. — Geoffrey Wolff

words.definition: A spoken curse
words.origin: From *imprecate* + *-ion*. *Imprecate*: Latin *imprecatus*, past participle of *imprecari*, from *in-* + *precari* to pray. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An official licence to print, given by a church; any authoritative approval
words.origin: New Latin, let it be printed, from *imprimere* to print, from Latin, to imprint, impress. First known use: 1640.
examples: … putting the sports establishment's **imprimatur** on an event that was once the exclusive province of renegades. — Curry Kirkpatrick

words.definition: Disrespectfully bold
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *impudent-, impudens*, from *in-* + *pudent-, pudens*, present participle of *pudēre* to feel shame. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Lisa is often out of the house and in motion … contending with **impudent** youths … — Robert Lloyd
When I refused to be the child they knew and accepted me to be, I was called **impudent** and my muteness sullenness. — Maya Angelou

words.definition: To dispute the truth or honesty of
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *empugner*, from Latin *inpugnare*, from *in-* + *pugnare* to fight. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Powerlessness or weakness; an inability to act or to change things
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from *in-* + *puissance* puissance, power. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A woman with whom one is in love
words.origin: Italian *innamorata*, from feminine of *innamorato*, past participle of *innamorare* to inspire with love, from *in-* (from Latin) + *amore* love, from Latin *amor*. First known use: 1651.

words.definition: Exhaustion caused by lack of nourishment; lack of mental or spiritual vigour
Crimson or flesh-coloured; to colour something crimson, as in Macbeth
words.origin: Middle French *incarnadin*, from Old Italian *incarnadino*, from *incarnato* flesh-coloured, from Late Latin *incarnatus*. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: Never-ending; continual
words.origin: Middle English *incessaunt*, from Late Latin *incessant-, incessans*, from Latin *in-* + *cessant-, cessans*, present participle of *cessare* to delay. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Just begun and not fully formed
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *incohātus, inchoātus* "only begun, unfinished, imperfect," from past participle of *incohāre* "to start work on, begin, initiate," perhaps, if the original sense was "to yoke a plow to a team of oxen," from *in-* in-:2 + *-cohāre,* verbal derivative of *cohum* "hollow in the middle of a yoke into which a pole is fitted" or "strap used to attach the pole to the yoke," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1534.
examples: … misty, **inchoate** suspicions that all is not well with the nation … — J. M. Perry
Until an employee has earned his retirement pay … his retirement pay is but an **inchoate** right …

words.definition: In an initial stage; beginning to happen
words.origin: Latin *incipient-, incipiens*, present participle of *incipere* to begin. First known use: 1633.

words.definition: Sharp and penetrating in thought; clear and direct
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *incisivus*, from Latin *incisus*, past participle of *incidere* to cut into.

words.definition: Thoughtless; inconsiderate; lacking the power of thought or reflection
words.origin: Latin *incogitant-, incogitans*, from *in-* + *cogitant-, cogitans*, present participle of *cogitare* to cogitate. First known use: 1628.

words.definition: Badly composed or constructed, as clumsy verse; crude and unpolished
words.origin: Latin *inconditus*, from *in-* + *conditus*, past participle of *condere* to put together, from *com-* + *-dere* to put. First known use: 1539.

words.definition: Out of place; not in harmony
words.origin: Late Latin *incongruus*, from Latin *in-* + *congruus* congruous. First known use: 1582.

words.definition: Not able to be corrected or reformed
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *incorrigibilis*, from Latin *in-* + *corrigere* to correct. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A male demon believed to lie on sleepers; a cause of oppressive distress
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin, from Latin *incubare*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Books printed before 1501; the earliest stages of something's development
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *incunabula*, plural, bands holding the baby in a cradle, from *in-* + *cunae* cradle. First known use: 1820.

words.definition: A book printed before 1501; the earliest stage of something
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *incunabula*, plural, bands holding the baby in a cradle, from *in-* + *cunae* cradle. First known use: 1820.

words.definition: To search out or investigate; to examine thoroughly, as a scholar or detective
words.origin: Latin *indagatus*, past participle of *indagare*, from *indago* ring of hunters encircling game, act of searching, from Old Latin *indu* in + Latin *agere* to drive. First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: A female investigator
words.origin: Latin, feminine of *indagator* investigator.

words.definition: Persisting tirelessly
words.origin: Middle French, from Latin *indefatigabilis*, from *in-* + *defatigare* to fatigue, from *de-* + *fatigare* to fatigue. First known use: 1608.

words.definition: Impossible to erase or forget
words.origin: Middle English *indelyble*, from Medieval Latin *indelibilis*, alteration of Latin *indelebilis*, from *in-* + *delēre* to delete. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Angry at unfair treatment
words.origin: Latin *indignant-, indignans*, present participle of *indignari* to be indignant, from *indignus* unworthy, from *in-* + *dignus* worthy. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: To write or compose a poem, speech or letter, especially in a formal style
words.origin: Middle English *enditen*, from Anglo-French *enditer* to write, compose, from Vulgar Latin **indictare*, frequentative of Latin *indicere* to make known formally, proclaim, from *in-* + *dicere* to say. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Wanting to avoid activity; lazy
words.origin: Late Latin *indolent-, indolens* insensitive to pain, from Latin *in-* + *dolent-, dolens*, present participle of *dolēre* to feel pain. First known use: 1663.

words.definition: Impossible to subdue or defeat
words.origin: Late Latin *indomitabilis*, from Latin *in-* + *domitare* to tame. First known use: 1634.

words.definition: Lenient; permitting pleasure
words.origin: Latin *indulgent-, indulgens*, present participle of *indulgēre*. First known use: 1509.

words.definition: Too great to be expressed in words
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *ineffabilis*, from *in-* + *effabilis* capable of being expressed, from *effari* to speak out, from *ex-* + *fari* to speak. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Unable to be resisted or avoided
words.origin: Latin *ineluctabilis*, from *in-* + *eluctari* to struggle clear of, from *ex-* + *luctari* to struggle, wrestle; akin to Latin *luxus* dislocated. First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: Lacking the ability to move or act
words.origin: Latin *inert-, iners* unskilled, idle, from *in-* + *art-, ars* skill. First known use: 1647.

words.definition: Impossible to stop or prevent
words.origin: Latin *inexorabilis*, from *in-* + *exorabilis* pliant, from *exorare* to prevail upon, from *ex-* + *orare* to speak. First known use: 1542.

words.definition: A person having a bad reputation. verb tr.: To defame: to attack the reputation or to disgrace
words.origin: From Latin *infamare*, from *in-* not + *fama* reputation.

words.definition: Too odious or horrible to be spoken of; unspeakable, as infandous crimes
words.origin: From Latin *infandus* unspeakable.

words.definition: Beneath one's dignity, as a task one thinks too lowly; from Latin infra dignitatem
words.origin: Short for Latin *infra dignitatem*. First known use: 1824.
examples: … while his work … was financially profitable, it was just a bit **infra dig**. — John McCarten

words.definition: Unbreakable; inviolable, as a law, principle or bond that cannot be broken
words.origin: Middle French, from Late Latin *infrangibilis*, from Latin *in-* + *frangere* to break. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: Funnel-shaped
words.origin: From Latin *infundibulum* funnel + *-form*.

words.definition: Clever and inventive
words.origin: Middle English *ingenyous*, from Middle French *ingenieus*, from Latin *ingeniosus*, from *ingenium* natural capacity. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Innocent and unsuspecting
words.origin: Latin *ingenuus* native, freeborn, from *in-* + *gignere* to beget. First known use: 1588.
examples: … her **ingenuous** thirst for experience … — Christopher Rawson

words.definition: A fire burning on a domestic hearth; a fireplace, as in the cozy ingle nook
words.origin: Scottish Gaelic *aingeal*. First known use: 1508.

words.definition: A cosy space beside a large fireplace
To swallow greedily; to gulp down or engulf, as food or a whirlpool might
words.origin: Latin *ingurgitatus*, past participle of *ingurgitare*, from *in-* + *gurgit-, gurges* whirlpool. First known use: circa 1570.

words.definition: An innocent, unsophisticated young woman, especially as a stage role
words.origin: French, feminine of *ingénu* ingenuous.

words.definition: Tending to obstruct or harm; hostile
words.origin: Late Latin *inimicalis*, from Latin *inimicus* enemy. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: Grossly immoral behaviour
words.origin: Middle English *iniquite*, from Anglo-French *iniquité*, from Latin *iniquitat-, iniquitas*, from *iniquus* uneven, from *in-* + *aequus* equal. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Pedantically or affectedly learned, of words borrowed to sound bookish
Inborn; natural
words.origin: Middle English *innat*, from Latin *innatus*, past participle of *innasci* to be born in, from *in-* + *nasci* to be born. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Not harmful or offensive
words.origin: Latin *innocuus*, from *in-* + *nocēre*. First known use: 1631.
examples: … newly aware that the behaviour isn't as **innocuous** as they imagined. — Conor Friedersdorf

words.definition: An animal living in the nest, burrow or home of another
words.origin: Latin *inquilinus* tenant, lodger, from *in-* + *colere* to cultivate, dwell. First known use: 1879.

words.definition: Unhealthy, especially of a climate or place; seedy and run-down
words.origin: Latin *insalubris*, from *in-* + *salubris* healthful. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Tasteless; without flavour
words.origin: From *in-* not + Latin *sapor* taste.

words.definition: Impossible to satisfy
words.origin: Middle English *insaciable*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *insatiabilis*, from *in-* + *satiare* to satisfy. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The unique inner essence of a person, place or thing
words.origin: Coined by the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins.

words.definition: An isolated rocky hill rising from a plain
words.origin: German, from *Insel* island + *Berg* mountain. First known use: 1913.

words.definition: Proceeding in a subtle way, but with harmful effects
words.origin: Latin *insidiosus*, from *insidiae* ambush, from *insidēre* to sit in, sit on, from *in-* + *sedēre* to sit. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: An assertion or hint that's disparaging and suggestive
words.origin: A blend of *insinuation* and *innuendo*.

words.definition: Lacking flavour or interest
words.origin: French & Late Latin; French *insipide*, from Late Latin *insipidus*, from Latin *in-* + *sapidus* savory, from *sapere* to taste. First known use: 1609.

words.definition: Rude and disrespectful
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *insolent-, insolens* unaccustomed, overbearing, from *in-* + *solens*, present participle of *solēre* to be accustomed; perhaps akin to Latin *sodalis* comrade. First known use: 1678.
examples: … the shifty slouch of their movements and the **insolent** way they throw their cigarette ends … around the streets. — Jan Morris

words.definition: Carefree lack of concern
words.origin: French, from *in-* + *soucier* to trouble, disturb, from Old French, from Latin *sollicitare*. First known use: 1799.

words.definition: Casually unconcerned
words.origin: French, from *in-* + *soucier* to trouble, disturb, from Old French, from Latin *sollicitare*. First known use: 1799.

words.definition: To thicken or congeal, as a sauce or syrup by evaporation; to condense
words.origin: Late Latin *inspissatus*, past participle of *inspissare*, from Latin *in-* + *spissus* slow, dense; akin to Greek *spidnos* compact, Lithuanian *spisti* to form a swarm. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: A stage in the life of an insect between two molts, prior to reaching maturity
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, equivalent. First known use: 1895.

words.definition: To blow or breathe into
words.origin: Middle English *insufflacion*, from Late Latin *insufflation-, insufflatio*, from *insufflare* to blow upon, from Latin *in-* + *sufflare* to inflate, from *sub-* + *flare* to blow. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Impossible to overcome, as a difficulty, obstacle or objection
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *insuperabilis*, from *in-* + *superare* to surmount, from *super* over. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To mix, insert or intersperse, especially with something extraneous
words.origin: Middle French *entrelarder*, from Old French, from *entre* inter- + *larder* to lard, from *lard*, noun. First known use: circa 1587.

words.definition: A person who takes part in a dialogue or conversation, especially a formal one
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *interlocūtor* "mediator, participant in a dialogue," from Latin *interlocū-,* variant stem of *interloquī* "to speak between, interrupt, issue an interlocutory decree" (from *inter-* inter- + *loquī* "to speak") + *-tor,* agent suffix. First known use: circa 1518.

words.definition: Destructive to both sides in a conflict; relating to conflict within a group
words.origin: Latin *internecinus*, from *internecare* to destroy, kill, from *inter-* + *necare* to kill, from *nec-, nex* violent death. First known use: 1642.

words.definition: Punctuation
words.origin: From Latin *interpunctio*, from *interpungere* to point between.

words.definition: A period when normal government is suspended, as between two reigns
words.origin: Latin, from *inter-* + *regnum* reign. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: The lower or inner curve of an arch or vault, as seen from beneath
words.origin: French, from Latin *intra* within + French *dos* back. First known use: 1772.

words.definition: Unwilling to change one's views
words.origin: Spanish *intransigente*, from *in-* + *transigente*, present participle of *transigir* to compromise, from Latin *transigere* to come to an agreement. First known use: circa 1879.

words.definition: Fearless and adventurous
words.origin: Latin *intrepidus*, from *in-* + *trepidus* alarmed. First known use: 1680.

words.definition: To flood; to overwhelm
words.origin: Latin *inundatus*, past participle of *inundare*, from *in-* + *unda* wave. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: To accustom to something unpleasant
words.origin: Middle English *enuren*, from *in ure* customary, from *putten in ure* to use, put into practice, partial translation of Anglo-French *mettre en ovre, en uevre*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Policies that **inure** to the benefit of employees

words.definition: Insulting, abusive language
words.origin: Middle English *invectif*, from Middle French, from Latin *invectivus*, from *invectus*, past participle of *invehere*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To speak or write about something with great hostility; to rail
words.origin: Latin *invehi* to attack, inveigh, passive of *invehere* to carry in, from *in-* + *vehere* to carry. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: To persuade by deception or flattery
words.origin: Anglo-French *enveegler, aveogler, avogler* to blind, hoodwink, from *avogle, enveugle* blind, from Medieval Latin *ab oculis*, literally, lacking eyes. First known use: 1539.

words.definition: Having a long-established habit
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *inveteratus*, from past participle of *inveterare* to age (transitive verb), from *in-* + *veter-, vetus* old. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **inveterate** tendency to overlook the obvious

words.definition: Easily made angry
words.origin: Middle French, from Late Latin *irascibilis*, from Latin *irasci* to become angry, be angry, from *ira*. First known use: circa 1530.

words.definition: Aiming for peace or reconciliation, especially between churches; conciliatory
words.origin: Greek *eirēnikos*, from *eirēnē* peace. First known use: circa 1864.

words.definition: Showing shifting rainbow colours
words.origin: Greek *īrid-, îris* "rainbow, iridescent halo around the moon, a flame, etc." + -escent. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: Cruel; unfeeling
words.origin: From *iron* + *hearted*.

words.definition: One advocating the restoration of territory that earlier belonged to one's country
Not able to be refuted or disproved, as irrefragable evidence; indisputable
words.origin: Late Latin *irrefragabilis*, from Latin *in-* + *refragari* to oppose, from *re-* + *-fragari* (as in *suffragari* to vote for); akin to Latin *suffragium* suffrage. First known use: 1533.

words.definition: Showing a lack of respect
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *irreverent-, irreverens*, from *in-* + *reverent-, reverens* reverent. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Equal in time
words.origin: Greek *isochronos*, from *is-* + *chronos* time. First known use: 1680.

words.definition: Occurring at the same time or at equal intervals, as a pendulum's swing
words.origin: Greek *isochronos*. First known use: 1706.

words.definition: Travelling from place to place
words.origin: Late Latin *itinerant-, itinerans*, present participle of *itinerari* to journey, from Latin *itiner-, iter* journey, way; akin to Hittite *itar* way, Latin *ire* to go. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: Nonsensical or wildly incoherent speech or writing. verb intr.: To speak or write in this manner
words.origin: From Lewis Carroll's poem *Jabberwocky*.

words.definition: An impertinent, conceited person; a cheeky child; once, a tame monkey
words.origin: Middle English *Jack Napis*, nickname for William de la Pole †1450 duke of Suffolk. First known use: circa 1529.

words.definition: Unskilled; unscrupulous; incompetent
words.origin: Jack + *-leg* (as in *blackleg*). First known use: 1833.

words.definition: A peasant uprising, from the French revolt of 1358 against the nobility
words.origin: Middle French, from the French peasant revolt in 1358, from *jacque* peasant. First known use: 1523.

words.definition: Boasting or boastfulness
words.origin: From Latin *jactantia*, from *jactare* to boast.

words.definition: Boasting
words.origin: From Latin *jactatio*, from *jactare* to toss, boast.

words.definition: A false boast, especially to the harm of another; restless tossing in illness
words.origin: Late Latin *jactitation-, jactitatio*, from *jactitare*, frequentative of Latin *jactare* to throw. First known use: 1665.

words.definition: Having two faces, sides or contrasting aspects
words.origin: From *Janus*, the two-faced Roman god + *-form*.

words.definition: A practical joke; a jest or prank, as played by schoolboys or court jesters
words.origin: From Middle English *jape*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A joke so unfunny one can't help laughing
words.origin: Indonesian slang.

words.definition: Naive and simplistic; also, dull
words.origin: Latin *jejunus* empty of food, hungry, meagre. First known use: 1646.
examples: … the "literary" fiction being written in this country nowadays strikes me as so **jejune**, self-absorbed and lifeless that I am just about unable to read it, much less pass fair judgment on it. — Jonathan Yardley

words.definition: Relating to breakfast, as a jentacular cup of tea taken before the day's work begins
words.origin: From Latin *jentaculum* breakfast.

words.definition: A long, mournful complaint or lamentation, like those of the prophet Jeremiah
words.origin: French *jérémiade*, from *Jérémie* Jeremiah, from Late Latin *Jeremias*. First known use: 1780.
examples: … the warnings became **jeremiads** against the folly of overemphasis on science and technology at the expense of man's subjective and emotional life. — Ada Louise Huxtable

words.definition: Remote, unimportant or small
words.origin: From *jerkwater* rural train. First known use: 1888.

words.definition: A very large wine bottle, holding four times a standard bottle or more
words.origin: *Jeroboam* I died about 912 b.c. king of the northern kingdom of Israel. First known use: 1889.

words.definition: To throw away or abandon
words.origin: Derivative of jettison. First known use: 1848.
examples: … must be prepared to **jettison** many romantic notions … — Christopher Catling

words.definition: An intense will to live
words.origin: Hindi, from Sanskrit *jijīviṣā* the desire to live.

words.definition: A state of nervousness; the jitters; delirium tremens; also pyjamas
words.origin: Perhaps alteration of *delirium tremens*. First known use: 1852.

words.definition: A stupid person; a blockhead, literally a stupid head
words.origin: From obsolete *jobard* fool + *noll* head.

words.definition: A petty official who insists on following trivial rules at the expense of common sense
words.origin: From the phrase "it's more than my job's worth".

words.definition: Playful or humorous
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *jocōsus* "fond of jokes, given to joking, laughable," from *jocus* "joke, jest" + *-ōsus* -ose. First known use: 1673.

words.definition: Cheerful and lighthearted
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *jocundus*, alteration of Latin *jucundus*, from *juvare* to help. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a poet could not but be gay, in such a **jocund** company … — William Wordsworth

words.definition: Exuberant enjoyment of life
words.origin: French, literally, joy of living. First known use: 1889.
examples: He radiates a vitalizing energy, the zest and gaiety of an inexhaustible **joie de vivre**. — Robert Kuttner

words.definition: An itinerant minstrel in medieval France who sang, juggled and told tales
words.origin: French, from Old French *jogleour*. First known use: 1782.

words.definition: A large drinking bowl or vessel, or the punch it holds, as at a festive gathering
words.origin: Perhaps from *Joram* in the Bible who "brought with him vessels of silver" (2 Samuel 8:10—King James Version). First known use: 1730.

words.definition: Pleasure; ecstasy
Doubtful; undecided; hesitating
words.origin: American dialect alteration of *dubious*.

words.definition: Joyful and triumphant
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *jūbilant-, jūbilans,* present participle of *jūbilāre* "to let out whoops, invoke with shouts" (Late Latin, "sing hymns of joy, be joyous"), from **jū, jō,* exclamation expressing strong emotion + *-bilāre,* as in *sībilāre* "to hiss"; **jū* going back to Indo-European **i̯ū,* whence also Middle High German *jū, jūch,* exclamation of joy, *jūchezen* "to rejoice," Old Icelandic *ýla* "to howl," Greek *iȳ́,* exclamation of amazement, *iȳ́zein* "to shout, yell". First known use: 1667.

words.definition: Showing good judgment; wise
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *judicieux,* from Latin *jūdicium* "legal proceedings, court, judgment, faculty of judging, discernment" + Middle French *-eux,* going back to Old French *-eus,* earlier *-os, -ous,* going back to Latin *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: A sweet drink, especially one of bourbon, sugar and fresh mint
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Arabic *julāb*, from Persian *gulāb*, from *gul* rose + *āb* water. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A youthful state
Becoming young or youthful; growing young again, as if renewed
To place side by side for contrast
words.origin: Probably back-formation from *juxtaposition*. First known use: 1851.
examples: … **juxtapose** unexpected combinations of colours, shapes and ideas … — J. F. T. Bugental

words.definition: The opportune moment for action
words.origin: Greek, the right moment.

words.definition: Continuous improvement through small steps
words.origin: Borrowed from Japanese, literally, "betterment, improvement," from *kai-* "change, modify" + *zen* "good, goodness". First known use: 1983.
examples: In companies that implement **kaizen**, workers look continuously for small improvements that can be implemented immediately. — Sarah Manguso

words.definition: Government by the least suitable or competent citizens of a state
words.origin: From Greek *kakistos* worst + *-kratia* rule.

words.definition: The fear of failure or defeat
words.origin: From Greek *kakorraphia* plotting of evil + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Brightly varied in colour and pattern; ever-changing
words.origin: Greek *kalos* beautiful + *eidos* form + English *-scope*. First known use: 1817.

words.definition: The ideal of being both beautiful and good
words.origin: Greek, from *kalos* beautiful + *kai* and + *agathos* good.

words.definition: Beauty that is more than skin deep
words.origin: Greek, the beautiful.

words.definition: Taboo
words.origin: Hawaiian, sacred, forbidden.

words.definition: Death from overwork
words.origin: Japanese, from *ka* excess + *rō* labour + *shi* death.

words.definition: A hangover; a state of distress, confusion or clamour, from German for cats' wailing
words.origin: German, from *Katze* cat + *Jammer* distress. First known use: 1834.

words.definition: The gleam of a river in the dark
words.origin: Japanese, from *kawa* river + *akari* light.

words.definition: Joyful passion and high spirits
words.origin: Greek, from Turkish *keyif* pleasure, from Arabic *kayf*.

words.definition: The renunciation of divine nature by Christ in becoming human; self-emptying
words.origin: Late Greek *kenōsis*, from Greek, action of emptying, from *kenoun* to purge, empty, from *kenos* empty. First known use: 1873.

words.definition: Conspicuous; easily recognized, as a kenspeckle figure about town
words.origin: Probably of Scandinavian origin; akin to Norwegian *kjennspak* quick to recognize. First known use: 1616.

words.definition: A cut, notch, slit, etc. made by a cutting tool
words.origin: Middle English, action of cutting, from Old English *cyrf*; akin to Old English *ceorfan* to carve. First known use: 1523.

words.definition: A commotion or fuss, especially one caused by conflicting views
words.origin: Respelling of Scots *cerfuffle, carfuffle,* derivative of *cerfuffle,* verb, "to disorder, throw into confusion," from *cer-, car-* (intensive prefix, perhaps borrowed from Scottish Gaelic *car-,* prefixal use of *car* "kink, quirk, twist, turn") + *fuffle* "to dishevel, ruffle," of imitative origin. First known use: 1908.
examples: In all the **kerfuffle**, nobody seemed to have noticed Harry, which suited him perfectly. — J. K. Rowling
It's not the only school with dress code issues; almost every week there's a local story about some **kerfuffle** over what kids wear to school. — Belinda Luscombe

words.definition: A meddler who offers unwanted advice, especially to card players
words.origin: Borrowed from Yiddish *kibetser,* from *kibetsn* "to kibitz" + *-er* -er. First known use: 1922.

words.definition: A fancy but insubstantial dish of food; a trinket or bauble, from French quelque chose
words.origin: By folk etymology from French *quelque chose* something. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: The giddy, fluttery thrill of being near someone you like
words.origin: Tagalog, the thrill or exhilaration of romance; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2016.

words.definition: To set alight; to arouse
words.origin: Middle English, probably modification of Old Norse *kynda*; akin to Old High German *cunte*sal fire. First known use: 13th century.
examples: Using dry twigs to **kindle** a fire

words.definition: The study of body movements, such as gestures or facial expressions, as a form of communication
words.origin: Greek *kinēsis* motion + English *-ics*. First known use: 1952.

words.definition: Repairing broken pottery with gold, honouring the cracks
words.origin: Borrowed from Japanese, from *kin* "gold" + *tsugi* "patch". First known use: 2008.
examples: Poetically translated to "golden joinery," **kintsugi** … is the centuries-old Japanese art of fixing broken pottery. — Kelly Richman-Abdou
The Japanese aesthetic of wabi-sabi is the appreciation of imperfections in objects. The **kintsugi** method of repair not only embraces the imperfections but highlights them. — Sandy Knowles

words.definition: A woman's gown or outer petticoat in medieval times; a man's tunic or coat
words.origin: Middle English *kirtel*, from Old English *cyrtel*, from Old English **curt* short, from Latin *curtus* mutilated, curtailed. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Fate or destiny
words.origin: Turkish, from Arabic *qisma* portion, lot. First known use: 1828.
examples: … we left much of the trip planning to **kismet** and synchronicity, grateful for a chance to lose ourselves in the magic generated by anomalies, towering redwoods and sea air. — Tanya Ward Goodman
They didn't know it right away, but when Heather Juergensen and Jennifer Westfeldt met at a New York theatre retreat in the late '90s, it was **kismet**. — Elaina Patton

words.definition: One's friends, acquaintances and neighbours, in the phrase kith and kin
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *cȳthth*; akin to *cūth* known. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: An inelegant, improvised solution to a problem
words.origin: Of uncertain origin. First known use: 1962.
examples: Just getting your documents into and out of the iPad is a **kludge**. You must e-mail them back and forth to yourself or sync to your computer using iTunes software. — Steve Morgenstern

words.definition: A clumsy or stupid person
words.origin: Yiddish *klots*, literally, wooden beam, from Middle High German *kloz* lumpy mass. First known use: 1959.

words.definition: Dishonest or unscrupulous behaviour; roguery, as of a knave in a play
words.origin: From *knave* + *-ry*. *Knave*: Middle English, from Old English *cnafa*; akin to Old High German *knabo* boy. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: The sound of a bell rung solemnly for a death or funeral; an omen of an end
examples: Sounded the death **knell** for our hopes

words.definition: The feeling on meeting someone that love is inevitable
words.origin: Japanese, premonition of love.

words.definition: Sunlight filtering through leaves
words.origin: Japanese, from *ko* tree + *more* leak through + *bi* sun.

words.definition: A meeting, discussion, conversation or storytelling session. verb intr.: To speak, talk or discuss
words.origin: Māori *kōrero* to speak, talk.

words.definition: Life out of balance; a way of life that cannot last
words.origin: Hopi, life out of balance.

words.definition: Weight gained from emotional overeating
words.origin: German, grief bacon.

words.definition: To complain persistently
words.origin: Yiddish *kvetshn*, literally, to squeeze, pinch, from Middle High German *quetschen*. First known use: circa 1950.

words.definition: Thinking of the perfect reply too late
words.origin: French, staircase wit; from Denis Diderot.

words.definition: A weakening, shaking or downfall, as of a state, belief or structure
words.origin: From Latin *labefacere* to cause to totter.

words.definition: Intricate and confusing, like a maze
words.origin: From *labyrinth* + *-ine*. *Labyrinth*: Middle English *laborintus*, from Latin *labyrinthus*, from Greek *labyrinthos*. First known use: 1632.

words.definition: Like a lizard, in form or movement; relating to lizards
words.origin: From Latin *lacerta* lizard.

words.definition: Inducing tears
words.origin: From Latin *lacrima* tear + *-genic*.

words.definition: Tearful; inclined to weep
words.origin: Latin *lacrimosus*, from *lacrima* "tear". First known use: circa 1727.
examples: Tended to become **lachrymose** when he was drunk

words.definition: Lacking enthusiasm and determination; carelessly lazy
words.origin: Irregular from *lackaday* + *-ical*. First known use: 1768.
examples: Teachers who are impatient with **lackadaisical** students

words.definition: One who lacks intelligence
words.origin: From *lack* + *wit*.

words.definition: Using very few words
words.origin: Latin *laconicus* Spartan, from Greek *lakōnikos*; from the Spartan reputation for terseness of speech. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: An unfilled space or interval; a gap or missing portion, as in a manuscript
words.origin: Latin, pool, pit, gap. First known use: 1652.
examples: … the evident **lacunae** in his story. — Shirley Hazzard
… despite all these **lacunae**, those reforms were a vast improvement …

words.definition: Goods or wreckage lying on the seabed, often marked by a buoy for recovery
words.origin: Middle French *lagan* or Medieval Latin *laganum* debris washed up from the sea. First known use: 1641.

words.definition: A small gift given to a customer with a purchase; something extra, a bonus
words.origin: American French, from American Spanish *la ñapa* the lagniappe, from *la + ñapa, yapa*, from Quechua *yapa* something added. First known use: 1844.
examples: The waiter added a cup of lobster bisque as a **lagniappe** to the meal.

words.definition: Just the right amount
words.origin: Swedish, just right.

words.definition: To spend time aimlessly; to idle or dawdle, especially when there is work to do
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1862.
examples: We were slow because the girl was **lollygagging**, the photographer was photographing, and I was on crutches. — James Robison

words.definition: The relief of stress, anxiety, pain or frustration through swearing
words.origin: From Greek *lalia* "speech, talk" + *chezein* "to relieve oneself". A medical term, first used in the early 20th century.

words.definition: A soft, flickering glow
Softly glowing or flickering
words.origin: Latin *lambent-, lambens*, present participle of *lambere* to lick. First known use: 1647.

words.definition: To express grief or regret
words.origin: Middle English *lementen*, from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *lamenter*, from Latin *lamentari*, from *lamentum*, noun, lament. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … nightingales **lament** without ceasing … — L. P. Smith
… must regret the imprudence, **lament** the result … — Jane Austen

words.definition: A female demon or monster of Greek legend who preyed on children; a witch
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin, from Greek, devouring monster; akin to Greek *lamyros* gluttonous. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To publicly ridicule through satire
words.origin: Borrowed from 17th-century French *lampon,* perhaps from *lampons!* "let us drink up!", first plural imperative of *lamper* "to drink up, drink to the bottom quickly," nasalized variant of *laper* "to lap, lap up," going back to Vulgar Latin **lappāre,* of expressive origin; allegedly from the use of *lampons!* in the refrains of verse satires. First known use: 1645.
examples: He said such ridiculous things that he was often the target of **lampoons** in the press.

words.definition: Loudness and clarity of voice; a ringing, distinct manner of speaking
words.origin: From Greek *lampros* clear + *phōnē* voice.

words.definition: Relaxed and unhurried; lacking energy
words.origin: Middle French *languide*, from Latin *languidus*, from *languēre* to languish. First known use: 1595.
examples: … arms too **languid** with happiness to embrace him … — John Galsworthy

words.definition: To weaken; to suffer neglect
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *languiss-*, stem of *languir*, from Vulgar Latin **languire*, from Latin *languēre*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Fine, soft hair, especially that covering the body of a newborn
words.origin: Latin, down, from *lana* wool. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Elegant and concise, as if engraved in stone; a cutter of gems
words.origin: Latin *lapidarius* of stone, from *lapid-, lapis* stone. First known use: 1724.

words.definition: Absurdly fanciful or impractical
Relating to or guilty of theft; thieving, as larcenous intentions
Pretentious; affected; dandyish
words.origin: Victorian slang, perhaps from *la-di-da*.

words.definition: Generosity in giving
words.origin: Middle English *largesse*, from Anglo-French, from *large*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: Projects depending on a flow of federal **largesse**

words.definition: Physical or mental weariness
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *lassitudo*, from *lassus* weary; probably akin to Old English *læt* late. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The patient complained of headache, nausea, and **lassitude**.
… surrendering to an overpowering **lassitude**, an extreme desire to sit and dream. — Alan Moorehead

words.definition: Present but hidden or undeveloped
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *latent-, latens*, from present participle of *latēre* to lie hidden; akin to Greek *lanthanein* to escape notice. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A hiding place; a cosy refuge
words.origin: From Latin *latibulum*, from *latere* to lie hidden.

words.definition: Tolerant of variations in religious opinion or doctrine; broad-minded
Deserving praise
examples: She has shown a **laudable** devotion to her children.

words.definition: An alcoholic solution of opium once widely used as a painkiller
words.origin: From New Latin *laudanum*. First known use: circa 1603.

words.definition: A poor and diseased person, especially one with leprosy, after Lazarus
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *lazarus*, from Late Latin *Lazarus*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An isolation hospital for people with infectious diseases; a quarantine station
words.origin: Italian *lazzaretto*, alteration of *Nazaretto*, quarantine station in Venice, from *Santa Maria di Nazareth*, church on the island where it was located. First known use: 1549.

words.definition: A meadow or open grassland
words.origin: Middle English *leye*, from Old English *lēah*; akin to Old High German *lōh* thicket, Latin *lucus* grove, *lux* light. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Loyal and honest; faithful, as in the Scots phrase the land o' the leal
words.origin: Middle English *leel*, from Anglo-French *leal*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Weary of life; recklessly daring
words.origin: German, from *Leben* life + *müde* tired.

words.definition: Sleight of hand; deceptive skill
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *leger de main* light of hand. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The … performer devised a show that attached orchestral music to her feats of **legerdemain**. — Steven Brown
… a remarkable piece of diplomatic **legerdemain** … — Anthony West

words.definition: Nimbleness of mind or body
words.origin: Middle French *legereté*, from Old French, lightness, from *leger* light, from Vulgar Latin **leviarius*, from Latin *levis*. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: Soothing or alleviating pain, as a lenitive balm; a soothing medicine
words.origin: Middle English *lenitif*, from Middle French, from Medieval Latin *lenitivus*, from Latin *lenitus*, past participle of *lenire*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to or living in still water
words.origin: Latin *lentus* sluggish. First known use: circa 1935.

words.definition: Slowness or sluggishness
words.origin: From Latin *lentitudo* slowness, from *lentus* slow.

words.definition: Having a thin skin
words.origin: From Greek *leptos* thin + *derma* skin.

words.definition: Forgetfulness; oblivion
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *Lēthē,* locale or a river in the Underworld, borrowed from Greek *lḗthē* "forgetfulness, oblivion" (personified as a goddess of forgetfulness, also a plain in the Underworld), derivative from the base of *lanthánein* "to escape one's notice," *lanthánesthai* "to forget". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The inability to remember a particular word or name; tip-of-the-tongue frustration
words.origin: From Greek *lēthē* forgetfulness + *logos* word.

words.definition: Humour or frivolity, especially when out of place
words.origin: Latin *levitat-, levitas*, from *levis* light in weight. First known use: 1564.
examples: She would tolerate no **levity** in the classroom.
… the **levity** … of the brisk fire. — Charles Dickens

words.definition: A compiler of dictionaries
words.origin: Late Greek *lexikographos*, from *lexikon* + Greek *-graphos* writer, from *graphein* to write. First known use: 1625.

words.definition: Using pretentious words and language
words.origin: From Greek *lexiphanēs* phrase-monger, from *lexis* word + *phainein* to show.

words.definition: A drink poured out as an offering to a deity; a drink, used humorously
words.origin: Middle English *libacioun*, from Latin *libation-, libatio*, from *libare* to pour as an offering; akin to Greek *leibein* to pour. First known use: 14th century.
examples: They offered a **libation** at the temple.

words.definition: A person who freely indulges in sensual pleasures
words.origin: Middle English, "freedman," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *libertin,* borrowed from Latin *lībertīnus,* noun derivative from *lībertīnus,* adjective, "of a freedman," from *lībertus* "freedman" (probably back-formation from *lībertās* "freedom, liberty") + *-īnus* -ine. First known use: 1577.
examples: … **libertines** indulging a variety of amorous impulses. — Mel White

words.definition: One who reads in bed
words.origin: From Latin *liber* book + *cubiculum* bedroom; coined by Christopher Morley.

words.definition: Promiscuous and unprincipled
words.origin: Latin *licentiosus*, from *licentia*. First known use: 1535.

words.definition: At great speed
words.origin: Probably irregular from lick + *split*. First known use: 1818.

words.definition: A person who behaves obsequiously to those in power; a toady
Trivial or very small, like the tiny people of Lilliput in Gulliver's Travels
A pleasant rise and fall in the voice
words.origin: Middle English *lulten* to sound an alarm. First known use: 1722.

words.definition: Having delicate, pale hands, unaccustomed to manual labour
words.origin: From *lily* + *handed*.

words.definition: The state of being infatuated with another person
words.origin: *limer-,* alleged to be an arbitrary formation by the coiner of the word + -ence. First known use: 1977.
examples: This is the crazy love phase known by psychologists as **limerence**: your heart palpitates, your palms sweat and your pupils dilate … — Catherine Armitage
**Limerance** is that first stage of mad attraction where all the hormones are flowing and things feel so right. — Miriam Stoppard

words.definition: At a boundary or threshold; in between
words.origin: Latin *limin-, limen* threshold. First known use: 1875.
examples: … in the **liminal** state between life and death. — Deborah Jowitt

words.definition: To depict or describe in painting or words; to illuminate a manuscript
words.origin: Middle English *limnen* to illuminate (a manuscript), probably back-formation from *lymnour* illuminator, alteration of *lumenur*, from Anglo-French *aluminer, enluminer* to illuminate, ultimately from Latin *illuminare*. First known use: 1592.
examples: … he was **limned** by a streetlight. — Stephen Coonts

words.definition: Fond of or living in inland bodies of water such as lakes, pools
words.origin: From Greek *limnē* marsh + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: Clear and transparent
words.origin: French or Latin; French *limpide*, from Latin *limpidus*, perhaps from *lympha* water. First known use: 1598.
examples: … the benign effects of a **limpid** childhood …

words.definition: The omission of a letter or syllable in writing
words.origin: From Greek *leipein* to leave out + *-graphia* writing.

words.definition: The long tail of a graduate's hood; a silly person
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *liripipium*, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Slim, supple and graceful
words.origin: Alteration of *lithesome*. First known use: 1763.

words.definition: A tedious recital or repetitive series
words.origin: Middle English *letanie*, from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French, from Late Latin *litania*, from Late Greek *litaneia*, from Greek, entreaty, from *litanos* supplicant. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … a **litany** of cheering phrases. — Herman Wouk

words.definition: Torment at the sudden sight of one's own misery
words.origin: Czech *lítost* sorrow, regret.

words.definition: Understatement by denying the opposite, as "not bad"
words.origin: Greek *litotēs*, from *litos* simple, perhaps from *lit-, lis* linen cloth. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: Relating to or situated on the shore of the sea or a lake; a coastal region
words.origin: Latin *litoralis*, from *litor-, litus* seashore. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: A lout; a thick gruel
words.origin: Probably from English dialect *lob* to boil + obsolete English dialect *lolly* broth. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: Skill in using or coining words
words.origin: From Greek *logodaidalia*, from *logos* word + *daidalos* cunning.

words.definition: A dictator about words and their use
words.origin: From Greek *logos* word + *agōgos* leading.

words.definition: An obsession with words
words.origin: From Greek *logos* word + *lēpsis* seizure.

words.definition: An argument about words or the meaning of words; a war of words
words.origin: Greek *logomachia*, from *log-* + *machesthai* to fight. First known use: 1569.

words.definition: A lover of words
A tendency to extreme loquacity; an uncontrollable flow of words
words.origin: From New Latin *logorrhea*. First known use: circa 1892.

words.definition: An exceptional person, thing or event
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1896.

words.definition: To dawdle or fool around; to waste time
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1862.
