examples: We were slow because the girl was **lollygagging**, the photographer was photographing, and I was on crutches. — James Robison

words.definition: Patience in the face of hardship or provocation; forbearance
words.origin: Middle English *longanymyte*, from Late Latin *longanimitat-, longanimitas*, from *longanimis* patient, from Latin *longus* long + *animus* soul. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Tending to talk a great deal
words.origin: Latin *loquāc-, loquāx* "talkative, verbose" (from *loquī* "to talk, speak" + *-āc-,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1634.
examples: … not often the most **loquacious** man when it comes to talking to the media … — Bill Reiter
The moderators have largely held their ground, … cutting off **loquacious** candidates. — Eliza Collins

words.definition: Spectacles held by a long handle
words.origin: French, from *lorgner* to take a sidelong look at, from Middle French, from *lorgne* squinting. First known use: 1803.

words.definition: A man who behaves selfishly and irresponsibly in his sexual relationships
words.origin: *Lothario*, seducer in the play *The Fair Penitent* (1703) by Nicholas Rowe. First known use: 1756.

words.definition: Relating to or living in flowing water
words.origin: Latin *lotus*, past participle of *lavere*. First known use: 1916.

words.definition: Disreputable or sordid in a rakish or appealing way, as a louche nightclub
words.origin: French, literally, cross-eyed, squint-eyed, from Latin *luscus* blind in one eye. First known use: 1819.

words.definition: Dark and threatening, as a sky
words.origin: Middle English *louren*; akin to Middle High German *lūren* to lie in wait. First known use: 13th century.
examples: An overcast sky **lowered** over the village

words.definition: Pining from unrequited love
An imaginary herb said to cause laziness
words.origin: From *lubber* lazy lout + *wort* plant.

words.definition: Lewd; also, smooth and slippery
words.origin: Latin *lūbricus* "slippery, hard to hold, hazardous" (Late Latin also "morally weak, lascivious") + -ious. First known use: 1535.

words.definition: Glowing with or giving off light; translucent, as lucent pearls or water
words.origin: Middle English, "bright, shining," borrowed from Latin *lūcent-, lūcens,* present participle of *lucēre* "to emit light, shine" (Old Latin, "to cause to shine"). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Clear and easy to understand
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *lūcidus* "bright, shining, light (of a place or time of day), clear to the understanding," adjective derivative, with the suffix *-idus,* corresponding to the verb *lūcēre* "to emit light, shine". First known use: 1591.
examples: Her **lucid** prose is precise and pointed … — Daniel Swift

words.definition: Avoiding light, as cockroaches, bats and some nocturnal animals do
words.origin: From Latin *lucifugus*, from *lux* light + *fugere* to flee.

words.definition: Money, especially gained dishonourably
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *lucrum* "material gain, profit," going back to Indo-European **lh2u-tló-* "seizure, gain," from **leh2u-* "seize, capture" + **-tlo-,* noun suffix, typically of instruments; **leh2u-* also in Greek *apolaúein* "to benefit (from), have pleasure or enjoyment," *leíā,* Doric* lāíā* "plunder, spoil," Germanic **launa-* "recompense, reward" (see guerdon). First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To study or write by lamplight
words.origin: From Latin *lucubrare* to work by lamplight.

words.definition: Laborious study, especially at night
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *lūcubrātiōn-, lūcubrātiō* "study done by lamplight," from *lūcubrāre* "to work by lamplight" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action; *lūcubrāre* derivative of **lūcubrum* "lamp, lamplight," from *lūc-, lūx* "light" + *-brum,* variant (after stems with an *-l-*) of *-bulum,* suffix of instruments (going back to Indo-European **-dhlom*); *-u-* presumably from *-i-/-e-* by rounding before a labial. First known use: 1595.

words.definition: Clearly expressed, as a luculent explanation; lucid and easily understood
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *lūculentus,* going back to Latin, "splendid, excellent, fine," from *lūc-, lūx* "light" + *-ulentus* -ulent. First known use: circa 1548.

words.definition: Lavish and luxurious, especially of food
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *Lūcullānus* "of Licinius lucullus," from *Lūcullus* + *-ānus* -an; from his reputation for luxurious banquets. First known use: 1861.

words.definition: Playful; spontaneously aimless
words.origin: Borrowed from French *ludique,* from Latin *lūdus* "sport, play, game" (derivative of *lūdere* "to play") + French *-ique* -ic. First known use: 1940.

words.definition: Playful, flirtatious love
words.origin: Latin, play, game.

words.definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal
words.origin: Latin *lugubris*, from *lugēre* to mourn; akin to Greek *lygros* mournful. First known use: 1585.
examples: … dark, dramatic and **lugubrious** brooding … — V. S. Pritchett
The tour de force of **lugubrious** cliche is ten times longer than this review — Martin Amis

words.definition: A large marine worm that lives in burrows on the shore, used as fishing bait
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1802.

words.definition: An inspiring, influential person
words.origin: Middle English *luminarye* "lamp, source of spiritual light," borrowed from Anglo-French *luminarie, luminaire* "celestial body, source of light, important person, lamp, candle," borrowed from Late Latin *lūmināria,* plural (later taken as feminine singular) of *lūmināre* "opening to let in light, source of light, lamp, torch, heavenly body, important person," from Latin *lūmin-, lūmen* "light, source of light, opening to let in light" + *-ar, -āre,* variant (after stems with an *l*) of *-al, -āle,* nominalized forms of *-ālis* -al. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Skywatchers … will see one more bright **luminary** below Orion and Canis Major — Martin Ratcliffe

words.definition: Giving off light; bright, shining or radiant
words.origin: Middle English *luminouse, luminose,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *luminous,* borrowed from Latin *lūminōsus* "full of light, dazzling," from *lūmin-, lūmen* "light, source of light" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … **luminous** objects—the nebula, the stars, the planets … — Lincoln La Paz

words.definition: Boorish and stupid; belonging to the dispossessed underclass
words.origin: German *Lumpenproletariat* degraded section of the proletariat, from *Lump* contemptible person (from *Lumpen* rags) + *Proletariat*. First known use: 1936.

words.definition: The time between two new moons, about 29 and a half days. A lunar month
words.origin: Middle English *lunacioun,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *lunaison, lunaciun,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *lūnātiōn-, lūnātiō,* from Latin *lūna* "moon" + *-ātiōn-, -ātiō* -ation. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A slow-witted person
words.origin: Probably alteration of *lump* + *head*. First known use: 1851.
examples: “Where I lived, in Central Square, Cambridge, you had the working class and the university life—you'd have to be a **lunkhead** not to be keenly aware of it,” says [Ben] Affleck. — Steven Daly
[Bruce] Willis played the **lunk** who ran a down-and-out detective agency that came to life when model Cybill Shepherd became his partner. — Stephen Dubner

words.definition: Vivid in a shocking or garish way
words.origin: Latin *luridus* pale yellow, sallow. First known use: 1603.
examples: The tabloids gave all the **lurid** details of floating wreckage and dismembered bodies.
… paperbacks in the usual **lurid** covers. — T. R. Fyvel

words.definition: To purify by means of rituals or ceremonies
words.origin: Latin *lustratus*, past participle of *lustrare*. First known use: 1653.

words.definition: A period of five years; a ritual purification in ancient Rome
words.origin: From Latin *lustrum*. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: Mixing two or more languages, especially vernacular words with Latin, in verse
words.origin: New Latin *macaronicus*, from Italian dialect *maccarone* macaroni. First known use: 1638.

words.definition: A plot or scheme
words.origin: Middle English *machynacion,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *māchinātiōn-, māchinātiō* "making of a machine, piece of machinery, mechanism," from *māchinārī* "to invent, devise, contrive" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … backstage **machinations** and power plays that have dominated the film industry … — Peter Bogdanovich

words.definition: A sky dappled with rows of small clouds
words.origin: From the clouds' resemblance to a mackerel's markings.

words.definition: Having a well-developed sense of smell
words.origin: From Greek *makros* large + *osmē* smell.

words.definition: Spotted or stained; morally impure, the opposite of immaculate
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *maculātus,* past participle of *maculāre* "to cover with stains, soil, disgrace, mark with coloured patches," derivative of *macula* "stain, spot, blemish". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Patronage of artists, musicians or writers
words.origin: From Maecenas, patron of Virgil and Horace.

words.definition: Generous or forgiving, especially to a rival
words.origin: Latin *magnanimus*, from *magnus* great + *animus* spirit. First known use: 1547.
examples: … a **magnanimous** and moving gesture, suitable to the spirit of the holiday. — Maurizio Valsania
He'd have been **magnanimous** in victory and gracious in defeat. — Liam Thorp

words.definition: A wealthy, influential businessperson
words.origin: Middle English *magnates*, plural, from Late Latin, from Latin *magnus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Using high-flown or bombastic language, as an overblown speech or speaker
words.origin: Back-formation from *magniloquence*. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: A person who works with, rides and tends an elephant, especially in India
words.origin: Hindi & Urdu *mahāwat, mahāut*. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: A household
words.origin: From Old French *mainpast*, from *main* hand + *past* food.

words.definition: Something put on a scale to make up the required weight; a filler
A general feeling of unease or discomfort
words.origin: French *malaise*, from Old French, from *mal-* + *aise* comfort. First known use: 1768.
examples: An infected person will feel a general **malaise**.
… a **malaise** of cynicism and despair … — Malcolm Boyd

words.definition: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one
words.origin: Mrs. *Malaprop*, character noted for her misuse of words in R. B. Sheridan's comedy *The Rivals* (1775). First known use: 1826.
examples: "Jesus healing those leopards" is an example of **malapropism**.

words.definition: A person who is dissatisfied and rebellious, always ready to complain or resist
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French, derivative of *malcontent* malcontent. First known use: 1581.
examples: …**malcontents** … bitter and almost choking with self-pity. — E. W. Griffiths

words.definition: A curse
words.origin: Middle English *malediccioun*, from Late Latin *malediction-, maledictio*, from *maledicere* to curse, from Latin, to speak evil of, from *male* badly + *dicere* to speak, say. First known use: 14th century.
examples: But I taunted him, ridiculed him, and loaded him with **maledictions** … — Sir Walter Scott

words.definition: Wishing harm on others
words.origin: Latin *malevolent-, malevolens*, from *male* badly + *volent-, volens*, present participle of *velle* to wish. First known use: 1509.
examples: … scheming, of both the benevolent and **malevolent** sort, designed to steer or derail the course of love. — Don Aucoin
And then there's Helen, the **malevolent** Sicilian neighbour who wishes everyone dead … — Judith Newman

words.definition: To pretend illness to avoid duty
words.origin: French *malingre* sickly. First known use: 1820.
examples: His boss suspected him of **malingering** because of his frequent absences from work.

words.definition: A curse
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *maleiçun*, from Late Latin *malediction-, maledictio*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Easily shaped or influenced
words.origin: Middle English *malliable*, from Medieval Latin *malleabilis*, from *malleare* to hammer, from Latin *malleus* hammer. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Corrupt behaviour in a position of trust, especially in public office
words.origin: Middle French, from *malverser* to be corrupt, from *mal* + *verser* to turn, handle, from Latin *versare*, frequentative of *vertere* to turn. First known use: 1549.

words.definition: To tease or deceive, especially by flattery
words.origin: Trinidadian English, perhaps from Spanish *mamar gallo* to tease.

words.definition: A look shared by two people, each wishing the other would act first
words.origin: Yaghan, a language of Tierra del Fuego; often cited as one of the world's most concise words.

words.definition: Wealth regarded as an evil influence or false object of worship
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *mammona*, from Greek *mamōna*, from Aramaic *māmōnā* riches. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A spoiled child
words.origin: From Greek *mammothreptos* brought up by a grandmother.

words.definition: A powerful official or senior bureaucrat; a person of influence
words.origin: Portuguese *mandarim*, from Malay *mĕntĕri*, from Sanskrit *mantrin* counselor, from *mantra* counsel. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: Having failed to become what one might have been, as a poet manqué
words.origin: French, missed, failed.

words.definition: Meekness; gentleness, a quiet and mild disposition
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *mansuetudo*, from *mansuescere* to tame, from *manus* hand + *suescere* to accustom; akin to Greek *ēthos* custom. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Release from slavery, servitude or restraint
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *manumission-, manumissio*, from *manumittere*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Withering without falling off
words.origin: From Latin *marcescere* to wither.

words.definition: Withered; wasted away
words.origin: From Latin *marcidus* withered.

words.definition: Notes written in the margins of a book
words.origin: New Latin, from Medieval Latin, neuter plural of *marginalis*. First known use: 1819.

words.definition: Affected writing style
words.origin: From Pierre de Marivaux, French playwright of witty courtship.

words.definition: Like marble; cold and smooth
words.origin: Latin *marmoreus*, from *marmor* marble. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: A person who spoils a plot or plan by meddling, after a character in an old comedy
A strict disciplinarian
words.origin: Jean *Martinet*, 17th century French army officer. First known use: 1737.
examples: The prison's warden was a cruel **martinet**.
A **martinet** in conducting meetings of the society, he never tolerated any sign of "levity or indecorum." — Daniel J. Boorstin

words.definition: A swallow or swift; a footless bird in heraldry, borne by younger sons
words.origin: Alteration of *martinet*, from Middle French, probably from St. *Martin*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To chew food thoroughly; to grind or knead into a pulp, as rubber
words.origin: Late Latin *masticatus*, past participle of *masticare*, from Greek *mastichan* to gnash the teeth; akin to Greek *masasthai* to chew. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: Characteristic of or in the manner of, an aunt
words.origin: From Latin *matertera* maternal aunt.

words.definition: Of or occurring in the morning, as a matutinal walk or cup of coffee
words.origin: Late Latin *matutinalis*, from Latin *matutinus*. First known use: 1567.

words.definition: Getting out of bed in a bad mood
words.origin: A modern coinage, not a dictionary entry: from *Matuta*, the Roman goddess of the dawn, + Greek *lypē* "grief, sorrow".

words.definition: Self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental
words.origin: Alteration of Mary *Magdalene*; from her depiction as a weeping penitent. First known use: 1509.
examples: … a mob of **maudlin** rummies … sing hymns … — Joseph Mitchell
Would crack open another beer and become **maudlin** — Patrick Moore

words.definition: An unorthodox, independent thinker
words.origin: Samuel A. *Maverick* †1870 American pioneer who did not brand his calves. First known use: 1866.

words.definition: My darling; an Irish term of endearment, from Irish mo mhúirnín
words.origin: Irish *mo mhuirnín*. First known use: 1800.

words.definition: A hypocrite who makes a show of piety; originally, a worm living in the stomach or gut
words.origin: From *maw* "stomach" + *worm*. The "hypocrite" sense comes from Mawworm, a canting preacher in Isaac Bickerstaffe's play *The Hypocrite* (1769).

words.definition: Sentimental in an exaggerated way
words.origin: Middle English *mawke* maggot, probably from Old Norse *mathkr*. First known use: circa 1697.

words.definition: Like a maze; winding
To wander along a winding course
examples: … across the ceiling **meandered** a long crack. — John Galsworthy
… he **meandered** with the sightseers gawping at the boat people … — John le Carré

words.definition: To move in a furtive manner
words.origin: From Middle English *michen* to pilfer, skulk.

words.definition: A deserved reward or share
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *mēd*; akin to Old High German *miata* reward, Greek *misthos*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: One obsessed with their own power or greatness
words.origin: Megalo- + -mania, after German *Megalomanie* or French *mégalomanie*. First known use: 1881.

words.definition: Low spirits, usually in the plural; a whim or fancy; a migraine
words.origin: Middle English *migreime*, from Middle French *migraine*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … had the power to jolly her out of her **megrims**. — Colleen McCullough

words.definition: Deliberate understatement
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *meiōsis* diminution, from *meioun* to diminish, from *meiōn* less; akin to Sanskrit *mīyate* he diminishes. First known use: 1550.

words.definition: A feeling of deep sadness; depression
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin, going back to Late Latin, "preponderance of black bile". First known use: circa 1553.
examples: Tense, irritable, I crashed into a fit of **melancholia** and found myself crying over inconsequential problems. — Susan Wood
A depressed Johnson was not the father figure that Boswell, himself prey to … bouts of **melancholia** and insecurity, wanted to celebrate. — Brooke Allen

words.definition: A deep, pensive sadness
words.origin: Middle English *malencolie, melancolie* "black bile, preponderance or excess of black bile, state (as anger or sorrow) produced by excessive black bile," borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *malencolie, melencolie,* borrowed from Late Latin *melancholia* (Medieval Latin *malencolia,* by association with the prefix *mal-* mal-), borrowed from Greek *melancholía,* from *melan-,* athematic variant of *melano-* melano- + *cholḗ* "bile" + *-ia* -ia. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Mitchell sounds utterly alone in her **melancholy**, turning the sadness into tender art.
Mordecai let his hands fall, and his head sink in **melancholy**: for the moment he had lost hold of his hope. — George Eliot

words.definition: The belief that the world can be improved by human effort, between optimism and pessimism
Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear
words.origin: Middle English *mellyfluous*, from Late Latin *mellifluus*, from Latin *mell-, mel* honey + *fluere* to flow; akin to Goth *milith* honey, Greek *melit-, meli*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An inordinate enthusiasm for music
words.origin: From Greek *melos* song + *mania*.

words.definition: By memory; by heart
words.origin: Latin, adverb, by memory, from *memor*. First known use: 1827.

words.definition: Likely to be remembered; notable
words.origin: From Latin *memor* mindful.

words.definition: Not telling the truth; lying
words.origin: Latin *mendac-, mendax*. First known use: 1616.

words.definition: A beggar
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *mendicant-, mendicans*, present participle of *mendicare* to beg, from *mendicus* beggar. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: , plural menschen (MEN-chuhn, MEN-shuhn) or mensches A decent, upright, honorable person
words.origin: Yiddish *mentsh* human being, from Middle High German *mensch*, from Old High German *mennisco*; akin to Old English *man* human being, man. First known use: 1856.

words.definition: Foul-smelling, as gases from a swamp or cave; noxious or poisonous
Pouring soul and love into one's work
words.origin: Modern Greek, from Turkish *merak* passion, curiosity.

words.definition: Subject to sudden changes of mood
words.origin: From *mercury* + *-al*. *Mercury*: Latin *Mercurius*, Roman god and the planet. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … he has a **mercurial** personality, a quality that leaves him hard to predict. — Kim Marcus
… the **mercurial**, nimble-witted types, persons given to animated speech and repartee … — A. C. Partridge

words.definition: A lake or pond
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *merus*; akin to Old English ā*merian* to purify and perhaps to Greek *marmairein* to sparkle. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Showily attractive but of little value
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *meretrīcius* “of women who engage in sex for financial considerations” (adjective derivative of *meretrīc-, meretrīx* “woman who engages in sex acts for financial considerations,” from *mere-,* stem of *merēre* “to earn” + *-trīc-, -trīx,* feminine agent suffix) + -ous. First known use: 1626.
examples: The paradise they found was a piece of **meretricious** trash. — Carolyn See
… scholarly names to provide fig-leaves of respectability for **meretricious** but stylish books.

words.definition: A prostitute, from the Latin for one who earns; a word found in old legal and church texts
words.origin: Latin, prostitute, from *merere* to earn.

words.definition: Naming a whole by its two extremes, as "young and old"
words.origin: From Greek *merismos* division.

words.definition: To puzzle or to mystify
words.origin: From French *métagraboulizer*, coined by Rabelais.

words.definition: A transformative change of heart
words.origin: Greek, from *metanoiein* to change one's mind, repent, from *meta-* + *noein* to think, from *nous* mind. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: The transposition of letters, sounds or syllables in a word. Example: aks for ask
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek, from *metatithenai* to transpose, from *meta-* + *tithenai* to place. First known use: circa 1538.

words.definition: Extremely careful and precise
words.origin: Earlier, "fearful," borrowed from Latin *metīculōsus, metūculōsus* "timid, apprehensive," from *metū-,* stem of *metus* "fear, dread" (of uncertain origin) + *-culōsus* (in *perīculōsus* "involving danger, perilous"). First known use: 1827.
examples: He is **meticulous** about updating his calendar.
The **meticulous** hand-beading process took over 300 hours, the brand says. — Bailey Richards

words.definition: Naming something by something closely associated, as the crown for the monarch
words.origin: Latin *metonymia*, from Greek *metōnymia*, from *meta-* + *-ōnymon* -onym. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: A mania for writing poetry
words.origin: From Greek *metron* metre + *mania*.

words.definition: To cry feebly or querulously, as a baby or kitten; to whimper
words.origin: Imitative. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: An unpleasant or unhealthy atmosphere
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek, defilement, from *miainein* to pollute. First known use: 1665.
examples: … freed from the **miasma** of poverty … — Sir Arthur Bryant

words.definition: To make small or insignificant
words.origin: From Greek *mikros* small + *-ify*.

words.definition: Small and delicately pretty, as a mignon face; dainty
A person's social environment
words.origin: French, from Old French, midst, from *mi* middle (from Latin *medius*) + *lieu* place, from Latin *locus*. First known use: 1854.
examples: In this diverse **milieu**, the children found their way to a new common language. — Rebecca Mead

words.definition: A timid, meek person
words.origin: Caspar *Milquetoast*, comic strip character created by H. T. Webster †1952 American cartoonist. First known use: 1935.

words.definition: The imitation of the real world in art and literature; mimicry in nature
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *mimēsis*, from *mimeisthai*. First known use: circa 1586.

words.definition: Threatening or menacing
words.origin: From Latin *minax* threatening.

words.definition: A slender tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is made
words.origin: French, from Turkish *minare*, from Arabic *manāra* lighthouse. First known use: 1682.

words.definition: Expressing a threat
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *minātōrius,* from Latin *minor, minārī* "to threaten, speak or act menacingly, hold out the threat of" (verbal derivative of *minae,* plural only, "threats, menaces, portents of evil") + *-tōrius,* deverbal adjective suffix originally forming derivatives from agent nouns ending in *-tōr-, -tor*; *minae* probably, if originally "projecting points, overhang," noun derivative of the verbal base **men-* seen in *ēminēre* "to stick out, protrude," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1532.
examples: … stabbing the air with a **minatory** forefinger. — Robert B. Silvers et al.

words.definition: To decorate a manuscript, book, etc., with colours, gold, silver
words.origin: From Latin *miniare* to paint with red lead.

words.definition: Wonderful; working wonders
words.origin: From Latin *mirificus*, from *mirus* wonderful + *facere* to make.

words.definition: Amusement expressed in laughter
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *myrgth*, from *myrge* merry. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: His clumsy attempt at dancing caused much **mirth**.

words.definition: A person who dislikes humankind
words.origin: Greek *misanthrōpos* hating humankind, from *misein* to hate + *anthrōpos* human being. First known use: 1683.

words.definition: Compassion, pity or mercy
words.origin: Medieval Latin *misericordia* seat in church, from Latin, mercy, from *misericord-, misericors* merciful, from *misereri* + *cord-, cor* heart. First known use: circa 1515.

words.definition: A hatred of new ideas
words.origin: From Greek *misos* hatred + *kainos* new.

words.definition: An intolerance of certain sounds, such as chewing, slurping
words.origin: *miso-* (as in misogyny) + -phonia. First known use: 2001.

words.definition: The deliberate concealment of a crime; a misunderstanding or misreading
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *mesprisun* error, wrongdoing, from *mesprendre* to take by mistake, from *mes-* mis- + *prendre* to take, from Latin *prehendere* to seize. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A remedy once thought to protect against all poisons, after a king of Pontus
words.origin: Medieval Latin *mithridatum*, from Late Latin *mithridatium*, from Latin, dogtooth violet (used as an antidote), from Greek *mithridation*, from *Mithridatēs* Mithridates VI. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: To make less severe
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *mitigatus*, past participle of *mitigare* to soften, from *mitis* soft + *-igare* (akin to Latin *agere* to drive); akin to Old Irish *moíth* soft. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The modern mom who's trying to **mitigate** any kind of conflict with her mother-in-law … — Nicole Ari Parker, quoted in *The Hollywood Reporter*
Emergency funds are being provided to help **mitigate** the effects of the disaster.

words.definition: An emotional bond between people kept apart
words.origin: Hebrew, watchtower; from Genesis 31:49.

words.definition: Light rain; drizzle, a fine misty rain that hangs in the air
words.origin: Middle English *misellen*; akin to Dutch dialect *mizzelen* to drizzle, Middle Dutch *mist* fog, mist. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A small quantity
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin, neuter of *modicus* moderate, from *modus* measure. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Had only a **modicum** of mathematical skills

words.definition: A fashionable milliner or dressmaker, especially one in Paris
words.origin: French, from *mode* style, mode. First known use: 1802.

words.definition: To calm someone's anger
words.origin: Middle English *mollifien*, from Middle French *mollifier*, from Late Latin *mollificare*, from Latin *mollis* soft; akin to Greek *amaldynein* to soften, Sanskrit *mṛdu* soft, and probably to Greek *malakos* soft, *amblys* dull, Old English *meltan* to melt. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A pampered or overprotected person. verb tr.: To overprotect or pamper
words.origin: *Molly*, nickname for *Mary*. First known use: 1837.

words.definition: A magic herb in Greek myth
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *mōly*. First known use: 1546.

words.definition: A carping critic
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *Mōmos*. First known use: 1561.

words.definition: An isolated hill of hard rock standing above an eroded plain
words.origin: Mount *Monadnock*, New Hampshire. First known use: 1893.

words.definition: A sophisticated man; a man belonging to fashionable society
words.origin: French, worldly, fashionable.

words.definition: A misheard word or phrase, especially in a song or poem, that gives a new meaning
words.origin: From the mishearing in a Scottish ballad of "laid him on the green" as "Lady Mondegreen". First known use: 1954.

words.definition: A gentle sadness at the passing of things
words.origin: Japanese, the pathos of things.

words.definition: A fight between two people or forces
words.origin: From Greek *monomachia*, from *monos* single + *machē* fight.

words.definition: A rainbow made by moonlight
words.origin: From *moon* + *rainbow*.

words.definition: A daydreamer or absent-minded person
examples: He was a helpless **mooncalf** of a man, poorly equipped for … a grueling life … — Peter Schjeldahl

words.definition: The bright path of moonlight on water
words.origin: From *moon* + *glade* bright path.

words.definition: A simpleton; a native of Wiltshire, from a legend of smugglers
words.origin: From the Wiltshire tale of smugglers raking a pond for the moon.

words.definition: In a dreamy state
examples: … who can forget the '50s **moonstruck** lyrics of Elvis … or the Everly Brothers … — Eileen Wood
**Moonstruck** partners pledging eternal love may be the current definition of marriage, but this starry-eyed picture has relatively modern origins. — Tia Ghose

words.definition: The strangeness of familiar things seen afresh
words.origin: *Coffee-room* read backwards through a glass door, after Dickens; used by G. K. Chesterton and Tolkien.

words.definition: A small child, especially a sweet or endearing one; a darling
words.origin: Obsolete English *mop* fool, child. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: An extreme softness, smoothness or delicacy, especially in works of art, sculpture, music
words.origin: Italian, softness, delicacy.

words.definition: Biting or caustic in manner or speech, as mordacious wit; given to biting
words.origin: From Latin *mordax* biting.

words.definition: Sharply sarcastic
words.origin: Middle French, present participle of *mordre* to bite, from Latin *mordēre*; perhaps akin to Sanskrit *mṛdnāti* he presses, rubs. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Of a marriage between a royal and a commoner, whose children cannot inherit
words.origin: New Latin *matrimonium ad morganaticam*, literally, marriage with morning gift. First known use: 1728.

words.definition: At the point of death; in terminal decline
words.origin: Latin *moribundus*, from *mori* to die. First known use: circa 1721.
examples: In the **moribund** patient deepening stupor and coma are the usual preludes to death. — Norman Cameron
Prune the **moribund** files from your disk forever — D. S. Janal

words.definition: Sullen and ill-tempered
words.origin: Latin *morosus*, literally, capricious, from *mor-, mos* will. First known use: 1565.

words.definition: Feeble-mindedness
words.origin: From Greek *mōrōsis*, from *mōros* foolish.

words.definition: Relating to sleep or dreams
words.origin: From *Morpheus*, god of dreams.

words.definition: To move in a leisurely manner
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1829.
examples: … **moseyed** around the general store … — Eric Sevareid

words.definition: A person who deceives others to trick them out of money; a charlatan
words.origin: Italian *montimbanco*, from *montare* to mount + *in* in, on + *banco, banca* bench. First known use: 1566.

words.definition: Feeling, expressing or causing sorrow
words.origin: From *mourn* + *-ful*; *mourn* from Old English *murnan*.

words.definition: Sticky and gelatinous, like the mucilage of seaweed or some plants
words.origin: Middle English *muscilaginous*, from Late Latin *mucilaginosus*, from *mucilagin-, mucilago*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A person of great importance; a bigwig, from a Chinook jargon word for food
words.origin: Short for *high-muck-a-muck*. First known use: 1883.

words.definition: Joy in the good fortune of others
words.origin: Sanskrit and Pali, joy.

words.definition: A person who remains aloof or independent, especially in politics
words.origin: Obsolete slang *mugwump* kingpin, from Massachusett *mugquomp, muggumquomp* war leader. First known use: 1884.

words.definition: To extract money from by fine, taxation or deceit; a fine or penalty
words.origin: Latin *multa, mulcta*. First known use: 1584.

words.definition: A fit of low spirits; a stomach ache
words.origin: A whimsical 16th-century coinage, perhaps from *mully* + *grub*.

words.definition: Rubbish or refuse; worthless rock left from mining; nonsense
words.origin: From Middle English *mul* dust, rubbish.

words.definition: Many and of various types; having great variety, as multifarious interests
words.origin: Medieval Latin *multifarius*, from Latin *multifariam* in many places. First known use: 1593.
examples: Participated in **multifarious** activities in high school

words.definition: A toothless beggar
words.origin: From *mumble* to chew toothlessly + *crust*.

words.definition: Ridiculous ceremony, especially in religious ritual; mime performed by mummers
words.origin: Middle French *momerie*, from *momer*. First known use: circa 1530.

words.definition: A stubborn adherence to error despite correction
Dull and ordinary
words.origin: Middle English *mondeyne*, from Anglo-French *mundain*, from Late Latin *mundanus*, from Latin *mundus* world. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the National Gallery had paid too little heed to **mundane** questions of security. — Edward Dolnick

words.definition: To wash, cleanse or purify
words.origin: From Latin *mundificare*, from *mundus* clean.

words.definition: Very generous
words.origin: Back-formation from *munificence*, from Latin *munificentia*, from *munificus* generous, from *munus* service, gift. First known use: 1565.

words.definition: Dark and gloomy; cloudy, as water; obscure or questionable
words.origin: From *murk* + *-y*. *Murk*: Middle English *mirke*, probably from Old Norse *myrkr* darkness; akin to Old English *mirce* gloom. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Handicapped by my seasickness and by the **murky** skies, I hardly ever could make my star sights work. — Robert Shenk

words.definition: A flock of starlings moving in shifting, swirling patterns across the sky
words.origin: From Latin *murmuratio* a murmuring.

words.definition: A mediocre musician
words.origin: From *music* + *-aster* inferior.

words.definition: Muttering; moving the lips without making a sound, as in silent prayer
words.origin: From Latin *mussitare* to mutter.

words.definition: Utterly, desolately alone
words.origin: German, literally mother-soul alone.

words.definition: Borrowed
words.origin: From Latin *mutuatitius*, from *mutuari* to borrow.

words.definition: A mushroom enthusiast
A countless number
words.origin: Greek *myriad-, myrias*, from *myrioi* countless, ten thousand. First known use: 1555.
examples: … he listened to the **myriads** of humming cicadas and the call of the geckos. — Nina Fitzpatrick

words.definition: A follower or subordinate of a powerful person, especially an unscrupulous one
words.origin: Middle English *Mirmydon*, Latin *Myrmidon-, Myrmido*, from Greek *Myrmidōn*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The road-like reflection of the moon on water
words.origin: Swedish, from *måne* moon + *gata* street.

words.definition: Lustrous and iridescent, like mother-of-pearl, as nacreous clouds
words.origin: From *nacre* + *-ous*. *Nacre*: French, from Middle French, from Old Italian *naccara* drum, nacre, from Arabic *naqqāra* drum. First known use: 1819.

words.definition: The lowest point
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Arabic *naḍhīr* opposite. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A water nymph said to inhabit a river, spring or waterfall; a graceful swimmer
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French or Latin; Middle French *naïade*, from Latin *naiad-, naias*, from Greek, from *nan* to flow. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Proud joy, especially in one's children
words.origin: Yiddish, from Hebrew *naḥat* contentment.

words.definition: The study of sacred buildings
words.origin: From Greek *naos* temple + *-logy*.

words.definition: Just beginning to develop
words.origin: Latin *nascent-, nascens*, present participle of *nasci* to be born. First known use: circa 1624.

words.definition: Swimming or floating, as a leaf on water; in heraldry, depicted as swimming
words.origin: Middle English *natand*, from Latin *natant-, natans*, present participle of *natare* to swim; akin to Latin *nare* to swim; akin to Greek *nein, nēchein* to swim, Sanskrit *snāti* he bathes. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Nevertheless; notwithstanding
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *nā thē lǣs* not the less. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Bringing back fond memories
words.origin: Japanese, dear, longed-for.

words.definition: Causing shipwreck
words.origin: From Latin *naufragus*, from *navis* ship + *frangere* to break.

words.definition: The confidence that comes from being loved
words.origin: Urdu, from Persian *nāz* pride, coquetry.

words.definition: A person, especially a man, who is regarded as pitifully ineffectual
words.origin: Yiddish *nebekh* poor, unfortunate, from Czech *nebohý*. First known use: 1907.

words.definition: Unclear, vague or ill-defined
words.origin: Latin *nebulosus* misty, from *nebula*. First known use: 1674.
examples: … this **nebulous** thing called jazz. — Josef Woodard
… the **nebulous** region between mere suspicion and probable cause — W. R. LaFave & J. H. Israel

words.definition: The supposed practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future
words.origin: Middle English *nycromancie* "sorcery, conjuration of spirits," borrowed from Late Latin *necromantīa* "divination from an exhumed corpse," borrowed from Late Greek *nekromanteía* "divination by conjuration of the dead," from Greek *nekro-* necro- + *-manteia* -mancy; replacing earlier Middle English *nigromance, nygromancye,* borrowed from Anglo-French *nigromance, nigromancie,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *nigromantia,* alteration of *necromantia* by association with Latin *nigr-, niger* "black". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The novel centres on the practice of **necromancy** and its influence on the world of the living.

words.definition: One who can't take a hint
words.origin: Czech, one who can't take a hint.

words.definition: So wicked as to defy description: abominable, appalling
words.origin: From Latin *nefandus* unspeakable.

words.definition: Wicked or criminal
words.origin: Latin *nefarius*, from *nefas* crime, from *ne-* not + *fas* right, divine law; perhaps akin to Greek *themis* law, *tithenai* to place. First known use: 1567.
examples: The more **nefarious** of these supervillains hide in plain sight. — Amelia Tait
The town itself is a classic of the genre, full of scheming locals, buried secrets and **nefarious** elites trying to make a quick buck. — David Faris

words.definition: A cloud-walker; one who lives in their imagination
words.origin: Portuguese, from Greek *nephelē* cloud + *bates* walker.

words.definition: Failing to take proper care
words.origin: Middle English *necligent, negligent,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *neglegent-, neglegens* (also *neclegens, negligens*), present participle of *neglegere, neclegere* "to disregard, do nothing about, fail to care for". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … was a careless workman, **negligent** of details. — Edith Hamilton

words.definition: One who walks barefoot
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; recorded in early modern English.

words.definition: A lover of woods and forests
words.origin: From Greek *nemos* grove + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: Relating to a forest; wooded
words.origin: From Latin *nemorosus*, from *nemus* grove.

words.definition: A newly coined word or expression
words.origin: Borrowed from French *néologisme* "the habit of forming new words, a newly formed word," from *néologie* "coining of new words" (from *néo-* neo- + *-logie* -logy) + *-isme* -ism. First known use: 1754.

words.definition: One who loves new or novel things
words.origin: From Greek *neos* new + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: A beginner
words.origin: Middle English *neophite,* borrowed from Late Latin *neophytus,* borrowed from Greek *neóphytos* "newly planted" (in New Testament and patristic Greek, "newly converted, new convert"), from *neo-* neo- + *-phytos,* verbal adjective of *phýein* "to bring forth, produce". First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **neophyte** when it comes to computers
**Neophytes** fresh from graduate schools of business

words.definition: A drug or potion that brings forgetfulness of sorrow or trouble
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *nēpenthes,* borrowed from Greek *nēpenthés,* neuter (modifying *phármakon* "drug") of *nēpenthḗs* "removing grief," from *nē-,* privative prefix (probably going back to Indo-European **n-,* privative prefix, and a sequence of laryngeal and consonant) + *-penthēs,* adjective derivative of *pénthos* "sorrow, grief". First known use: 1577.

words.definition: Lack of knowledge; ignorance, especially of something unknowable
words.origin: Late Latin *nescientia*, from Latin *nescient-, nesciens*, present participle of *nescire* not to know, from *ne-* not + *scire* to know. First known use: 1612.

words.definition: Soft; sensitive to cold
words.origin: From Old English *hnesce* soft.

words.definition: To blink or wink, as a bird does with its translucent third eyelid
words.origin: Alteration of *nictate* to wink, from Latin *nictatus*, past participle of *nictare*. First known use: 1713.

words.definition: A coward; a base or contemptible person, a word from old ballads
words.origin: From a misreading of Middle English *nithing* coward.

words.definition: Well-developed and able to leave the nest soon after hatching
words.origin: Latin *nidus* nest + *fugere* to flee. First known use: 1896.

words.definition: To build a nest, as birds do in spring, gathering twigs, moss and down
words.origin: From Latin *nidificare*, from *nidus* nest.

words.definition: Plural nidi or niduses 1. A nest
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin. First known use: 1734.

words.definition: Blackish; tending toward black, as nigrescent clouds or plumage
words.origin: From Latin *nigrescere* to grow black.

words.definition: A luminous cloud or halo surrounding a supernatural being; a rain cloud
words.origin: Latin, rainstorm, cloud; probably akin to Latin *nebula* cloud. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: To behave like a tyrant
words.origin: From Nimrod, the mighty hunter of Genesis.

words.definition: A foolish person
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1668.
examples: … they could easily find some **nincompoop** to give them yet more money … — Kevin Maney
“A bunch of **nincompoops** … that could not find themselves out of a restroom.” — Jill Zuckman

words.definition: A miser
words.origin: Naval slang for a purser, from *nip* + *cheese*.

words.definition: A coward
words.origin: From Old Norse *níðingr* villain.

words.definition: Bright; glossy; shining, as nitid leaves or polished stone
words.origin: Latin *nitidus*. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Growing in or living among snow
words.origin: From Latin *nivalis*, from *nix* snow.

words.definition: God
words.origin: Coined by William Blake, from *nobody* + *daddy*.

words.definition: A harmless substance that causes harm because it is believed to
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *nocēbō* "I will harm" (1st person singular of *nocēre* "to damage, harm"), on the model of placebo. First known use: 1961.

words.definition: Harmful
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *nocent-, nocens* "injurious, guilty," from present participle of *nocēre* "to damage (things), injure, harm (persons)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One who stays up late; a night owl
words.origin: French, from *noce* revelry.

words.definition: A sleepwalker; a person who walks about during sleep
words.origin: New Latin *noctambulus* "sleepwalker" (earlier *noctambulō,* with *-ōn-, -ō,* agent suffix, from Latin *noct-, nox* night + *-ambul-,* noun derivative of *ambulāre* "to walk") + -ist. First known use: circa 1731.

words.definition: Shining at night
words.origin: From Latin *nox* night + *lucere* to shine.

words.definition: Wandering at night, as owls, foxes or restless poets do
words.origin: From Latin *nox* night + *vagari* to wander.

words.definition: A record of what passes in the night
words.origin: From Latin *nox* night, on the model of *diary*.

words.definition: A dreamy piece of music or painting of night
words.origin: Borrowed from French, noun derivative of *nocturne* "of the night," going back to Middle French, borrowed from Latin *nocturnus*. First known use: 1814.

words.definition: Disgusting, especially in smell; harmful
words.origin: Middle English *noysome*, from *noy* annoyance, alteration of *anoi*, from Anglo-French *anui*, from *anuier* to harass, annoy. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The period of one's minority, before legal adulthood; a period of immaturity
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from *non-* + *age* age. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Calm and casually unconcerned
words.origin: French, from Old French, from present participle of *nonchaloir* to disregard, from *non-* + *chaloir* to concern, from Latin *calēre* to be warm. First known use: circa 1734.
examples: Few rappers are able to combine a **nonchalant** flow with the ups and downs of Black American life.
With her oversized red-and-blue plaid flannel, charcoal wide-legged pants, and blue bucket hat, the actor offered a more **nonchalant** take to her father's rockstar style. — Hannah Jackson

words.definition: Having no match or equal; unrivalled; a person or thing without equal
words.origin: Middle English *nounparalle*, from Middle French *nompareil*, from *non-* + *pareil* equal, from Vulgar Latin **pariculus*, from Latin *par* equal. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: So surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react; bewildered
examples: She was **nonplussed**, but quickly collected herself, explained that the plumbing had been acting up for days, and told them to pay it no mind. — Diane Ackerman
Cedric looked **nonplussed**. He looked from Bagman to Harry and back again as though sure he must have misheard what Bagman had said. — J. K. Rowling

words.definition: Nagging, pestering, annoying or complaining
words.origin: From Yiddish *nudyen* to bore, pester.

words.definition: The sphere of human thought around the earth
words.origin: Borrowed from French *noosphère,* from Greek *noo-,* combining form of *nóos,* contracted *noûs* "mind, intellect" (of uncertain origin) + French *-sphère* -sphere. First known use: 1930.

words.definition: A small bunch of flowers, typically one that is sweet-scented
words.origin: Middle English, from *nose* nose + *gay* ornament, literally, something gay, from *gay*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The systematic description of diseases
words.origin: From Greek *nosos* disease + *-graphia* writing.

words.definition: A sentimental longing for the past
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin, from Greek *nóstos* "return, homecoming" (nominal derivative, with o-ablaut and the suffix *-to-,* from the base of *néomai, neîsthai* "to come/go [home, back], return") + *-o-* -o- + *-algia* -algia; *néomai* going back to the Indo-European verbal base **nes-* "escape danger, return safely," whence also Germanic **nesan-* "to be saved, return safely" (whence Old English *nesan, genesan* "to be saved, survive" [strong verb class V], Old Saxon *ginesan* "to be saved, convalesce," Old High German, "to recover, be saved," Gothic *ganisan* "to be saved"), Sanskrit *násate* "approaches, resorts to someone, joins"; from a causative stem **nos-éi̯e-* Germanic **nazjan-,* whence Old English *nerian* "to save, preserve," Old Frisian *nera* "to save, nourish, Old Saxon *nerian* "to rescue, redeem, nourish," Old High German *nerien, nerren* "to nourish, support, save, heal," Gothic *nasjan* "to save, heal"; and from lengthened grade **nōzjan-* Old Icelandic *nœra* "to refresh, nourish". First known use: 1756.
examples: They were filled with **nostalgia** for their college days.
His family once worked at the local slaughterhouse, but their jobs have been automated into oblivion, leaving them with nothing but **nostalgia** for their old day-to-day. — Jackson Arn

words.definition: A favourite but ineffective remedy
words.origin: Latin, neuter of *noster* our, ours, from *nos* we. First known use: 1602.
examples: … is put to work at county fairs, promoting a quack **nostrum** for pain relief. — Patrick McGrath
… an audience eager to believe he had found the **nostrum** for all of society's ills. — Warren Sloat

words.definition: Someone or something that turns out to be inconsequential
examples: Is that piece of evidence a **nothing burger** or a big freakin' deal? — Mark Kiszla

words.definition: A thing as it is in itself, beyond perception
words.origin: German, from Greek *nooumenon* that which is apprehended by thought, from neuter of present passive participle of *noein* to think, conceive, from *nous* mind. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: Desiring powerful change in one's life
words.origin: From Latin *novaturire* to desire change.

words.definition: New and unusual; interestingly original
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *novellus*, diminutive of *novus* new.

words.definition: A beginner
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French, "probationer in a religious community" (continental Old French also, "inexperienced person"), borrowed from Late Latin *novīcius,* going back to Latin, "newly enslaved person, person recently entered into a condition," as adjective, "newly imported, recently discovered, fashionable," from *novus* "new" + *-īcius* -itious. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **novices** spend part of each day in prayer and meditation.

words.definition: Newly invented
words.origin: From Latin *novicius* new.

words.definition: Cloudy or foggy; obscure or vague, as a nubilous argument
words.origin: From Latin *nubilus* cloudy.

words.definition: Wandering among the clouds
words.origin: From Latin *nubes* cloud + *vagari* to wander.

words.definition: One who believes that faith alone is sufficient for salvation
words.origin: From Latin *nudus* naked + *fides* faith.

words.definition: A pestering, nagging or irritating person; a bore who will not let up
words.origin: Yiddish *nudnik*, from *nudyen* to bore, from Polish *nudzić*, from *nuda* boredom. First known use: 1916.

words.definition: Triviality; futility; a trifling or worthless thing
words.origin: From Latin *nugax* trifling.

words.definition: Of no value or importance
words.origin: Latin *nugatorius*, from *nugari* to trifle, from *nugae* trifles. First known use: 1603.
examples: The law was unenforced and thus rendered **nugatory**.

words.definition: The state of being nowhere
words.origin: From Latin *nullibi* nowhere.

words.definition: A person having no religious faith or belief; a sceptic or unbeliever
words.origin: From Latin *nullus* none + *fides* faith.

words.definition: Having a strong spiritual or divine quality
words.origin: Latin *numin-, numen* numen. First known use: 1647.

words.definition: A fool
words.origin: Scottish slang, perhaps from *numps* a silly person.

words.definition: The subtle art of reading a room
words.origin: Korean, eye measure.

words.definition: Drooping; nodding
words.origin: From Latin *nutare* to nod.

words.definition: A love of darkness or night
words.origin: From Greek *nyx* night + *-philia* love.

words.definition: To walk about aimlessly; to wander here and there with no destination
words.origin: From Latin *obambulare* to walk about.

words.definition: Numbness of a limb that has fallen asleep from pressure
words.origin: From Late Latin *obdormitio*, from Latin *obdormire* to fall asleep, from *ob-* + *dormire* to sleep.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin *obdūrātus,* going back to Latin, past participle of *obdūrāre* "to harden, be persistent, hold out," from *ob-,* perfective prefix + *dūrāre* "to harden, hold out, endure". First known use: 15th century.
examples: Remaining **obdurate** to her husband's advances — Edith Wharton

words.definition: Deferential respect or homage; a gesture such as a bow that expresses it
words.origin: Middle English *obeissance, obeysaunce* "obedience, submission, gesture indicating submission," borrowed from Anglo-French *obeissaunce*, from *obeis*ant "willing to obey" (from present participle of *obeir* "to submit to the authority of, obey") + *-aunce* -ance. First known use: 14th century.
examples: After making his **obeisances** he approached the altar.

words.definition: To mark a word as doubtful or spurious
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *obelízein,* from *obelós* obelus + *-izein* -ize. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: A dagger-shaped mark used in old manuscripts to flag doubtful passages
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin, borrowed from Greek *obelós, odelós* (Doric) "spit, four-sided pointed pillar, obol, line in a manuscript marking a passage as spurious," perhaps of pre-Greek substratal origin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To make obscure or unclear
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *obfuscātus, offuscātus,* past participle of *obfuscāre, offuscāre* "to obscure, darken, depreciate," from Latin *ob-,* perfective prefix + *-fuscāre,* verbal derivative of *fuscus* "dark-coloured, sombre, dark-skinned or -complected". First known use: 1536.
examples: Moisture caused minerals in the stone and brick walls to rise up and **obfuscate** the frescoes with a thin coating of white salts. — Elizabeth Helman Minchilli
… the strong performance of the few can **obfuscate** the mediocrity of the many. — Christopher Lynch

words.definition: To scold or rebuke severely; to berate in harsh terms
words.origin: Middle English *objurgacyon,* borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *objurgacion,* borrowed from Latin *objūrgātiōn-, objūrgātiō,* from *objūrgāre* "to reprove, rebuke, find fault with" (from *ob-* "against" + *jūrgāre, jūrigāre* "to quarrel, wrangle, utter reproaches," from *jūr-, jūs* "law, right, prerogative" + *-igāre,* causative and factitive suffix) + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A thing presented or offered to God or a god; a pious donation
words.origin: Middle English *oblacioun,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *oblacion,* borrowed from Late Latin *oblātiōn-, oblātiō* "offering, sacrifice, offering of the eucharistic elements," going back to Latin, "offering, tender, presentation," from *oblā-,* suppletive stem of *offerre* "to put in a person's path, provide, offer" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Strong public criticism; disgrace
words.origin: Middle English *obloquie, obloqui,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *obloquie,* borrowed from Late Latin *obloquium,* from *obloquī* "to speak against, blame" (going back to Latin, "to break in on, interrupt," from *ob-* "against" + *loquī* "to speak") + Latin *-ium,* deverbal suffix of function or state. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Held to their convictions in the face of **obloquy**
Living out his days in the **obloquy** of one who had betrayed a solemn trust

words.definition: To darken, cloud or obscure, as clouds the sky or worry the mind
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *obnūbilātus,* past participle of *obnūbilāre* "to make dark or obscure, becloud, darken (the mind)," from *ob-* "toward, facing" + *nūbilāre* "to become cloudy or overcast," derivative of *nūbilus* "cloudy, overcast, dark, dim, confused," from *nūbēs* "cloud" + *-ilus,* denominative adjective suffix. First known use: 1583.

words.definition: Not well known; hard to understand
words.origin: Middle English, "dark, unenlightened, incomprehensible," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *oscur, obscur* "dark, dull, enigmatic," borrowed from Latin *obscūrus* "dim, dark, appearing faintly, imperfectly known, concealed from knowledge, incomprehensible," of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **obscure** dusk of the shuttered room

words.definition: To beg or implore earnestly; to beseech, as in prayer
words.origin: From Latin *obsecrare* to beseech.

words.definition: Excessively eager to please or obey
words.origin: Middle English, compliant, from Latin *obsequiosus*, from *obsequium* compliance, from *obsequi* to comply, from *ob-* toward + *sequi* to follow. First known use: 1602.
examples: Was always followed around by his **obsequious** minions
There are no hushed voices, white tablecloths or **obsequious** waiters. — Isabelle Kliger

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *obstinat*, Latin *obstinatus*, past participle of *obstinare* to be resolved, from *ob-* in the way + *-stinare* (akin to *stare* to stand). First known use: 14th century.
examples: Only this austerity of voice, this **obstinate** refusal to capitulate to the romantic tone, rescues the novel from bathos. — Francine Du Plessix Grey
You've seen movies in which there's one **obstinate** juror who blocks conviction, perhaps someone enticed to that obstinacy by the accused. — Philip Bump

words.definition: Noisy and difficult to control
words.origin: Latin *obstreperus*, from *obstrepere* to clamour against, from *ob-* against + *strepere* to make a noise. First known use: circa 1600.

words.definition: Slow to understand
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *obtusus* blunt, dull, from past participle of *obtundere* to beat against, blunt, from *ob-* against + *tundere* to beat. First known use: 15th century.
examples: He is too **obtuse** to take a hint.
It is also, unfortunately, ill-written, and at times **obtuse** and often trivial. — Shirley Hazzard

words.definition: To turn so as to show a different side
words.origin: From Latin *obvertere* to turn toward.

words.definition: To remove a need or difficulty
words.origin: Late Latin *obviatus*, past participle of *obviare* to meet, withstand, from Latin *obviam*. First known use: 1567.
examples: The new medical treatment **obviates** the need for surgery.

words.definition: To stop, close up or obstruct an opening, passage or view, as a blood vessel
words.origin: Latin *occludere*, from *ob-* in the way + *claudere* to shut, close. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: The state of being hidden or blocked
words.origin: Middle English *occultacion,* borrowed from Latin *occultātiōn-, occultātiō* "concealment, interruption of light from a celestial body," from *occultāre* "to prevent from being seen, conceal, keep secret" + *-tiōn- -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Having eyelike spots
words.origin: From Latin *ocellus* little eye.

words.definition: Government by the mob; mob rule
words.origin: Greek & Middle French; Middle French *ochlocratie*, from Greek *ochlokratia*, from *ochlos* mob + *-kratia* -cracy. First known use: 1594.

words.definition: A fear or dislike of crowds
words.origin: From Greek *ochlos* crowd + *-phobia*.

words.definition: Letting the eyes wander
words.origin: From Latin *oculus* eye + Greek *planē* wandering.

words.definition: A female slave or concubine in a harem; a reclining nude in painting
words.origin: French, from Turkish *odalık*, from *oda* room. First known use: circa 1681.

words.definition: Extremely unpleasant; repulsive
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *odiosus*, from *odium*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A lover of wine
words.origin: French *œnophile*, from *œno-* (from Greek *oinos* wine) + *-phile* -phile. First known use: 1865.

words.definition: Asserting authority in an annoyingly interfering way
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *officiōsus* "ready to fulfill obligations, dutiful, attentive, (in pejorative sense) importunate," from *officium* "beneficial act in fulfillment of an obligation, duty, functions in a position, post, office" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
examples: **Officious** people who are always ready to offer unasked advice

words.definition: Family, including chosen family, bound to care for one another
words.origin: Hawaiian *ʻohana* family.

words.definition: A person perceived as uncouth, unpleasant and of lower social standing
words.origin: British slang, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Oily or greasy; exaggeratedly and distastefully complimentary
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *oleagineux*, from Latin *oleagineus* of an olive tree, from *olea* olive tree, from Greek *elaia*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Foul-smelling
words.origin: From Latin *olidus*, from *olere* to smell.

words.definition: A miscellaneous collection of things; a spicy stew of meat and vegetables
words.origin: Modification of Spanish *olla*. First known use: circa 1842.
examples: The Spanish restaurant offered an **olio** containing a variety of ingredients.
… an incredible bourgeois **olio** of fancy stonework, stained glass, and light-opera staircases … — R. H. Rovere

words.definition: Something that provides protection from the rain, especially an umbrella
words.origin: From Greek *ombros* rain + Latin *fugere* to flee.

words.definition: One who hates or fears rain
words.origin: From Greek *ombros* rain + *-phobos* fearing.

words.definition: Threatening; giving a sense of something bad to come
examples: … in Italy, it's Friday the 17th that's considered **ominous** … — Sarah Otter
It was quiet in an **ominous** way; it was quiet in the way of small, frightening sounds. — Kate DiCamillo

words.definition: Having read everything
words.origin: From Latin *omnis* all + *legere* to read.

words.definition: A situation that is a complete mess, especially when resulting from mismanagement
words.origin: Coined in the BBC satire *The Thick of It*, from *omni-* + *shambles*.

words.definition: Contemplation of one's navel as an aid to meditation; self-absorbed musing
words.origin: Greek *omphalós* "navel" + *-o-* -o- + *sképsis* "perception, taking notice, examination, inquiry," from *skep-*, base of *sképtomai, sképtesthai* "to look at, expect, observe, inquire" + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 1925.
examples: … a preponderance of emotional self-awareness has sent us sliding dangerously into **omphaloskepsis** … — Fiona McCann

words.definition: The inability to tell fantasy from reality
words.origin: From Greek *oneiros* dream + *ataxia* disorder.

words.definition: Involving heavy effort; burdensome
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *honereus*, from Latin *onerosus*, from *oner-, onus* burden; akin to Sanskrit *anas* cart. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Worship of the donkey or ass
words.origin: From Greek *onos* ass + *latreia* worship.

words.definition: A word that imitates the sound it names
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *onomatopoiia*, from *onomat-, onoma* name + *poiein* to make. First known use: circa 1553.
examples: … some of our most beloved **onomatopoeias**: crackle, sizzle, pop, slurp. — Yotam Ottolenghi

words.definition: The habit of biting one's nails, often from nervousness
words.origin: From Greek *onyx* nail + *-phagia* eating.

words.definition: Money or cash
words.origin: Yiddish, from German *auf dem Tisch* on the table.

words.definition: Showing many small points of shifting colour
Not transparent; hard to understand
words.origin: Latin *opacus*. First known use: 1641.
examples: The **opaque** water of the muddy river

words.definition: Harsh public criticism
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, derivative (with *-ium,* deverbal suffix of function or state) of *opprobrāre* "to bring up as a reproach," from *ob-* ob- + *-probrāre,* verbal derivative of *probrum* "reproach, insult, disgrace," probably noun derivative of **pro-fro-* "brought up against someone (as a reproach)," going back to Indo-European **pro-bhr-o,* from **pro-* "before" + **bhr-,* ablaut grade of **bher-* "carry, bring". First known use: 1647.
examples: Collaborators with the enemy did not escape the **opprobrium** of the townspeople.
The bombing of the church was met with widespread **opprobrium**.

words.definition: A person who begins to learn or study only late in life
words.origin: From Greek *opsimathēs*, from *opse* late + *manthanein* to learn.

words.definition: An excessive longing for a particular food
words.origin: From Greek *opson* delicacy + *mania*.

words.definition: Ostentatiously rich and luxurious
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Latin *opulentus* "abounding in resources, wealthy," from *op-, *ops* "power, ability, wealth" + *-ulentus* "having in quantity, full of" (probably dissimilated from **-o-u̯ent-os,* with Indo-European **-u̯ent-,* suffix of possession). First known use: circa 1518.

words.definition: Relating to appetite or desire
words.origin: From Greek *orektikos*, from *oregein* to stretch out, desire.

words.definition: In Iroquoian belief, a spiritual power in all things that can effect change
words.origin: From Huron (Wendat), an Iroquoian word for a spiritual force; brought into English by anthropologist J. N. B. Hewitt in 1902.

words.definition: A large upper-storey window projecting from a wall, supported by corbels
words.origin: Middle English, porch, oriel, from Anglo-French *oriol*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A banner or symbol that inspires devotion
words.origin: Middle English *oriflamble*, the banner of St. Denis, from Middle French, from Old French *ori flambe*, small flag. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: A prayer, especially a spoken one, as in Hamlet's in thy orisons
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *ureisun, oreison*, from Late Latin *oration-, oratio*, from Latin, oration. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Full, round and imposing, of a voice; pompous or pretentious, of writing
words.origin: Modification of Latin *ore rotundo*, literally, with round mouth. First known use: 1799.

words.definition: Melodious
words.origin: From *Orpheus* + *-an*. *Orpheus*: Latin, borrowed from Greek *Orpheús*.

words.definition: Mystic and entrancing
A clockwork model of the solar system that shows the planets in motion
words.origin: Charles Boyle †1731 4th Earl of *Orrery*. First known use: 1713.

words.definition: Drowsiness or inattention; the act of yawning; dullness
words.origin: From Latin *oscitare* to yawn.

words.definition: To kiss, used formally or humorously; of curves, to touch and share a tangent
words.origin: Latin *osculatus*, past participle of *osculari*, from *osculum* kiss, from diminutive of *os* mouth. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: To become rigid and unable to change
words.origin: Latin *oss-, os* + English *-ify*. First known use: 1699.
examples: … so easy for the mind to **ossify** and generous ideals to end in stale platitudes. — John Buchan

words.definition: Stated or appearing true, but not necessarily so
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *ostensibilis* "perceptible, visible, capable of demonstration," from Latin *ostensus,* variant of *ostentus,* past participle of *ostendere* "to hold out for inspection, show, make clear by one's actions, demonstrate" (from *os-,* assimilated variant of *obs-,* variant of *ob-* "toward, facing, against" + *tendere* "to extend outward, stretch, spread out") + *-bilis* "capable (of acting) or worthy (of being acted upon)". First known use: 1771.

words.definition: Designed to impress; showy
words.origin: Ostentati(on) + -ous, after contention : contentious and like pairs. First known use: 1590.
examples: The **ostentatious** = very large and expensive summer homes of rich industrialists

words.definition: To exclude from a group
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *ostrakízein* "(in 5th-century Athens) to banish an individual chosen after a vote taken by writing names on potsherds," from *óstrakon* "earthen vessel, potsherd" + *-izein* -ize. First known use: 1649.
examples: Despite his victories, Themistocles was **ostracized** by the Athenians.
… a lonely dissenter, **ostracized** as an enemy of the people … — Robert Brustein

words.definition: Making the familiar seem strange
words.origin: Russian, estrangement; coined by Viktor Shklovsky.

words.definition: The act or policy of refusing to face reality or unpleasant facts
words.origin: From the ostrich's supposed habit of burying its head.

words.definition: Unusual; bizarre; risqué or indecent
words.origin: A whimsical British coinage of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Of another kind
words.origin: Alteration of English dialect *othergates*. First known use: 1632.

words.definition: Serving no practical purpose or result, as otiose words; futile; idle
words.origin: Latin *otiosus*, from *otium* leisure. First known use: 1795.

words.definition: A stanza of eight lines rhyming abababcc, as in Byron's Don Juan
words.origin: Italian, literally, eighth rhyme. First known use: 1776.

words.definition: A secret dungeon reached through a trapdoor
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from *oublier* to forget, from Old French *oblier*, from Vulgar Latin **oblitare*, frequentative of Latin *oblivisci* to forget. First known use: 1777.

words.definition: To emit strange noises, such as bellowing, whistling and shrieking
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in *Jabberwocky*.

words.definition: Unusual and startling; beyond the bounds of convention; bizarre
words.origin: French, exaggerated, past participle of *outrer* to overdo.

words.definition: Outside of; beyond
The day after tomorrow
words.origin: From Middle English *overmorwe*, from *over* + *morrow*.

words.definition: Showing excessive confidence or pride; presumptuous and arrogant
words.origin: Middle English *overwening*, present participle of *overwenen* to be arrogant, from *over* + *wenen* to ween. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a school with **overweening** pride in its own rectitude. — S. L. Price

words.definition: The armpit, a word still heard in Scotland and northern England
words.origin: Middle English (Scots), alteration of Old English *ōxta*; akin to Old English *eax* axis, axle. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A phrase pairing contradictory terms
words.origin: Late Greek *oxymōron*, from neuter of *oxymōros* pointedly foolish, from Greek *oxys* sharp, keen + *mōros* foolish. First known use: 1656.
examples: More than recognizing **oxymorons** or simply thinking these examples are clever, students need to understand that they represent moments in which the speaker feels contradictory sentiments. — Kenneth J. Smith
Of course, "objective parent" is something of an **oxymoron**, if not an outright lie. — Michael Martin

words.definition: Bland or insipid intellectual matter, entertainment or writing; food
words.origin: Latin, food, fodder; akin to Latin *pascere* to feed. First known use: circa 1661.

words.definition: Golden; lavish
words.origin: From the Pactolus, a river in Lydia said to carry gold.

words.definition: An expression of praise, joy or triumph, typically in the form of a song
words.origin: Latin, hymn of thanksgiving especially addressed to Apollo, from Greek *paian, paiōn*, from *Paian, Paiōn*, epithet of Apollo in the hymn. First known use: 1589.
examples: … unite their voices in a great **paean** to liberty. — Edward Sackville-West
Wrote a **paean** to the queen on her 50th birthday

words.definition: Any of the twelve warriors of Charlemagne's court; a knightly champion
words.origin: Middle French, from Italian *paladino*, from Old French *palatin*, from Medieval Latin *palatinus* courtier, from Late Latin, imperial official. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: A covered litter for one passenger, carried on poles by bearers
words.origin: Portuguese *palanquim*, from Malay or Javanese *pelangki*, of Indo-Aryan origin; akin to Bengali *pālaṅka* bed. First known use: 1588.

words.definition: Prolonged, idle fuss or talk
words.origin: Portuguese *palavra* word, speech, from Late Latin *parabola* parable, speech. First known use: 1735.

words.definition: A docile horse used for ordinary riding, especially by women
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *palefrei*, from Medieval Latin *palafredus*, from Late Latin *paraveredus* post-horse for secondary roads, from Greek *para-* beside, subsidiary + Late Latin *veredus* post-horse, from a Gaulish word akin to Welsh *gorwydd* horse; akin to Old Irish *réidid* he rides. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: A repetition of words, especially for emphasis
words.origin: From Greek *palillogia*, from *palin* again + *logos* word.

words.definition: A manuscript written over an earlier, partly erased text
words.origin: Latin *palimpsestus*, from Greek *palimpsēstos* scraped again, from *palin* + *psēn* to rub, scrape; akin to Sanskrit *psāti, babhasti* he chews. First known use: 1825.
examples: Canada … is a **palimpsest**, an overlay of classes and generations. — Margaret Atwood
Too short a time to get to know the **palimpsest** of Genevan societies, let alone those of Switzerland — George Steiner

words.definition: A poem in which the poet retracts something said in an earlier poem
words.origin: Greek *palinōidia*, from *palin* + *aeidein* to sing. First known use: 1579.

words.definition: Compulsively repeating an act until it is perfect
words.origin: From Greek *palin* again + *nous* mind.

words.definition: Wise or learned
A safeguard or source of protection; a rare silvery-white metal
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin, from Greek *palladion*, from *Pallad-, Pallas*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … this political persecution being, somehow or other, the grand **palladium** of our liberties … — Washington Irving
… lend authority to the view that the true **palladium** of every people is its language … — Ferdinand Schevill

words.definition: To make less severe without curing
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *palliatus*, past participle of *palliare* to cloak, conceal, from Latin *pallium* cloak. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Pale; lacking vigour
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *pallidus* "pale, colourless". First known use: 1590.
examples: The movie is a **pallid** version of the classic novel.

words.definition: Of supreme importance; outstanding; praiseworthy
words.origin: Latin *palmarius* deserving the palm, from *palma*. First known use: 1657.

words.definition: A stupid, clumsy or uncouth person; a mediocre or inexperienced boxer
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1920.

words.definition: Strong, dangerous winds
words.origin: American, from the Palouse region of Washington and Idaho.

words.definition: Small or meagre; petty and worthless
words.origin: Obsolete *paltry* trash, from dialect *palt, pelt* piece of coarse cloth, trash; akin to Middle Low German *palte* rag. First known use: 1565.
examples: They in their greatness don't have to bother with such **paltry** restrictions — Vanessa Feltz

words.definition: A cure for all ills
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *panacēa* "universal remedy, cure-all," going back to Latin, "any of various medicinal plants," borrowed from Greek *panákeia* "name of a medicinal plant, universal remedy, (as a personified abstraction) a goddess of healing," derivative of *panakḗs* "all-healing," from *pan-* pan- + *-akēs,* adjective derivative of *ákos* (neuter s-stem) "cure, remedy, relief," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1548.
examples: The law will improve the lives of local farmers, but it is no **panacea**.

words.definition: Flamboyant confidence of style
words.origin: Middle French *pennache*, from Old Italian *pennacchio*, from Late Latin *pinnaculum* small wing. First known use: 1553.
examples: The palace guard had a **panache** on his helmet.
… flashed his … smile and waved with the **panache** of a big-city mayor. — Joe Morgenstern

words.definition: Stretching and yawning, especially on waking: contraction, expansion, release
words.origin: From Latin *pandiculari* to stretch oneself.

words.definition: A public speech or text in praise of someone
words.origin: Latin *panegyricus*, from Greek *panēgyrikos*, from *panēgyrikos* of or for a festival assembly, from *panēgyris* festival assembly, from *pan-* + *agyris* assembly; akin to Greek *ageirein* to gather. First known use: 1603.
examples: Composed a **panegyric** about Tchaikovsky for the concert program

words.definition: Blindly or unreasonably optimistic
words.origin: *Pangloss*, optimistic tutor in Voltaire's *Candide* (1759). First known use: 1831.
