words.definition: A person who has or claims to have a great deal of authority or influence
words.origin: Grand *Panjandrum*, burlesque title of an imaginary personage in some nonsense lines by Samuel Foote. First known use: 1825.

words.definition: A circular prison watched from a single central tower
A large van for moving furniture; once, a bazaar for furniture
words.origin: Short for *pantechnicon van*, from *pantechnicon* storage warehouse. First known use: 1891.

words.definition: An advocate or helper; in Christian thought, the Holy Spirit
words.origin: Middle English *Paraclit, Paraclyte,* borrowed from Late Latin *Paraclētus, Paraclītus* "advocate, comforter," borrowed from Greek *paráklētos* "advocate, helper, comforter," an epithet of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel of John (as John 14:26), derivative of *paráklētos,* adjective, "called to one's aid," verbal adjective of *parakaleîn* "to call in, send for, summon, exhort, comfort, console," from *para-* para-:1 + *kaléō, kaleîn* "to call, summon". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A detailed imaginary world, often one created in childhood
words.origin: From Greek *para-* beside + *kosmos* world; coined in the 1970s.

words.definition: A typical model or pattern
words.origin: Late Latin *paradigma*, from Greek *paradeigma*, from *paradeiknynai* to show side by side, from *para-* + *deiknynai* to show. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Her book provides us with a new **paradigm** for modern biography.
An entrepreneur who became a **paradigm** of success

words.definition: A model of excellence
words.origin: Middle French, from Old Italian *paragone*, literally, touchstone, from *paragonare* to test on a touchstone, from Greek *parakonan* to sharpen, from *para-* + *akonē* whetstone, from *akē* point; akin to Greek *akmē* point. First known use: circa 1548.

words.definition: One who lives by the sea
words.origin: From Greek *paralios* by the sea, from *para* beside + *hals* sea.

words.definition: Drawing attention to something by professing to pass over it, as I won't mention
words.origin: From Greek *paraleipsis* omission.

words.definition: More important than anything else; supreme
words.origin: Anglo-French *paramont*, from *par* by (from Latin *per*) + *amunt* above, from *a* to (from Latin *ad*) + *munt* mountain. First known use: 1530.
examples: Unemployment was the **paramount** issue in the election.

words.definition: A lover, especially the illicit partner of a married person
words.origin: Middle English, from *par amour* for the sake of love, willingly, from Anglo-French *par amur*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Her account put him in the position of looking like the duped lover believing the cheating married **paramour's** protestation of love … — Bettina Drew

words.definition: A flourish added after a signature, once a safeguard against forgery
words.origin: Middle French, modification of Latin *paragraphus* paragraph. First known use: 1584.

words.definition: A sentence whose ending surprises
words.origin: From Greek *para* beyond + *prosdokia* expectation.

words.definition: Extremely dry; very thirsty
words.origin: From Middle English *parch*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: He was **parched** after the long hike.

words.definition: Seeing faces or patterns in random things
words.origin: Borrowed from German *Pareidolie*, from Greek *par-* para-:1 + *eídōlon* "image, reflection" + German *-ie* -ia. First known use: 1962.
examples: The scientific explanation for some people is **pareidolia**, or the human ability to see shapes or make pictures out of randomness. Think of the Rorschach inkblot test. — Pamela Ferdinand

words.definition: An outcast
words.origin: Tamil *paṟaiyan*, literally, drummer. First known use: 1613.
examples: … the mordant wit and unsettling insight that once made [Mark] Twain practically a **pariah** in Middle America. — Roy Reed
A nation, it seemed, had become a global **pariah** overnight. — Adam Westbrook and Kirk Semple

words.definition: Full of danger or uncertainty; precarious; dangerously clever
words.origin: Middle English, variant of *perilous* perilous (through loss of medial syllable and regular lowering and backing of *e*). First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A writer or collector of proverbs
words.origin: From Greek *paroimia* proverb + *-graphos* writer.

words.definition: A pun; wordplay on similar sounds
words.origin: Latin, from Greek, from *paronomazein* to call with a slight change of name, from *para-* + *onoma* name. First known use: 1577.

words.definition: A sudden attack or violent outburst of emotion or activity; a spasm
words.origin: Middle English *paroxism*, from Medieval Latin *paroxysmus*, from Greek *paroxysmos*, from *paroxynein* to stimulate, from *para-* + *oxynein* to provoke, from *oxys* sharp. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Convulsed … in the **paroxysms** of an epileptic seizure — Thomas Hardy

words.definition: Unwilling to spend money; stingy
words.origin: Parsimony + -ous. First known use: 1598.

words.definition: A person from a humble background who has rapidly gained wealth or position
words.origin: French, from past participle of *parvenir* to arrive, from Latin *pervenire*, from *per* through + *venire* to come. First known use: 1787.

words.definition: A satire or lampoon, originally one displayed or posted in a public place
words.origin: Middle French, from Italian *pasquinata*, from *Pasquino*, name given to a statue in Rome on which lampoons were posted. First known use: 1658.

words.definition: A work imitating the style of another
words.origin: French, from Italian *pasticcio*. First known use: 1866.
examples: His building designs are **pastiches** based on classical forms.
The research paper was essentially a **pastiche** made up of passages from different sources.

words.definition: The dialect of the common people of a region, differing from the standard
words.origin: From French *patois*. First known use: 1643.

words.definition: A scarcity
words.origin: Middle English *paucite*, from Latin *paucitat-, paucitas*, from *paucus* little. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Like a peacock; resembling the iridescent colours of a peacock's tail
words.origin: From Latin *pavoninus*, from *pavo* peacock.

words.definition: Liable to sin or err, as all mortals are said to be; fallible
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *peccabilis*, from *peccare* to sin.

words.definition: A small, relatively unimportant offence
words.origin: Spanish *pecadillo*, diminutive of *pecado* sin, from Latin *peccatum*, from neuter of *peccatus*, past participle of *peccare*. First known use: 1591.
examples: The movie star's **peccadilloes** made tabloid headlines.

words.definition: Affecting benevolence or high moral principles; hypocritical, after Dickens
words.origin: Seth *Pecksniff*, character in *Martin Chuzzlewit* (1843–44) by Charles Dickens. First known use: 1844.

words.definition: A teacher, especially a strict or pedantic one; in Greece, a slave who led boys to school
words.origin: Middle English *pedagoge, petegoge* "teacher," borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *pedagoge, pedagogue* "person escorting a child to school, tutor," borrowed from Latin *paedagōgus* "slave in charge of children," borrowed from Greek *paidagōgós* "slave who escorted children to and from school and supervised them while outdoors, attendant on a child, tutor, guide, mentor," from *paid-* ped- + *agōgós* "leading, guiding," derivative (with reduplication) of *ágein* "to lead, carry off". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules
words.origin: From *pedant* + *-ic*. *Pedant*: Middle French, from Italian *pedante*. First known use: 1628.
examples: … **pedantic** grading rubrics and exams … — C. Brandon Ogbunu
… if we're going to be exactingly correct and **pedantic**, I'd point out that there's no such thing … — Alasdair Wilkins

words.definition: Pale and sickly-looking
words.origin: Scots, perhaps imitative of a feeble wail.

words.definition: A woman's light, loose dressing gown or negligee, often of silk or lace
words.origin: French, literally, garment worn while combing the hair, from Middle French, from *peigner* to comb the hair, from Latin *pectinare*, from *pectin-, pecten* comb. First known use: 1835.

words.definition: The belief that the world is becoming worse
words.origin: From Latin *pejor* worse.

words.definition: Money, especially when gained in a dishonest or dishonourable way
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *pelfre* booty. First known use: circa 1505.

words.definition: Translucently clear; easy to understand
words.origin: Latin *pellucidus*, from *per* through + *lucidus* lucid. First known use: 1563.

words.definition: A strong liking or inclination
words.origin: Borrowed from French, noun derivative from present participle of *pencher* "to lean, slope, be inclined, tend," going back to Old French *pengier,* going back to Vulgar Latin **pendicāre,* from **pendere* "to hang" + **-icāre,* verb formative. First known use: 1672.

words.definition: Involving repetitive or cyclical efforts, often with little apparent progress
words.origin: From Penelope, who wove and unwove a shroud each day in the *Odyssey*.

words.definition: The innermost, secret or hidden parts of something
words.origin: Latin, the innermost part, from *penetrare* to penetrate.

words.definition: Feeling sorrow for wrongdoing
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *penitent*, from Latin *paenitent-, paenitens*, from present participle of *paenitēre* to cause regret, feel regret, perhaps from *paene* almost. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: One who steals jewellery, especially by substituting a fake for the real one
words.origin: From *pennyweight*, a small unit of weight for gold.

words.definition: Engaged in deep, often sad thought
words.origin: Middle English *pensif* "sad, anxious, thoughtful, lost in thought," borrowed from Anglo-French (also continental Old French), from *penser* "to think of, consider, ponder" (borrowed from Latin *pensāre* "to weigh, counterbalance, weigh in the mind, consider," iterative of *pendere* "to weigh, have a weight of, pay [out], estimate, consider") + *-if* -ive. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … her face had the **pensive** mournfulness of a seraph in an old sad painting. — Herman Wouk

words.definition: A task given, especially as a punishment
words.origin: Latin, a weight of wool to be spun, a task.

words.definition: Second to last
A demand made before an ultimatum
words.origin: A blend of *penultimate* and *ultimatum*.

words.definition: A partly shaded outer region; a borderland
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *paene* almost + *umbra* shadow. First known use: 1665.
examples: The seventeenth century lay in the **penumbra** of the middle ages … — Edward Eggleston
The **penumbra** of the Bill of Rights

words.definition: Partly shaded; dimly lit
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *paene* almost + *umbra* shadow. First known use: 1665.

words.definition: Extremely poor; also, stingy
words.origin: From *penury* + *-ous*. *Penury*: Middle English, from Latin *penuria, paenuria* want; perhaps akin to Latin *paene* almost. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: Extreme poverty; destitution, a state of having almost nothing at all
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *penuria, paenuria* want; perhaps akin to Latin *paene* almost. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Perhaps; by chance; uncertainty or doubt, as in beyond peradventure
words.origin: Middle English *par aventure*, from Anglo-French, by chance. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To walk or travel through
words.origin: Latin *perambulatus*, past participle of *perambulare*, from *per-* through + *ambulare* to walk. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Perceptive; discerning
words.origin: Latin *percipient-, percipiens*, present participle of *percipere* to perceive. First known use: 1659.

words.definition: In Christian theology, a state of eternal punishment; utter ruin or destruction
words.origin: Middle English *perdicion*, from Anglo-French *perdiciun*, Late Latin *perdition-, perditio*, from Latin *perdere* to destroy, from *per-* through + *dare* to give. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Permanent or everlasting; enduring continuously, as perdurable fame
words.origin: Middle English, long-lasting, eternal, from Anglo-French *pardurable*, from Late Latin *perdurabilis*, from Latin *perdurare* to endure, from *per-* throughout + *durare* to last. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A long, meandering journey
Foreign; coming from abroad; wandering, as the peregrine falcon
words.origin: Middle French *peregrin*, from Medieval Latin *peregrinus*, from Latin, foreign. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: To postpone until the day after tomorrow; to defer, again and again
words.origin: From Latin *perendinare*, from *perendie* the day after tomorrow.

words.definition: Lasting a very long time; recurring
words.origin: Latin *perennis*, from *per-* throughout + *annus* year. First known use: circa 1660.

words.definition: Intense and impassioned; burning with zeal, sometimes to an excessive degree
words.origin: New Latin *perfervidus*, from Latin *per-* thoroughly + *fervidus* fervid. First known use: 1833.

words.definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy
words.origin: From *perfidy* + *-ous*. *Perfidy*: Latin *perfidia*, from *perfidus* faithless, from *per-* detrimental to + *fides* faith. First known use: circa 1538.

words.definition: Done with minimal effort or reflection
words.origin: Late Latin *perfunctorius*, from Latin *perfungi* to accomplish, get through with, from *per-* through + *fungi* to perform. First known use: 1593.

words.definition: The point in an orbit closest to the sun
words.origin: New Latin, from *peri-* + Greek *hēlios* sun. First known use: 1666.

words.definition: Travelling from place to place
words.origin: Middle French & Latin; Middle French *peripatetique*, from Latin *peripateticus*, from Greek *peripatētikos*, from *peripatein* to walk up and down, discourse while pacing (as did Aristotle), from *peri-* + *patein* to tread; akin to Sanskrit *patha* path. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A sudden reversal of fortune
words.origin: Greek, from *peripiptein* to fall around, change suddenly, from *peri-* + *piptein* to fall. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: The use of indirect and circumlocutory speech or writing; a roundabout phrase
words.origin: Latin, from Greek, from *periphrazein* to express periphrastically, from *peri-* + *phrazein* to point out. First known use: 1533.

words.definition: Relating to pigeons
words.origin: From Greek *peristera* dove.

words.definition: The assemblage of bubbles, in a glass of champagne, for example
words.origin: French, from *perle* pearl.

words.definition: Having a harmful effect, often gradually
words.origin: Middle English, "evil, wicked," "(of an illness) extremely serious, fatal," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *perniciōsus* "destructive of health or life, ruinous, fatal," from *perniciēs* "physicial destruction, ruin, undoing" (from *per-* per- + *nec-,* base of *necāre* "to kill, destroy" —derivative of *nec-, nex* "violent death, killing"— + *-iēs,* deverbal suffix of abstract nouns) + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The study highlights just how **pernicious** this metal can be, even at low levels. — Bradley Allf

words.definition: A benefit to which one is entitled because of one's position; a perk
words.origin: Middle English, property acquired by means other than inheritance, from Anglo-French *perquisit*, Medieval Latin *perquisitum*, from neuter of *perquisitus*, past participle of *perquirere* to purchase, acquire, from Latin, to search for thoroughly, from *per-* thoroughly + *quaerere* to seek. First known use: 1567.

words.definition: Light and slightly contemptuous mockery or banter, as in witty drawing-room talk
words.origin: French, from *persifler* to banter, from *per-* thoroughly + *siffler* to whistle, hiss, boo, ultimately from Latin *sibilare*. First known use: 1757.

words.definition: Having keen insight and understanding
words.origin: Latin *perspicac-, perspicax*, from *perspicere*. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action
words.origin: Latin *pertinac-, pertinax*, from *per-* thoroughly + *tenac-, tenax* tenacious, from *tenēre*. First known use: 1583.

words.definition: To read carefully
words.origin: Middle English, to use up, deal with in sequence, from Latin *per-* thoroughly + Middle English *usen* to use. First known use: circa 1520.
examples: "Do you know me?" asked Mr. Huntingdon, intently **perusing** his features. — Anne Brontë
The wretched plumber had been **perusing** my private documents. — Myles na gCopaleen (Flann O'Brien)

words.definition: Spreading through every part of something
words.origin: From Latin *pervasus*, past participle of *pervadere* to go through, + English *-ive*.
examples: Social media's **pervasive** influence on our culture
This is one of the most persistent and **pervasive** problems in the music business. — Shaun Harper

words.definition: The pleasant smell of rain on dry earth
words.origin: Petr(o)- + ichor. First known use: 1964.
examples: Australian scientists first documented the process of **petrichor** formation in 1964 … — Tim Logan
The intensity of the **petrichor** smell can vary with the type of soil and how heavily the rain is falling. — John Boyer

words.definition: So frightened one cannot move; turned to stone
words.origin: From past participle of petrify. First known use: 15th century.
examples: And at the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History's annual dinosaur ball, about 800 patrons in black tie or gown waltz among the **petrified** remains of the once-glorious creatures. — Sheldon Teitelbaum

words.definition: One who quibbles over trivial details; a petty lawyer
words.origin: Probably from *petty* + obsolete English *fogger* pettifogger. First known use: 1564.

words.definition: Petty quibbling over trivial details
words.origin: Probably from *petty* + obsolete English *fogger* pettifogger. First known use: 1564.

words.definition: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered
words.origin: Earlier, "immodest, impudent," borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French, "lively, impudent," borrowed from Latin *petulant-, petulans* "impudent, self-assertive, immodest," perhaps re-formation (as a present participle) of **petulus,* adjective derivative of *petere* "to make for (with hostile intent), seek to" with *-ulus,* suffix denoting repeated or prolonged action; modern senses (since the 18th century) probably by association with pet, pettish. First known use: 1755.
examples: The person most capable of running a group of obscenely wealthy, often **petulant** twentysomethings is an obscenely wealthy, **petulant** manager. — Roy S. Johnson
"What is it all about?" cried Dorian in his **petulant** way, flinging himself down on the sofa. — Oscar Wilde

words.definition: A sequence of real or imaginary images like those seen in a dream
words.origin: Borrowed from French *phantasmogorie* (later *fantasmagorie*) "theatrical show using magic lanterns in a darkened performance space to suggest supernatural phenomena," from *fantasme* phantasm + *-ogorie, -agorie,* of uncertain origin. First known use: circa 1802.

words.definition: Dreamlike and rapidly shifting
words.origin: Borrowed from French *phantasmogorie* (later *fantasmagorie*) "theatrical show using magic lanterns in a darkened performance space to suggest supernatural phenomena," from *fantasme* phantasm + *-ogorie, -agorie,* of uncertain origin. First known use: circa 1802.

words.definition: The love of money; greed
words.origin: From Greek *philargyria*, from *philos* loving + *argyros* silver.

words.definition: A bitter attack or denunciation, after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip
words.origin: Middle French *philippique*, from Latin & Greek; Latin *philippica, orationes philippicae*, speeches of Cicero against Mark Antony, translation of Greek *philippikoi logoi*, speeches of Demosthenes against Philip II of Macedon, literally, speeches relating to Philip. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: A collector of matchboxes, matchbooks or their labels
words.origin: *phil-* + Latin *lumen* light. First known use: 1943.

words.definition: The love of beauty
words.origin: From Greek *philokalia*, from *philos* loving + *kalos* beautiful.

words.definition: A lover of cats
words.origin: From Greek *philos* loving + Latin *feles* cat.

words.definition: A lover of learning
words.origin: From Greek *philomathēs*, from *philos* loving + *manthanein* to learn.

words.definition: A poetry lover
words.origin: From Greek *philos* loving + *Mousa* muse.

words.definition: A drink supposed to excite sexual love in the one who drinks it; a love potion
words.origin: Middle French *philtre*, from Latin *philtrum*, from Greek *philtron*; akin to Greek *philos* dear. First known use: circa 1563.

words.definition: Face; facial expression
words.origin: By shortening & alteration from *physiognomy*. First known use: 1685.

words.definition: Calm and unemotional
words.origin: Middle English *fleumatik, flemmatik, fleugmatik,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *fleumatike,* borrowed from Late Latin *phlegmaticus* "relating to or producing the humour phlegm," borrowed from Greek *phlegmatikós* "abounding in phlegm," from *phlegmat-, phlégma* "flame, inflammation, phlegm" + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Light seen with closed eyes, as when they are rubbed
words.origin: International Scientific Vocabulary *phos-* + Greek *phainein* to show. First known use: 1852.
examples: Early studies have demonstrated that direct electrical stimulation to neurons of the visual system will cause a subject to perceive points of light (**phosphenes**). — George Scarlatis

words.definition: Emitting light without combustion or perceptible heat; softly glowing
Relating to the adventures of a likeable rogue
words.origin: Spanish *picaresco*, from *pícaro*. First known use: 1810.

words.definition: Petty; worthless; of little value or importance, from a small old Louisiana coin
words.origin: Occitan *picaioun*, a small coin, from *picaio* money, from *pica* to jingle, of imitative origin. First known use: 1805.

words.definition: Nonsense; trivial or foolish talk, dismissed with a wave of the hand
words.origin: Perhaps blend of *piddle* and *trifle*. First known use: 1847.

words.definition: A darling; a pet name for a sweetheart
words.origin: From Middle English *pigges eye* pig's eye, a term of endearment.

words.definition: A symbol (¶) used to indicate paragraph breaks
words.origin: From Middle English *pylcrafte*, an alteration of *paragraph*.

words.definition: To attack or ridicule publicly; a wooden frame for public punishment
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *pilori*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Appearing valuable but actually cheap or tawdry; an alloy imitating gold
words.origin: Christopher *Pinchbeck* †1732 English watchmaker. First known use: 1734.

words.definition: Unwilling to spend or give money
, plural pineta An arboretum of coniferous trees such as pines
words.origin: Latin, from *pinus*. First known use: 1838.

words.definition: Devoutly religious
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *pius*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a hypocrite,—a thing all **pious** words and uncharitable deeds. — Charles Reade

words.definition: Pleasantly sharp in taste; stimulating
words.origin: Middle French, from present participle of *piquer*. First known use: 1645.
examples: To start, we pureed cilantro, spinach and a jalapeno in a blender to form a bright, **piquant** base for cooking the rice. — Lawman Johnson
… along the way we learn such **piquant** details as the fact that the great physicist Michael Faraday knew no math to speak of. — Tracy Kidder

words.definition: Sorcery; witchcraft; spell
words.origin: Irish *piseog* charm, witchcraft.

words.definition: An ant, from its sharp, vinegary smell; once a common country word
words.origin: Middle English *pissemire*, from *pisse* urine + *mire* ant, of Scandinavian origin; akin to Old Norse *maurr* ant; akin to Latin *formica* ant, Greek *myrmēx*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Concise and full of meaning
words.origin: From *pith* + *-y*. *Pith*: Middle English, from Old English *pitha*; akin to Middle Dutch & Middle Low German *pit* pith, pit. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: Crazy, confused or eccentric, as though led astray by pixies; tipsy
words.origin: Irregular from *pixie*. First known use: 1848.

words.definition: To make less angry
words.origin: Latin *placatus*, past participle of *placare*. First known use: 1678.

words.definition: Calm and peaceful, with little movement or excitement
words.origin: Latin *placidus*, from *placēre* to please. First known use: 1614.

words.definition: Loud, reverberating and often melancholy, especially of sound
words.origin: Latin *plangent-, plangens*, present participle of *plangere* to strike, lament. First known use: 1666.

words.definition: A gentle splash
words.origin: Probably imitative. First known use: circa 1522.

words.definition: A remark used too often to be interesting
words.origin: French, from *plat* flat, dull. First known use: 1762.
examples: … he seemed to breathe only for the purpose of perpetrating puns—things of so despicable a **platitude** … — Edgar Allan Poe
… monologues with a few too many **platitudes** … — Michael Musto

words.definition: An expression of praise
words.origin: Latin *plaudite* applaud, plural imperative of *plaudere* to applaud. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: Seemingly reasonable or probable
words.origin: Latin *plausibilis* worthy of applause, from *plausus*, past participle of *plaudere*. First known use: 1565.
examples: … a swindler …, then a quack, then a smooth, **plausible** gentleman … — Ralph Waldo Emerson
The argument was both powerful and **plausible**

words.definition: To entwine or interlace branches to form a hedge or arbour, as in a formal garden
words.origin: Middle English *plechen*, of uncertain origin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Excessive talking
words.origin: From Latin *plenus* full + *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: A person, especially a diplomat, invested with full power to act for a government
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *plēnipotentiārius,* from *plēnipotentia* "full power or authority" (noun derivative of Late Latin *plēnipotent-, plēnipotens* "invested with full power, plenipotent") + Latin *-ārius* -ary. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: The state of being full
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *plēnitūdō,* from *plēnus* "full" + *-i-* -i- + *-tūdō* -tude. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The use of more words than are necessary to convey meaning, as see with one's eyes
words.origin: Late Latin *pleonasmus*, from Greek *pleonasmos*, from *pleonazein* to be excessive, from *pleiōn, pleōn* more. First known use: 1610.

words.definition: An excess
words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *plēthōra, plētūra* "fullness, overabundance of a humour," borrowed from Greek *plēthṓra* (Ionic *plēthṓrē*) "fullness, crowdedness (of a marketplace at peak hour), excess of a humour or blood," from *plēth-,* base of *plḗthein* "to be full" + *-ōra, -ōrē,* probably dissimilated variant of *-ōlē,* suffix of deverbal nouns; *plḗthein* going back to Indo-European **pléh1-dh-,* extended form of the verbal base **pleh1-* "become full," with **-dh-* marking a completed state. First known use: circa 1541.
examples: … Grand Cayman offers a **plethora** of bustling restaurants, ritzy resorts and comfortable condos … — Susanne Cummings
… a world whose credibility is threatened by the meaningless **plethora** of material goods it goes on producing. — W. Roy Niblett

words.definition: Of or relating to plums
examples: Got a **plummy** role in the movie

words.definition: A group of political, business and financial interests engaged in exploiting the public
words.origin: From *plunder* + German *Bund* league.

words.definition: Richly luxurious and comfortable
words.origin: Middle French *peluche*. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: A person whose power derives from their wealth, especially one who governs by it
words.origin: Greek *ploutokratia*, from *ploutos* wealth; akin to Greek *plein* to sail, float. First known use: 1631.

words.definition: A lover of rain
words.origin: From Latin *pluvia* rain + Greek *-philos* loving; a modern coinage.

words.definition: A person who asks too many questions
words.origin: Russian, from *pochemu* why.

words.definition: A person who writes inferior poetry; a dabbler who thinks himself a poet
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *poeta* + *-aster* -aster. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: A dense winter fog having ice particles
words.origin: Shoshone *paγɨnappɨh* cloud. First known use: 1865.

words.definition: The cutting of a beard; shaving
words.origin: From Greek *pōgōn* beard + *-tomia* cutting.

words.definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret
words.origin: Middle English *poynaunt*, from Anglo-French *poinant, poignant*, present participle of *poindre* to prick, sting, from Latin *pungere*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **poignant** story of love, courage, and sacrifice

words.definition: A strong verbal or written attack
words.origin: French *polémique*, from Middle French, from *polemique* controversial, from Greek *polemikos* warlike, hostile, from *polemos* war; perhaps akin to Greek *pelemizein* to shake, Old English eal*felo* baleful. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: An utter coward; a spiritless wretch, a word of strong contempt
words.origin: Middle French *poultron*, from Old Italian *poltrone*, probably akin to *poltro* colt, ultimately from Latin *pullus* young of an animal. First known use: circa 1529.

words.definition: A person of great or wide learning. Also polyhistorian
words.origin: Greek *polyistōr* very learned, from *poly-* + *istōr, histōr* learned. First known use: 1588.

words.definition: The use of many conjunctions in a row
words.origin: New Latin, from Late Greek, neuter of *polysyndetos* using many conjunctions, from Greek *poly-* + *syndetos* bound together, conjunctive. First known use: circa 1577.

words.definition: A vain or conceited person, especially one who dresses or behaves extravagantly
words.origin: Middle English *papejay* parrot, from Middle French *papegai, papejai*, from Arabic *babghā'*. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: A sign that something momentous will happen
words.origin: Latin *portentum*, from neuter of *portentus*, past participle of *portendere*. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: A word blending the sounds and meanings of two others, as brunch; a travelling bag
words.origin: Middle French *portemanteau*, from *porter* to carry + *manteau* mantle, from Latin *mantellum*. First known use: 1553.
examples: A **portmanteau** of “costume” and “play,” cosplay by definition is the act of dressing up as a fictional character, with many of the costumes you find inspired by video games, film, or TV. — Stephanie LaCava

When the steamboat bumped against the … pilings, the crowd eased back to allow the hands to erect the gangplank and bear trunks and **portmanteaux** to the dock for passengers to claim. — Loren D. Estleman

words.definition: With great speed
words.origin: Post. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: A hairpiece
words.origin: French, from Spanish *postizo*. First known use: 1867.

words.definition: During or relating to the period after dinner or lunch, as a postprandial nap
A person displaying boldness or courage while drunk
words.origin: From *pot* drink + *valiant*.

words.definition: The act of drinking, especially alcohol; a drink or draught
words.origin: Middle English *potacioun*, from Anglo-French *potation*, from Latin *potation-, potatio* act of drinking, from *potare* to drink. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A book, painting or recording produced purely to make the creator a living
A commotion or fuss over something trivial; a choking cloud of smoke or dust
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1591.

words.definition: A longing for someone absent
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin, earlier genus name for the plant (*Pothos aureus,* later reclassified as *Scindapsus aureus* and *Epipremnum aureum*), Linnaeus's re-formation of earlier *Potha,* borrowed from Sinhalese *pōṭā væl* or *pōṭǣ,* names for the plant *Pothos scandens*. First known use: 1822.

words.definition: A soft, moist mass of material applied to the body to relieve soreness
words.origin: Middle English *pultes*, from Medieval Latin, literally, pap, from Latin, plural of *pult-, puls* porridge. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to the Roman emperor's bodyguard, notorious for making emperors; corrupt or venal
words.origin: From *praetor* + *-ian*. *Praetor*: Middle English *pretor*, from Latin *praetor*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically
words.origin: Latin *pragmaticus* skilled in law or business, from Greek *pragmatikos*, from *pragmat-, pragma* deed, from *prassein* to do. First known use: circa 1612.
examples: At its core the Marshall Plan was a **pragmatic** approach to a tough problem. — Timothy Naftali

words.definition: During or relating to dinner or lunch, as prandial conversation
words.origin: Latin *prandium* late breakfast, luncheon. First known use: 1781.

words.definition: To talk foolishly or at tedious length about something, without sense or point
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle Dutch; akin to Middle Low German *pratten* to pout. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To talk at length in a foolish way
words.origin: Low German *pratelen*; akin to Middle Dutch *praten* to prate. First known use: 1532.
examples: They **prattled** on into the night about the old days.

words.definition: Dangerously unstable
words.origin: Latin *precārius* "given as a favour, depending on the pleasure or mercy of others, of questionable force or permanence, uncertain" + -ous. First known use: 1626.
examples: … forced to earn a **precarious** living as a door-to-door salesman. — Peter Ackroyd
Their wealth was **precarious**, liable to be seized by the sultan if they fell from favour … — Albert Hourani

words.definition: Done suddenly and without careful thought; hasty
words.origin: Latin *praecipitatus*, past participle of *praecipitare*, from *praecipit-, praeceps*. First known use: 1528.

words.definition: Having developed abilities at an unusually early age
words.origin: Latin *praecoc-, praecox* early ripening, precocious, from *prae-* + *coquere* to cook. First known use: 1650.
examples: … Einstein was a **precocious** child. — Gemma Tarlach et al.
The wisdom out of the mouth of a **precocious** 3-year-old has, from then on, been the family's motto. — Michelle Matthews

words.definition: A preference or special liking
words.origin: French *prédilection*, from Medieval Latin *praediligere* to love more, prefer, from Latin *prae-* + *diligere* to love. First known use: 1742.
examples: … a wonderfully spunky heroine with a smart mouth, a bad attitude and a **predilection** for trouble. =a tendency to get into trouble

words.definition: Characteristic of the time before the Fall of Man; innocent and unspoilt
words.origin: *pre-* + Latin *lapsus* slip, fall. First known use: 1879.

words.definition: Having knowledge of events before they happen
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *praescientia*, from Latin *praescient-, praesciens*, present participle of *praescire* to know beforehand, from *prae-* + *scire* to know. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Magic tricks performed as entertainment, especially card tricks; sleight of hand
words.origin: French, from *prestidigitateur* prestidigitator, from *preste* nimble, quick (from Italian *presto*) + Latin *digitus* finger. First known use: 1859.

words.definition: Beyond what is normal or natural; exceptional, almost supernatural
words.origin: Medieval Latin *praeternaturalis*, from Latin *praeter naturam* beyond nature. First known use: 1580.
examples: … wits trained to **preternatural** acuteness by the debates … — G. L. Dickinson

words.definition: To speak evasively
words.origin: Latin *praevaricatus*, past participle of *praevaricari* to act in collusion, literally, to straddle, from *prae-* + *varicare* to straddle, from *varus* bowlegged. First known use: circa 1625.

words.definition: One overly concerned with their personal appearance: dandy
words.origin: From *prick* to dress up + *me* + *dainty*.

words.definition: Self-righteously moralistic and superior; primly fussy about propriety
words.origin: Probably from prig. First known use: 1676.

words.definition: The right of succession belonging to the firstborn child, especially the eldest son
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Late Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Late Latin *prīmogenitūra,* from *prīmogenitus* "firstborn" (from Latin *prīmus* "first, earliest" + *-o-* -o- —for expected *-i-* -i- — + *genitus,* past participle of *gignere* "to bring into being, beget, give birth to") + Latin *-ūra* -ure. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To spruce up or dress up fussily, as before a mirror; to primp or preen
words.origin: Probably alteration of prank. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: In its original, unspoiled condition
words.origin: Latin *pristinus*; akin to Latin *prior*. First known use: 1534.

words.definition: Strong moral principles; integrity
words.origin: Middle English *probite*, from Latin *probitat-, probitas*, from *probus* honest. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A natural tendency
words.origin: Latin *proclivitas*, from *proclivis* sloping, prone, from *pro-* forward + *clivus* slope. First known use: 1561.

words.definition: Enforcing uniformity or conformity without regard to natural variation
Spending money or resources recklessly
words.origin: Latin *prodigus*, from *prodigere* to drive away, squander, from *pro-, prod-* forth + *agere* to drive. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … nature has been so **prodigal** of her bounty … — H. T. Buckle

words.definition: Remarkably great in size or degree
words.origin: From *prodigy* + *-ous*. *Prodigy*: Middle English, from Latin *prodigium* omen, monster, from *pro-, prod-* + *-igium* (akin to *aio* I say). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A young person of exceptional talent
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *prodigium* omen, monster, from *pro-, prod-* + *-igium* (akin to *aio* I say). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The feeling or the belief that everyone around is out to get you
words.origin: From Latin *proditor* traitor + *mania*.

words.definition: An early symptom that indicates the onset of a disease or an episode of something such as a migraine
words.origin: French, literally, precursor, from Greek *prodromos*, from *pro-* before + *dromos* act of running, racecourse. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful
words.origin: Latin *profligatus*, from past participle of *profligare* to strike down, from *pro-* forward, down + *-fligare* (akin to *fligere* to strike); akin to Greek *phlibein* to squeeze. First known use: 1617.

words.definition: Very great or intense; deeply insightful
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *parfunt, profond* deep, from Latin *profundus*, from *pro-* before + *fundus* bottom. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Her books offer **profound** insights into the true nature of courage.

words.definition: To foretell or prophesy an event in the future, often from signs or symptoms
words.origin: Middle English *pronosticaten* "to make a prediction, make a prognosis, portend," borrowed from Medieval Latin *pronōsticātus,* past participle of *prognōsticāre, pronōsticāre* "to predict, forecast, portend," derivative of Late Latin *prognōsticum* prognostic. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A critical or discursive introduction to a book or a subject of study
words.origin: Greek, neuter present passive participle of *prolegein* to say beforehand, from *pro-* before + *legein* to say. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: Anticipating and answering an objection
words.origin: Greek *prolēpsis*, from *prolambanein* to take beforehand, from *pro-* before + *lambanein* to take. First known use: 1578.

words.definition: To increase rapidly in number
words.origin: Back-formation from *proliferation*, from French *prolifération*, from *proliférer* to proliferate, from *prolifère* reproducing freely, from Latin *proles* + *-fer* -ferous. First known use: 1866.

words.definition: Tediously lengthy
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *prolix*, from Latin *prolixus* extended, from *pro-* forward + *liquēre* to be fluid. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To make widely known; to put a law or decree into effect by proclamation
words.origin: Latin *promulgatus*, past participle of *promulgare*, from *pro-* forward + *-mulgare* (probably akin to *mulgēre* to milk, extract). First known use: 1530.
examples: … the huge meeting served primarily as the occasion on which to **promulgate** the official doctrine … — Roger Shattuck
From the beginning our objective has been to develop and **promulgate** new models for the calculus-based introductory course. — John S. Rigden et al.

words.definition: The state of being close to someone or something; proximity or kinship
words.origin: Middle English *propinquite*, from Latin *propinquitat-, propinquitas* kinship, proximity, from *propinquus* near, akin, from *prope* near. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Giving a good chance of success
words.origin: Middle English *propycyous*, from Anglo-French *propicius*, from Latin *propitius*, probably from *pro-* for + *petere* to seek. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A fortress; defence; protection
words.origin: Latin, bulwark, from *propugnare* to fight in defence.

words.definition: To discontinue a session of parliament without dissolving it
words.origin: Middle English *prorogen*, from Anglo-French *proroger*, from Latin *prorogare*, from *pro-* before + *rogare* to ask. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Commonplace; lacking poetic beauty
words.origin: Late Latin *prosaicus*, from Latin *prosa* prose. First known use: 1692.

words.definition: A writer of prose
words.origin: French, from Italian *prosatore*, from Medieval Latin *prosator*, from Latin *prosa*. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: To forbid
words.origin: Latin *proscribere* to publish, proscribe, from *pro-* before + *scribere* to write. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A study of a group in history through the collected lives of its members
words.origin: Borrowed from German *Prosopographie*, borrowed from New Latin *prosopographia* "description of an individual's personal appearance," from Greek *prósōpon* "face, mask, role, person" + New Latin *-graphia* -graphy. First known use: 1896.

words.definition: A figure of speech in which an absent or imaginary person is made to speak
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *prosōpopoeia*, borrowed from Greek *prosōpopoiía*, from *prósōpon* "face, mask, role, person" (from *pros-* "facing, opposite" + *-ōp-* "eye, sight," hence, "the eyes, or sight, opposite own's own") + *-poiia* "making," from *poi-*, base of *poieîn* "to make" + *-ia* -ia. First known use: 1550.

words.definition: Able to change frequently or easily
words.origin: From *proteus* + *-an*. *Proteus*: New Latin, from Latin, Proteus. First known use: 1594.

words.definition: The study of how humans use space and the effect of distance on behaviour
words.origin: *prox*imity + *-emics* (as in *phonemics*). First known use: 1963.

words.definition: Acting with care for the future
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Latin *prudent-, prudens*, contraction of *provident-, providens*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: It seems **prudent** to wait until we know more.
Our forecasts helped inform **prudent** decisions and keep people safe, which is the ultimate goal. — Jason Samenow

words.definition: Covered with a whitish, frosty bloom
words.origin: Latin *pruinosus* covered with hoarfrost, from *pruina* hoarfrost. First known use: circa 1826.

words.definition: The whispering of wind through trees
words.origin: From Greek *psithurisma* whispering.

words.definition: The mechanical, parrot-like repetition of words without thought
words.origin: From Greek *psittakos* parrot.

words.definition: One who loves to bathe outdoors in cold water
words.origin: From Greek *psychros* cold + *louein* to bathe.

words.definition: Playful, especially in a mischievous way, like Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream
words.origin: Puck. First known use: 1831.

words.definition: Modesty; bashfulness, especially an excessive sense of shame
words.origin: Latin *pudentia*, from *pudent-, pudens*, present participle of *pudēre* to be ashamed, make ashamed. First known use: circa 1616.

words.definition: Childishly silly
words.origin: French or Latin; French *puéril*, from Latin *puerilis*, from *puer* boy, child; akin to Sanskrit *putra* son, child and perhaps to Greek *pais* boy, child. First known use: 1527.

words.definition: Relating to childbirth or the period immediately following it
words.origin: Latin *puerpera* woman in childbirth, from *puer* child + *parere* to give birth to. First known use: 1716.

words.definition: Eager or quick to argue or fight
words.origin: Latin *pugnac-, pugnax*, from *pugnare* to fight. First known use: 1642.

words.definition: Having great power or influence; mighty, as a puissant prince or army
Physical beauty
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *pulchritudin-, pulchritudo*, from *pulchr-, pulcher* beautiful. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Physically beautiful
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *pulchritudin-, pulchritudo*, from *pulchr-, pulcher* beautiful. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Cushion-shaped; swollen or bulging, as some leaf bases or architectural friezes
words.origin: From Latin *pulvinatus*, from *pulvinus* cushion.

words.definition: A fine or petty point of conduct or procedure; strict observance of formality
words.origin: Italian & Spanish; Italian *puntiglio* point of honour, scruple, from Spanish *puntillo*, from diminutive of *punto* point, from Latin *punctum*. First known use: 1596.

words.definition: Showing great attention to correct behaviour
words.origin: From *punctilio* + *-ous*. *Punctilio*: Italian & Spanish; Italian *puntiglio* point of honour, scruple, from Spanish *puntillo*, from diminutive of *punto* point, from Latin *punctum*. First known use: 1617.

words.definition: Having impaired or defective vision; lacking awareness or understanding
words.origin: Middle English *pur blind*, from *pur* purely, wholly, from *pur* pure. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To flow with a soft murmur
words.origin: From Middle English *purl*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The area near or surrounding a place; one's usual haunts or bounds
words.origin: Middle English *purlewe* land severed from an English royal forest by perambulation, from Anglo-French *puralé* perambulation, from *puraler* to travel through, measure, from *pur-* thoroughly + *aler* to go. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To steal, typically something of small value; to filch, as in Poe's purloined letter
words.origin: Middle English, to put away, misappropriate, from Anglo-French *purluigner* to prolong, postpone, set aside, from *pur-* forward + *luin, loing* at a distance, from Latin *longe*, from *longus* long. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Short of breath, especially because of being overweight; puckered
words.origin: Middle English *pursi, pursif*, from Anglo-French *porsif*, alteration of **polsif*, from Old French *pousser* to exert pressure, breathe heavily. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Showing a lack of courage
words.origin: Late Latin *pusillanimis*, from Latin *pusillus* very small (diminutive of *pusus* boy) + *animus* spirit; perhaps akin to Latin *puer* child. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Any of various birds of prey
words.origin: From Middle English *puttok*, a kite or buzzard.

words.definition: A pain in the buttocks
words.origin: From Greek *pygē* buttocks + *algos* pain.

words.definition: Of a victory, won at too great a cost to have been worthwhile
words.origin: Latin *pyrrhichius*, from Greek (*pous*) *pyrrhichios*, from *pyrrhichē*, a kind of dance. First known use: 1610.

words.definition: Extreme or absolute skepticism
words.origin: French *pyrrhonisme*, from *Pyrrhon* Pyrrho, 4th century b.c. Greek. philosopher, from Greek *Pyrrhōn*. First known use: 1693.

words.definition: Sitting together in the dark, waiting for something to burst forth
words.origin: Inuit, recorded by the explorer Knud Rasmussen.

words.definition: A person who dishonestly claims knowledge of medicine; a quack
words.origin: Obsolete Dutch (now *kwakzalver*). First known use: 1579.

words.definition: To drink something heartily, especially an alcoholic drink, in deep draughts
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1534.
examples: At Fort William, goods were exchanged, bills were tallied, brandy was **quaffed**, songs were sung. — Will Ferguson
Young Cheltenham ladies and gentlemen in striped shirts and Barbours **quaffed** their drinks and guffawed loudly. — John Ayto

words.definition: An awkward, complex or hazardous situation
An uneasy feeling of doubt
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1530.
examples: Had no **qualms** about asking for their help
It was about an enduring secular world where people did unspeakable things, seemingly without **qualm** and without any grave consequences to themselves. — Jim Holt

words.definition: The first person met on leaving home on New Year's Day
words.origin: Manx, from *quaail* to meet.

words.definition: A state of uncertainty over what to do
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: Sloping downward from a centre in all directions
words.origin: From Late Latin *quaquaversus*, from *quaqua* wherever + *versus* turned.

words.definition: A crossroads; a critical decision point
words.origin: From Old French *quatre voies* four ways.

words.definition: A bold, impudent woman; a young girl
words.origin: Middle English *quene*, from Old English *cwene*; akin to Old English *cwēn* woman, queen. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: To put an end to; to suppress
words.origin: Middle English, to kill, quell, from Old English *cwellan* to kill; akin to Old High German *quellen* to torture, kill, *quāla* torment, Lithuanian *gelti* to hurt. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A place where one feels safe and at home
words.origin: Spanish, from *querer* to love, want.

words.definition: An unknown person
words.origin: Latin, somebody.

words.definition: The inherent nature of a thing; a quibble
words.origin: Middle English *quidite*, from Medieval Latin *quidditat-, quidditas* essence, from Latin *quid* what, neuter of *quis* who. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Complaining in a whining manner
words.origin: Middle English *querelose*, from Latin *querulus*, from *queri* to complain. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Fussing over trifles; wasting time on things that don't matter
words.origin: From the verb *quiddle* "to trifle, dawdle," of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A busybody forever asking what's new; one hungry for the latest gossip
words.origin: Latin *quid nunc* what now? First known use: 1709.

words.definition: In a state of inactivity
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *quiēscent-, quiēscens,* present participle of *quiēscere* "to repose, fall asleep, rest, be quiet," inchoative derivative of a base *quiē-,* going back to Indo-European **kwi̯eh1-* "have a rest". First known use: 1605.

words.definition: Death or something that causes death; release from life; a final settlement
words.origin: Middle English *quietus est*, borrowed from Medieval Latin, "he is quit," formula of discharge from obligation. First known use: 1540.

words.definition: To quibble
words.origin: Perhaps from Latin *quidlibet* whatever you please.

words.definition: An arrangement of five objects with four at the corners and one in the centre
words.origin: Latin *quincunc-, quincunx*, literally, five twelfths, from *quinque* five + *uncia* twelfth part. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: Recurring every five years or lasting for five years, as a quinquennial plan
The most perfect example of its kind
examples: Jerry's your **quintessential** streetwise New Yorker … — Kai Wright
This is the **quintessential** Los Angeles restaurant, casual but never frumpy, lively but not overheated … — Harvey Steiman

words.definition: A set of folded sheets of paper
words.origin: Middle English *quair* four sheets of paper folded once, collection of sheets, from Anglo-French *quaier*, from Vulgar Latin **quaternum* set of four, from Latin *quaterni* four each, set of four. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A traitor who collaborates with an enemy force occupying their country
words.origin: Vidkun *Quisling* †1945 Norwegian politician who collaborated with the Nazis. First known use: 1940.

words.definition: Trivial; worthless
words.origin: From Latin *quisquiliae* rubbish.

words.definition: Exceedingly idealistic; unrealistic
words.origin: Don *Quixote*. First known use: 1718.
examples: What started as an act of rather **quixotic** nostalgia has grown into one of the most sophisticated preservation efforts in the country. — Richard Todd
… the **quixotic** search for cities of gold. — Thomas Y. Canby

words.definition: Absurdly chivalrous, idealistic or impractical ideas or behaviour
words.origin: Don *Quixote*, hero of the novel *Don Quixote de la Mancha* (1605, 1615) by Cervantes. First known use: 1648.

words.definition: A subtle point for debate; a light-hearted musical medley of tunes
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *quodlibetum*, from Latin *quodlibet*, neuter of *quilibet* any whatever, from *qui* who, what + *libet* it pleases, from *libēre* to please. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Relating to a discussion or debate involving subtle or hypothetical points
words.origin: From Latin *quodlibet* what pleases.

words.definition: That once was; former, as a quondam friend or quondam professor
words.origin: Latin, at one time, formerly, from *quom, cum* when; akin to Latin *qui* who. First known use: 1539.

words.definition: Of or occurring every day; ordinary
words.origin: Middle English *cotidian*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *quotidianus, cotidianus*, from *quotidie* every day, from *quot* (as) many as + *dies* day. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A person who speaks with the intention of inflaming the emotions of a crowd
Suffering from rickets, a disease of soft bones; feeble or rickety
words.origin: New Latin *rachitis* rickets, from Greek *rhachitis* spinal disease, from *rhachis*. First known use: 1797.

words.definition: A skilled teller of stories
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from *raconter* to tell, from Old French, from *re-* + *aconter, acompter* to tell, count. First known use: 1819.

words.definition: Red ocher, used for marking animals, colouring, etc. verb tr.: To mark or paint with red ocher
words.origin: Middle English *radel,* probably variant of *rodel* ruddle. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Unconventional and slightly disreputable, especially in an attractive manner
words.origin: From *raff* + *-ish*. *Raff*: Middle English *raf* rubbish. First known use: 1795.

words.definition: A person, typically a child, in ragged, dirty clothes; an urchin
words.origin: Middle English *Ragamuffyn*, name for a ragged, oafish person. First known use: 1586.

words.definition: Having a row of oblique notches
words.origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from *ragged*.

words.definition: Good-humoured teasing
words.origin: French *raillerie*, from Middle French, from *railler* to mock. First known use: 1643.

words.definition: A licentious or immoral person
Boisterously unruly
words.origin: Probably alteration of *rumbustious*. First known use: 1830.

words.definition: Badly made and falling apart
words.origin: Alteration of earlier *ransackled*, from past participle of obsolete *ransackle*, frequentative of *ransack*. First known use: 1830.

words.definition: Bitterness or resentfulness
words.origin: Middle English *rancour*, from Anglo-French *rancur*, from Late Latin *rancor* rancidity, rancour, from Latin *rancēre*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A wild, reckless or rakish person; wild and disorderly in behaviour
words.origin: Perhaps from *rant* + *poll* head.

words.definition: Aggressively greedy
words.origin: Latin *rapāc-, rapāx* "given to seizing or catching things (as prey), carrying away, excessively grasping" (from *rapere* "to seize and carry off" + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1651.

words.definition: A re-establishment of friendly relations
words.origin: French, from *rapprocher* to bring together, from Middle French, from *re-* + *approcher* to approach, from Old French *aprochier*, from Late Latin *appropiare*. First known use: 1809.

words.definition: A mischievous person; a rascal or rogue, often a likeable one
words.origin: Alteration of earlier *rascallion*, irregular from *rascal*. First known use: 1648.
examples: If a little prince with a permissive nanny can get bumptious on occasion, a regal **rapscallion** without any nanny could fast become a royal pain.

The kidnapper is none other than the nefarious Captain Hook (Dustin Hoffman), who still hasn't gotten over the loss of his hand. That **rapscallion** Peter Pan is to blame, and Hook will have his revenge. — Nora Lee

words.definition: A feeling of intense joy
words.origin: Rapt + -ure; (sense 3) probably after the use of *rapere* in the Vulgate (1 Thessalonians 4:17) to translate Greek *harpázein* "to take hold of, seize, snatch up". First known use: 1594.

words.definition: Esoteric; distant from ordinary life
words.origin: Middle English *rarefien, rarifien*, modification of Latin *rarefacere*, from *rarus* rare + *facere* to make. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The bliss of a meditative trance
words.origin: Sanskrit, from *rasa* essence + *āsvāda* tasting.

words.definition: Early; coming before others
words.origin: Middle English, quick, from Old English *hræth*, alteration of *hræd*; akin to Old High German *hrad* quick. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Bring the **rathe** primrose that forsaken dies … — John Milton

words.definition: The process of exact thinking, as in a detective's deductions; a reasoned train of thought
words.origin: From *ratiocinate* + *-ion*. *Ratiocinate*: Latin *ratiocinatus*, past participle of *ratiocinari* to reckon, from *ratio* + *-cinari* (as in *vaticinari* to prophesy). First known use: 1532.

words.definition: Extremely hungry; fiercely eager for satisfaction
words.origin: Middle English *ravynous, raveynous,* from *ravyn, raveyn* "robbery, rapacity" + *-ous* -ous. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Foggy; damp; cold
words.origin: English dialect, from *roke* mist.

words.definition: To rob or plunder
words.origin: Middle English *reven*, from Old English *rēafian*; akin to Old High German *roubōn* to rob, Latin *rumpere* to break. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Unattractive and objectionable; repellent or irritating, as rebarbative prose
words.origin: French *rébarbatif*, from Middle French, from *rebarber* to be repellent, from *re-* + *barbe* beard, from Latin *barba*. First known use: 1892.

words.definition: To express sharp disapproval
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *rebucher, rebouker* to blunt, check, reprimand. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Uncooperative toward authority
words.origin: Late Latin *recalcitrant-, recalcitrans*, present participle of *recalcitrare* to be stubbornly disobedient, from Latin, to kick back, from *re-* + *calcitrare* to kick, from *calc-, calx* heel. First known use: 1797.
examples: Unfortunately, her new student proved particularly **recalcitrant**. — Leonardo Bevilacqua
The touch switches for the heater and the air conditioner can be **recalcitrant** as well. — Rich Ceppos

words.definition: Rare, exotic or obscure, as recherché references; excessively refined or contrived
words.origin: French, sought after.

words.definition: Care or concern. verb tr., intr.: To care or concern
words.origin: Middle English, to take heed, from Old English *reccan*; akin to Old High German *ruohhen* to take heed. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Avoiding the company of others
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *reclus*, literally, shut away, from Late Latin *reclusus*, past participle of *recludere* to shut up, from Latin *re-* + *claudere* to close. First known use: 13th century.
examples: While Stephen King is far from **reclusive**, he doesn't spend much time promoting his horror-filled novels. — Sarah Lyall
… sit under the **reclusive** calm of the acacia tree. — H. E. Bates

words.definition: Little known; abstruse
words.origin: Latin *reconditus*, past participle of *recondere* to conceal, from *re-* + *condere* to store up, from *com-* + *-dere* to put. First known use: 1619.
examples: … mentioned some more or less **recondite** fact about the origin of the holiday … — Floyd Dell

words.definition: Unfaithful to a cause, duty, person, belief
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from present participle of (*se*) *recreire* to give up, yield, from Medieval Latin (*se*) *recredere* to resign oneself (to a judgment), from Latin *re-* + *credere* to believe. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To break out again after a period of dormancy or abatement, as a disease
words.origin: Latin *recrudescere* to become raw again, from *re-* + *crudescere* to become raw, from *crudus* raw. First known use: 1713.

words.definition: Moral uprightness
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Late Latin *rectitudo*, from Latin *rectus* straight, right. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A knockout blow
words.origin: A mock-Latin coinage from *recumbent*.

words.definition: A person who refuses to submit to an authority or to comply with a regulation
words.origin: Latin *recusant-, recusans*, present participle of *recusare* to reject, oppose, from *re-* + *causari* to give a reason, from *causa* cause, reason. First known use: circa 1553.

words.definition: Loving in return
words.origin: From Latin *redamare* to love in return.

words.definition: To advise
words.origin: Middle English *reden* "to counsel, order, decide, guide, govern, realize, grasp the meaning of, interpret, explain, look at and understand (written symbols), say aloud (something written)". First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Come back to life; reborn, used after a noun, as in Caesar redivivus
words.origin: Late Latin, from Latin, reused. First known use: 1675.

words.definition: Strongly reminiscent of; fragrant
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Latin *redolent-, redolens*, present participle of *redolēre* to emit a scent, from *re-, red-* + *olēre* to smell. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Formidable, especially as an opponent
words.origin: Middle English *redoutable*, from Anglo-French, from *reduter* to dread, from *re-* + *duter* to doubt. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Refreshment by food or drink; a light meal, especially in a monastery
words.origin: Middle English *refeccioun*, from Anglo-French *refectiun*, from Latin *refection-, refectio*, from *reficere* to restore, from *re-* + *facere* to make. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Shining brightly
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *refulgentia* "resplendence, brilliance," derivative of *refulgent-, refulgens,* present participle of *refulgere* "to radiate light, shine brightly, shine with reflected light," from *re-* re- + *fulgere* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten". First known use: 1634.

words.definition: Stubborn or unmanageable
words.origin: Alteration of *refractary*, from Latin *refractarius*, irregular from *refragari* to oppose, from *re-* + *-fragari* (as in *suffragari* to support with one's vote). First known use: 1606.
examples: After recovery they were **refractory** to infection

words.definition: Reigning, as a queen regnant; currently having the greatest influence; dominant
words.origin: Latin *regnant-, regnans*, present participle of *regnare* to reign, from *regnum*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To give up willingly
words.origin: Middle English *relinquisshen*, from Anglo-French *relinquiss-*, stem of *relinquir*, from Latin *relinquere* to leave behind, from *re-* + *linquere* to leave. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Slowly **relinquished** his grip on the bar

words.definition: A container for holy relics
words.origin: French *reliquaire*, from Medieval Latin *reliquiarium*, from *reliquia* relic. First known use: 1550.

words.definition: To make a forcefully reproachful protest
words.origin: Medieval Latin *remonstratus*, past participle of *remonstrare* to demonstrate, from Latin *re-* + *monstrare* to show. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: Deep regret for a wrong
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *remors*, from Medieval Latin *remorsus*, from Late Latin, act of biting again, from Latin *remordēre* to bite again, from *re-* + *mordēre* to bite. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Bellowing again
words.origin: From Latin *remugire* to bellow back.

words.definition: Becoming active or popular again, as a renascent movement; reborn
words.origin: Latin *renascent-, renascens*, present participle of *renasci*. First known use: 1662.

words.definition: To formally give up
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *renuncer*, from Latin *renuntiare*, from *re-* + *nuntiare* to report, from *nuntius* messenger. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: [the first syllable is nasal] A person who lives on income from rent, interest
words.origin: French, from Old French, from *rente*. First known use: 1798.

words.definition: To feel or express discontent; to fret or complain about one's lot
words.origin: From *rep* + *-ine*. *Rep*: French *reps*, modification of English *ribs*, plural of *rib*. First known use: 1529.

words.definition: Filled or well supplied
words.origin: Middle English *replet, replete, repleet* "filled (with), filled with food or drink, sated, having an excess of humours," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *replet* "filled," borrowed from Latin *replētus* "full (of), fully endowed (with)," from past participle of *replēre* "to make full again, replenish, restore, fill up, sate," from *re-* re- + *plēre* "to fill". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a book **replete** with … delicious details … — William Safire

words.definition: A temporary relief or cancellation of punishment
words.origin: Probably blend of obsolete *repreve* to reprove (from Middle English) and obsolete *repry* to remand, postpone, from Anglo-French *repri-*, past stem of *reprendre* to take back. First known use: 1596.

words.definition: To restore something to its original condition or purity
words.origin: *re-* + *pristine* + -ate. First known use: 1659.

words.definition: An unprincipled person
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *reprobatus*, past participle of *reprobare*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Scrooge, a curmudgeon and a **reprobate**, is able to … become a beacon of generosity, kindness and goodwill. — Emery Cummins

words.definition: To refuse to accept; to reject
words.origin: Latin *repudiatus*, past participle of *repudiare*, from *repudium* rejection of a prospective spouse, divorce, probably from *re-* + *pudēre* to shame. First known use: 1545.
examples: … unless they **repudiated** the failed policies of the past and took decisive action, the party might fracture or lose its hold on the electorate. — Walter A. McDougall
"The incident was witnessed by … the Marquess Zanipolo, who, in consequence, has already **repudiated** his unhappy bride." — Edith Wharton

words.definition: To return a favour or avenge a wrong
words.origin: *re-* + obsolete *quite* to quit, pay, from Middle English *quiten*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: His love for her was not **requited**.

words.definition: To revoke or cancel
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *rescinder* "to reduce, cut, cancel, break (a contract)," borrowed from Latin *rescindere* "to remove or lay bare by hewing and cutting, cut or tear open, cancel, annul," from *re-* re- + *scindere* "to split, cleave, separate". First known use: 1579.
examples: "… from this day I diet him on bread and water— **rescind** his pocket-money! …" — George Meredith
… the bean counters send letters that seem to suggest they can **rescind** the patient's good health unless he pays up immediately. — Karen Stabiner

words.definition: The restless excitement before a journey
words.origin: Swedish, from *resa* travel + *feber* fever.

words.definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty
words.origin: Latin *resilient-, resiliens*, present participle of *resilire* to jump back, recoil, from *re-* + *salire* to leap. First known use: 1674.

words.definition: The jocular belief that objects resent people
words.origin: Coined by humorist Paul Jennings in 1948, a pun on *existentialism*.

words.definition: Shining brilliantly; splendid in appearance
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *resplendent-, resplendens*, present participle of *resplendēre* to shine back, from *re-* + *splendēre* to shine. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Restless; resisting control
words.origin: Middle English *restyf*, from Anglo-French *restif*, from *rester* to stop, resist, remain. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Not revealing one's thoughts readily
words.origin: Latin *reticent-, reticens*, present participle of *reticēre* to keep silent, from *re-* + *tacēre* to be silent. First known use: 1825.
examples: He is **reticent**, positively closemouthed about private matters … — Tom Gliatto
The room has an aspect of **reticent** dignity. — A. N. Whitehead

words.definition: Urinating backward, as some animals, including cats and camels, do
words.origin: From Latin *retro* backward + *mingere* to urinate.

words.definition: The joy of finding someone again after a long time
words.origin: French, from *retrouver* to find again.

words.definition: A person who has returned, especially supposedly from the dead
words.origin: French, from present participle of *revenir* to return. First known use: 1818.

words.definition: Feeling deep respect
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *reverent-, reverens,* present participle of *reverērī* "to stand in awe of, revere". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A state of pleasant daydreaming
words.origin: French *rêverie*, from Middle French, delirium, from *resver, rever* to wander, be delirious. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Showing stern and inflexible judgment, like the judge of the underworld; strictly just
words.origin: Rhadamanthus + -ine. First known use: 1659.

words.definition: Ecstatically enthusiastic
Referring to sex in an amusingly rude way
words.origin: Middle English *ribaud* person of low status, scoundrel, lecher, from Anglo-French, from Old French *riber* to be debauched, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *rīban* to be in heat, copulate, literally, to rub. First known use: circa 1500.

words.definition: A long, complicated procedure
words.origin: Alteration of obsolete *ragman roll* long list, catalog. First known use: circa 1736.
examples: I went to my insurers and started the usual **rigmarole**. — Cliff Ballinger
The whole **rigmarole** of getting a visa didn't even exist until recent decades. — Mary Sanchez

words.definition: Covered with frost
words.origin: From *rim* + *-y*. *Rim*: Middle English, from Old English *rima*; akin to Old Norse *rimi* strip of land. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Relating to or situated on the banks of a river, as riparian woodland or rights
words.origin: Latin *riparius*. First known use: 1807.

words.definition: Something or someone remarkable in excellence, intensity, strength
Such as to provoke laughter; ludicrous, as a risible excuse
words.origin: Late Latin *risibilis*, from Latin *risus*, past participle of *ridēre* to laugh. First known use: 1557.

words.definition: Extravagantly ornate
words.origin: French, irregular from *rocaille* rocaille. First known use: 1830.

words.definition: A vain boaster
words.origin: From Rodomonte, a boastful king in Ariosto's *Orlando Furioso*.

words.definition: To enjoy oneself or celebrate in a noisy or boisterous way, as revellers do
words.origin: Middle French *rustre* lout, alteration of *ruste*, from *ruste*, adjective, rude, rough, from Latin *rusticus* rural. First known use: 1549.

words.definition: A swaggering buffoon or reveler
words.origin: From the 16th-century comedy *Ralph Roister Doister*.

words.definition: A false story or slander, especially one spread for political purposes
words.origin: From an attack on James K. Polk in 1844 purporting to quote from an invented book by a Baron von *Roorback*. First known use: 1855.

words.definition: Like a rose, especially in colour: pink, red
words.origin: Middle English *roseat,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *roseātus,* from, Latin *roseus* "made of roses, rose-coloured, reddish" (from *rosa* rose + *-eus* -eous) + *-ātus* -ate. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A cheap or inferior alcoholic drink
A person of low rank; a commoner
words.origin: From Middle French *roturier*. First known use: 1586.

words.definition: Reddening; blushing, as a rubescent cheek or sky at dawn
words.origin: From Latin *rubescere* to grow red.

words.definition: Ruddy; having a healthy red colour
words.origin: Middle English *rubicunde*, from Latin *rubicundus*, from *rubēre* to be red; akin to Latin *rubeus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A rude, boorish person
words.origin: From *rude* + *-by*, as in a surname; used by Shakespeare.

words.definition: Regret; a bitter herb
words.origin: Middle English *rewen, rowen, ruwen, ruen* "to affect with sorrow, distress, regret, be sorry, have pity for," going back to Old English *hrēowan* (class 2 strong verb) "to distress, grieve, affect with pity, cause to regret, make repent" and *hrēowian* (weak verb) "to grieve, lament," going back to Germanic **hrewwan-* (whence also Old Frisian *riōwa, riouwa* "to make regret," Old Saxon *hreuwan,* Old High German *hriuwan, riuwan*) and **hrewwōjan-* (whence Old Saxon *hreuwon* "to repent of," Old High German *hriuwōn, riuwōn*), going back to pre-Germanic **kreu̯(H)-e-,* of uncertain origin. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: Reddish
words.origin: Latin *rufescent-, rufescens*, present participle of *rufescere* to become reddish, from *rufus* red. First known use: 1817.

words.definition: A violent, lawless person
words.origin: Middle French *rufian*. First known use: circa 1525.

words.definition: Wrinkled; corrugated; covered in ridges, as rugose leaves or coral
words.origin: Latin *rugosus*, from *ruga*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To think deeply about something
words.origin: Latin *ruminatus*, past participle of *ruminari* to chew the cud, muse upon, from *rumin-, rumen* rumen; perhaps akin to Sanskrit *romantha* act of chewing the cud. First known use: 1533.
examples: … **ruminating** the contents of that last batch of letters … — Aldous Huxley

words.definition: An uproar or commotion
words.origin: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from *rumpus*.

words.definition: A utensil that is a combination of a fork and spoon. Also known as a spork
words.origin: Coined by Edward Lear.

words.definition: Relating to, composed of or carved on rocks
words.origin: From Latin *rupes* rock.

words.definition: An action intended to deceive
words.origin: French, from Old French, roundabout path taken by fleeing game, trickery, from *reuser*. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: Reddish-brown
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from *russet*, adjective, russet, from *rus, rous* red, from Latin *russus*; akin to Latin *ruber* red. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: To go to, live in or spend time in the country; to suspend from university
An icicle-like formation of rust, as on an underwater shipwreck
words.origin: From *rust* + *icicle*; coined by Robert Ballard.

words.definition: Compassion
words.origin: Middle English *rewþe, rowthe, ruthe* "pity, compassion, sorrow, cause for sorrow," from *rewen, ruwen* "to affect with sorrow, be sorrowful, rue" + *-th* -th, after an Old Norse predecessor of Old Icelandic *hryggð* "affliction, sorrow". First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: Glowing, shining or glittering with a red or golden light
words.origin: Middle English *rutilaunt*, from Latin *rutilant-, rutilans*, past participle of *rutilare* to glow reddish, from *rutilus* ruddy; probably akin to Latin *ruber* red. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A warmed-over dish; a rehash of old ideas
words.origin: French, reheated.

words.definition: The worship of stars
words.origin: From Hebrew *ṣābāʼ* host (of heaven).

words.definition: Excessively sweet or sentimental, as a saccharine film; relating to sugar
words.origin: Latin *saccharum*. First known use: circa 1674.

words.definition: A supreme chief of some North American Indigenous peoples; a political leader
words.origin: Narragansett *sâchim*. First known use: 1622.

words.definition: Too important to be interfered with
words.origin: Latin *sacrosanctus*, probably from *sacro sanctus* hallowed by a sacred rite. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: Having keen judgment; wise
words.origin: Latin *sagac-, sagax*, from *sagire* to perceive keenly; akin to Latin *sagus* prophetic. First known use: 1607.
