examples: The judge was fair and **sagacious**. — Keith C. Burris
… the standard post-election postmortem, in which the winner is praised for his **sagacious** grasp of the hopes and anxieties of the public … — Hendrik Hertzberg

words.definition: Keen wisdom and judgment
Having undue interest in sexual matters
words.origin: Latin *salac-, salax*, from *salire* to move spasmodically, leap. First known use: circa 1645.
examples: … have fiercely denounced the book's sketches of melodramatic lovers and **salacious** partygoers … — Casey Greenfield

words.definition: Most noticeable or important
words.origin: Latin *salient-, saliens*, present participle of *salire* to leap. First known use: 1646.
examples: One of the **salient** features of these Celtic structures … is the extreme narrowness of the buildings in proportion to their length. — Farley Mowat
For commuters in suburban communities … safety on the city's public transportation network is a uniquely **salient** topic. — Tim Balk

words.definition: A dish of chopped meat, eggs and vegetables; a general mixture or miscellany
words.origin: French *salmigondis*. First known use: circa 1674.

words.definition: The action of leaping or dancing; an abrupt evolutionary change
words.origin: Latin *saltation-, saltatio*, from *saltare* to leap, dance, frequentative of *salire* to leap. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: A mountebank or charlatan who performs on a bench to sell remedies
words.origin: Italian, from *saltare* to leap + *in* on + *banco* bench.

words.definition: Health-giving; pleasant
words.origin: Latin *salubris*; akin to *salvus* safe, healthy. First known use: 1547.

words.definition: Healthfulness, as of air or climate
words.origin: Latin *salubris*; akin to *salvus* safe, healthy. First known use: 1547.

words.definition: Having the power to save or redeem
words.origin: Late Latin *salvificus*, from Latin *salvus* safe + *-ficus* -fic. First known use: 1591.
examples: … the **salvific** life and death of Christ … — E. A. Walsh

words.definition: Making a show of moral superiority
words.origin: From *sanctimony* + *-ous*. *Sanctimony*: Middle French *sanctimonie*, from Latin *sanctimonia*, from *sanctus*. First known use: 1604.
examples: The king's **sanctimonious** rebuke — G. B. Shaw

words.definition: A very happy person
words.origin: From the phrase "as happy as a sandboy", a boy who sold sand.

words.definition: Composure or coolness, sometimes excessive, in danger or under trying circumstances
words.origin: French *sang-froid*, literally, cold blood. First known use: 1750.

words.definition: Optimistic, especially in a bad situation
words.origin: Middle English *sanguin*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *sanguineus*, from *sanguin-, sanguis*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Some of us hear the term AI and picture a dystopian future. … Others are more **sanguine** about our ability to control and harness technology to achieve more and greater things. — Georgene Huang
The trustees chose to take a **sanguine** approach to the future. — Michael Hiltzik

words.definition: Going back to retrieve what was lost from the past
words.origin: Twi (Akan), go back and get it.

words.definition: Having a pleasant taste or flavour
words.origin: Latin *sapidus* tasty, from *sapere* to taste. First known use: 1623.

words.definition: Deep wisdom
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *sapientia*, from *sapient-, sapiens*, present participle. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Wise, or attempting to appear wise, often used ironically
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Latin *sapient-, sapiens*, from present participle of *sapere* to taste, be wise. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A slow, stately Spanish dance in triple time; music for it, as in Bach's suites
words.origin: French *sarabande*, from Spanish *zarabanda*. First known use: 1616.

words.definition: Grimly mocking or cynical
words.origin: Re-formation, with the suffix -ic, of earlier *sardonian,* from Greek *sardónios,* alteration (after *Sardónios* "Sardinian") of earlier *sardánios* "(of laughter or smiling) bitter, scornful" (of obscure origin) + -an. First known use: 1638.
examples: A **sardonic** little jab that made her visitor quiet and subdued for the rest of the night
"The Great War," used interchangeably with "the First World War" (so named in 1918 by a **sardonic** English journalist, who knew it would not be the last such conflict) … — Benjamin Schwarz

words.definition: Relating to tailoring, clothes or style of dress, as sartorial elegance
words.origin: Medieval Latin *sartor*. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: To satisfy fully
words.origin: Latin *satiatus*, past participle of *satiare*, from *satis* enough. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To satisfy the minimum requirements in a given situation
words.origin: A blend of *satisfy* and *suffice*; popularized by Herbert Simon.

words.definition: A provincial governor in ancient Persia; a subordinate or local ruler
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *satrapes*, from Greek *satrapēs*, from Old Persian *khshathrapāvan*, literally, protector of the dominion. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Thoroughly soaked; holding as much as it can absorb
words.origin: Latin *saturatus*, past participle of *saturare*, from *satur* well-fed. First known use: 1538.
examples: If more material is added to a **saturated** solution, no further dissolving will take place. The extra material will simply settle to the bottom of the solution. — Merill C. Fellger
The early spring sky is a deep **saturated** blue next to the muddy brown of the dry, scrubby hills … — Sonia Shaw

words.definition: Marked by unrestrained revelry, overindulgence, licentiousness
words.origin: Latin, from neuter plural of *saturnalis* of Saturn, from *Saturnus*. First known use: 1538.

words.definition: Slow and gloomy; sullen
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Medieval Latin *sāturnīnus* (Latin *Sāturnīnus,* a Roman cognomen), from Latin *Sāturnus* saturn + *-īnus* -ine. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A deep longing for something absent or lost
words.origin: Portuguese, from Latin *solitas* solitude.

words.definition: A fiery speaker, especially a preacher
words.origin: Italian, bench-warmer.

words.definition: Related to climbing
words.origin: From Latin *scandere* to climb.

words.definition: A mischievous or wayward person, especially a young one; a rascal
words.origin: Scape. First known use: 1763.

words.definition: A boastful but cowardly person; a stock character in Italian comedy
words.origin: French *Scaramouche*, from Italian *Scaramuccia*, from *scaramuccia* skirmish. First known use: 1677.

words.definition: To make shallow incisions in the skin; to criticize severely and hurtfully
words.origin: Middle English *scarifien*, from Middle French *scarefier*, from Late Latin *scarificare*, alteration of Latin *scarifare*, from Greek *skariphasthai* to scratch an outline, sketch. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One who spends wastefully
Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune, from German harm and joy
words.origin: German, from *Schaden* damage + *Freude* joy. First known use: 1868.
examples: His arrest … brought out ugly **schadenfreude** on social media from those who view the incident in which no one was hurt as some sort of … karmic retribution. — Lisa Respers France

words.definition: Excessive sentimentality, especially in music or film; melted chicken fat
words.origin: Yiddish *shmalts*, literally, rendered fat. First known use: 1850.
examples: “ … It's not showbiz **schmaltz**; it's a story about the battle to overcome hardship. … ” — Elton John
A lot of people make fun of this show, pegging it as pure **schmaltz**.

words.definition: Fighting with shadows or imaginary enemies
words.origin: From Greek *skiamachia*, from *skia* shadow + *machē* fight.

words.definition: A tiny trace
words.origin: From Latin *scintilla*. First known use: 1661.

words.definition: To emit flashes of light; to sparkle; to be brilliant and witty
words.origin: Latin *scintillatus*, past participle of *scintillare* to sparkle, from *scintilla* spark. First known use: circa 1623.
examples: Imagine it's a cool summer night, the stars **scintillate** brilliantly in the sky overhead and the campfire blazes away. — Thomas E. Young
The Jay Tarses sitcom, which **scintillates** with whacked-out wit, was dropped by NBC in 1988 because it was deemed too quirky. — Lawrence Eisenberg

words.definition: One who never works hard
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; recorded from the 16th century.

words.definition: A person who flouts the law, especially by failing to comply with a minor law
Carved or engraved bone or ivory, typically made by sailors on long voyages
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1821.

words.definition: A room for copying manuscripts
words.origin: Medieval Latin, from Latin *scribere*. First known use: 1695.

words.definition: Having a consuming urge to write
words.origin: From Latin *scripturire* to long to write.

words.definition: A clerk, scribe or notary; a person who writes out documents
words.origin: Middle English *scriveiner*, alteration of *scrivein*, from Anglo-French *escrivein*, from Vulgar Latin **scriban-, scriba*, alteration of Latin *scriba* scribe. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Morally degenerate or corrupt; affected by scrofula, a form of tuberculosis
examples: … **scrofulous** characters … so quick to smear … — John Garrity

words.definition: To make a scraping or grating sound
words.origin: Imitative.

words.definition: To squeeze, press or crowd
words.origin: Alteration of English dialect *scruze* to squeeze. First known use: 1755.

words.definition: Diligent and thorough; very honest
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *scrupulosus*, from *scrupulus*. First known use: 1542.

words.definition: A servant assigned the most menial kitchen tasks, such as scrubbing pots
words.origin: Middle English *sculioun*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To disgust or sicken. verb intr.: To feel disgust or to flinch
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *skunniren*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Fed up; disgusted
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *skunniren*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Making scandalous claims to damage a reputation
examples: … **scurrilous** imposters who used a religious exterior to rob poor people … — Edwin Benson

words.definition: Occurring every other day
words.origin: From Latin *secundus* second.

words.definition: Showing dedication and diligence
words.origin: Latin *sedulus*, from *sedulo* sincerely, diligently, from *sed-, se* without + *dolus* guile. First known use: 1540.

words.definition: An intense longing for something indefinable
words.origin: German, from *sehnen* to yearn + *Sucht* addiction.

words.definition: Strange; marvellous; unfamiliar, a word from Old English seldom known
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *seldcūth*, from *seldan* seldom + *cūth* known. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A lover of the moon
words.origin: From Greek *selēnē* moon + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: Reproducing only once in a lifetime
words.origin: Latin *semel* "a single time, once" (from the same base as *simul* "together, at the same time," *similis* "having characteristics in common, like") + -parous. First known use: 1954.

words.definition: Eternal and unchanging
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *sempiternalis*, from Latin *sempiternus*, from *semper* ever, always, from *sem-* one, same (akin to Old Norse *samr* same) + *per* through. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Old age
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *senectitūdin-, senectitūdō,* re-formation, with Latin *-tūdin-, -tūdō* -tude, of Latin *senectūt-, senectūs* "old age," from *senec-,* variant stem of *sen-, senex* "old, aged" + *-tūt-, -tūs,* suffix of abstract nouns. First known use: 1796.

words.definition: The condition or process of deterioration with age, in people, cells or plants
words.origin: Senesc(ent) + -ence. First known use: 1695.
examples: The life of a mosquito—and this may be the only good news about the insect—is brutal and short. Roughly one in five die every day, and not from **senescence**. — Gary Taubes
Until we're all brain patterns on computers, there are still forces that do not bend to our wants, including **senescence** and death. — John Hodgman

words.definition: A week; seven nights, just as a fortnight is fourteen, as in this day sennight
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *seofon nihta* seven nights. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Given to pompous moralizing
words.origin: Middle English, full of meaning, from Latin *sententiosus*, from *sententia* sentence, maxim. First known use: 1509.

words.definition: Of the north; northern, from the seven stars of the Great Bear
words.origin: From *septentrion* + *-al*. *Septentrion*: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *septentriones*, plural, the seven stars of Ursa Major or Ursa Minor, from *septem* seven + *triones* plowing oxen. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Relating to a tomb or interment; gloomy and dismal, as a sepulchral voice
Lacking independence or originality of thought; following without question
words.origin: Latin *sequac-, sequax* inclined to follow, from *sequi*. First known use: 1643.

words.definition: Angelically serene
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *seraphicus,* from Late Latin *seraph*im seraphim + *-icus* -ic. First known use: 1536.
examples: … the immortal / Choir of Heaven's **seraphic** host. — Luther C. Riggs
“You believe it all, I suppose?” she asked with **seraphic** gravity. — Edith Wharton

words.definition: Finding good things by chance
words.origin: *Serendip,* variant of *Sarandīb,* Persian and Arabic name for Sri Lanka + -ity; from its possession by the heroes of the Persian fairy tale *The Three Princes of Serendip*. First known use: 1754.
examples: … materials researchers, who now rely mostly on rules of thumb, trial-and-error and **serendipity** for developing new materials. — I. Amato
… the pleasure of wandering while lost and discovering by **serendipity** interesting new places. — Katie Davis and Howard Gardner

words.definition: Calm, peaceful and untroubled
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *serenus* clear, cloudless, untroubled. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The moon, **serene** in glory … — Alexander Pope

words.definition: Taking one subject after another in regular order; point by point
words.origin: Medieval Latin, from Latin *series*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Excessively willing to serve or please
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *servil,* borrowed from Latin *servīlis* "of a slave, slavish, abject," from *servus* "slave" + *-īlis* "pertaining to or characteristic of (such persons)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Characterized by long words
words.origin: Latin *sesquipedalis*, literally, a foot and a half long, from *sesqui-* + *ped-, pes* foot. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: The practice of using big words
words.origin: From Latin *sesquipedalis* a foot and a half long.

words.definition: Chaotic, disorganized or mismanaged, as a shambolic meeting or campaign
words.origin: Probably from *shambles*. First known use: 1970.

words.definition: Secret or dishonest activity or manoeuvring; silly or high-spirited behaviour
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1854.
examples: … takes attention away from the **shenanigans** of corporate executives … — Anthony Lewis

words.definition: A custom or phrase that distinguishes a group
words.origin: Hebrew *shibbōleth* stream; from the use of this word in Judges 12 as a test to distinguish Gileadites from Ephraimites. First known use: 1638.
examples: … the old **shibboleths** come rolling off their lips … — Joseph Epstein
… today this book publishing **shibboleth** is a myth. — L. A. Wood

words.definition: A thick stick of blackthorn or oak used in Ireland as a weapon
words.origin: *Shillelagh*, town in Ireland. First known use: 1772.

words.definition: To hesitate and be indecisive
words.origin: Irregular reduplication of *shall I*. First known use: 1700.

words.definition: Forest bathing
words.origin: Japanese, forest bath.

words.definition: A chronically unlucky person
words.origin: Yiddish, from German *schlimm* bad + Hebrew *mazzāl* luck.

words.definition: Wobbly; unsteady
words.origin: Scots, from *shoogle* to shake.

words.definition: To hear the confession of, assign penance to and absolve, as a priest does
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *scrīfan* to shrive, prescribe (akin to Old High German *scrīban* to write), from Latin *scribere* to write. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A side road taken to avoid a toll road. verb intr.: To travel on a side road
Spraying saliva when speaking
words.origin: From Greek *sialon* saliva + Latin *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: Making a hissing sound
words.origin: Latin *sibilant-, sibilans*, present participle of *sibilare* to hiss, whistle, of imitative origin. First known use: 1669.

words.definition: Prophetic and mysterious; cryptically foreboding
words.origin: Middle English *sibile, sybylle*, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *sibile*, from Latin *sibylla*, from Greek. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Of or with respect to the distant stars, as sidereal time measured by them
words.origin: Latin *sidereus*, from *sider-, sidus* star, constellation. First known use: 1612.

words.definition: Extremely funny; causing uproarious laughter
words.origin: From *side* + *splitting*, as if laughter could split one's sides.

words.definition: A fairy
words.origin: Irish *sídhe* fairy mounds.

words.definition: Soft, smooth and lustrous, like silk
words.origin: Old English *seolcen*, from *seolc* silk + *-en*.
examples: … the same **silken** surroundings encountered at the restaurant's far more expensive evening meal. — Elaine Tait

words.definition: The trail of scent left in the air by someone's perfume; a wake
words.origin: French, the wake of a ship, from *sillon* furrow.

words.definition: Living or growing in woods
words.origin: From Latin *silva* wood + *colere* to inhabit.

words.definition: A woman who lives in the woods
words.origin: From Latin *silva* wood + *cultrix* inhabitant.

words.definition: The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges, such as pardons
words.origin: Middle English *symonie*, from Anglo-French *simonie*, from Late Latin *simonia*, from *Simon* Magus, Samaritan sorcerer in Acts 8: 9–24. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: To smile in an affectedly coy or ingratiating manner; a silly, simpering smile
words.origin: Akin to Middle Dutch *zimperlijc* elegant, Danish dialect *simper* affected, coy. First known use: 1562.
examples: Through force of will, she escaped the narrowness of Victorian daughterhood, the polite world of needlework and **simpering** over teacups that had always bored her. — Matthew Dennison

words.definition: An image or imitation, often unsatisfactory
words.origin: Middle English, "image, representation," borrowed from Latin *simulācrum* "likeness, visual representation, image, statue, outward appearance of a person or thing (as in the imagination or a dream), phantom, sham appearance," from *simulāre* "to pretend, produce a fraudulent imitation of, imitate" + *-crum,* suffix of instruments (dissimilated from **-clum,* going back to **-tlom*). First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a reasonable **simulacrum** of reality … — Martin Mayer

words.definition: A paid position requiring little work
words.origin: Medieval Latin *sine cura* without cure (of souls). First known use: 1662.

words.definition: A hiccup
words.origin: Latin, a sob, hiccup.

words.definition: Left-handedness
words.origin: From Latin *sinister* left.

words.definition: Having many curves and turns
words.origin: Latin *sinuosus*, from *sinus*. First known use: 1578.

words.definition: A fine, misty drizzle
words.origin: Spanish, from Basque *zirimiri*.

words.definition: Grit and resilience in the face of adversity
words.origin: Finnish, from *sisus* innards.

words.definition: Endless and futile, like Sisyphus's task
A secluded nook for sitting out
words.origin: Scots, from *sit oot* sit out.

words.definition: The ability to sit through or endure long tasks
words.origin: German, sitting flesh.

words.definition: To scatter out, spill or disperse. verb tr.: To dismiss or to disband an assembly, group, etc
words.origin: Scots, from Old Norse *skilja* to separate.

words.definition: To depart quickly or hurriedly; to run away, as soldiers fleeing in panic
words.origin: Perhaps extended form of British dialect (Nottinghamshire) *scaddle* "to run off in a fright," derivative of dialectal *scaddle,* adjective, "wild, timid, skittish," going back to Middle English *scathel, skadylle* "harmful, fierce, wild," borrowed from Old Norse **skǫþull* "harmful," going back to Germanic **skaþulo-* (whence also Old High German *scadel* "bad, wicked," Gothic *skaþuls** "harmful, hurtful"), from **skaþjan-* "to harm" + *-ul-,* deverbal adjective suffix. First known use: 1859.
examples: I've got to **skedaddle** or I'll be late.
Whenever there was work to be done, he **skedaddled**.

words.definition: A splinter
words.origin: Scots, from Old English *scylf* ledge.

words.definition: Askew; mixed-up; confused
words.origin: American dialect, from *skew*.

words.definition: Closeness built through touch
words.origin: Korean and Japanese English, from *skin* + *-ship*.

words.definition: A shrill sound, as of bagpipes
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *skrillen, skirlen* to scream, shriek, of Scandinavian origin; akin to Norwegian dialect *skræla* to cry aloud; akin to Old English *scrallettan* to resound loudly. First known use: circa 1665.

words.definition: A coward
words.origin: Of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Underhanded or unscrupulous behaviour; trickery, as in political skulduggery
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1845.

words.definition: A small, loosely run unit formed to foster innovation
words.origin: From the Skonk Works in the *Li'l Abner* comic strip.

words.definition: Dirty and untidy; slovenly in appearance or housekeeping
examples: … fifty unpainted and **slatternly** dwellings all fronting onto muddy roads. — David Guterson
I am … **slatternly**; I seldom put, and never keep things in order; I am careless … — Charlotte Brontë

words.definition: A slovenly, worthless person; a dirty wretch, a word of 17th-century abuse
words.origin: From *slubber* to slobber + a fanciful ending.

words.definition: One who lazily lies in bed late
words.origin: From *slug* to be lazy + *abed* in bed. First known use: late 16th century.

words.definition: Slow-moving or inactive; lacking energy
words.origin: From *slug* + *-ish*. *Slug*: Middle English *slugge*, of Scandinavian origin; akin to Norwegian dialect *slugga* to walk sluggishly. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An insignificant contemptible person
words.origin: Scots, a small, contemptible person.

words.definition: To talk ignorantly or superficially; to dabble, giving us smattering
words.origin: Middle English *smateren* to make dirty, talk idly. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One with only superficial knowledge
words.origin: Middle English *smateren* to make dirty, talk idly. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Spirit, pluck and good sense
words.origin: Scots, from Old English *smedma* fine flour.

words.definition: A habitual fault-finder; a grumbler, Sterne's name for a carping traveller
words.origin: Laurence Sterne's nickname for the grumbling travel writer Tobias Smollett.

words.definition: A fine drizzle
words.origin: Scots, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A special, hidden place of solace
words.origin: Swedish, wild strawberry patch.

words.definition: A large knife; a fight with knives
words.origin: Obsolete *snick or snee* to engage in cut-and-thrust fighting, alteration of earlier *steake or snye*, from Dutch *steken of snijden* to thrust or cut. First known use: circa 1775.

words.definition: A shrewd, unprincipled person, especially a politician
words.origin: Probably alteration of *snallygaster* a mythical creature that preys on poultry and children. First known use: 1845.
examples: Truman lamented that Dwight Eisenhower had given in to congressional "**snollygosters**"—unprincipled politicians. — Orme Wilson

words.definition: A good-looking person
words.origin: From *snout* + *fair*.

words.definition: A white glare on clouds above snowfields
words.origin: From *snow* + *blink* a gleam.

words.definition: Lingering at the table in conversation after a meal
words.origin: Spanish, over the table.

words.definition: A nickname
words.origin: From French *sobriquet*. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: A decisive blow; something outstanding
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1830.

words.definition: A confraternity or association, especially a Roman Catholic religious guild
words.origin: Latin *sodalitat-, sodalitas* comradeship, club, from *sodalis* comrade. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: Comfort or consolation in a time of distress
words.origin: Middle English *solas*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *solacium*, from *solari* to console.

words.definition: A grammatical mistake; a breach of etiquette
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *soloecismus,* borrowed from Greek *soloikismós,* from *solikízein* "to use language incorrectly" (from *sóloikos* "non-Greek, barbarian" —of uncertain origin— + *-izein* -ize) + *-ismos* -ism; associated by popular etymology with *Sóloi,* Athenian settlement in Cilicia whose inhabitants were alleged to have spoken poor Greek. First known use: circa 1555.

words.definition: Formal and dignified; serious
words.origin: Middle English *solempne*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *sollemnis* regularly appointed, solemn. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **solemn** reminder of the price of freedom
The mood in the room grew **solemn**.

words.definition: Showing interest or concern
words.origin: Latin *sollicitus*. First known use: 1563.

words.definition: The view that the self is all that can be known to exist; extreme self-absorption
words.origin: Latin *solus* alone + *ipse* self. First known use: 1836.

words.definition: Wandering alone
words.origin: From Latin *solus* alone + *vagari* to wander.

words.definition: Dark or dull; gravely serious
words.origin: French *sombre*. First known use: 1760.

words.definition: Somewhat; to some degree
To some place; somewhere
A sleepwalker; a person who walks about while still asleep
Sleepy; drowsy
words.origin: Middle English *sompnolent*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *somnolentus*, from *somnus* sleep; akin to Old English *swefn* sleep, Greek *hypnos*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Deep and full in sound
words.origin: Latin *sonorus*; akin to Latin *sonus* sound. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Buxom, comely and good-natured
words.origin: Scots *sons* health, from Scottish Gaelic *sonas* luck, happiness. First known use: 1720.

words.definition: Truth

words.definition: Clever but false argument meant to deceive
words.origin: From *sophist* + *-ry*. *Sophist*: Latin *sophista*, from Greek *sophistēs*, literally, expert, wise man, from *sophizesthai* to become wise, deceive, from *sophos* clever, wise. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Pretentious or juvenile; conceited and overconfident of knowledge but immature
Soundness of mind, as expressed in moderation, self-control and prudence
words.origin: Greek, soundness of mind, moderation.

words.definition: Tending to induce sleep
words.origin: Probably from French *soporifique*, from Latin *sopor* deep sleep; akin to Latin *somnus* sleep. First known use: 1665.

words.definition: The practice of foretelling the future from a card or lot drawn at random
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *sortilegium*, from Latin *sortilegus* foretelling, from *sort-, sors* lot + *-i-* + *legere* to gather. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To make a soft murmuring sound, as wind
words.origin: Middle English *swoughen*, from Old English *swōgan*; akin to Goth ga*swogjan* to groan, Lithuanian *svagėti* to sound. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Of a reddish-brown colour
words.origin: From Latin *spadix* date-brown.

words.definition: To throw violently into the air
words.origin: Northern English dialect, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Old and decrepit; out of condition; affected by a disease of horses' hocks
words.origin: From *spavin* + *-ed*. *Spavin*: Middle English *spavayne*, from Middle French *espavin*, alteration of Old French *esparvains*, probably of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *sparo* sparrow (likened to a lump). First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Superficially plausible, but actually wrong; misleadingly attractive
words.origin: Middle English, visually pleasing, from Latin *speciosus* beautiful, plausible, from *species*. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: A person who explores caves, especially as a hobby; a caver
words.origin: Latin *spēlunca* "cave" (borrowed from Greek *spēlynk-,* stem of *spêlynx* "cave") + -er. First known use: 1942.

words.definition: A trivia-monger; a gatherer of gossip
words.origin: From Greek *spermologos* seed-picker, babbler.

words.definition: Spray blown from the crests of waves by the wind; driving snow
words.origin: Alteration of Scots *speendrift*, from *speen* to drive before a strong wind + English *drift*. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: A small thicket

words.definition: An eel split, cut into pieces and cooked. verb tr.: To treat severely
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; compare *spatchcock*.

words.definition: Extraordinarily impressive; magnificent

words.definition: Bad-tempered or spiteful, once thought caused by the spleen; peevish
words.origin: Late Latin *spleneticus*, from Latin *splen* spleen. First known use: 1697.

words.definition: Fussy and officious
words.origin: 19th-century slang of uncertain origin.

words.definition: A verbal error in which initial sounds are switched, as tease my ears for ease my tears
words.origin: William A. *Spooner* †1930 English clergyman & educator. First known use: 1892.

words.definition: Occurring at irregular intervals
words.origin: Medieval Latin *sporadicus*, from Greek *sporadikos*, from *sporadēn* here and there, from *sporad-, sporas* scattered; akin to Greek *speirein* to sow. First known use: 1652.

words.definition: An intuitive feel for language
words.origin: German, feeling for language.

words.definition: To spread one's legs wide apart, as a newborn foal; to sprawl
words.origin: Perhaps blend of *straddle* and *sprawl*. First known use: 1632.

words.definition: Effortless grace that hides great effort
To work feebly
words.origin: From *spud* + *-le*.

words.definition: False, though seeming genuine
words.origin: Late Latin & Latin; Late Latin *spurius* false, from Latin, of illegitimate birth, from *spurius*, noun, bastard. First known use: circa 1567.
examples: The **spurious** eminence of the pop celebrity

words.definition: Extremely dirty and unpleasant; morally sordid
words.origin: Latin *squalidus* rough, dirty, from *squalēre* to be covered with scales or dirt, from *squalus* dirty; perhaps akin to Latin *squama* scale. First known use: 1596.

words.definition: The practice of spending money recklessly
words.origin: From *squander* + *mania*.

words.definition: A short piece of satirical writing; a small firework that hisses before exploding
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1525.

words.definition: Tall, graceful and dignified, like a statue
words.origin: From *statue* + *-esque*.

words.definition: Loyal and committed
words.origin: Middle English *staunche, stanch* "watertight, solidly made, in good repair," borrowed from Anglo-French *estanc,* feminine *estaunche* "stanched (of blood), watertight," derivative of *estancher* "to stop (blood from flowing), (of a wound) stop bleeding, (of water) be stanched, dry up". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Very loud and powerful, of a voice
words.origin: From *stentor* + *-ian*. *Stentor*: Latin, from Greek *Stentōr* Stentor, a Greek herald in the Trojan War noted for his loud voice. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: Noisy and laboured, of breathing, as of a heavy sleeper; snoring
words.origin: From *stertor* + *-ous*. *Stertor*: New Latin, from Latin *stertere* to snore; akin to *sternuere* to sneeze. First known use: 1802.

words.definition: A person employed at a dock to load and unload ships; a longshoreman
words.origin: Spanish *estibador*, from *estibar* to pack. First known use: 1788.

words.definition: Enduring pain without complaint
Enduring hardship without complaint
Calm and showing little emotion
words.origin: Latin *stolidus* dull, stupid. First known use: circa 1600.

words.origin: Greek, natural affection.

words.definition: Straw-coloured
words.origin: From Latin *stramineus*, from *stramen* straw.

words.definition: A plan to outwit an opponent
words.origin: Italian *stratagemma*, from Latin *strategema*, from Greek *stratēgēma*, from *stratēgein* to be a general, maneuver, from *stratēgos* general, from *stratos* camp, army (akin to Latin *stratus*, past participle, spread out) + *agein* to lead. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To wander about aimlessly; to stroll, a word from Scots and Irish speech
words.origin: Probably by shortening & alteration from *extravagate*. First known use: 1773.

words.definition: To wander aimlessly
words.origin: Probably by shortening & alteration from *extravagate*. First known use: 1773.

words.definition: Loud and harsh; forceful
words.origin: Latin *strident-, stridens*, present participle of *stridere, stridēre* to make a harsh noise. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: Shrill; making a harsh grating sound
words.origin: From Latin *stridulus* creaking.

words.definition: To make a shrill, jarring sound by rubbing body parts together, as crickets do
words.origin: Back-formation from *stridulation*, from French, high-pitched sound, from Latin *stridulus* shrill. First known use: 1838.

words.definition: The joy of being able to say "to hell with it"
words.origin: A modern coinage of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Someone very old and decrepit
words.origin: From the immortal but decrepit Struldbruggs in *Gulliver's Travels*.

words.definition: A woman of loose morals; a prostitute, a word of old-fashioned abuse
words.origin: From Middle English *strumpet*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: EMILIA. Fie, fie upon thee, **strumpet**! / BIANCA. I am no **strumpet**, but of life as honest / As you that thus abuse me. — William Shakespeare
… the networks aired at least half a dozen TV movies featuring prostitutes as heroines. Farrah Fawcett, Loni Anderson and Ann Jillian were among those who played **strumpets**. — Leah Rozen

words.definition: To make feel dull or stifled
words.origin: Late Latin *stultificare* to make foolish, from Latin *stultus* foolish; akin to Latin *stolidus* stolid. First known use: 1737.

words.definition: Foolish talk
words.origin: From Latin *stultus* foolish + *loqui* to speak.

words.definition: To make someone unable to think or feel properly; to astonish and shock
words.origin: Middle English *stupifien*, modification of Latin *stupefacere*, from *stupēre* to be astonished + *facere* to make, do. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Having the place to oneself
words.origin: German, storm-free.

words.definition: Extremely dark and gloomy
words.origin: Latin *stygius*, from Greek *stygios*, from *Styg-, Styx* Styx. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: Fragrant; sweet-smelling, as some flowers and herbs are
words.origin: From Latin *suaveolens*, from *suavis* sweet + *olere* to smell.

words.definition: Dull or gloomy; dark academic dress worn for formal occasions at Oxford
words.origin: Latin *subfuscus* brownish, dusky, from *sub-* + *fuscus* dark brown. First known use: 1710.

words.definition: Of such excellence as to inspire awe
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *sublimer*, from Medieval Latin *sublimare* to refine, sublime, from Latin, to elevate, from *sublimis*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Belonging to this world as contrasted with a better or more spiritual one
words.origin: Modification of Late Latin *sublunaris*, from Latin *sub-* + *luna* moon. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: Deceit used to achieve a goal
words.origin: Late Latin *subterfugium*, from Latin *subterfugere* to escape, evade, from *subter-* secretly (from *subter* underneath; akin to Latin *sub* under) + *fugere* to flee. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: A quantity or number to be subtracted from another, the minuend
words.origin: Latin *subtrahendus*, gerundive of *subtrahere*. First known use: 1685.

words.definition: A substitute, especially for a medicine or drug; a stand-in remedy
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *succēdāneum,* noun derivative from neuter of Latin *succīdāneus, succēdāneus* "killed as a substitute or addition, exposed to a danger in place of another," from *succīdere* "to cut from below or at the base, kill (a sacrificial victim) as a second offering" (from *suc-,* assimilated form of *sub-* sub- + *caedere* "to strike, cut through, fell, kill") + *-āneus,* suffix forming adjectives from compound verbs. First known use: 1641.

words.definition: Briefly and clearly expressed
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *succinctus* having one's clothes gathered up by a belt, tightly wrapped, concise, from *sub-* + *cinctus*, past participle of *cingere* to gird. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Gave a **succinct** overview of the project
As a judge, she is known more for being detailed and thorough … than for crisp and **succinct** rulings. — Patricia Mazzei and Charlie Savage

words.definition: Assistance and support in times of hardship and distress; to give such aid
words.origin: Middle English *socour, sucurs* (taken as plural), from Anglo-French *sucur, sucors*, from Medieval Latin *succursus*, from Latin *succurrere* to run to the rescue, bring aid, from *sub-* + *currere* to run. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Causing or relating to sweating, as a sudorific herb or remedy
words.origin: New Latin *sudorificus*, from Latin *sudor*. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: To gradually spread through or over, as light, colour or a feeling
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *suffūsus,* past participle of *suffundere* "to pour on or in (as an addition), cause (a liquid, colour, light) to well up or rise to the surface, fill with a liquid, colour or light that wells up from below," from *suf-,* assimilated form of *sub-* sub- + *fundere* "to pour, shed, cast, send forth, disperse". First known use: 1590.
examples: The northern horizon was **suffused** with a deep red glow … — P. M. Leschak

words.definition: Lasting happiness regardless of circumstances
words.origin: Sanskrit and Pali, happiness.

words.definition: A bright spot of light beside the sun
words.origin: Latin *parelion*, from Greek *parēlion*, from *para-* + *hēlios* sun. First known use: 1571.

words.definition: Obsolete through age or new developments; retired with a pension
words.origin: Medieval Latin *superannuatus*, past participle of *superannuari* to be too old, from Latin *super-* + *annus* year. First known use: circa 1634.

words.definition: Proud; insolent
words.origin: From Latin *superbia* pride.

words.definition: Behaving as if superior to others
words.origin: Latin *superciliosus*, from *supercilium* eyebrow, haughtiness, from *super-* + *-cilium* eyelid (akin to *celare* to hide). First known use: 1543.
examples: Reacted to their breach of etiquette with a **supercilious** smile

words.definition: Beyond what is required or expected, as supererogatory kindness; superfluous
More than is needed
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *superfluus*, literally, running over, from *superfluere* to overflow, from *super-* + *fluere* to flow. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Desserts after meals as sweet as these might be **superfluous**. — Sam Sifton
The concept of a summer scarf—even one this light—is **superfluous** yet chic. — Liana Satenstein

words.definition: Situated beyond the moon
words.origin: Latin *super-* + *luna* moon. First known use: 1614.

words.definition: Relating to the sky or the heavens; celestial; of exceptional quality
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *supernel*, from Latin *supernus*, from *super* over, above. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Lying face upward; failing to act or protest as a result of moral weakness
words.origin: Middle English *suppyne*, from Latin *supinus*; akin to Latin *sub* under, up to. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An excessive amount

words.definition: Done secretly
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *surrepticius*, from *surreptus*, past participle of *surripere* to snatch secretly, from *sub-* + *rapere* to seize. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Whispering or rustling
words.origin: Latin, hum, whisper. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: A whispering or rustling sound

words.definition: A young lover or suitor; a country youth, as in pastoral poetry

words.definition: A low, often marshy hollow

words.definition: To swagger, bluster, behave recklessly

words.definition: A swaggering or daring adventurer, typically one in a historical story

words.definition: A vision seen in sleep; a dream
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *swefn* sleep, dream, vision. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: To faint from strong emotion
words.origin: Middle English *swounen*, probably back-formation from *swouning, swowening*, from *iswowen, aswoune*, from Old English *geswōgen* in a swoon. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: A person devoted to luxury and pleasure
A person who flatters to gain advantage
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *sȳcophanta,* borrowed from Greek *sȳkophántēs,* literally, "one who shows the fig," from *sŷkon* "fig" (perhaps in reference to an apotropaic gesture made by inserting the thumb between the index and second fingers) + *-phantēs,* agentive derivative of *phaínein* "to reveal, show, make known"; perhaps from the use of such a gesture in denouncing a culprit. First known use: 1575.
examples: … bumbling **sycophants** whose self-importance far outstrips their actual abilities. — Alison Herman

words.definition: Deductive reasoning from two premises
words.origin: Middle English *silogisme*, from Anglo-French *sillogisme*, from Latin *syllogismus*, from Greek *syllogismos*, from *syllogizesthai* to syllogize, from *syn-* + *logizesthai* to calculate, from *logos* reckoning, word. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Of the woods; wooded and pastoral
words.origin: Medieval Latin *silvanus, sylvanus*, from Latin *silva, sylva* wood. First known use: circa 1586.

words.definition: A part standing for the whole
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *synekdochē*, from *syn-* + *ekdochē* sense, interpretation, from *ekdechesthai* to receive, understand, from *ex* from + *dechesthai* to receive; akin to Greek *dokein* to seem good. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the sun, moon and Earth
words.origin: Late Latin *syzygia* conjunction, from Greek, from *syzygos* yoked together, from *syn-* + *zygon* yoke. First known use: circa 1847.

words.definition: A happy solution where everyone wins
words.origin: Arabic, mutual satisfaction.

words.definition: Things better left unsaid
words.origin: Latin, things to be kept silent.

words.definition: A style of action painting using dabs or splotches of colour
words.origin: French *tachisme*, from *tache* stain, spot, blob, from Old French *teche, tache*, of Germanic origin; akin to Old Saxon *tēkan* sign, Old High German *zeihhan*. First known use: 1955.

words.definition: Understood without being stated
words.origin: Middle French or Latin; Middle French *tacite*, from Latin *tacitus* silent, from past participle of *tacēre* to be silent; akin to Old High German *dagēn* to be silent. First known use: circa 1650.
examples: The blush … was a **tacit** answer … — Bram Stoker

words.definition: Reserved; saying little
words.origin: French or Latin; French *taciturne*, from Middle French, from Latin *taciturnus*, from *tacitus*. First known use: 1734.

words.definition: A fat, greasy lump of a person

words.definition: Perceptible by touch; real
words.origin: Late Latin *tangibilis*, from Latin *tangere* to touch. First known use: 1589.
examples: There is no **tangible** evidence to support their claim.
By December of that year, there was a **tangible** sign of fresh progress. — Hal Bernton

words.definition: Equivalent in seriousness to
words.origin: Obsolete *tantamount*, noun, equivalent, from Anglo-French *tant amunter* to amount to as much. First known use: 1641.

words.definition: At full gallop; a hunting cry; a rapid gallop, as of hounds and riders
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1641.
