words.origin: From Mark Tapley, a relentlessly cheerful character in Dickens's *Martin Chuzzlewit*.

words.definition: Musically induced ecstasy
words.origin: Arabic *ṭarab* ecstasy, delight.

words.definition: A petty lie; pretentious nonsense
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1796.

words.definition: An overwhelming urge to dance
words.origin: New Latin *tarantismus*, from *Taranto*, Italy. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: Used to express surprise, anger, irritation, annoyance, etc
words.origin: Alteration of *darnation*, euphemism for *damnation*. First known use: 1790.

words.definition: To hesitate when introducing someone whose name one forgets
words.origin: Scots, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: The public face one shows to the world
words.origin: Japanese, façade.

words.definition: A person in tattered clothing; a ragamuffin; ragged or dilapidated
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1608.

words.definition: A jack of all trades
words.origin: German, from *tausend* thousand + *Sasa*, a cry of encouragement.

words.definition: Showy but cheap and of poor quality
words.origin: *tawdry lace* a tie of lace for the neck, from *St. Audrey* (St. Etheldreda) †679 queen of Northumbria. First known use: 1655.
examples: Any trip there carries with it more than its share of drabness, **tawdry** hotels and second-rate service, all of which tax the forbearance of the most patient traveller. — John F. Burns
A **tawdry** attempt to smear his opponent

words.definition: A small object that is decorative rather than strictly functional; a trinket
words.origin: Yiddish *tshatshke* trinket, from obsolete Polish *czaczko*. First known use: 1971.
examples: Carlene's furniture was garish and awful and every shelf or corner held **tchotchkes** and gewgaws and other tacky trinkets. — Ingrid Law
… collecting every sort of art, from Old Masters to precious textiles, from rare books and manuscripts to antique **tchotchkes**. — Diane Wood Middlebrook

words.definition: Too long and dull
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *taediosus*, from Latin *taedium*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A natural outer covering of a body or part, such as a seed coat
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *tegumentum*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A carved male figure used as a pillar to support an entablature
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *telamōn* bearer, supporter; akin to Greek *tlēnai* to bear. First known use: circa 1706.

words.definition: Of or inhabiting the earth; an inhabitant of the earth, as opposed to a Martian
words.origin: From Latin *tellus* earth.

words.definition: To violate something sacred
words.origin: From Latin *temerare* to violate.

words.definition: Excessive confidence or boldness
words.origin: Middle English *temeryte,* borrowed from Latin *temeritāt- temeritās,* from *temere* "blindly, recklessly, haphazardly" + *-itāt- -itās* -ity; *temere* going back to adverbialized locative singular of a noun **temes-* "darkness," going back to Indo-European **temH-es-,* whence also Sanskrit *tamas-* "darkness, gloom," Avestan *tǝmah-,* and, from the base **temH-,* Lithuanian *témsta, témti* "to become dark," *tamsà* "darkness," *tim͂sras* "dark red (of a horse), sorrel," Old Church Slavic *tĭma* "darkness," *tĭmĭnŭ* "dark, gloomy," and from a **-ro-* adjectival derivative Sanskrit *tamra-* "darkening, oppressive," Germanic **þemra-* "darkness," whence Old High German *demar* "dusk, twilight". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To avoid making a decision or committing oneself in order to gain time
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *temporiser, temporisier* "to last, pass one's life, postpone, gain time," probably borrowed from Medieval Latin *temporizāre* "to delay," from Latin *tempor-, tempus* "time, period of time" + Medieval Latin *-izāre* -ize. First known use: 1579.
examples: … you'd have to **temporize** until you found out how she wanted to be advised. — Mary Austin

words.definition: Persistent; holding firmly
words.origin: Latin *tenāc-, tenāx* "holding fast, clinging, persistent" (from *tenēre* "to hold, occupy, possess" + *-āc-,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1607.
examples: … made a name for himself as a powerful and **tenacious** midfielder, … propelling his side forward with aplomb.

words.definition: Producing or causing darkness, as tenebrific clouds or moods
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *tenebrae* "darkness" + Latin *-i-* -i- + *-ficus* -fic. First known use: 1785.

words.definition: Dark; shadowy
words.origin: Middle English *tenebrose, tenebrus,* borrowed from Anglo-French *tenebreus,* borrowed from Latin *tenebrōsus,* from *tenebrae* "darkness" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One of various hooks used for stretching cloth on a frame
words.origin: Tenter + hook. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Very weak or slight
words.origin: Latin *tenuis* "fine-drawn, thin, narrow, slight" + -ous. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: To make conflicting or evasive statements; to change one's loyalties
words.origin: Latin *tergiversatus*, past participle of *tergiversari* to show reluctance, from *tergum* back + *versare* to turn, frequentative of *vertere* to turn. First known use: 1590.

words.definition: Misleading, evasive or ambiguous speech or action
words.origin: From *tergiversate* + *-ion*. *Tergiversate*: Latin *tergiversatus*, past participle of *tergiversari* to show reluctance, from *tergum* back + *versare* to turn, frequentative of *vertere* to turn. First known use: 1570.

words.definition: A harsh-tempered or overbearing woman
words.origin: From Middle English *termagant*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: Relating to dancing, after Terpsichore, the muse of dance and choral song
As slow as a tortoise
words.origin: From Latin *testudo* tortoise.

words.definition: Relating to the sea, especially to smaller or inland seas, as the Mediterranean
words.origin: French *thalassique*, from Greek *thalassa* sea. First known use: 1883.

words.definition: A reflection upon death
words.origin: From Greek *thanatos* death + *opsis* view; the title of a poem by William Cullen Bryant.

words.definition: A worker of wonders and performer of miracles; a magician or conjuror
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *thaumatūrgus* "worker of miracles," borrowed from Late Greek *thaumatourgós,* going back to Greek, "performer of wonders (as an acrobat)," from *thaumat-, thaûma* "wonder, object of wonder or admiration, marvel" (probably derivative from the base of *théā* "sight, spectacle") + *-ourgos* "performing, carrying out (the thing specified)," going back to **-o-wergos* or **-o-worgos,* derivative of Indo-European **u̯erǵ-* "make, bring about" (whence, as a nominal derivative, Greek *érgon* "work"). First known use: 1715.

words.definition: A battle among the gods or other powerful entities
words.origin: From Greek *theomachia*, from *theos* god + *machē* battle.

words.definition: The operation or effect of a supernatural or divine agency in human affairs
words.origin: Late Latin *theurgia*, from Late Greek *theourgia*, from *theourgos* miracle worker, from Greek *the-* + *ergon* work. First known use: circa 1569.

words.definition: Muscle or tendon
words.origin: Middle English, personal quality, virtue, from Old English *thēaw*; akin to Old High German *thau* custom. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A dense growth of shrubs
words.origin: Middle English **thikket*, from Old English *thiccet*, from *thicce* thick. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A careless error in thinking
words.origin: From *think* + *-o*, on the model of *typo*.

words.definition: To endure something without complaint; to tolerate, a word still alive in Scots
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *tholian*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Bragging or boastful, after Thraso, a braggart soldier in Terence
words.origin: Latin *Thrason-, Thraso* Thraso, braggart soldier in the comedy *Eunuchus* by Terence. First known use: 1564.

words.definition: Stubborn and contrary
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *thrawin*, from past participle of Middle English *thrawen* to twist. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A song or poem of lament
words.origin: Greek *thrēnōidia*, from *thrēnos* dirge + *aeidein* to sing. First known use: 1634.

words.definition: A purposeless incompetent in public office
words.origin: From Alexander Throttlebottom, a hapless vice-president in the musical *Of Thee I Sing*.

words.definition: A light meal, especially lunch, as eaten in India; the tin it is carried in
words.origin: Probably alteration of *tiffing*, gerund of obsolete English *tiff* to eat between meals. First known use: 1800.

words.definition: A tambourine or similar ancient instrument, as played by Miriam in Exodus
words.origin: Diminutive of obsolete English *timbre* small drum, tambourine, from Middle English, from Anglo-French, drum. First known use: circa 1520.

words.definition: In good time
words.origin: From *time* + *-ous*. *Time*: Middle English, from Old English *tīma*; akin to Old Norse *tīmi* time, Old English *tīd*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Showing nervousness or fear
words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *timorosus*, from Latin *timor* fear, from *timēre* to fear. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … reproached myself with being so **timorous** and cautious … — Daniel Defoe
… proceed with doubtful and **timorous** steps. — Edward Gibbon

words.definition: To take a neighbour's things by borrowing them one by one
words.origin: Pascuense, the language of Easter Island.

words.definition: Someone who pretends to have money, skill, influence, etc
A clamour; a confused uproar
words.origin: French, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: To ring like a bell
words.origin: From Latin *tintinnabulum* bell.

words.definition: A ringing or tinkling sound
words.origin: Latin *tintinnabulum* bell, from *tintinnare* to ring, jingle, from *tinnire*. First known use: 1831.

words.definition: A long, angry speech
words.origin: French, shot, tirade, from Middle French, from Old Italian *tirata*, from *tirare* to draw, shoot. First known use: 1802.

words.definition: An instance of panic, temper, upset
words.origin: Coined by Shakespeare, perhaps from *terror*.

words.definition: Hat
words.origin: By shortening & alteration from *tit for tat*, rhyming slang for *hat*. First known use: circa 1930.

words.definition: To make small enhancing alterations to one's appearance; to spruce up
words.origin: Perhaps from tidy + reno*vate*. First known use: 1824.

words.definition: A tiny amount or part of something; a small written mark, as a dot on an i
words.origin: Middle English *titel*, from Medieval Latin *titulus*, from Latin, title. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: A lively movement; caper. verb intr.: To move in an exaggerated prancing manner
words.origin: Imitative of the sound of a horse's hooves. First known use: 1868.

words.definition: Unsteady movement, such as the staggering, lurching or nodding of the head or the body
words.origin: From Latin *titubare* to stagger.

words.definition: Splitting a word with another, as "abso-bloody-lutely"
words.origin: Late Latin, from Greek *tmēsis* act of cutting, from *temnein* to cut. First known use: 1550.

words.definition: A person who behaves obsequiously to someone important; a sycophant
words.origin: Toad(eater) + -y. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: Chaos; utter confusion, from the Hebrew for the formless void of Genesis
words.origin: From Hebrew *tōhū wā-bōhū* formless and void.

words.definition: Foolish or silly behaviour
words.origin: Tomfool + -ery, after foolery. First known use: 1812.

words.definition: The part of a monk's or priest's head left bare on top by shaving
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Medieval Latin *tonsura*, from Latin, act of shearing, from *tonsus*, past participle of *tondēre* to shear. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: An annuity shared by subscribers, the whole going to the last survivor
words.origin: French, from Lorenzo *Tonti* †1695 Italian banker. First known use: 1765.

words.definition: The art of clipping shrubs or trees into ornamental shapes, as peacocks or spirals
words.origin: Latin *topiarius*, from *topia* ornamental gardening, irregular from Greek *topos* place. First known use: 1592.

words.definition: Haughty; pretentious
words.origin: Probably from the phrase *top loft*. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: The love for or the emotional connection to a particular place
words.origin: From Greek *topos* place + *-philia* love.

words.definition: A rocky peak on a hill
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *torr*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Clumsy; awkward
words.origin: Spanish, clumsy.

words.definition: Mentally or physically inactive; sluggish
words.origin: Middle English, "inattentive, lazy," borrowed from Latin *torpidus* "numbed, paralyzed," adjective derivative corresponding to the stative verb *torpēre* "to be numb, lack sensation, be struck motionless, be sluggish or lethargic," going back to dialectal Indo-European **tr̥p-eh2-* (whence also Old Church Slavic *trĭpěti* "to be patient, suffer," Lithuanian *tirpstù, tir͂pti* "to become stiff, lose feeling, fall asleep [of limbs]"), zero-grade derivative of a verbal base perhaps seen also in the Germanic adjective **þerba-* (from **terp-o-*), whence Old English *þeorf* "unleavened," Old Frisian *therve, derve* "rough, violent," Old High German *therp, derp* "unleavened," Old Icelandic *þjarfr* "unleavened, fresh (of water), insipid, flat". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Scorchingly hot; full of passion or intensity
words.origin: Borrowed from French & Latin; French *torride,* going back to Middle French, borrowed from Latin *torridus* "dried by exposure to heat, parched, scorched," adjective derivative from the stem of *torreō, torrēre* "to heat so as to dry, scorch, parch". First known use: 1545.

words.definition: The fear that time is running out
words.origin: German, gate-closing panic.

words.definition: A deep spiritual anguish without cause
words.origin: Russian, yearning, anguish.

words.definition: A habitual drinker; a drunkard, one who tosses off pot after pot
A whirlwind or whirlpool
words.origin: Anglo-French *turbeillun*, ultimately from Latin *turbin-, turbo*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The practice of, love of or addiction to, archery
words.origin: Greek *toxon* bow, arrow + *philos* dear, loving. First known use: 1794.

words.definition: Easy to control or influence
words.origin: Latin *tractabilis*, from *tractare* to handle, treat. First known use: 1502.

words.definition: A treatise; a formal written essay on a subject, especially a religious one
words.origin: Latin *tractatus*, from *tractare* to draw out, handle, treat. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To speak badly of or tell lies about someone so as to damage their reputation
words.origin: Latin *traducere* to lead across, transfer, degrade, from *tra-, trans-* trans- + *ducere* to lead. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: Free from disturbance; calm
words.origin: Middle English *tranquill*, from Latin *tranquillus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Lasting only a short time
words.origin: Latin *transeunt-, transiens*, present participle of *transire* to cross, pass by, from *trans-* + *ire* to go. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: To transform in a surprising or magical way
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: On the other side of a bridge, especially south of the Thames; melodramatic
words.origin: *trans-* + Latin *pont-, pons* bridge. First known use: 1844.

words.definition: Guilty of betrayal; hazardous where danger is hidden
words.origin: Middle English *trecherous*, from Anglo-French *trecherus*, from *trecher* to cheat.

words.definition: Shaking or quivering slightly, as a tremulous voice; timid or nervous
words.origin: Latin *tremulus*. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Vigorous and incisive
words.origin: Middle English *trenchaunt*, from Anglo-French, present participle of *trencher*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **trenchant** divisions between right and wrong … — Edith Wharton

words.definition: A hearty eater
A feeling of fear about what may happen
words.origin: Latin *trepidation-, trepidatio*, from *trepidare* to tremble, from *trepidus* agitated; probably akin to Old English *thrafian* to urge, push, Greek *trapein* to press grapes. First known use: 1605.
examples: Travers sent the book to press with some **trepidation**, fearing that a children's book might undermine her hard-won literary cachet. — Caitlin Flanagan

words.definition: A witty reply thought of too late
words.origin: German, staircase wit.

words.definition: A hat with a brim turned up on three sides, as worn in the 18th century
words.origin: Latin *tricornis*. First known use: 1823.

words.definition: Sad; melancholy, a word found in Shakespeare and older verse
words.origin: Middle English *trist* sad, from Anglo-French *triste*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a **tristful** harpist completes recollections of rainy afternoons … — Simon Schama

words.definition: Of little value or importance
words.origin: Latin *trivialis* found everywhere, commonplace, from *trivium* crossroads, from *tri-* + *via* way. First known use: 1589.
examples: A **trivial** solution to a linear equation

words.definition: A person who lived in a cave; a person regarded as deliberately ignorant
words.origin: Latin *troglodytae*, plural, from Greek *trōglodytai*, from *trōglē* hole, cave (akin to Greek *trōgein* to gnaw, Armenian *aracem* I lead to pasture, graze) + *dyein* to enter. First known use: 1555.

words.definition: One's pledged word, loyalty or fidelity
words.origin: Middle English *trouth*, from Old English *trēowth*. First known use: 12th century.
examples: … I don't remember the details or, by my **troth**, even the gist … — Stanley Elkin

words.definition: A lucky find; something lovely discovered by chance
words.origin: French, from *trouver* to find.

words.definition: To act in a servile manner. verb tr.: To move or roll on small wheels
words.origin: From the lower position of the truckle bed. First known use: 1647.
examples: Walt Whitman became a pop star for reminding his countrymen of the duty never to **truckle** … — Virginia Heffernan

words.definition: Eager to argue or fight; defiant
words.origin: Latin *truculentus*, from *truc-, trux* savage; perhaps akin to Middle Irish *trú* doomed person. First known use: circa 1540.
examples: … he stood, hands on hips, at his most evidently **truculent** … — John Arlott

words.definition: Attractive articles of little value or use; practices or beliefs that are worthless
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *trompery* deceit, from Middle French, from *tromper* to deceive. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a wagon loaded with household **trumpery** … — Washington Irving

words.definition: Buying books and letting them pile up unread
words.origin: Japanese, from *tsunde* piling up + *oku* to leave + *doku* reading.

words.definition: Thick, dark and scary
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in *Jabberwocky*.

words.definition: Swollen or bulging; pompous or bombastic, especially in style
words.origin: Latin *tumidus*, from *tumēre*. First known use: 1541.

words.definition: Tediously pompous; also, swollen
words.origin: Latin *turgidus*, from *turgēre* to be swollen. First known use: 1620.

words.definition: Depravity; wickedness
words.origin: Middle French, from Latin *turpitudo*, from *turpis* vile, base. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One who poses as a model of deportment: the way in which one conducts oneself
words.origin: From Mr Turveydrop, a pompous dancing master in Dickens's *Bleak House*.

words.definition: Serving as a protector, guardian or patron, as a tutelary deity of a city
Trivial or foolish speech or writing; nonsense, as sentimental twaddle
words.origin: Probably alteration of English dialect *twattle* idle talk. First known use: 1782.

words.definition: Two
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *twēgen*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Idle talk; nonsense. verb intr.: To talk idly
words.origin: Perhaps a variant of *tattle*.

words.definition: Infatuated; giddily in love
words.origin: Popularized by Disney's *Bambi*, from *twitter* + *pate* head.

words.definition: Charity given as a moral duty
words.origin: Hebrew, righteousness, charity.

words.definition: To be unwilling to spend time or money on something
words.origin: Icelandic.

words.definition: Found everywhere
words.origin: From *ubiquity* + *-ous*. *Ubiquity*: Latin *ubique* everywhere, from *ubi* where + *-que*, enclitic generalizing particle; akin to Latin *quis* who and to Latin *-que* and. First known use: 1772.
examples: From the sky to the water, blue is one of the most **ubiquitous** colours in nature. — Marissa Hermanson

words.definition: The belief that we are who we are through others
words.origin: Nguni Bantu, humanity.

words.definition: Lying awake before dawn, worrying
words.origin: Old English, from *ūht* the hour before dawn + *caru* care.

words.definition: To walk in the wind to clear one's head
words.origin: Dutch, from *uit* out + *waaien* to blow.

words.definition: An edict of the Russian tsar; an arbitrary or peremptory command
words.origin: French & Russian; French, from Russian *ukaz*, from *ukazat'* to show, order; akin to Old Church Slavic *u-* away, Latin *au-*, Sanskrit *ava-* and to Old Church Slavic *kazati* to show. First known use: 1729.

words.definition: The amount by which a container, such as a wine bottle or cask, falls short of full
words.origin: Middle English *ulage*, from Anglo-French *ulliage*, from **ullier* to fill a partially empty cask, from Old French (Picard dialect) *oel* bunghȯle, literally, eye, from Latin *oculus* eye. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: One who gives opinions beyond their knowledge
words.origin: From Latin *ultra crepidam* beyond the sandal, after the painter Apelles' rebuke to a shoemaker.

words.definition: Voluntary; spontaneous
words.origin: From Latin *ultroneus*, from *ultro* of one's own accord.

words.definition: To howl or wail, as a sign of grief or celebration, with a trilling sound
words.origin: Latin *ululatus*, past participle of *ululare*, of imitative origin. First known use: circa 1623.
examples: … eight singers took to the aisle, dancing with ferocious energy as the chorus sang, **ululated** and clapped in an exuberant, multisensory ode to joy. — Susan Saccoccia
As soon as he said our mother's name, my sisters began to wail: keening, **ululating** cries, the Greek expression of sorrow for the dead. — Nicholas Gage

words.definition: The fully shaded inner region of a shadow, as in a total eclipse
words.origin: From Latin *umbra*. First known use: 1638.

words.definition: Offence or annoyance
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *umbraticum*, neuter of *umbraticus* of shade, from *umbratus*, past participle of *umbrare* to shade, from *umbra* shade, shadow; akin to Lithuanian *unksmė* shadow. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the shock jock turned media power broker vacillated between contrition and **umbrage** … — Raina Kelley et al.
If someone disagrees with him, he doesn't **take umbrage**. — Fred Barnes

words.definition: Inclined to take offence easily
words.origin: From *umbrage* + *-ous*. *Umbrage*: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *umbraticum*, neuter of *umbraticus* of shade, from *umbratus*, past participle of *umbrare* to shade, from *umbra* shade, shadow; akin to Lithuanian *unksmė* shadow. First known use: 1587.

words.definition: Casting a shadow
words.origin: From Latin *umbra* shade + *ferre* to bear.

words.definition: Complete and unreserved; pure, as unalloyed joy; of metal, not mixed
Impossible to attack, defeat or question
words.origin: From *un-* + *assailable*, from *assail*, ultimately from Latin *ad-* + *salire* to leap.

words.definition: A day other than one's birthday
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in *Through the Looking-Glass*.

words.definition: Excessively flattering; oily
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French or Medieval Latin; Middle French *unctueus*, from Medieval Latin *unctuosus*, from Latin *unctus* act of anointing, from *unguere* to anoint. First known use: 14th century.
examples: An **unctuous** appraisal of the boss's decision
… delectably **unctuous** bacon-wrapped black cod. — Caroline Bates

words.definition: To move with a smooth wavelike motion
words.origin: Latin *undulatus*, from **undula*, diminutive of *unda* wave. First known use: 1658.

words.definition: A soft, greasy or viscous substance used as ointment or for lubrication
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *unguentum*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Calm and composed; not upset or agitated
words.origin: From *un-* + *ruffled*, past participle of *ruffle*.

words.definition: Serious; unmitigated
words.origin: From the phrase "hell unshirted".

words.definition: Unaware; unintentional
examples: Kept the truth from their **unwitting** friends

words.definition: Unaccustomed or unusual, as unwonted generosity from a miser
examples: … made his comeback with an **unwonted** show of humility. — Walter Goodman

words.definition: A tree with poisonous sap; a corrupting or harmful influence
words.origin: Indonesian Malay *pohon upas* poison tree. First known use: 1814.

words.definition: To scold
words.origin: Middle English *upbreyden*, from Old English *ūpbregdan*, probably from *ūp* up + *bregdan* to snatch, move suddenly. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … **upbraids** all forms of ceremony … — W. B. Yeats
**Upbraided** them for not helping their grandparents

words.definition: Courteous and refined
words.origin: Latin *urbanus* urban, urbane. First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: Having the form or appearance of a bear
words.origin: From Latin *ursus* bear + *-form*.

words.definition: The act of burning or searing
words.origin: From Latin *ustulare* to scorch.

words.definition: Charging excessive rates, especially for lending money
words.origin: From *usury* + *-ous*. *Usury*: Middle English *usurie*, from Anglo-French, from Medieval Latin *usuria*, alteration of Latin *usura*, from *usus*, past participle of *uti* to use. First known use: 1610.

words.definition: To take a position or power illegally
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *usorper*, from Latin *usurpare* to take possession of without legal claim, from *usu* (ablative of *usus* use) + *rapere* to seize. First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Usurped** the rights to her life story
Must not let stock responses based on inherited prejudice **usurp** careful judgment

words.definition: A beer enjoyed outdoors on a sunny day
words.origin: Norwegian, from *ute* outside + *pils* lager.

words.definition: An imagined perfect place
words.origin: *Utopia*, imaginary and ideal country in *Utopia* (1516) by Sir Thomas More, from Greek *ou* not, no + *topos* place. First known use: 1533.

words.definition: Having or showing an excessive or submissive fondness for one's wife
words.origin: Latin *uxorius* uxorious, uxorial, from *uxor* wife. First known use: 1598.

words.definition: Wandering where the journey matters more than the destination
words.origin: Spanish, wavering; popularized by John Steinbeck.

words.definition: To waver between opinions
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vacillātus*, past participle of *vacillāre* "to be unsteady, totter, be weak or inconstant, waver," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: Showing a lack of thought or intelligence
words.origin: Latin *vacuus* "empty, unoccupied, idle" + -ous. First known use: circa 1660.

words.definition: A handbook carried for constant reference
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, "go with me". First known use: 1629.

words.definition: An unexpected and inexplicable change in a situation or in someone's behaviour
words.origin: Perhaps borrowed from Latin *vagārī* "to wander, roam". First known use: 1579.

words.definition: Excessively proud of oneself
words.origin: Middle English *vaynegloryous*, from *vaynglorie* vainglory + *-ous* -ous, after Middle French *vaneglorious* and Medieval Latin *vāniglōrius*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A valley
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French *val*, going back to Latin *vallēs, vallis*, of uncertain origin. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Serving as a farewell
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *valedictōrius*, from Latin *valedic-*, alternate stem of *vale dīcere, valedīcere* "to say goodbye" + *-tōrius*, adjective suffix (originally derivatives of agent nouns ending in *-tōr-, -tor*). First known use: 1651.

words.definition: A person who is unduly anxious about their health; an invalid
words.origin: Valetudinary + -an. First known use: 1684.

words.definition: Offering nothing stimulating; bland
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vapidus* "(of wine) having lost freshness, flat"; akin to Latin *vappa* "wine that has gone flat" and perhaps to *vapor* "exhalation, steam". First known use: circa 1656.
examples: … a gossipy, **vapid** woman, obsessed by her own elegance … — R. F. Delderfield
London was not all **vapid** dissipation — V. S. Pritchett

words.definition: Consisting of or full of vapour, as a misty valley; insubstantial or vague
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vaporōsus* "full of steam," from *vapor* "steam, vapour" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 1527.

words.definition: Marked with patches of different colours
words.origin: From past participle of variegate. First known use: 1615.

words.definition: To foretell the future; to prophesy, as an oracle or seer does
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vāticinātus*, past participle of *vāticinārī* "to make divinely inspired predictions, prophesy, warn," verbal derivative of **vāticinium* "act of prophesying," from *vātēs* "prophet, seer" + *canere* "to sing, chant, utter" + *-ium*, deverbal noun suffix. First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: The forefront; vanguard
words.origin: Middle English *vauntwarde, vanwarde, vaward*, borrowed from Anglo-French **vantwarde, vantgarde* vanguard. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … the **vaward** of our youth … — William Shakespeare

words.definition: Showing strong feeling; forceful
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French, going back to Old French, borrowed from Latin *vehement-, vehemens, vēmens* "violent, vigorous, (of feelings) overmastering, powerful," perhaps from *vehere* "to convey, carry along, drive" + *-mens*, adjective suffix (as in *clēmens* "mild, calm") of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The faintest kind of wanting: an inclination too weak to stir any effort to fulfil it
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *velleitāat-, velleitās*, from Latin *velle* "to want, will" + *-itāt, -itās* -ity. First known use: 1618.

words.definition: Fine parchment made from calfskin
words.origin: Middle English *velym*, borrowed from Anglo-French *velim, veeslin*, noun derivative of **veelin* "of a calf," from *veel* "calf" + *-in* -ine. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Soft and smooth like velvet
words.origin: From New Latin *velutinus* velvety.

words.definition: Open to bribery; corrupt
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vēnālis* "that may be bought, for sale," from **vēnus* "sale" (attested only in accusative *vēnum* and dative *vēnō, vēnuī*; akin to Greek *ônos* "price," Sanskrit *vasna-* "price, value") + *-ālis* -al. First known use: 1652.

words.definition: Respected because of age or wisdom
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *venerābilis* "entitled to respect," from *venerārī* "to solicit the good will of (a deity), hold in awe, venerate" + *-bilis* "capable of (acting or being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To regard with great respect
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *venerātus*, past participle of Latin *venerārī* "to solicit the good will of (a deity), worship, pay homage to, hold in awe," verbal derivative of *vener-, venus* "sexual desire, qualities exciting desire, charm, (as proper noun) goddess personifying sexual attractiveness" (probably originally in cognate accusative phrase *Venerem venerārī* "to propitiate Venus," extended to other deities). First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: Sexual indulgence; the practice of hunting game, especially with hounds
words.origin: Middle English *venerie*, borrowed from Anglo-French, from Old French *vener* "to hunt with dogs" (going back to Latin *vēnārī* "to hunt") + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Having a large belly; gluttonous, with a mighty appetite to match
words.origin: From Latin *venter* belly + *potens* powerful.

words.definition: Truthfulness
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *vērācitāt-, vērācitās*, from Latin *vērāc-, vērāx* "truthful" + *-itāt-, -itās* -ity. First known use: 1614.

words.definition: Speech or writing that uses too many words or excessively technical expressions
words.origin: Borrowed from French, from *verbier* "to trill, warble" (going back to Middle French *verboier* "to twitter," altered from Middle French dialect (Picard) *verbloier, guerbloier*, derivative of *werbler* "to sing expressively, trill") + *-age* -age. First known use: circa 1721.
examples: … such a tangled maze of evasive **verbiage** as a typical party platform … — Marcia Davenport
… sportswriters guarded their **verbiage** so jealously. — Raymond Sokolov

words.definition: To obsessively repeat
words.origin: From Latin *verbigerare* to chatter.

words.definition: A mania for words
words.origin: From Latin *verbum* word + *mania*.

words.definition: Using more words than needed
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *verbōsus*, from *verbum* "word, verb" + *-ōsus* -ose. First known use: circa 1531.

words.definition: Green with grass or vegetation
words.origin: Contracted from Middle French *verdoyant*, from present participle of *verdoyer* "to be green, turn green," going back to Old French *verdoier*, from *verd, vert* "green" (going back to Latin *viridis*, from a base **wir-*, whence *virēre* "to show green growth, be green" of uncertain origin) + *-oier*, factitive verb suffix, going back to Latin *-idiāre*, originally representing variant pronunciation (or spelling variant) of *-izāre* -ize. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: Bluish-green; sea-green
words.origin: From French *vert* green + *azur* blue.

words.definition: A bright bluish-green coating formed on copper or brass by oxidation
words.origin: Middle English *vertegrese*, borrowed from Anglo-French *verdegrece, vert de Grece*, literally, "green of Greece". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Shy, modest and bashful; inclined to blush, from the Latin for feeling shame
words.origin: From Latin *verecundus* modest.

words.definition: Having the appearance of truth or reality
words.origin: Latin *vērī similis, vērīsimilis* "having the appearance of truth" (from *vērī*, genitive of *vērum* "truth," noun derivative of *vērus* "true" + *similis* "like, similar") + -ar. First known use: 1681.

words.definition: The appearance of being true or real
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vērīsimilitūdō*, from *vērī similis, vērīsimilis* "having the appearance of truth" + *-tūdō*, suffix of abstract nouns. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: Overcome with emotion
words.origin: Borrowed from Yiddish *farklemt* "depressed, grieving," past participle of *farklemen* "to grip, press," going back to Middle High German *verklemmen*, from *ver-*, *vir-*, *vor-*, verb prefix, here with intensive force (going back to Old High German *fir-*, *far-* for-) + *klemmen* "to press, squeeze," going back to Old High German *-klemmen* (in *biklemmen* "to block, oppress"), going back to Germanic **klammjan-*, derivative from a base **klamm-*, whence Old English *clam*, *clom* "bond, fetter". First known use: 1991.
examples: Hunched over my tiny screens lately, I've found myself … **verklempt** over an old video I posted of my son blowing bubbles in the bathtub. — James Poniewozik

words.definition: Marked with sinuous or wavy lines, like the tracks of worms in wood or stone
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vermiculātus* "marked with wavy lines," from *vermiculus* "insect larva, grub" (from *vermis* "worm" + *-culus*, diminutive suffix) + *-ātus* -ate. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: The ordinary language of a region
words.origin: Latin *vernāculus* "belonging to the household, domestic, native" (from *verna* "slave born in the household"—of uncertain origin— + *-āculus*, perhaps originally diminutive suffix, though derivation is unclear) + -ar. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: Of, in or appropriate to spring, as the vernal equinox or vernal blossoms
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vernālis,* from *vernus* "of spring" (going back to pre-Latin **u̯esri-no-,* adjective derivative from the base of Latin *vēr* "spring") + *-ālis* -al; *vēr* "spring," going back to Indo-European **u̯ḗs-r̥-, *u̯es-n̥-s,* whence also Old Norse *vár* "spring," Old Frisian *wars, wērs,* Welsh *gwanwyn* (Old Welsh *guiannuin,* from British Celtic **u̯esantēno-*), Middle Irish *errach* (probably from **u̯esrāko-,* with generalization of the lenited initial consonant), Old Church Slavic *vesna,* Russian *vesná,* Lithuanian *vãsara* "summer," Greek *éar* "spring" (from **u̯ehar,* from **u̯esr*̥), Armenian *garun* (*gar-* from **gehar-,* from **u̯esr̥-* + a suffix), Sanskrit *vasantá-,* Avestan *vaŋri* (locative) "in the spring". First known use: 1530.

words.definition: To make something worse while trying to improve it
words.origin: German, from *verschlimmern* to worsen + *verbessern* to improve.

words.definition: The left-hand page of a book
words.origin: New Latin *verso* (*folio*) the page being turned. First known use: 1839.

words.definition: Understanding human actions through empathy
words.origin: German, to understand.

words.definition: Extremely high or steep; causing dizziness
words.origin: Latin *vertiginosus*, from *vertigin-, vertigo*. First known use: 1608.

words.definition: Relating to, occurring or active in the evening, as vespertine flowers or bats
words.origin: Latin *vespertinus*, from *vesper*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Forming a very small remnant of something that was once much larger
words.origin: Latin *vestigium* + English -al. First known use: 1843.
examples: Kiwis lack an external tail, and their **vestigial** wings are entirely hidden beneath a curious plumage—shaggy, more like fur than feathers … — Stephen Jay Gould
It's held in the Gold Room, a **vestigial** ballroom of the kind that every downtown hotel uses for banquets and conventions. — William Zinsser

words.definition: Causing annoyance, frustration or worry
words.origin: From *vexation* + *-ous*; ultimately from Latin *vexare* to harass.

words.definition: The Eucharist given to a person near death; provisions for a journey
words.origin: From Latin *viaticum*. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: Experienced through another person's actions
words.origin: Latin *vicarius*, from *vicis* change, alternation, stead. First known use: 1637.
examples: **Vicarious** menstruation manifested by bleeding from the nose

words.definition: A neighbourhood or surrounding district; the people who live near
words.origin: Middle English *vesinage*, from Anglo-French *veisinage*, from neighbouring, from Vulgar Latin **vecinus*, alteration of Latin *vicinus*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A change of circumstances, often unwelcome
words.origin: Middle French, from Latin *vicissitudo*, from *vicissim* in turn, from *vicis* change, alternation. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: Food or provisions, usually in the plural victuals; to provide with food
words.origin: Middle English *vitaille, victuayle*, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *victualia*, plural, provisions, victuals, from neuter plural of *victualis* of nourishment, from Latin *victus* nourishment, way of living, from *vivere* to live. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Things worth seeing
words.origin: Latin, things to be seen.

words.definition: Relating to or based on the number twenty, as counting in scores
words.origin: Latin *vicesimus, vigesimus* twentieth; akin to Latin *viginti* twenty, Greek *eikosi*. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: To speak about in an abusively disparaging way
words.origin: Middle English *vilifien*, from Late Latin *vilificare*, from Latin *vilis* cheap, vile. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Relating to wine
words.origin: Latin *vinaceus* of wine, from *vinum* wine. First known use: 1678.

words.definition: To clear of blame or suspicion
words.origin: Latin *vindicatus*, past participle of *vindicare* to lay claim to, avenge, from *vindic-, vindex* claimant, avenger. First known use: circa 1571.
examples: A nonprofit group that works to **vindicate** those wrongly convicted
They have evidence that will **vindicate** =exonerate her.

words.definition: A domineering, violent or bad-tempered woman
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *viragin-, virago*, from *vir* man. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Greenish or becoming green, as leaves in early spring
words.origin: Latin *virescent-, virescens*, present participle of *virescere* to become green, inchoative of *virēre* to be green. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: Rain that evaporates before reaching the ground
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin, branch, rod, streak in the sky suggesting rain. First known use: 1938.

words.definition: Bright green
words.origin: Latin *viridis* green. First known use: 1600.

words.definition: Greenness; youthful freshness
words.origin: Middle English *viridite*, from Latin *viriditat-, viriditas*, from *viridis*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Knowledge of or expertise in the fine arts; curios or objets d'art collectively
words.origin: Italian *virtù*, literally, virtue, from Latin *virtut-, virtus*. First known use: 1722.

words.definition: Showing dazzling technical skill, especially in music
words.origin: Virtuoso + -ic. First known use: 1879.
examples: Generally speaking, the banjo and jazz parted ways many decades back, but **virtuosic** banjoist Bela Fleck is almost single-handedly lobbying for reconciliation. — Gina Arnold
Yet it was from his craftsman father that he learned everything that there was to know about brick, and his use of that humble but infinitely versatile material was **virtuosic**. — Martin Filler

words.definition: Extremely severe or harmful; bitterly hostile
words.origin: Middle English, "discharging watery pus, purulent," borrowed from Latin *vīrulentus* "full of poison, venomous," from *vīrus* "venom, poisonous fluid" + *-ulentus* "having in quantity, full of". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A person's face, with reference to the form or proportions of the features
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from *vis* face, from Latin *visus* sight, from *vidēre* to see. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The grimy **visage** of a mining town

words.definition: Glutinous and sticky, as viscid sap, honey or the coating on some leaves
words.origin: Late Latin *viscidus*, from Latin *viscum* birdlime. First known use: 1635.

words.definition: Thick and sticky
words.origin: Middle English *viscouse*, from Anglo-French *viscos*, from Late Latin *viscosus* full of birdlime, viscous, from Latin *viscum* mistletoe, birdlime; akin to Old High German *wīhsila* cherry, Greek *ixos* mistletoe. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To spoil or impair the quality or efficiency of; to destroy the legal validity of
words.origin: Latin *vitiatus*, past participle of *vitiare*, from *vitium* fault, vice. First known use: 1534.
examples: … the comic impact is **vitiated** by obvious haste … — William Styron

words.definition: Filled with bitter criticism
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *vitriole*, from Medieval Latin *vitriolum*, alteration of Late Latin *vitreolum*, neuter of *vitreolus* glassy, from Latin *vitreus* vitreous. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To blame or insult in strong language
words.origin: Latin *vituperatus*, past participle of *vituperare*, from *vitium* fault + *parare* to make, prepare. First known use: 1542.

words.definition: Attractively lively
words.origin: Latin *vivac-, vivax* long-lived, vigorous, high-spirited, from *vivere* to live. First known use: circa 1645.

words.definition: Strikingly bright or lifelike
words.origin: Latin *vividus*, from *vivere* to live. First known use: 1634.

words.definition: Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully
words.origin: Latin *vōciferārī* "to utter with a loud voice, shout, yell" + -ous. First known use: 1700.

words.definition: The faculty of using one's will
words.origin: French, from Medieval Latin *volition-, volitio*, from Latin *vol-* (stem of *velle* to will, wish) + *-ition-, -itio* (as in Latin *position-, positio* position). First known use: 1605.

words.definition: The turn of thought in a sonnet
An act of turning around so as to face in the opposite direction; a reversal
words.origin: French, from Italian *voltafaccia*, from *voltare* to turn + *faccia* face, from Vulgar Latin **facia*. First known use: 1819.

words.definition: Fluent, ready talk
words.origin: Middle English *volible, voluble* "able to turn, changing," borrowed from Latin *volūbilis* "turning on its axis, rolling, flowing, (of speech) readily flowing, fluent," from *volū-,* variant stem of *volvere* "to set in a circular course, cause to roll" + *-bilis* "capable (of acting) or worthy (of being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Speaking fluently and incessantly
words.origin: Middle English *volible, voluble* "able to turn, changing," borrowed from Latin *volūbilis* "turning on its axis, rolling, flowing, (of speech) readily flowing, fluent," from *volū-,* variant stem of *volvere* "to set in a circular course, cause to roll" + *-bilis* "capable (of acting) or worthy (of being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Wanting great quantities; insatiable
words.origin: Latin *vorac-, vorax*, from *vorare* to devour; akin to Old English ā*cweorran* to guzzle, Latin *gurges* whirlpool, Greek *bibrōskein* to devour. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: A gulf or abyss; a whirlpool that swallows everything
words.origin: Latin, abyss, from *vorare* to swallow.

words.definition: Joyful anticipation
words.origin: German, pre-joy.

words.definition: Sharp
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in *Jabberwocky*.

words.definition: A person, such as a monk or nun, who has made vows; a devoted follower
words.origin: Latin *votum* vow. First known use: 1543.

words.definition: Something used for the healing of wounds
words.origin: Latin *vulnerarius*, from *vulner-, vulnus*. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Of or relating to foxes; crafty and cunning, as a vulpine smile
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *vulpinus*, from *vulpes* fox; perhaps akin to Greek *alōpēx* fox. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Exhausted
words.origin: Scots, of uncertain origin.

words.definition: Rustic simplicity and quiet elegance
words.origin: Japanese, rustic simplicity.

words.definition: Beauty in imperfection and impermanence
words.origin: Borrowed from Japanese, from *wabi* "austere beauty" (Old Japanese, "loneliness, disheartenment," noun derivative from the base of *wabiru* "to feel disheartened") + *sabi* "aged appearance, rustic patina" (Old Japanese, "rust, patina," noun derivative from the stem of *sabiru* "to feel lonely, rust, corrode"). First known use: 1963.
examples: To discover **wabi-sabi** is to see the singular beauty in something that may first look decrepit and ugly. — Robyn Griggs Lawrence
I'm really informed and inspired by the Japanese philosophy of **Wabi-Sabi** which says you find beauty in things that are imperfect. — Joyce Seymore

words.definition: Humorous in a playful way
words.origin: From *wag* + *-ish*. *Wag*: Middle English *waggen*; akin to Middle High German *wacken* to totter, Old English *wegan* to move. First known use: 1589.

words.definition: An area of wooden panelling on the lower part of the walls of a room
words.origin: Middle English, from Middle Dutch *wagenschot*, probably from *wagen* wagon + *schot* shot, crossbar. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: The feeling of being alone in the woods
words.origin: German, forest solitude.

words.definition: To move unsteadily or totter; to feel nauseated, as a queasy stomach
words.origin: Middle English *wamlen*; akin to Danish *vamle* to become nauseated, Latin *vomere* to vomit. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A strong desire to travel
words.origin: German, from *wandern* to wander + *Lust* desire, pleasure. First known use: 1875.

words.definition: To decrease gradually
words.origin: Middle English *wanien, wanen*, going back to Old English *wanian*, going back to Germanic **wanōjan-* (whence Old High German *wanōn* "to lessen," Old Norse *vana*), weak verb derivative from **wano-* "deficient, absent," whence Old English & Old High German *wan* "lacking, deficient," Old Norse *vanr*, Gothic *wans*; akin to Latin *vānus* "empty, vain," Greek *eûnis* "bereft (of), without," Sanskrit *ūna-* "deficient, defective". First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Despair
words.origin: From Middle English *wan-* lacking + *hope*.

words.definition: Deliberate and unprovoked; also, unrestrained
words.origin: Middle English, from *wan-* deficient, wrong, mis- (from Old English, from *wan* deficient) + *towen*, past participle of *teen* to draw, train, discipline, from Old English *tēon*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A fool; one lacking good sense
words.origin: From *want* + *wit*.

words.definition: Cautious about possible dangers
words.origin: Ware + -y. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A wasteful or good-for-nothing person who squanders time and money
words.origin: Irregular from waste. First known use: circa 1841.

words.definition: An annual summer party or outing held by a printing house for its workers
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; a printers' annual outing.

words.definition: Fate or destiny
words.origin: From construal as an adjective of weird in *weird sisters,* name for the Fates of Greek and Roman myth (early Scots *werd sisteris,* Middle English *wyrde systeres,* Shakespeare *weyard/weyward sisters,* applied to the witches in *Macbeth*). First known use: 1817.

words.definition: The sky; the vault of heaven
words.origin: Middle English, literally, cloud, from Old English *wolcen*; akin to Old High German *wolkan* cloud. First known use: 12th century.
examples: The sun of heaven … made the western **welkin** blush … — William Shakespeare

words.definition: A comprehensive view of the world
words.origin: German, from *Welt* world + *Anschauung* view. First known use: 1868.
examples: … she possesses a **weltanschauung** that is unremittingly positive … — Leonore Fleischer
In my personal **Weltanschauung**, there is nothing wrong with arm hair, giant headphones are silly and skin-lightening products are creepy and grim. — Victoria Coren Mitchell

words.definition: A confused mass or jumble
words.origin: Middle English *welteren, weltryn* "to turn over, tumble, writhe, take unrestrained pleasure (in)," frequentative derivative of *welten* "to topple, overturn, fall over," by-form (perhaps from a Germanic weak verb **waltjan-*) of *walten* "to turn over, upend, be overturned, cast, throw, surge," going back to Old English *-wæltan* (in *gewæltan* "to roll"), going back to a Germanic verbal base **walt-, *welt-* "roll," found in a variety of attested formations (as Old English *awyltan* "to roll away," *unwealt* "steady," Middle High German *walzen* "to roll over," Old Icelandic *velta* [strong verb, intransitive] "to roll, roll over," *velta* [transitive] "to set rolling," Gothic *waltjan* "to surge against [of waves]," *uswaltjan* "to overturn"), going back to Indo-European **u̯el-d-,* extended form of **u̯el(H)-* "roll," whence, with various vowel grades and stem formations, Old Irish *fillid* "(s/he) bends, turns back" (< **u̯el-n-*), Old Church Slavic *valiti sę* "to roll (intransitive)," Lithuanian *veliù, vélti* "to full (cloth), roll," Greek *eiléō, eileîn* "wind, turn round, roll up" (< **u̯el-né-*), *íllō, íllein* in same sense (< **u̯i-u̯l-ō*), Armenian *glem* "to roll". First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: World-weariness
words.origin: German, from *Welt* world + *Schmerz* pain. First known use: 1864.

words.definition: A benign tumor of the skin
words.origin: Middle English *wenn*, from Old English; akin to Middle Low German *wene* wen. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: That which constitutes the fundamental nature of a thing: the essence or inherent quality
To employ endearments or flattery to persuade someone to do something
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1661.

words.definition: To submerge
words.origin: From Middle English *whelm*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … **whelmed** with a rush of joy … — G. A. Wagner

words.definition: To bury deep; to cover over
words.origin: From Middle English *whelven* to overturn.

words.definition: To neigh
words.origin: Imitative. First known use: 1753.

words.definition: To vacillate; to blow in light puffs
words.origin: Probably frequentative of *whiff*. First known use: 1568.

words.definition: Former; formerly, as in the whilom glory of a fallen house
words.origin: Middle English, literally, at times, from Old English *hwīlum*, dative plural of *hwīl* time, while. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: Playfully quaint or fanciful
words.origin: *whimsy*. First known use: 1653.

words.definition: Playfully quaint or fanciful behaviour
words.origin: Irregular from *whim-wham*. First known use: 1605.
examples: The designer's new line showed a touch of **whimsy**

words.definition: To whine or to complain
words.origin: Middle English **whingen*, from Old English *hwinsian*; akin to Old High German *winsōn* to moan. First known use: 12th century.

words.definition: A young and inexperienced person considered to be presumptuous
words.origin: Alteration of *snippersnapper*. First known use: 1700.

words.definition: A spinning toy; a constant whirl of activity
words.origin: Middle English *whirlegigg*, from *whirlen* to whirl + *gigg* top. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Hush; be quiet
words.origin: Middle English; imitative. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; anticlockwise
words.origin: Middle Low German *weddersinnes*, from Middle High German *widersinnes*, from *widersinnen* to go against, from *wider* back against (from Old High German *widar*) + *sinnen* to travel, go; akin to Old High German *sendan* to send. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: One who deserves to be hanged; a rogue
words.origin: Scots, from *widdy* gallows rope + *-ful*.

words.definition: A dabbling duck with mainly reddish-brown and grey plumage; a fool
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1508.

words.definition: Scatterbrained; ditzy
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1918.
examples: She portrays a wealthy but **wifty** widow who wants her family home for the holidays. — Ed Weiner

words.definition: A creature or being; a ghost
words.origin: Middle English, creature, thing, from Old English *wiht*; akin to Old High German *wiht* creature, thing, Old Church Slavic *veštĭ* thing. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Haphazardly; whether one likes it or not
words.origin: Alteration of *will I nill I* or *will ye nill ye* or *will he nill he*. First known use: 1608.

words.definition: A person who manipulates or exerts control from behind the scenes
words.origin: From puppetry, one who pulls the wires.

words.definition: A person with an affectation of wisdom or knowledge; a know-it-all
words.origin: Middle Dutch *wijssegger* soothsayer, modification of Old High German *wīzzago*; akin to Old English *wītega* soothsayer, *witan* to know. First known use: 1595.

words.definition: Knew
words.origin: Alteration of *wis*. First known use: 1508.

words.definition: Having a feeling of vague, regretful longing
words.origin: Blend of *wishful* and obsolete English *wistly* intently. First known use: 1714.

words.definition: An Anglo-Saxon national council or parliament of nobles and churchmen
words.origin: Old English *witena gemōt*, from *witena* (genitive plural of *wita* sage, adviser) + *gemōt* gemot. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A man who knows of and tolerates his wife's infidelity; a complaisant husband
words.origin: Middle English *wetewold*, from *weten, witen* to know + coke*wold* cuckold. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An addiction to telling inappropriate jokes
words.origin: German, joking addiction.

words.definition: Shrivelled or wrinkled with age
words.origin: Middle English *wisenen*, from Old English *wisnian*; akin to Old High German *wesanēn* to wither, Lithuanian *vysti*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Sad or miserable in appearance
words.origin: Middle English *wo begon*, from *wo*, noun + *begon*, past participle of *begon* to go about, beset, from Old English *begān*, from *be-* + *gān* to go. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A piece of high, open, uncultivated land
words.origin: Middle English *wald, wold*, from Old English *weald, wald* forest; akin to Old High German *wald* forest, Old Norse *vǫllr* field. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: One's habit or custom
words.origin: Middle English *woned, wont*, from past participle of *wonen* to dwell, be used to, from Old English *wunian*; akin to Old High German *wonēn* to dwell, be used to, Sanskrit *vanoti* he strives for. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Indulgence in aimless thought or dreamy imagining; absent-mindedness
A hobgoblin, scarecrow or a person of frightening appearance
words.origin: Scots, from *worry* + *cow* goblin.

words.definition: Ruinous
words.origin: Wrack + -ful. First known use: 1558.

words.definition: A ghost or ghostlike image
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: Twisted; coiled; contorted
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English, from past participle of *wrīthan*. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Unfair, lacking propriety, illegal
words.origin: From *wrong* + *-ous*. *Wrong*: Middle English, from Old English *wrang*, from **wrang*, adjective, wrong.

words.definition: Dryly humorous
words.origin: Middle English *wrien*, from Old English *wrigian* to turn; akin to Middle High German *rigel* kerchief wound around the head, Greek *rhiknos* shriveled, Avestan *urvisyeiti* he turns. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A cabinet of curiosities
words.origin: German, chamber of wonders.

words.definition: One who succeeds remarkably young
words.origin: German, from *Wunder* wonder + *Kind* child. First known use: 1873.

words.definition: Yellow or yellowish
words.origin: From Greek *xanthos* yellow.

words.definition: Relating to hospitality or relations between host and guest, as xenial gifts
words.origin: From Greek *xenia* hospitality.

words.definition: A person attracted to foreign peoples, cultures or customs; the opposite of a xenophobe
words.origin: Xeno- + -phil, perhaps after French *xénophile*. First known use: 1948.

words.definition: Relating to very dry conditions
words.origin: *xer-* (in xerophytic) + -ic. First known use: 1926.

words.definition: Growing on or living in wood
words.origin: From Greek *xylon* wood + *-philos* loving.

words.definition: To talk loudly and incessantly; to whine or complain at length
words.origin: Middle English *yameren*, alteration of *yomeren* to murmur, be sad, from Old English *gēomrian*; akin to Old High German *jāmaron* to be sad. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … caused the purists to **yammer** for censorship. — D. W. Maurer

words.definition: By the name of; called, a mock-archaic word, as a pub yclept the Red Lion
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *geclipod*, past participle of *clipian* to cry out, name.

words.definition: Someone who is the same age as oneself
words.origin: From Middle English *ȝeliche*, an equal in age.

words.definition: The young of an animal, especially of a sheep or a goat
To have an intense longing
words.origin: Middle English *yernen*, from Old English *giernan*; akin to Old High German *gerōn* to desire, Latin *hortari* to urge, encourage, Greek *chairein* to rejoice. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: A man holding and cultivating a small landed estate; a reliable worker
words.origin: Middle English *yoman, yeman*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Did a **yeoman's** job in seeing the program through

words.definition: Yesterday evening
words.origin: From *yester-* + *eve*.

words.definition: Last night
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *gystran niht*, from *giestran* yesterday + *niht* night. First known use: before 12th century.

words.definition: Yesterday evening
words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *yistrevin*, from *yister*day + *evin* evening, alteration of Middle English *even*. First known use: 1773.

words.definition: Prestige, social status or pedigree
words.origin: Yiddish, from Hebrew *yiḥus* lineage.

words.definition: An uneducated and unsophisticated person from the countryside
words.origin: Perhaps from English dialect *yokel* green woodpecker, of imitative origin. First known use: circa 1819.

words.definition: The stress of speaking a foreign language
words.origin: Japanese, a meal eaten sideways, a pun on horizontal writing.

words.definition: Absent-minded; distant
words.origin: English dialect, from *yonder*.

words.definition: Time long past
words.origin: Middle English, from *yore*, adverb, long ago, from Old English *gēara*, from *gēar* year. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: A binding fate that brings people together
words.origin: Mandarin *yuánfèn* fate, destiny.

words.definition: A profound, mysterious sense of beauty
words.origin: Japanese, mysterious grace.

words.definition: Having a full, rounded figure; pleasantly plump, from Yiddish for juicy
words.origin: Yiddish *zaftik* juicy, succulent, from *zaft* juice, sap, from Middle High German *saf, saft*, from Old High German *saf*. First known use: 1926.

words.definition: To get something done through connections
words.origin: Polish, to arrange, to settle.

words.definition: A sleeve or holder designed to hold a hot cup
words.origin: Arabic *ẓarf* vessel.

words.definition: A person who is fanatical in their beliefs
words.origin: Late Latin *zelotes*, from Greek *zēlōtēs*, from *zēlos*. First known use: 1537.

words.definition: Full of fervent enthusiasm
words.origin: From *zeal* + *-ous*. *Zeal*: Middle English *zele*, from Late Latin *zelus*, from Greek *zēlos*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The defining spirit or mood of an era
words.origin: German, from *Zeit + Geist* spirit. First known use: 1835.

words.definition: The highest point reached
words.origin: Middle English *cenyth, senyth*, from Middle French *cenit*, from Medieval Latin, from Old Spanish *zenit*, modification of Arabic *samt* (*al-ra's*) way (over one's head). First known use: 14th century.
examples: … at the **zenith** of his powers … — John Buchan

words.definition: Square of a number
words.origin: From German *zensus* square, from Latin *census*.

words.definition: The eighth power of a number
words.origin: Coined by Robert Recorde in 1557 for the eighth power.

words.definition: A soft, gentle breeze
words.origin: Middle English *Zephirus*, west wind (personified), from Latin *Zephyrus*, god of the west wind & *zephyrus* west wind, zephyr, from Greek *Zephyros* & *zephyros*. First known use: 1567.

words.definition: Light and breezy
words.origin: From *zephyr* + *-ous*. *Zephyr*: Middle English *Zephirus*, west wind (personified), from Latin *Zephyrus*, god of the west wind & *zephyrus* west wind, zephyr, from Greek *Zephyros* & *zephyros*.

words.definition: A figure of speech in which a word applies to two others in different senses
words.origin: Middle English *zeuma*, from Medieval Latin, from Latin *zeugma*, from Greek, literally, joining, from *zeugnynai* to join; akin to Latin *jungere* to join. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: The delusion that one is a beast
words.origin: From Greek *zōon* animal + *anthrōpos* human.

words.definition: A faint glow in the night sky along the zodiac
words.origin: From *zodiac*.

words.definition: A 19th-century toy that produces the illusion of motion from spinning images
words.origin: From Greek *zōē* life + *tropos* turning.

words.definition: A harsh, petty critic
words.origin: From Zoilus, a harsh Greek critic of Homer.

words.definition: Restlessness at the beginning of a migration period
words.origin: German, migratory restlessness.

words.definition: A position where any move worsens one's position
words.origin: German, compulsion to move.

words.definition: The space in between
words.origin: German, space between.

words.definition: Having a single plane of symmetry: divisible into two mirror-image halves along only one axis
The study or practice of fermentation in brewing, winemaking or distilling
words.origin: From Greek *zymē* leaven + *-ourgia* working.

words.definition: Energy, style and enthusiasm
words.origin: French, from *élancer* to dart.

words.definition: The vital force driving life and growth
words.origin: French, vital impetus; coined by Henri Bergson.

words.definition: A small ornamental case for needles or cosmetics
words.origin: French, a case.
